ORDER 


WHEREAS there is apprehension of the occurrence 
of rioting, affrays and other disturbances of the public 
tranquillity within the area in the schedule hereto 
(hereinafter referred to as the said area); 


AND WHEREAS, I, H. S. Ghose Chaudhuri, Com- 
missioner of Police, Calcutta, being a Presidency 
Magistrate, have been specially empowered by the 
State Government under Notification No. 2627-G.A., 
dated the Sth August 1955, to act under section 144 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 


1898); oO 

AND WHEREAS, in my opinion, there is sufficient 
ground for procecding under the said section for the 
immediate prevention of disturbances of the public 
tranquillity and of riots and affrays. within the said 
area;

Now THEREFORE, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (/) of section 144 of the Code 
of Criminal Procecure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), read 
with sub-section (3) of the said section, I, the said 
H. S. Ghase Chaudhuri, Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta, do hereby prohibit from the 180 day of July 
1956, until further orders, any ass¢mbly of five or 
more persons within the said area, or the carrying of 
any lathis or other dangerous weapons or the doing 
of any act which is likely to cause a disturbance of the 
public tranquillity or a riot or an affray within the 
said areas 


The Schedule 


The area within the jurisdiction of Hare Street 
police-station in the Town of Calcutta bounded— 

On the north by Hastings Street (the strect being 
excluded); 

On the south by Auckland Road and Lawrence 
Road up to the South Gate of Raj Bhawan 
(the roads being included); 

On the east by Government Place West (the road 
being included); and 

On the west by Strand Road (thé road being 
excluded). 


Explanation.——In this schedule “Town of Calcutta” 
means the Town of Calcutta as defirted in section 3 of 
the Calcutta Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act IV of 
1866).

State Government for the election of a member of the Board of Trusteas 
fur the Improvement of Calcutta, referred to in sub-rule (2) of rule 3, hereé- 
inafter referred to as the date for the election of the Secretary to the 
Chamber, by the member of which the election is to be held, hereinufte 
referred to as the Secretary, shall invite nominations from the members o 
the Chamber who are entitled to exercise the rights of voting at ৪9 
election under the Articles of Association of the Chamber. 


2. Nominations shall reach the Secretary at least ten clear days before 
the date for the election; any nominations received later shall be rejected.: 


3. The President of the Chamber shall thereupon examine the nomina- 
tions and shall instruct the Secretary to issue ut least seven days before 
the date for the election, a ballot paper signed and numbered by him and 
containing the names of the persons whose nominations are found to be in 
order to every member of the Chamber referred to in paragraph 1. 


4, (a) Every such member shall have one vote only. 
(b) Every such member desirous of voting at the election shall record 


his vote on the ballot paper supplied to him by putting a cross mark against 
the name of the person whom he desires to vote.for and sign it, end shall 
return the same to the Secretary so as ty reach him on or before the date 


for the election. 


(c) Any ballot paper which is not received by the Secretary within the 
due date shall be rejected. 


5. The ballot papers shall then be examined by two Scrutineers 
appointed by the President of the Chamber from among the members of the 
Chamber who have not offered themselves as candidates for the election.

6. The Scrutineers shal] report the result of the examination of the 
ballot papers to the Secretary. 


7. The candidate who, on such report, is found to have obtained the 
largest number of votes shall be declared by the Secretary to be elected, and 
the report of the Scrutineers shall be ‘conclusive evidence of his election. 


Provided that if the voting has resulted in an equality of votes between 
two or more candidates, lots shall be drawn in the presence of the Secretary 
of such other officer and in such manner us may be directed by the President 
of the Chamber, to determine which’ of such candidates shall be declared 
to be elected.

No. 2613W.T.—19th June 1956.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 
1919 (Bengal Act I of 1919), the Governor is pleased to make the follww- 
ing by-laws for the Bhadreswar Municipality in the district of Hooghly :-- 


By-laws 


1. Appointment and duties of the Ragistering Officer.—Every cycle 
rickshaw in the Bhadreswar Municipality shall be annually registered by 
w Registering Officer uppointed for registering hackney-carriages. 


2. Qualifications and duties of bearers.—Every person applying for a 
تعنص‎ benrer’s license shull be required to satisfy the Registering 
cer— 


(i) that he knows how to drive and control a cycle-rickshaw and is in all 
respects a fit person for such employment; 


(ii) that he is well acquainted with the principal streets, offices and 
places in and around the town of Bhadreswa=; 


(111) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and 
distances prepared by the Commissioners; 


(iv) that he knows the rules of the read aad signals used by the bearers 
and drivers of vehicles and by the trattic police; and 


(v) that he is not less than 18 years of age.

a meeting.

furnished at the fore-end with a ring-shaped metal support and connected 
by collision guard. . 


(x) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
tight. :

Appearances : 
For the Company: Shri Kunja Behari Mookherjee, Director of the Com- 
pany. 


For the Union: Shri Naren Sen, General Secretary of the Union. - 


Disputes between Messrs. India Metal Manufacturing Co., Ltd., and their 
employees 0 baffled solution through the process of conciliation, the 
(tovernment of West Bengal, by order No. 4981Dis./D/10L-118/55, dated 
Calcutta, the 8th October 1955, referred for adjudication the following 
issues : — 


(1) Is the lock-out of the factory with effect from 13th December 
justified P 


(2) What relief are the workmen’ entitled to for the period of lock-out? 


The lot of the workers, according to the written statement filed by the 
Union, was extremely hard. The scale of wages was low and there was no 
security of service. No provision was made for retirement benefits. In 
order to improve their lot the workers organised a Union. The Directors of 
the Company were displeased on the formation of the Union and started 
harassing operations. Some leading members of the Union were victimised 
but on the intervention of the Labour Commissioner, one of the discharged 
workmen was reinstated. 


2630 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 10660 [Parr | 


» On the 10th of September 1954, the Union: submitted a demand for 
Puja bonus. Nothing fruitful however resulted froin discussions that had 
taken place between the management and the representative of the work- 
men. A charter of demand was presented on the 3rd of November 1904. 
The management showed no inelination to treat these demands in a fair and 
responsive spirit. Driven to desperation the workers went on strike for one 
day. As a counter blast the Compary declared lock-out on 111) December 
1954. Since then though willing the workers have been prevented from 
going back to their duty as the Company persisted in continuing the lock-out. 


The written statement filed on behalf of the Company traversed the 
grounds raised in the Union statement. Regarding the action taken aguinst 
some workers which in the estimation of the workers was a measure of 
reprisal for inauguration of the Union, the Company’s reply is that they 
had caused heavy damage and financial loss by wilful acts and were rightly 
dismissed. It was not a fact that on aecount of the organisation of the 
Union the Company had started hostile operations against the members. 
The employees went on strike on 10th December 1954 without any previous 
warning or notice. The fact was communicated to the Labour Commissioner 
who addressed a letter asking the employees to resume work immediately. 
Vhe advise thus tendered fell on deaf ¢ars. The strike was continued and 
on the 13th December 1954, the Company was forced to declare a lock-out. 
The employees had gone on strike without justification and the lock-out was 
the sequel. They are not entitled to any relief. 


issues Nos. 1 and 2.—In the written statement of the workers sone allega- 
tions were made that the formation of the Union had flicked the! Directors 
on the raw. To take the wind out of the sail of the Union, the aythorities 
started persecuting the workers. Some prominent members tell victims to 
their rancour. The Company produced a letter Ext. B(1) addressed to the 
Secretary of the Unidn by the Assistant Secretary to the Government of 
West Bengal, Labour Department, intimating that on enquiry Government 
was satisfied that the workmen concerned were negligent in discharging their 
duties resulting in financial loss to the Company. The charges brought 
against them were bona fide. The Union’s grievance that the dJeading 
members of the organisation were victimised appears دز‎ the face of this 
communication to be frivolous. There was discharge 20 another person who 
was however reinstated on the recommendation.of-the Labour -Cemmissioner. 
So far the Company’s record appeurs quite clean. 


The demand for Puja honus was made by letter Ext. l(a), dated the 
10th of September 1954, The case of the Company is that its financial 
position was so unstable and precarious that the demand could not be sutis- 
fied. It uppears that the paid up capital of the business at Ns inuuguration 
was Rs. 49,000. The number*of workers employed is 32. The business was 
not started under favourable auspices for, a loan had to be taken from the 
(tovernment to the extent of Its. 24,000. The loan was repayable by instul- 
ments. Two instalments were paid but the 3rd instalment was defaulted. 
The result was that the Government took charge of the business. This dixmal 
history confirms the version presented on behalf of the Company that the 
financial: position not being sound the demand of the workers could not be 
inet. ' 


The charter of demands Ext. 100) was submitted on the 8rd of Novem- 
ber 1954. The Company could not see its way to give effect to the demands. 
As the workers could not obtain satisfaction of the demands, they went on 
strike on 10th December 1964. They went to the workshop but did not do 
any work. They remained in the workshop kicking their heels for the whole 
day. O.P.W. 1 Shri Kunja Behari Mookerjee one of the Directors went to 


Part 1| THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 2631 


the office of the Labour Commissioner and gave him information in writing 
(vide 146 B2) that the workers had gone on a stay-in strike. The Labour 
(‘commissioner issued a letter (Ext. 13) to the Secretary of the Union on the 
same day advising htm to persuade the workers to resume normal work. A 
copy was handed over to P.W. 1. His evidence is that returning to the 
workshop he put up a notice Ext. A(1) but it gid not work. The next day 
was a Saturday. According to 0.P.W.°1. the employees entered the work- 
shop and repeated the performance of the previous day by sitting idle. He 
went to the Labour Commissioner’s office once again and gave information 
by 1167 Ext. A(3). Returning toethe workshop he got the notice Ext. A(2) 
posted up. In this notice it is stuted that in spite of the uotice given the 
previous day, the workers had abstained from resuming duty up to 2 p.m. 
The Company would be forced to close down the business. The case of the 
Union 1s that on Saturday the workers flocked at the gate with the intention 
of restarting work but they were not allowed admission. The durwan told 
them that he had orders to keep the gates closed until the strike matter was 
finally settled. As against the evidence of P.W. 1 the Company has got 
the evidence of O.P.W. 1 Shri Kunja Behari Mookherjee, one of the Direc- 
tors of the Company and the durwan (0O.P.W. 2) Radha Pandey. The 
Tribunal was impressed by the transparent truthfulness of the witness Shri 
Kunja Behari Mookherjee. The evidence given by him bears the ring of 
truth. The durwan also gave his evidence in a straightforward way. ٤ 
we consider in this context that 0.۲7.۲۷۰. 1 had gone to the office to inform 
the Labour Commissioner that despite his good counsel the workers were 
holding back, persisting in continuing the strike and that the notice Ext. 
A(2). was posted up, I am not prepared to believe that the gate was kept 
closed and all the move taken was exhibitionism. On the 18th which was 
a Monday. the Company published lock-out notice Ext. A. The point for 
consideration 1s 11 the strike was justifiéd. Justification of a strike depends 
to a large extent upon whether or not the parties had tried all other avail- 
able means of setting the disputes according to law. The right to strike is 
a recognised weapon of the workers to be used as a last resort when all other 
avenues of settlement of industrial disputes have proved futile. In the 
present iystance the Union did not explore all avenues of settlement by 
peaceful mneans before advising its members to take the extreme step. When 
the Company’s attitudé was found to be unresponsive the Union might seek 
intervention of the Conciliation Officer and have conciliation proceeding 
started. Instead of taking that course, the Union or for the matter of that, 
the workers went on strike. Not having exhausted all possible megns of 
82111010109 settlement,*the workers must be held ty have gone on a strike which 
was unjustified. On the Company’s evidence the Tribunal is satisfied that 
the situation did not improve on the following day. The workers remained 
in the workshop déwning thelr tools. The lock-out declared ‘by the Company 
was hence fully justified. No adverse finding 0811 be made against the Com- 
pany for the action it had taken, in view of the conduct of the workers. 
Since the lockout was justified, the workers cannot legitimately claim any 
relief for the period of lock-out.

AWARD 


This is ام‎ complaint under aection 33A of_the Industrial Disputes Act 
filed on 4th August 1955 by workman, Jonab Nur Islam, who was a polisher 
in the opposite party Hotel. He allewed that he was জর suspended 
{rom Ist April 1955 during the pendency of an adjudication proceeding 
before this Tribunal; that the subsequent decision of the management to 
dismiss |him was unjust and unwarranted; that the petitioner had only 
suggested to Shri A. K. Sep Roy that a particular polish might be more 


Part J} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 2633 


suitable and thus committed no offence and that the opposite party was 


delaying filing petition under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for 
obvious reasons. 


On these allegations the petitioner prayed for an award directing with- 
drawal of the suspension order as also management’s decision to dismiss tlie 
petitioner from service, ٠ : 


The opposite party Grand Hotél opposed the application. It contended 
that the application under section 33A was not mainteinable and pleaded the 
circumstances in which the petitioner was suspended and the subsequent 
decision to dismiss him was taken. It was said that both the suspension 
and the decision to dismiss the petitioner were just and proper and that there 
was no intentional delay to apply under section 33 seeking permission to 
dismiss him. 


DECISION 


The petitioner was admittedly a polisher in the opposite party Grand 
Hotel working directly at the relevant time under the Paint Technologist ot 
the opposite party, Shri A. K. Sen Roy (2506 D.W.1). The Engineer of the 
opposite party, Shri B. K. Ghosh (D°W. 1) was the head of the department 
(ode P.W. 1). The petitioner was directed by Shri A. K. Sen Roy to use 
a new polish. The petitioner did not admittedly use the new 
polish as directed by Shri Sen Roy (ude ط‎ W. 1). So 
after interrogation on 3)et March 1955, Shri A. K. Sen 
Roy made written complaint (Ext. A) of insubordination against the pcti- 
tioner to the Engineer, Shri B. K. Ghosh. It was inter alw stated therein 
that notwithstanding his direction the petitioner réfused to use the new 
polish and that he was not only insubordinate but rude and insolent, and 
that the petitioner sdid that he would not obey either the Engineer’s or his 
instruction regarding polishing. Qn receipt of the said complaint the 
Engineer, Shri B. K. Ghosh (D.W. 1), sent for the petitioner and asked 
him to explain his conduct tor refusing to obey the order of Shri Sen Roy 
and for having been insolent and ryde to him. D.W. 1 further deposed that 
upon this the petitioner said that he was not bound to give explanation to 
him nor was he bound to carry out the instructions. Thereupon the Eng- 
neer D.W. 1 forwarded the written complaint of Shri Sen Roy (Ext. A) 
with his remarks (Ext. B) to the Manager of the opposite party Grand Hotel 
on that very day (81st March 1955). In the written report (Ext. B), the 
Engineer stated that on receipt of the réport of Shri Sen Roy he called for 
the petitioner and asked him to éxplain why he was insolent and disobedient 
to Shri Sen Roy. It was further stated that the petitioner reiterated that 
he would not obey anybody’s order from the Engineering Department 000 
that if the heads of the department so desired they could take any action 
they liked. Therefore, the Manager of the opposite party Grand Hotel, 
D.W. 2 Mr. Cecil Bernard Benson, issued a charge-sheet on Ist April 1959’ 
to the petitioner quoting from thd written complaint of Shr A. K. Sen Roy 
as already referred to. The petitioner was asked to submit his explanation 
to the charge by 2nd April 1955 and he was suspended with immedinte effect 
pending enquiry. 


On 2nd April 1955 the Manager of the opposite party Grand Hotel fixed 
4th April 1955 at 11 a.m. for enquiry and the petitioner was notified to he 
present at the time (Ext. 2). Als notified, the enquiry was held by the 
Manager on 4th April 1955 when the Chief Engineer, Skri B. K. Ghosh 
(D.W. 1) and the petitioner (P.W. 1) were present. Shri A. K. Sen Roy 
could not attend the enquiry having had in the meanwhile left for Gopalpur- 
on-sea on hotel duties in connection with the impending visit of the Prime 
Minister in the hotel there. Shri A. K. Sen Roy had also since left service 
of the opposite party Grand Hbtel. 


2634 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [Part ] 


Exhibit E is the minutes of the enquiry held on the 4th April 1955 at 
the office of {he Manager, Mr. Benson at 11 a.m. The petitioner admitted 
that he did not use the new paint ae Shri Sen Roy had asked him to do 
so. Thus the main charge against the petitioner of having flouted Shri 
Sen Roy was admitted and proved. The petitioner also admitted Shri B. K. 
Ghosh’s charge that the petitioner said that he would not give any explana- 
tion to anyone except the Manager. The petitioner was thus insuboidinate 
and insolent il Ag On conclysion of such enquiry the petitioner was 
intimated by a letter, dated 21st April 1955, that the management decided 
to dismiss him from service in view of his refusal to carry out the instruc- 
tions of Shri A. K. Sen Roy regarding the polish to be used and in view of 
his attitude towards the superiors, and that 16 was making necessary applica- 
tion under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for permission in that 
respect ard that until such permission was obtained, he (the petitioner) 
would continue to be unde: order of suspension (vide Ext. F). 


The petitioner admittedly did not receive any other communication 
subsequently. In his complaint under section 833A filed on 4th August 1900, 
it was also admitted that the opposite party did not dismiss him but kept 
him under suspension pending permission from the Tribunal. Said suspen- 
sion in the circumstances wos therefore not punishment within clause (b) of 
section 38. It cannot, therefore, be said that section 33 was :contravened. 
Section 834 of the Act allows a complaint only if section 33 Had been con- 
travened by the employer. As there has been no such violatign, the com- 
plaint under sertion 33A, it is obvious, is not maintainable. Nat only there 
was no such violation but, on the other hand, the opposite party made appli- 
cation under section 33 seeking permission from the Tribuna) to dismiss the 
petitioner. The fact of delay in making the said application would not by 
itself constitute a violation. The foundation for a complaint under 
section 383A is a ‘“‘contravention’’ of section 33 and there cannot be a con- 
travention of that provision when the employer applied for permission. 


On merits ton, on the facts and the circumstances as disclosed, I find 
nothing to impugn the action of the management. The question for consi- 
deration would be whether the case falls within any of the exceptions men- 
tioned in Buckingham & Carnatic Mills, Ltd. In the case before me, there 
is no question of want of bona fides, victimisation or unfair labour practice 
or violation of the principles of natural justice nor does any basic error of 
fact arise. Of course the application under section 83 was not earlier 
presented, but it appears that it was unintentional. The evidence shows 
that the officer of the opposite party Hotel who was dealing with these cases 
was away from the station in connection with the Hotel duties. Neither in 
the complaint nor in his evidence the petitioner could suggest any unfair 
motive on the part of the opposite party Hotel. It, therefore, appears that 
the action of the opposite party was not actuated by an indirect motive or 
want of good faith but was the result of the requirement of the situation. 
In this view of the matter, I am of opinion that the complaint must fail 
both on preliminary ground and on merits, 


Tt is awarded accordingly. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 


J. MAITRA, Judge. JITENDRA NATH MAITRA,

The reference made by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, by order No. 3574Dis. /D/11L-79(c) /55, dated Calcutta, the 4th August 
1955, and subsequent corrigendum No. 916Dis./D/11L-79(c)/55, dated 
Calcutta, the 7th March 1956, relates to a dispute between Messrs. National 
Tohacco Company? Ltd., and one of their employees Shri Suresh Chandra 
Sarkar arising out of the dismissal of the said employee. 


Schedule 


Is the dismissal of Shri Suresh Chandra Sarkar justified? To what relief by 
way of reinstatement and/or compensation is he entitled ? 


The employee’s grievance is that he was rendering meritorious service 
but had the misfortune to incur the ill-will of the chemist Shri 8. B. Dhar 
on account of his not rendering a personal service required by Shri Dhar. 
On the plea that reorganisation was necessary Shri Suresh Chandra Sarkar 
was served with a notice of discharge on 31st October 1952. As a matter of 
fact this action was taken not for the purpose of reorganisation but because 
he had fallen out of favour. This is a glaring instance of victimisation and 
unfair labour practice. 


The Company took a preliminary objection that this is not an industrial 
dispute and hence the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to enter into an adjudica- 
tion of the issue by the Government. It is also urged that there was no pre- 
existing dispute at the time of termination of service of this employee and 


2636 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [ Paxr 1 


উস 
আর, سج کو‎ 


hence he was not a workman as defined in the Industrial Disputes Act. On 
the merits the. Company's case is that in the yeur 1952, the Company'a 
business had suffered a set-batk. There was diminution of the volume of 
work. Retren¢hment was accordingly tndispensibly necessary. There was 
no sufficient work to keep this employee engaged. Notice of discharge was 
accordingly served on him for retren¢thment. Regarding the allegation that 
ou account of his failure to render personal service to the chemist he had 
incurred the displeasure 91 the chemist and the Factory Manager, the Com- 
pany’s case is that it was part of the duty of the employee to purchase rail- 
way ticket for the Company’s employees. He had tailed to do what waé 
his ordinary duty and was reprimanded! for disobedience of order by the 
Factory Manager. There was however no action taken against him. It 18 
a figment of his imagination that he has been victimised for failure to 
purchase railway ticket for the chemist. In view of the legal objection 
taken, an additional issue is framed in the following terms :— 


Issue No, 2.—Is the dispute an industrial one which the Tribunal 18 
competent to adjudicate upen? 


Issue No. &—At the date of the reference the dispute was between 
68815, National Tobaceo Co., Ltd., and an individual worker who was 
engaged in single combat with the Company. The other employees of the 
Company were not interested in the dispute and had taken no\part therein. 
No union or association had espoused the cause of this employed Shri 911 681) 
Chandra Sarkar who was fighting his own cause single-handed. This 
Tribunal has held that an individual dispute of this type is not an indus- 
trial dispute (vide 1956, 1, L.L.J., page 138, and 1956, 1.L.L.J., page 356). 


The order of reference was amehded hy Government order No. 916])is. | 
D/11L-79(e)/55, dated the 7th March 1956. The employee was described 
as represented 1) National Tobacco Company Employees’ Union. The 
question has arisen whether by this amendment the dispute has been con- 
verted into an industrial dispute. On other occasions I had to consider the 
effect of amendment of this nature. Two awards passed by me on this 
subject are published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 26th 4001 1956, at 
page 472 and June 7, 1956, at page 2156. Broadly speaking, my view on the 
point at issue is that (30৮61111017 can amend an order of reference to correct 
clerical errors or make good omissions and oversight. When the ground of 
amendment is some development taking place after the date of the reference 
when the Tribunal is in seisin, the Government is not the authority to make 
alterations. On the date of reference an individual employee was agitating 
for redress of his grievances. If during the pendency of the proceeding 
before the Tribunal he managed to persuade any Union to conduct his case, 
that would not create anv occasion for amendment of the reference. It 18 
entirely for the Tribunal to consider if such intervention will have any effect 
upon the proceeding started on the reference as made. Even if it 1s conceded 
that the cause of the employee heing taken up by a trade union, the dispute 
is transformed into an industrial dispute, the employee concerned secures no 
advancement of his interest inasmuch as the dispute so converted was not 
before the Tribunal on the reference made by Government. The conversion 
cannot be made to be operative from the date of the original reference. 


On behalf of the employee an argument was pressed that the case of 
Shri Santosh Bhattacherjee dealt with by the Tribunal] on the earlier occasion 
stands on a different footing from the present one inasmuch دہ‎ the Wnion 
which came to the aid of §}. Bhattacherjee was of an alien character, whereas 
in the instant case the Union is a body representing the workers of Messrs. 
National Tobacco Company. I do not think that this distinction makes any 
difference. In the first place, J have taken the view that the Government 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1996 2637 


পক সস 


has no power to make this sort of amendment and secondly that the amend- 
ment would not relate back to the date of the order of referetice. 


A marked line of distinction has been drawn between a Union merely 
helping an employee, who, it thinks, should be helped and fts taking up his 
cause as one which affects the general body of workmen and adopting it as 
its own. The distinction has been emphasised in the case reported in 1955, 
2, L.L.J., page 477. Ifa Union merely renders assistance to an emplovee 
without actually making the question an issue betw%en itself and the employer 
it remains an individual disputé. The Tribunal] has therefore to take stock 
of events that has happened since the date of the reference. The learned 
spokesman for the employee produced before me a letter addressed by the 
employee to the Assistant Labour Commissioner which I have marked X. 
In this letter Shrijut Sarkar stated that he did not desire to represent the 
case by himeelf. He had therefore authorised the Assistant Secretary, 
National Tobacco Employees’ Union, to represent the case, on his behalf, 
adding that he would also be present with him for the purpose. It was 
further stated that 16 was difficult on his part to represent the case himself 
without co-operation and help of the Union. The letter addressed hy the 
Assistant Secretary of the National Tobacco Co., Ltd., Employees’ Union to 
Assistant Labour Commissioner on 23rd January 1956 has been found in 
the file of the Lahour Department called for by the Tribunal. The letter is 
reproduced below:

1. 


The latter read in conjunction with Shri Suresh Chandra Sarkar’s letter io 
the Union makes it abundantly clear that the Union was persmaded to take 
up the cudgels on behalf of*the employee to conduct the case before the 


2638 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [Parr ] 


Tribunal. The representation was not of any wider range. The Union 
did not adopt the cause as-its own and turn the dispute into a collective dis- 
pute. This sort of representation 1s not equivalent to espousal of the cause 
as contemplated in the case reported above. The Union did not make the 
employee’s cause its own in the sense that it considered the interests involved 
of general importance desiring its active support in furtherance of its policy 
und the ereed it has undertaken to Uphold and propagate. In the result 
1 hold that the individual dispute has not been converted into an industrial 
dispute. 11 was an individual dispute at its origin and remains so even 
though for purposes of representation before the Tribunal, the Union has 
entered the arena of conflict. 


The learned Counsel also dwelt upon the question whether a discharged or 
dismissed employee would be a workman as defined in the Act if there be no 
pre-existing dispute. The matter is highly controversial. J do not think it 
necessary to start an investigation of the question since on the other point 
denlt with above the conclusion follows that the dispute is an individual 
dispute and as such outside the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. 


Having uo jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the issue referred by the 
Government, I do not find 16 necessary to enter into a discussion on the 
merits. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


This is a complaint filed by the ahove workmen under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act against their employers. The original reference, 
out of which this complaint has arisen, was made under Government order 
No. 4045Dis./D/11L-53/55, dated 9186 August 1999. 


The petitioners’ case is that during the pemdency of the original refer- 
ence before this Tribunal, the Opposite Party continued lay-off of the 
petitioners without the permission of the Tribunal, and thus section 33 of 
the Act was contravened. Accordingly, the petitioners prayed for payment 
of full wages for the period of lay-off, that is from 3lst August 1955 to 
4th September 1955. 


The application was resisted by the Opposite Party. It denied that 
there was any violation of section 33 of the Act, and contended that the 
application was not maintainable. According to the Opposite Party, such 
lay-off was a condition of service. 


I do not like 10 enter into the details or merits of the case, as on the 
date of hearing’ the Joint Secretary of the Empire Bone Mills Mazdoor 
Union filed a petition as per Annexure before the Tribunal that the peti- 
tioners for reasons stated therein wanted leave to withdraw the applica- 
tion under section 33A. The Opposite Party’s representative also stated 
that he had no objection, if the Tribunal allowed the application to be 
withdrawn. In the circumstances, I find no reason as to why I shall not 
allow withdrawal of the application as prayed for. So, the application 
riage section 33A of the Act is allowed to be withdrawn. I make no order 
or costs. 


The case 15 disposed of accordingly.

n joint petition of compromise. The workmen undertook to apply: for leave 
in such cases beforehand in future. In the circumstances thd opposite 
party Company agreed to pay wages to them for 24th J anuary 1956. The 
terms are fair. I accordingly accept the petition of compromise and make 
my award in terms thereof. The petition of compromise is made part of 


the award.

The case presented on behalf of the workers is that during the pendency 
of a reference proceeding, the Management applied under section 33 of the 
Industrial Dispntes Act for permission to dismiss 67 workers. The 
workers also made a petition under section 338A of the Industrial ]hisputes 


Part |] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 2645 


লস 
Act. The applications were heard by the Second Industrial Tribunal. 
Permission was granted to dismiss three workers and with regard to the 
rest the application made by the Management was rejected. The 
application under section 388A was allowed. Appeals were preferred 
against the orders made by the Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal 
upheld the order granting permission to .dismiss three workers and 
also the order refusing permission wifh regard to the rest. The award 
under section 894 was set aside as the application was found ہا‎ be 
unsustainable. Thereafter the Management issuede charge-sheets and gave 
intimation to the workers that aefresh enquiry would be held. Ultimately 
(4 workmen were dismissed. According’ to the workers the dismissal of 
these persons was illegal, mala fide and against all principles of natural 
justice. They are entitled to reinstatement with back wages and compen- 
gation. There’ was a further demand for compensation for non-implementa- 
tion of the awards of the Tribunals اھر‎ 


The Company in its written statement traced the history of the trouble. 
During the pendency of a reference the workers had, according to the 
Company, struck work on 6th October 1903 at 9-14 a.m. They also 
formed a cordon round the acting Working Manager Mr. 1), Cruz and kept 
him confined within a narrow space. The strikers behaved in such a lnw- 
less manner and were so disorderly that the Management had to summon 
)01109 help to save the situation. Mr. 1). Cruz was rescued by the police 
see the clutches of the strikers. As the workers did not listen to reason 
and go back to resume their duties the Company was forced to declare a 
lock-out. Application was thereafter made for permission to dismiss 67 
workers. The Tribunal granted permission to dismiss three of them and 
rejected the prayer so far as the others were concerned, An application 
made by the workem under section 338A was allowed. On appeal the uward 
under section 338A was set aside. The orders passed under section 3:3 were 
confirmed. Thereafter when no ban was in operation the Management 
issued charge-sheets and notices that enquiry would be held on appointed 
dates and hours. Some of the workers appeared at the enquiry but the 
majority kept away. On enquiry the authorities were satisfied that the 
charges were established and orders of dismissal were accordingly made 
which were fully warranted. The workers under reference are not entitled 
to any relief, 


issue No, 1.—Ext. 1 is the order passed hy the Second Industrial 
Tribunal on the ‘applications 7009 by the Company under section 33. 
Three workers, viz., Subhas Roy, Madhusudan Routh, and Bimal Ghose 
were found to have wrongfully confined Mr. 1), Cruz within the factory 
premises for a fairly Jong 1708. The Tribunal granted permission to 
dismiss these three men hut with regard to the rest the evidence was not 
considered convincing. Permission to dismiss the others was refused as 
there was reasonable doubt regarding their complicity in the incident. 
Ext. 1(b) is the Appellate order. Their Lordships held that the Manage- 
ment did not hold a proper enquiry in the presence of the persons 
concerned. The materials on record were accordingly scrutinised in order 
to reach a finding whether the charges had heen substantiated. Their 
Lordships recorded their agreement with the finding of the Tribunal of 
first instance that the allegation against the 64 workers had not been made 
out. In this view they confirmed the order passed by the State Tribunal. 
On behalf of the wopnkers it haa keen strenuously urged that in view of 
the finding of the State Tribunal which was affirmed by the Appellate 
Tribunal, the Management had no right to institute a fresh enquiry in 
respect of the same incidents and take action against persons deemed to 


2646 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 6-6 [Parr I 


be guilty. The spokesman for the workers submitted an argument Yhat 
the findings have the force of res judicata and this Tribunal cannot consti- 
tute itself a Court of Appeal, as it were, to reconsider the same mutter. 
In the first place I may point out that an enquiry under section 33 is of a 
summary ‘character. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is limited ‘to 
granting or refusing permission to the employer to take action. What is 
material is the order and rot the reasons leading up to the saine. In a 
case where permission is granted the effect thereof is not to validate the 
changes brought about by the employer. What happens is that the ban 
imposed by the 14981885079 upon the right of the employer to take disci- 
plinary action against the employees is removed on permission being granted. 
Findings reached in such a summary proceeding can have no finality and 
cannot debar a Tribunal dealing with a reference under section 10(1) from 
going into the matter unfettered by the conclusions arrived at in the 
summary proceeding. It has been held that orders under section 33 are 
not awards. The learned spokesman for the workers referred to awards 
made by Shri P. R. Mookherjee published in the Calcutta Gazette, under 
notification No. 40]4Lab., dated 24th July 1950, and hy Shr M. C. Baner- 
jee under notification No. 1716Lab., dated 6th April 1950, in support 
of his coptention that though the principle of res judicata is not directly 
applicable a principle analogous to it is applicable. He seems to have 
overlooked that the applicability of the principle was considered in relation 
to awards. The position is now entirely different since in the present 
case the order arose out of a proceeding started under section 33 of the 
Act, Since no award is passed in proceedings of this nature,| the question 
of the applicability of a principle analogous to the principle of res judicata 
cannot arise. 


The State Tribunal did not hold the charges disproved. There was in 
its view reasonable doubt. The Appellate Trihunal did not go any further. 
The sum and substance therefore 1s that the charges framed against the 
others were not proved not that they were disproved. In this view I can- 
not sustain the plea that the same question could not be reopened by the 
Management for purposes of a fresh enquiry. Both the State Tribunal 
and the Appellate Tribunal pointed out that the enquiry held by the 
Management was not in accordance with the principles of natural justice. 
Notices were not given and the persons concerned were denied the element- 
ary right to defend themselves. The Management had therefore the right 
4) remedy the defects and start afresh observing the formalities which 
would make’ it fool-proof. In my view the Managemsant did not assume 
a right not available to it in embarking upon a fresh enquiry. Admittedly 
all barriers were down by 29th March 1955. There was nothing to prevent 
the Management from awarding punishment upon the employees for any 
misconduct. By the date mentioned above no proceedings were pending 
te act as a clog on the rights of the Company. Charge-sheets in form as 
per Ext. A were issued afresh. Ext. A(1) is the form in which notices 
were issued under registered post. Ext. B series are the postal receipts. 
Jt appears that 28 persons were not found at the recorded addregs. Six 
persons had refused to accept the registered notices. Out of the reminder 
one Haroo Flalder appeared at the enquiry and pleaded guilty, 98 will 
appear from the enquiry report Ext. G (pages 3-4), Sixteen others serial 
numbers (2), (8), (11), (12), (15), (17),-418), (36), (42), (44), (58), 
(57), (58), (60), (61) and (62) in the list of workers attached to the 
Order of Reference tendered resignation voluntarily and left. The case 
of these 16 persons need not hence be considerd. 


As Haroo Halder had pleaded guilty, his dismissal is upheld as justified. 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 2647 


Fhe 23 persons bearing serial numbers (1), (3), (4), (5), (9), (19), 
(14), (16), (20), (22), (০), (26), (34), (40), (41), (45), (46), (48), 
(49), (50), (94), (56) and (59) who have not been served with notices 
could not be dismissed. On behalf of the Company the learned Advocate 
ressed the argument that notices being returned unserved the Company 
80 written to the Secretary of the Union the letter Ext. ہا‎ asking for the 
present address of those people. The Secretary of the Union vouchsafed 
no reply. The Company could not thefefore take any further steps ٥ 
give notice to them. The learned Advocate appeared to have the notion 
that the Company having done everything in its power, non-service of 
notice on those workers could beseoverlooked. 1 am afraid he has taken 
an erroneous view. The Company might have sent the notices to the 
Union Secretary for circulation to the absentees. The notices not having 
been served the position remains the same as at the time the State Tribunal 
dealt with the matter on the application under section 33. It was pointed 
out that according to the Standing Order of the Company, notice might be 
given by aflixture on the notice board of the factory. It should be borne 
in mind that the Company had declared a lock-out. The workers had no 
access to the factory during the lock-out period. The Works Manager 
addressed a letter to the Secretary of the Union on the 25th April 1955 
(Ext. 2d), that any workman in resject of whom enquiry would be hield 
would be treated as a trespasser and severe action would be taken against 
him if he entered the factory without permission. Practically the workers 
who had not capitulated and rejoined after tendering apology had no means 
of access to the factory. The notice in the notice board could not hence 
serve any useful purpose so far as they were concerned. In my view 
therefore service by affixture in the notice board was of no avail. The 23 
persons must hence be held to have been wrongfully dismissed. In regard 
to the rest, harring of course the 16 men who had voluntarily resigned, 
the action of the Corfipany cannot hut he justified as there was evidence 
recorded by the enquiring officer on the basis of which he could take the 
view that they were guilty of the charges framed. It has been held that 
if there is evidence to support the action of the Management, the Tribunal 
will not substitute its own judgment for that of the Management. 
Mr. Dungee, O.P.W. 1, had held the enquiry. Ext G is the record of the 
proceeding. He examined Mr, D. Cruz as witness. Evidence was taken 
regarding the identity of the persons who had participated in the strike 
and molestation of Mr. D. Cruz. No bias or ill-will was attributed to the 
Management. In the written statement no case was suggested that the 
Management was inspired by any vindictive motive. Since there was 
evidence and it was a possible view, the Tribunal must accept the finding 
and hold that the dismissal of those workers wus justified. 


The men wrongfully dismissed must he reinstated within 15 days from 
the date of the publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette. There 
was an illegal strike. The work was completely suspended. The Company 
had issued one notice after another, calling upon the workers to go back 
to their duties but no one paid heed. There is nothing to show that the 
persons ‘who are about to be reinstated had evinced any inclination to 
follow a different line of action from the rest. Out of sympathy or for 
some other reasons they had also abstained from resuming duty. ‘The 
Management was forced to declure a lock-out. It would not therefore he 
just and proper to allow these workers any wages or compensation. 


issue No. 2.—The strike, dated 6th October 1953, was illegal as at that 
time a reference proceeding was pending. The lock-out declared by the 
Company was fully justified. The strikers had taken up a_ belligerent 
attitude and had actually kept the acting Working Manager confined till 


2648 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 6 [Parr 1 


he was rescued late in the afternoon by the police. No compensati§n can 
legitimately be claimed for the period of enforced idleness from 6th 
October 1953, The applications under section 33 were finally disposed of 
by the Appellate Tribunal on 29th March 1955. As permission to dismiss 
these men was refused, they are to be treated us continuing in service. The 
correspondence Iixt. 2 (series) shows that the Union tried to persuade the 
Company to readmit tha workers to their respective posts. Ext. 2 is a 
letter, dated 80th March 1956, in which the Assistant Secretary of the 
Union affirmed that on the same day the workers had presented themselves 
at the factory gate: but they were not allowed admuission. The Works 
Manager replied by letter Ext. 2(a) that some 15 men had congregated ut 
the gate but did not report to the office. It was not possible to say 
whether they were workers or not. The Union had in the letter Ext. 2 
enquired when the workers should be directed to report for duty. To this 
no reply was given. The workers who were wrongfully dismissed and kept 
out when they were ready to come back are entitled to recover their wages. 
T award them wages and dearness allowance, if any, with effect from 151 
April 1955 up to the date of reinstatement. Payment must be made within 
15 days from the date of publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette. 


Issue No. 3.—Shri Subhas Rov, Madhusudan Routh and Bimal Ghose 
were permitted by the State Tribunal to be dismissed. The order was 
confirmed on appeal. Company’s prayer to dismiss 64 others were rejected 
both by the State Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal. Neither the State 
Tribunal nor the Appellate Tribunal made any order upon the Company 
fo do any positive act. The application under section 334 was allowed 
by the State Tribunal but the order was set aside on appeal [vide Ext. 1(d)] 
The application was held to be misconceived. As the order of 1179 
Appellate Tribunal in the matter of the application under section 33 was 
not directory and no duty was imposed upon the Company, there can | 
no question of implementation or non-implementation. No question of 
compensation can therefore arise.

Roth parties filed their written statements in the case. The Union 
which filed written statement on behalf of the workers, claimed 3 months’ 
wages as bonus for the year 1954, over and above the customary bonus paid 
to workmen. 


In a counter-statement, Messrs. Bhartia Electric Steel Co., Ltd. (herejn- 
after referred to as the Company) resisted the Union’s demand, and contend- 
ed inter alia that there was no surplus available after deducting all the prior 
charges from the trading results of the year, for which bonus was being 
claimed. The Company further stated that in spite of no surplus being 
available, it is a gesture of goodwill and with a view to obtain better labour- 
management relations, paid to the workmen a bonus equivalent to about 
15 days’ basic wages in 1954, and that it was unable to pay any further 
bonus in reapect of the year endipg 1954.

ceeding with the case, intimated that the dispute was amicably settled. A

Appendices was thereafter filed. The terms of settlement relating to bonus 
for the year 1954, which is.the subject-matter of the present reference 
appear to be fair and reasdnable, and as such they are accepted. Accord- 
ingly, an award is passed in terms thereof. The petition of compromise, s0 
far as it relates to the question of bonus for the year 1954, do form part 
of this award.

was pronounced on the 5th April 1956. The issue of bonus for 1954 has

Works in view of the setting up of a new rolling mill at Khardah, reclasai-

sive of Sundays, Festival holidays and other leave. For attendance for less

or payments already made shall be adjusted against the above payment.

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. National

The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. 6173Dis./D/10L-125/55, dated 20th December 1955, has referred the 
aforesaid dispute regarding the matter mentioned in the schedule below 
to this Tribunal for its adjudication. 


The issues as contained in the schedule to the order of reference stand 
as follows :— 


Whether the existing rates of wages are in accordance with the Major 
Engineering Tribunal Awards ? 


Tf not, in what way they should be improved? 


AWARD 


The case for the Union in short is that the National Sheet & Metal 
Works, Ltd., is at present a very prosperous concern. It has been making 
steady and continuous progress in all directions since the Second World 
War broke out, and has made great financial strides. But unfortunately, 
thia Company pays much lower wage and dearness allowance to its workers. 
Naturally, the workers became extremely dissatisfied. In October 1993, 
the workers through their Union demanded revision of their wages and 
dearness allowance with effect from Ist October 1953 in terms of the level 
fixed by the Engineering Industrial Tribunals. The matter was referred 
to the Conciliation Officer, Yabour Directorate. Though in course of 


2656 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [Parr I 


® 


conciliation proceedings, the Company ut the suggestion of the Concilia- 
tion Officer at first ugreed to introduce minimum wage scale inclusive otf 
dearness allowance at Rs. 61, which was the miniinum acale for unskilled 
workers awarded by the Major Kugimeering Tribunal, it subsequently 
declined to do this. Further conciliation proceedings were then held, 
but due to the attitude of the Company no amicable settlement could be 
arrived at. At last, it was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. As 
the wages given by the Company are extremely inadequate and cannot 
provide most ot the workers with the barest necessities of life, the Union 
prayed that the wages and dearness allowance of the workers must be 
revised, at least in terms of the Major Engineering ‘Tribunal Award with 
regard to unskilled and semi-skilled workers, and for the skilled, highly 
skilled and special grade workers, the basic wages should he Ks. 60—-100, 
Rs. 100—100 and Rs. 1580-200, respectively. 


Messrs. National Sheet & Metal Works, Ltd. (hereinafter called the 
Company) contends that it never agreed to introduce minimum wage scale 
inclusive of dearness allowance at Rs. 61. It did not also agree to any 
terms before the Conciliation Officer, but due to insistence of the Union, 
the said Conciliation Officer made some f£ecommendations, which could not 
be accepted by the Company. The Company expressed its inability to pay 
according to the recommendations accepted by the Union. The Company 
is not in a position to give any Increase in wages, or to fix ahy pay seule 
in view of its unstable financial condition. So, it should nof be saddled 
with the rates of wages as per Major Engineering Tribunal Awards, 
considering its status and capacity to pay. It stated further’ that = the 
minimum basic wages of the unskilled workers of this Company has been 
fixed by the Tribunal at Rs. 30, and the Company has been tollowing the 
game. Furthermore, this Company has given increases -in wages = from 
time to time, and the basic wages of unskilled workers and_ semi-skilled 
workers are in conformity with the Major Engineering Tribunal Awarda, 
which fixed such minimum basic wages at Rs. 30 and Rs. 30, respectively, 
for unskilled and semi-skilled workers. As regards skilled workers, 
highly skilled workers and special grade workers, the Major Engineernng 
Tribunal Award did not fix basic wages for them. It further contended 
that dearness allowance should be treated as outside the scope of adjudi- 
cation, because this would be evident from the pleadings of the Union and 
also from the issue as contained in the schedule to the order of reference. 
Finally, the Company said that in view of its financial position which was 
bad and unsatisfactory and owing to depression in business, it was not in 
a position to bear any further increase in wages, or to make payment of 
dearness allowance at the rate fired by the Major Engineering Tribunal 
Award of 1980, 


DECISION 


At the very outset, I would like to dispose of a point that has heen 
raised before the Tribunal on behalf of the Company. Tearned advocate 
appearing on behalf of the Company has argued that the question ot 
dearness allowance should be treated as outside the scope of adjudication 
in the present dispute. He has invited my attention in this respect to thie 
pleadings of the Union and also to the issue as-contained in the schedule 
to the order of the present reference. He has further drawn my attention 
to Ext. 2—charter of demands placed before the Labour Officer by the 
Union and also to Ext. 3—a letter addressed hy the Director of the 
Company to the Assistant Labour Commissioner. Relying on these docu- 
ments, he has voiced an argument that dearness allowance was a separate 
item, which was and has heen kept distinct all along from the wages, 


Pane 1| THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 2657 


Sather the basic wages, and that us the present reference was in respect of 
wages alone, the question whether or not there should be any increase in 
the existing dearness allowance of the workers, was beyond the scope ot 
the present reference. He hus further contended that the wording of the 
issue as ا‎ a the schedule, clearly excluded the adjudication of the 
question of dearness allowance. 1! have perused the relevant documents, 
and huve given my careful and anxious cpnsideration to the arguments 
put forward by the learned advocate’ of the Company. But I must say 
that 1 am unable to accept the interpretution he wanted to make. The 
issue as contained in the schedule to the order of,reference is as follows :— 


‘Whether the existing rates of wages are in accordance with 1116 
Major Engineering Tribunal Awards P’’ 


‘“Wages’’ has been defined in section 2(rr) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947. The definition of wages is that it means all remunerations 
capable of being expressed in terms of money......... and includes such 
allowance (including dearness allowance) as the workman is for the time 
being entitled to. So, the plain language of the definition of wages 
indicates that it includes dearness allowance. It being so, I have no doubt 
or hesitation in saying that in the issue as mentioned in the schedule to 
the order of reference, the word ‘*wuges’’ includes also dearness allowance. 
Accordingly, this Tribunal has the right and jurisdiction to enter into the 
question of dearness allowance also in determining the question whether 
the existing rates of wages are in accordance with the Major Engineering 
Tribunal Awards. 


Now let me enter into the merits of the case. Admittedly, the present 
sompany is an Engineering concern. It is a fact no doubt that this 
Company was not a party to the Major Engineering Tribunal. But tos 
fact by itself does, not matter much. The awards of the Major Engineering 
Tribunal can certainly be used as guide for determining what the wages 
should be for the workers of an Engineering concern. In fact, those 
awards help us as guide in the matters dealt with thereunder. For thut 
purpose, the rate decidendi of those awards is of great importance. It 
is up to this Tribunal to decide, whether or not such wages as fixed by 
the Major Engineering Tribunal Awards including dearness allowance 
should be given to the workers of the present Company. This Cmpany 
gives dearness allowance at the flat rate of Rs. 30 to all its workefs. 
This is not in conformity with the Major Engineering Tribunal Awards. 
Regarding wages, J, however, find that this Company gives munitnum 
basic wages as prescribed by the Major Engineering Tribunal for unskilled 
und skilled workers. The Major Engineering Tribunal fixed the minimum 
basic wage for the unskilled workers at Rs. 30 per month or Re. 1-2-0 
per day, and that of the semi-skilled workers at Ks.. 30 per month or 
Re. 1-0-0 per day. This Company has been giving such minimum basic 
wages to its unskilled and semi-skilled workers. ‘The charts which have 
been filed by both parties show that the minimum basic wages as stated 
above, do not fall দন of the minimum wages as prescribed by the Major 
Engineering Tribunal in case of unskied and semi-skilled workers ot the 
present Company. That being so, I do not think any interference is culied 
for so far as the question of basic wages of the unskilled and semi-skilled 
workers is concerned. Regarding skilled workers, highly skilled workers 
and special grade workers, the Major Engineering Tribunal did not fix any 
minimum basie wage, but it 1016 the matter with the Management of the 
different concerns with its recommendation that there should be some 
increments in their pay. In the present dispute, the Union 910 not 
produce any ৪001) material which justified ony increment in the pay olf 
these workers. So, any increment in the basic wages of skilled workers, 


2658 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [Parr I 


highly skilled workers and special grade workers of the present Company, 
cannot be entertained or gone into. ‘The bone of contention of the Union 
is that the cost of living has gone up. Even if it is accepted to be so, it 
does not support the Union’s contention for justifying any increment in 
the wages of all the workers—unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled, highly skilled 
and special grade workers—as demanded in this case. It may be state’ 
further that a rise of the cost of living index prima facie supports a case 
for revision of the dearness allowauce, and not of basic wages. The 
introduction of the Compulsory Provident Fund Scheme and the State 
Insurance Fund for the workers has given much-needed relief to the 
workers, and the contributions coming therefrom are to be treated as addi- 
tions to their wages. Hence, judging by all the available standards, the 
basic wages which are given at present to the workmen of this Company, 
cannot be said to be below the minimum or otherwise inadequate. So, 
the Tribunal holds that the demand for ad hoc increments over the existing 
rates of basic wages is neither justified nor expedient and proper, specially 
in view of the financial position of the Company as appearing from Ext. 
3(b). Furthermore, it appears that there are no grades with fixed scales 
of increment for the workers in this Company. Ad 1000 increments can 
only be granted if the two conditions are fulfilled, namely (£) there are 
certain grades and (22) time scales of pay. In the present case, both these 
conditions are absent. So, no increment in the basic wages would be 
proper in the circumstances of the case. So, to be precise, the Tribunal 
holds that the existing rates of basic wages given to the workers of this 
Company are in রি with the Major Engineering Tribynal Awards, 
and that it being so, they need no improvement or revision. Regarding 
dearness allowance, I have already observed that this Company gives 
dearness allowance at the flat rate of Rs. 30 to all its workers, which is not 
in conformity with the Major Engineering Tribunal Awards.‘ The First 
Major Engineering Tribunal by its award, dated 4th -June 1948, fixed 
dearness allowance for all categories of workmen under the Engineering 
firms at the following scale :—

»From what has been stated above, it is crystal clear that the dearness 
allowance, which this Company has been paying to its workers, is lesser 
than the deurness allowance admissible according to the awards of the 
Engineering Tribunal as atoresaid. The Company contends that it has no 
capacity to bear additional burden. It is urged on behalf of the Company 
that it is rather a small concern, and its financial position is bad and un- 
satistactory, and that in the circumstances, the dearness allowance as fixed 
in the awarda of the Major Kngineering Tribunal should not be applied to 
it. The resources of this Company are meagre. From Ext. 3(b)—a chart 
showing the statement of the Company’s financial position—it will be 
evident that the net profit after sales and payment of wages, has been 
gradually going down. In 1901-02 it was Rs. 25,204, but in 1954-06 it 
has come down to Rs. 11,088. Less than 200 workers are employed in tbis 
Company. Taking this financial stability and ability of this Company 
into consideration, it will not be just and proper if this Company be asked 
to implement fully the Major Engineering ‘Tribunal Awards regarding 
dearness allowance as awarded by the aforesaid Tribunal. Accordingly, 
this Tribunal directs dearness allowance at the following scale :—

Dearness allowance at the above rates 18 accordingly awarded to 911 
the workers of this concern. The dearness allowance as fixed above, will 
be payable within one month of the award coming into operation. I give 
no retrospective effect in this respect. 


In awarding the above dearness allowance, particularly at rates varying 
trom Rs. 31 to Re. 45, two important points which have emerged from the 
materials on record have also been taken into consideration. One is that 
the Union agreed to such rates of dearness allowance before the Assistant 
Labour Commissioner, while conciliation proceedings were going on before 
him. The other is that the range of basic wages of almost all the workers 
of this concern with the exception of one or two falls within the limit of 
Rs. 200. I am mindful of the fact that by this award, 1» few workers, 
whose basic wages will be ultimately above Rs. 200 per month, will be 
getting dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 50, a rate which will be 
higher than what was agreed to by the Union before the Assistant Labour 
Commissioner in the conciliation proceedings. But I do not think thal 
the Union can be pinned down to what was agreed by it during the 
conciliation proceedings. It is true no doubt that the Union agreed صا‎ 
accept what was suggested by the Conciliation Officer regarding dearness 
allowance. But at the same time, the stubborn fact remains that the 
Company did not accept that suggestion. So, it cannot be said that there 
was any concluded agreement between the parties in this respect. The 
matter did not take any definite shape, rather it remained in a duid ataye. 
In the circumstances, the Union cannot be forced 10 limit its demand for 
dearness allowance to what was suggested by the Conciliation Officer and 
agreed by it. 


2660 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 [Part 1 


An argument was made before me by the learned spokesman of the 
Union that sume portion of the dearness allowance should be incorporated 
into the basic wages. In my view, this claim is untenable. ] am_ fully 
alive to the fact that the trend of events leads one tq think that the prices 
of commodities are never going to stabilise at the pre-war level. So, 
dearness allowance has got practically to stay. Under such circumstances, 
the claim tor having at least a portion of it to be converted into basic 
wage, may not be unreasonable. But this move does not fetch more money 
into the pockets of the workers, It may affect one’s contribution ‘to the 
Provident Fund. It may affect his retiral benefit as gratuity. It may 
also have a bearing on the retrenchment relief. So, except for gratuity 
or bonus; incorporation of dearness allowance into the basic wage cannot 
be of much benefit to the workers. But whatever that might be, such 
incorporation of dearness allowance into the basic wage cannot be done wm 
a stray and individual case before a Tribunal. It is desirable that it should 
be done on a higher level, مھ‎ that the industries in general might be bound 
by such a provision. I do not think ft advisable to allow any incorpora- 
tion of dearness ullowance into the basi¢ wage in the present case, as it 
stands by itself. It has been represented to me that there is already a 
move in this direction. Let us only wait. 


Now ] give a summary below of my award. The existing rates of basic 
wages in this Company are in accordance with the Major Engineering 
1177৭] Awards, and us such the same need no revision or improvement. 
But the existing dearness allowance, which is part of the wages, ia not in 
accordance with the Major Enginecring Tribunal Awards, and ay such 11 
should be revised and improved for all categories of workmen as below :—

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 21st June 1956. 


Summary.—During the week under report there was rainfall in thirty-five subdivisions. The weather conditions wure 
unfavourable in eighteen subdivisions. Transplantation of Aman and Aus continuing in some subdivisions. The condition of the 
standing crop was on the whole fair. 

The fodder was reported to be insufficient in fourtoen subdivisions and cattle-disease was reported from seven subdivisions. 


The wages of the labourer varied from rupee one to rupees two and annas eight only during the week under report.

SUPPLEMENT TO 11117 CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 5, 1956 


DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, WEST 


BENGAL, 
Calcutta, the 19th March 1956. 


Second Forecast of Gram Crop of West Bengal for 
1955-56. 


f Note.—The estimates of area under and yield of 
Gram for last year have been taken from last 
year’s final forecast which was based on 
reports of sample survey and crop cutting 
experiments carried out by the State 
Statistical Bureau, West Bengal. The figures 
of this year as shown in the forecast are 
based on the reports furnished by the exten- 
sion staff of this Directorate. ] 


Season.—The weather conditions have in 
Hence been favourable, for the crop in all the 


a 


Area and yield.—325,100 acres are estimated to

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The object of the Rill.is (1) to remove certain administrative difficulties 
and (2) tg stop certain loopholes tor evasion. 


The reasons are explained in’ the notes on clauses appearing below. 


Notes on Clauses. 


Clause 2. 


Sub-clause (a).—Extends the scope of the present definition of ‘‘contract’’ 
by including river-going vessel and aireraft so that the sale price of goods 
supplied in the execution of a cuntract to construct, overhaul or repdir them 
may be preacribed under section )ا)2‎ 


Sub-clause (b).-—It is a consequeytial amendment. 


Clause 3. 


Recently the High Court of Calcutta has decided in a case that under 
the law, as it is noy, if during the pendency of a certificate case arising out 
of sales tax demand, such demand is in any way modified by a sales” tax 
Appellate or ‘Revisiunal authority, the original certificate proceedings will 
become void and fresh [80018111010 will have to be filed in respect of such 
demand. This will not only make the future certificate procedure very much 
cumbrous but may make a large number of claims time-barred when the time 
for re-filing arises. This provision seeks to make it ‘clear that such fresh 
requigjtion will not be necessagy. 


Clausé 4. 


Information about sales tax assessment cases cannot now be disclosed for 
the purposes of a suit or proceeding in a 611] Court or to any officer of 
Government tar the purposes of this Act. In the absence of such informa- 
tion Law Officers of Government are handicapped in contesting applications 
under article 226 of the (Constitution and in conducting prosecutions. 
Similarly, assessing officers are handicapped for their inability to refer to 
papers of other dtalers for the purpose of crose-checking. The proposed 
amendment seeks to remove these two handicaps. 


Clause de 
The sales tax on textiles was beipg évaded through two loopholes : 


(1) the exemption from registration ‘of dealers importing less than 
Rs.10,000 a year, and 


(2) the exemption from taxation of dhooties, lungi€s and sarees below 
certain price limits. 


Most of the dealers avoided registration by dtranging large imports in 
small consignments in the name of © numper of fictitious or berami dealers. 
Those who were registered avoided taxation by showing fictitiously in their 
books that mest of the sales were of items below the price limits. To stop 
this malpractice it was necessary to withdraw both types of exemption. 
The Legislature has already withdrawn the first exemption by enacting the 
Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) (Secopd Amendment) Act, 1955. Withdrawal 
of the second exemption required assent of the President and the consent of 
the Government of India was not so long available. The consent hag since 
hecome available. This clause seeks 18 withdraw this exemption.

8.8.0. 1519.—In exercise of the powers conferred by section 20-A of

NOTIFICATION 
No. 3800W.T.—10th July 1956.—The following 


draft of amendment which, in exercise of the power 
conferred by sub-section Ob and, in particular, by 
clause (za) of sub-section (2), of section 68 of the 
Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (1V of 1939), the 
Governor proposes to make in the Bengal Motor 
Vehicles Rules, 1940, published with notification 
No. 1930P1., dated the 2lst September 1940, at 
pages 2655-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta Gazette 
of the 10th October 1940, as subsequently amended, 
is hereby published, as required by sub-section (1) 
of section 133 of the said Act, for the information 
of persons likely to be affected thereby. 


2. The draft amendment will be taken into 
consideration on or after the 20th July 1956, and 
any objection or suggestion with respect thereto 
which may be received by the undersigned before 
that date shall be considered : 


Draft Amendment 


After rule 67A of the said rules, add the follow- 
ing new rule, namely :— 


“67B. Conveyance of long dastance goods 
trafic by private or public carrters.—Subject to the 
provisions of clause (9) of sub-section (1) of sec- 
tion 43 of the Act, the State Government may 
restrict throughout the State or in any area or on 
any route within the State, the conveyance of all 
or any of the following classes of goods, by private 
or public carriers, namely : 


(a) Tea and tea garden stores, 

(b) Cardamom, 

(c) Salt, 

(d) Oil of any kind or variety whatsoever, 
(e) Seed potatoes, and 


(f) Any other goods as may be deemed 
necessary. 


\ 
By order of the Governor, 
J. N. TALUKDAR, Secy.

No. 6911..—9th June 1956.—Whereaos I am of 


opinion, as the result of an enquiry held into the 
constitution, working and financial condition of the 
Berhampore Co-operative Stores Ltd. (Registered 
No. 247 of 1919) in the Berhampore subdivision 
of the district of Murshidabad, under sub-section 
(1) of section 84 of the Bengal Co-operative 
Societies Act, XXI of 1940, that the Society 
ought to be wound up. 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power confer- 
red by sub-section (1) of section 89 of the Bengal 
Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 (Bengal Act XXI 
of 1940), | hereby order the winding up of the 
said Society. 


And further, in exercise of the power conferred 
by section 90 of the said Act, I hereby appoint 
the Departmental Officer-in-charge of Liquidated 
Societies, Murshidabad district, to be Liquidator 
of the said Society,

ANNEXURE A 
TERMS OF SETTLEMENT 
BETWEEN 
THE VIJOY ENGINEERING CO., PRIVATE LTD., 
AND 


THEIR WORKERS REPRESENTED BY 
BELUR IRON & STEEL WORKERS’ UNION. 


1.—Minimum Scale of Wages 


It is agreed that the minimum wage of unskilled workers will be 
i ৫০3 per day. 


: The semi-skilled workers will be given a flat increment of annas 2 per 
ay. 


2718 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 [Part I 


ہے شس تسپ 


With regard to two skilled workers, the Management agrees to grant 
suitable increments at their discretion. 


2.—Leave 


The Management agrees to grant nine festival holidays. The nine 
festival holidays will include two National holidays, i.e., the 26th ٦ 
and 15th August. Qut of the remaining seven holidays three will be 
selected by the Management and four by the workers. 


3.—etrenchment of 49 workers 


(a) The retrenchment of 19 workers as per list enclosed will stand. 
They have already tuken retrenchment compensation and as such they will 
have no further claims on the Company. In case of any future vacancies 
preterence will be given to those persons, 


(8) The following three retrencked workers will be paid as و‎ special 
case a lump sum of four months’ wages in full and final settlement of their 
claims and they shall forfeit their claim for re-employment in future سے‎ 


(1) Bhajan Gopal Banerjee. 
(2) Ashutosh Roy. 
(3) Netai Chandra Ghosh. 


(c) The rest of the 27 workers have already been taken 0 service. 
There is, therefore, no dispute on their account. But out of these 27 
workers those who have not taken the retrenchment compensation will be 
treated as on leave without pay for the period of unemployment, and 11761 
service will be treated as continuous. Others who accepted the compen- 
sation, should be treated as re-employed. 


4,.—Bonus 


Having regard to the financial position of the Company the Union does 
not press its claim for bonus for the past years. ‘he Management on their 
part assure the Union that they will review the financial position to consider 
the question of paying bonus during the Pujas. 


5.—Dismissal 


(a) Chittaranjan Das.—His dismissal will stand. He will get one- 
fourth wages for the period of unemployment from the date of suspension, 
i.e., 8th September 1954 to the date of the agreement. 


(b) Ajit Kumar Samonta.—He will be treated as dismissed from 8th 
January 1956. The petitions under section 33 and 094 will be withdrawn. 
He will get one-fourth of the wages for the period from 8th January 1956 
go the date of agreement. 


(c) Birendra Nath Adhikari.—His dismissal will stand. He will get 
one-fourth of the wages from the date of dismissal, i.e., 14th December 
1905 tg the date of agreement.

Schedule 


Is the dismissal of Shri Radheshyam justified ?

Notices were issued on both parties. The Company refused the ‘otice 
and did not appear before the Tribunal. The Union filed written  state- 
ment on 14th December 1955. The case was heard ex parte in the absence 
of the Company. Shri T. B. Pakhrin, Secretary, and Shri M. A. Quraishi 
appeared for the workman. 


Parr I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 2721 


es সত 


‘Phe issue that arises for decision in this case is the same as that men- 
tioned in the order of reference and is as follows :— 


Issue 
Is the dismissal of Shri Radheshyam justifies ? 
To what relief is he entitled? 


AWARD 
Decisions 


The written statement of the worker shows that Shri Radheshyam was 
appointed by the Company as a Driver in June 1949 on a total emolument 
of Rs. 95 per month, and that the Driver served the Company faithfully 
for over four years. The plug of the car which Shri Radheshyam used to 
drive developed some mechanical trouble due to weak compression engine, 
and the workman brought the defect to the notice of the employer for 
necessary repair, hut the employer did not take any action to repair the 
defect. On 10th July 1954, Radheshyam reminded the employer about the 
defect, but the employer got annoyed and dismissed him with 172706018৮6 
effect without any notice and without any compensation. The Union, 
therefore, prays that the dismissal of Shri Radheshyam was unjustifiable 
and he should be reinstated with continuity of service and should be اہر‎ 
back wages for the period of forced unemployment commencing from the 
date of his dismissal being 10th July 1954 to the date of reinstatement. 


P.W. 1 Shri Radheshyam deposed and proved the statements made in 
the written statement filed by the Union. He states that the plug of the 
car which he used to drive developed some mechanical trouble and he 
brought the defect to the notice of the employer for repairs, but the 
employer did not take any step. On 10th July 1954, he reminded the 
employer, on which the latter took away the key of the car from the 
Driver and then discharged him. Shri Radheshyam prayed for reinstate- 
ment and emoluments for the period of non-employment. On the evidence 
on record, it appears that the dismissal of Shri Radheshyam was not 
justified. He should, therefore, be reinstated to his own job at his old 
pay of Rs. 95 per month. Shri Radheshyam was discharged on 10th July 
1954, and the order of reference is dated 13th October 1955. It appears 
to me that it will not be proper to allow back wages for the entire period 
of unemployment from 10th July 1954, aa the reference was made more 
than o year after the date of the discharge. In the circumstances, 14 18 
awarded that Shri Radheshyam should be paid by the Company full wages 
for four months by way of compensation for the period of non-employment. 
Shri Radheshyam should be reinstated within one month from the date on 
which this award comes into operation. The period of non-employment 
will = considered to be special leave on emoluments as are allowed in this 
award. 


M. 0. BANERJI, 


Judge, First Industrial Tribunal.
