AWARD 


During the pendency of the original dispute, the present complaint, 
dated 9th February 1956, purporting to be under section 394 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act was filed on 20th February 1956 by these two workers on 
the allegation that while the original dispute was pending before this 


Part I} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTR, JULY 12, 1956 2723 
ee —_____________—_____———_ ممسممسستسست ک س۰6 شش‎ 
Tr8unal, the Opposite Party, in contravention of the provisions of section 
49 of the Industrial Disputes Act, retrenched them unlawfully. 


The Opposite Pifrty has raised a preliminary objection regarding 
maintainability of the complaint. It is urged by the Opposite Vaity— 
Company that the petitioners were never under ity employment, aud as such 
they could have no cause of grievance against the present Company, which 


alone was concerned with the original order of reference. 


JT have heard the learned representative on both sides at length, and have 
considezed the evidence—both oral and documentary as furnished, 


Now let me turn to the order of reference of the main case. The relevant 
portion of the reference was in the following terms :— 


‘Whereas an industrial dispute exists between Messrs. Khemchand 
Rajkumar, 33 Netaji Subhas Road, Caleutta-1, and their workmen 
represented by Shri Rajani Mukherjee, Vice-President, Hind 
Mazdoor Sabha, 19913 Rash Behari Avenue, Caleutta-29, regarding 
the matters specified in the schedule, and whereas it 1৭5 expedient 
that the said dispute should he referred to an Industrial Tribunal 


constituted under section 7 ofthe Industrial Disputes Act ........... 
vise yee veee the Governor is pleased hereby to refer the said 
dispute to the Second Industrial Tribunal.............ccccecee میتی‎ 


for adjudication.’’ 


The plain language of the order of reference df the above industrial 
dispute for adjudication shows that the dispute arose between Messrs. 
Khemehand Rajkumer oy. the one hand and their workmen on the other. 
So. it 1৭ apparent that the subject-matter of the di pute was between that 
Jompany and its employees, and that no employee in other concerns could 
he aftected by the award that would be passed in the above dispute. From 
the description of the parties to the dispute on whom the award in the 
dispute could be binding and from the nature of the subject-matter of the 
dispute, 14 seems that the result was likely to concern none else except the 
workmen of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar. This was also the argument 
that was put forward by the learned representative on behalf of the Company. 
He has further argued that these two petitioners were never in the employ- 
ment of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar, and as such they were not entitled 
to present the application under section 38A of the Act, because they were 
not concerned in the original order of reference. But it is the positive case 
of the petitioners that they were employed under Messrs. Khemchand Raj- 
kumar. It 1৭ not their case that they worked under Messrs. Steel Rolling 
Mills of Bengal Ltd. The petitioners have also deposed at the time of 
hearing that thev used to work under Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar. They 
did not assert that they were under the employment of Messrs. Steel Rolling 
Mills of Bengal Ltd. It may be said in this connection that even if they 
were employed under Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal JAd. stil] they 
were not entifled to make such a complaint under section 33A, firstly 
hecause Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal 1540. were no parties to the 
original order of reference. Some of the proprietors of Messrs. Khemchand 
Rajkumar might also be the proprietors of Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of 
Bengal Ltd. But this fact does not and cannot necessarily mean that 
Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal Itd. could be deemed to be a party 
also to the original reference. I am mindful of the fact that in the srhedule 
to the original order of reference, there is mention of scales of pay for 
clerks of all the three concerns (vide No. 6 of the schedule). An attempt 
wad naturally made by the learned representative appearing on behalf of 
the petitioners to interprete that Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal J.id. was one 


724 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 [Parr I 


ot the three concerns of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar, and as such it shuld 
he deemed to be a party in the original order of reference. But I am not 
disposed to accept such interpretation. The three concerns as referred ما‎ in 
the order of reference mean, in my opinion, two yards of Messrs. Khemchand 
Rajkumar—one at Paharpore and the other at Salimar and the Head (ffice 
at 38 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1. This will also he evident from the 
complaint of the petitioners themselves, in which mention is also made of 
Paharpore and Salimar. Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal 1۸504. is a 
separate legal entity, and it is a Limited Company. That being so, it 
rannot be regurded as an allied concern of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar. 


Now the main point for consideration is, whether these two petitioners 
were really in the employment of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar. The 
petitioners have no doubt deposed that they were employees of Messrs. 
Khemchand Rajkumar, but their evidence, if carefully considered and 
scrutinised, clearly points to the direction that they never worked under 
Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar. Exhibits A, A(1), B and B(1), which are 
the extracts of wage sheets for certain periods, go to prove beyond doubt 
that these two petitioners were employed by the persons who were entrusted 
with the building construction of Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal 144. 
Both of the petitioners have admittéd their thumb impressions in the said 
wage sheets. This fact is also strengthened by what has transpired from 
the evidence of the petitioners themselves. Both of them were constrained 
to say that they worked as masons for some days, and thereafter they 
worked as Sardars for employing labourers. Furthermore, the petitioner— 
Fouzder Sahu (P.W. 2)—has admitted in his cross-examination that Messrs. 
Khemehand Rajkumar has got 0 factory, in which iron rods and such other 
things are manufactured. In view of this admission by one of \the 
wtitioners there could be no chance or possibility of these two petitioners 
ا‎ employed as masons and Sardars for employing labourers in Mesars. 
Khemehand Rajkumar. Fvidently, there was and could be no scope for 
8001) kind of work in the factory of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar, regard 
being had to what has heen stated above. My conclusion, therefore, is 
that there was no relationship of ‘‘employer and employee’ between the 
petitioners and Messrs. Khemchand pie, etal That being so, the present 
applieation is not maintainable, 


Another fact is worth mentioning. It appears from the materials that 
the main dispute that was referred to this Tribunal, was amicably settled 
between the parties on 29th March 1956. The terms of settlement welt 
embodied in an agreement. A copy of that agreement is to be found in the 
award (Ext. 1) which was ihe in the Calcutta Gazette on April 26, 
1900 and this agreement formed part of the award. In that agreement 
10 1 paragraph 3, it is clearly stated that at the time, all pending disputes 
were amicably settled, and that there were no other disputes of any other 
workmen, and no such issue would be entertained. This agreement was signed 
not only on behalf of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar, but also by Shri Rajani 
Mukherjee, Vice-President of the Union, on behalf of the workmen. That 
agreement has now culminated in an award, (010 the same date, another 
agreement was arrived at also between Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal 
lid. and their workmen represented by Shri Rajani Mukherjee, Vice- 
President of the Union. A copy of this agreement has been produced on 
behalf of the Opposite Party and it is Ext. 2. In this agreement, it is 
specifically mentioned that this agreement settled all the disputes pending 
till date. In the circumstances, it must be held that al] pending disputes 
bteween Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal Ltd. and their employees 
were settled and closed. Assuming for argument’s sake that the petitioners 
were either in the employment of Messrs. Khemchand Rajkumar or in the 


partI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 2725 


empyoyment of Messrs. Steel Rolling Mills of Bengal Ltd. they in view of 
the agreements mentioned above cannot be permitted to reopen the matter 
aun, Fe their discharge by way of retrenchment. Hence, in any view 
of the matter, they afe precluded from maintaining the present application 
ander section 33A of the Act. 


The result 1s that the application be rejected.

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, 7ص‎

Union, F2 Clive Buildings, Calcutta, regarding the matters specified ৪ 
u schedule to this Tribunal for adjudication. The award in respect of that 
proceeding was made by the Tribunal on 28th Muay 0۰ 


On 29th September 1955, Shri Chiva Ranjan Das applied under section 
33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), stating that he 
was a workman under the Opposite Party Company in the capacity of a 
Salesman in the category of 475 Grade Clerk being employed thereto 
with effect from 12th April 1948 and presently enjoying a_ salary of 
Rs. 403-4 per month including dearness allowance. It is stated that he 
was a party to the industrial dispute pending before this Tribunal under 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, Reference No. 8419Dis. / 
J) /11L-268/55, dated 28th July 1956. The petitioner is a permanent 
employee of the Opposite Party. He was elected to the Executive Com- 
mittee of the East Asiatic Co. (India), Ltd. Calcutta Employees’ Union. 
It is further stated that while the original dispute was pending before the 
Tribunal, the applicant was handed over o letter, dated 15th September 
1955, discharging him with effect from 30th September 1955 and declaring 
him a non-workman. The Opposite Party has contravened the provisions 
of section 33, clauses (a) and (b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, by 
categorising him as a non-workman without taking permission of | the 
Tribunal and without following the procedure 1881 down in section 20] of 
the Act. The petitioner, therefore, prays that he should be reinstated \and 
awarded such compensation as will be considered appropriate. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows :— 


The petition is not maintainable, as there has not been any contraven- 
tion of section 33 of the Act. The petitioner is not a workman within the 
meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. The petitioner was employed in 
the Opposite Party Company with effect from 12th April 1948, and that 
his present salary is Rs. 408-4. The petitioner was appointed as a Sales- 
man and was never put in any grade meant for clerical staff. As the 
petitioner was employed on salary basis. he was fitted in a certain pay 
scale. The mode of remunerating the Salesman in the Opposite Party 
Company varied from Salesman to Salesman. The petitioner was 4 
permanent employee of the Company prior to the termination of his service. 
The petitioner was never treated as a clerk. The nature of the work 
performed by the petitioner was neither clerical nor manual so as to render 
him a workman. The work of the petitioner mainly was to approuch the 
various dealers in machinery and push sales of the products in which the 
Company was dealing. The petitioner was engaged as a Machinery Sales- 
man. Since 1953, there has been a very considerable decline in the import 
und sales of machinery due to various reasons, which has 78511010901 the 
scope of business to a great extent and consequently the Company has heen 
incurring heavy losses. As a result of this aa decline of business ond 
in profit, the Opposite Party ona very careful consideration of all the 
circumstances were of the opinion that there was no chance of any improve- 
ment in business and that the petitioner was surplus to the requiremenf. 
The Opposite Party, therefare, terminated the services of the petitioner. 
The termination of service of the petitioner was bona fide and was fully 
justified und the present petition is misconceived. The petition under 
section 994. should be rejected.

In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Calcutta Tanneries

By Government Order No. 6124Dis./1)/11].-109(A)/55, dated 28th 
December 1955, the aforesaid dispute was referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication. The issue framed hy the Government was the same as the 
issue framed by this Tribunal and it was as follows:— 


To what relief Shri Nanda Gopal Chakrabarty is entitled as a result 
of his termination of service by the Company? 


Notice of the aforesaid dispute was served on both parties. The work- 
man filed his written statement on 27th February 1956 and the Compapv 
filed its written statement on 7th March 1956, 


The case for the employee in his written statement is that he had been in 
employ of the company’s factory at Kankinarah, 24-Parganas, from Ist 
September 1952 to loth April 1954 as an Assorter at a salary of Rs. 150 per 
month, that on 12th April 1954 the Director of the Company informed 
Shri Nanda Gopal Chakraharty by a letter stating that his services were no 
longer required from 13th April 1954, that the petitioner submits that the 
action of the Company by terminating his services from the said factory is 
illegal, unfair and amounts to clear unfair labour practice, that in the 
ciicumstances the employee prays for an Award directing the Company to 
pay the petitioner notice pay, leave pay and compensation for retrencliment 
and other reliefs. 

The Company, on the other hand, in its written statement contended 
that due to abnormal trade depression in this industry the Manugement 
decided to close down the factory early in October 1953 and issued a notice 


Parr T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1966 2729 


an 


10 this effect to all staff and workers of the factory on 3lst October 1963 
terminating their services as and when their individual responsibilities are 
finished, that all the workers and staff received their dues as usual, that on 
12th April 1954 it was observed that the works in the applicant’s department 
was completed and = aceordingly he was fjnally notified on the 
date and was offered his dues up to date, but he refused to accept it 
without assigning any reason that the Company agrees to pay to the 
applicant his dues up to 12th April 1954, that the allegations made in the 
applicant’s written statement are false, that the Company acted legally 
accoiding to exigency of circumstances and denies all charges, that in the 
circumstances, the Company submits that the prayer for notice pay, leave 
pay and compensation for retrenchment and other reliefs be rejected. 


AWARD 


It has heen proved by 0.P.W. 1 that due to trade depression the Com- 
pany has been suffering loss to the total extent of 14 lakh and consequently 
the business had to be closed down and the entire staff retrenched. 1 
therefore, in the circumstances hold that the retrenchment was bona fide 
and for good and sufficient reason. AM the workers have already left with 
retrenchment compensation. Qnly this worker did not accept his dues un- 
leas he was paid notice pay, leave pay and compensation. He has, however, 
subsequently settled up his dues with the Company and has granted a full 
discharge receipt on getting Rs.290 on the heads mentioned in Ext. A. 
T hold that Ext. A is true and it gives the Company full discharge and the 
worker cannot reopen the claim over again. I, therefore, hold that there 
wil] be a ‘‘no-dispute’’? Award in this case.

While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application was 
filed by Shri Bedananda Thakur and 40 others on the allegation that the

motive made payment for the month of December 1955 in February 1956 
“but again withheld the payment of wages to the workmen for the moriths 
of January and February 1956 up to date, that hy delaying and withholding 
payment of wages for the aforesaid months the Management altered the

Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the Opposite

the application is not maintainable دہ‎ it has been signed hy 34 workers 
instead of 41 workers inasmuch as the application is not in conformity with

Opposite Party submits that the application is misconcéived and should he 
dismissed with costs. 


The only point for decision t— 


Whether the application in the present’ form is tenable. 


AWARD 


Since only aggrieved را‎ cau apply under section 9384. of the Indus- 
trial Dispubeg Act, the present petition is tenable only with regard to 34 
mwisons who have signed the petition. With regard to others, there is no 
evidence that they have éfther signed or authorised the Secretary to file the 
application or to conduct their cases on their behalf. So with regard to 
others, there is no case. Besides, wages, etc., and their payment on the 
expiry of the month are terms of service rather than conditions of service. 
So, nan-phyment of monthly wages by itself is not a breach in the condition 
of service and as such complaint for stitch non-payment cannot he ad¥anced 
under section 388A of the Industrial Disputes Act and, therefore, the 
application in ‘the present form is not tenable. 


ا٦‎ wag however stated in the application under section 338A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act that the act of the Company amounted to victimisa- 
tion of workers only to sabotage their Union activities but on this point 
there is absolutely no evidence which can be acted on in the Court of Justice. 
P.W. 1, the ২ witness examined for the Union, did not venture to say 
so in hia orpl statement before the Tribunal and that circumstances do not 
support the existence of such a motive behind the non-payment. The 
Company admitted that due to financial stringency they had been irregular 
in payment to their staff and they had, for the same reason, to pay the wages 
for the month of December 1955 in February 1956 and that for January 1956 
in March 1966. Tt is clear from the Award published in the ‘‘Calcutta 
Gazette’, dated 4th June 1958, that the pecuniary condition of the Company 
was not at all sound and this ultimately led to the retrenchment of the staff. 
Besides, the alleged default in the payment of wages is not confined to 
only the Union workers and there is no evidence that the Uhion workers 
were singled out from other members of the staff for meeting out this punish- 
inent. So I hold that Union has failed to prove that the non-payment was 
due to any ulterior motive. That being so, the petitioners have no case on 
merits for mere non-payment without any ulterior motive does not make 
{he non-payment a breach in the condition of service. So, on merits algo 
petitioners have no case.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, filed by Shri Subal Chandra Das and 64 others against 
Messrs. Dhur Tin Factory of 101 Akshoy Kumar Mukherjee Road, 
Calcutta-36, in connection with an industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Dhur Tin Factory and their workmen referred under Government Order 
No. 695Dis., dated 13th February 1954 (case No. 116 of 1954). 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 
PRESENT : 
Suri 8. C. MUKHERJI, Dustrict Judge, Judye, Fourth Industrial 


Tribunal. 
For the Union: Shri Panchanan Bhattacharji. 
For the Company: Shn 1). K. Sanyal, Advocate. 


While the atoresaid dispute wus pending, the present application under 
section 034 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed by Shr; Subal 
Chandra Das and 64 others on the allegation that they are employees of 
Dhur Tin Factory, that they used to be allowed a holiday for the Dasahara 
festival since the last few years, that this year also they enjoyed the same 
holiday on 116) June 1954, that the petitioners on coming to the factory 
on 12th June 1954, found the gates of the factory closed and police-pickets 
posted, that they had been retused ontry since that time, that under the 
circumstances the petitioners pray that their employers may kindly be 
directed to allow them to resume work immediately and pay them wages 
for the period they may remain idle. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the Opposite 
Party, the Company filed its written statement in which it contended that 
the petitioners had no right to be allowed a holiday for the Dasahara 
festival nor they had ever enjoyed such a holiday as a matter of right, that 
whenever a holiday would be granted the Opposite Party would as a 
matter of right decide prior to the date of the holiday whether the same 
would be granted and would issue previous notice of such holidays if 
decided upon by it, that no holiday was declared by the Opposite Party 
for the 11th of June 1954 nor were the workmen entitled to enjoy the said 
date as a holiday, that on 116) day of June 1954 the workmen resorted to 
an illegal and wholly unjustified strike and threatened the Management 
with violence and to cause mischief to the factory and did not work although 
they came to the factory in the morning, that immediately thereupon the 
Opposite Party informed in writing the Officer-in-charge, Baranagore 
police-station, about the illegal strike and the threatening of violence and 
mischief given by the workmen, that on 12th June 1954 the Opposite Party 
handed over to the workmen charge-sheets for their misconduct of the 11th 
June 1954 whereupon they refused to accept the said charge-sheets and also 
to attend to their duties thus resorting to another illegal strike, that the 
Opposite Party never refused entrance to workmen, that the workmen con- 
tinued the illegal strike til] the 16th of June 1954 and thereafter joined 
their duties on and from the 17th day of June 1094) that the Opposite 
Party states that the application is not maintainable in law, that the 
Opposite Parfy states that the workmen having resumed their work on and 
from the 17th June 1954 the praver in this respect is wholly mala fide and 
the petitioners having indulged in illegal strike are not entitled to any 
wages for the period of the said strike, that the Company submits that in 
the circumstances the application is wholly mala fide, harassing and frivo- 
lous and should be dismissed, 


pant 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 2735 


Phe first point: raised by the Union that they have been improperly 
locked out by the Company cannot form the subject-matter of a complaint 
under section ddA, for ea aie is not a change in the cyndition of service. 
Just as a strike is a fundamental right in the hand of a worker to enforce 
his claim against the employer, so lock-out is a fyndamenta] weapon in the 
hand of the employer. So, 1 hold that a complaint under section JSA is not 
enable on the allegation that the workers lave been illegally locked out. 
So the only other point that remains for consideration is whether the 
‘ompany 1s justified in refusing to grant holiday on 118) June 1954. If 
not, what relief can the employees get. 


AWARD 


The certified standing order has been proved by the Company which 
contains direction as regards leave and holidays of the workers and clerks 
and also as to manner of publication of holidays. 1 am satisfied from the 
evidence that the standing order was duly certified after service of notice 
to the parties including Engineering Workers’ Federation, Bengal. In 
fact Engineering Workers’ Federation wrote this letter Ext. 3 acknowledg- 
ing receipt of a copy of the standing order. This certified stunding order 
is, therefore, binding on the parties. 


The Company’s case is that in accordance with the standing order they 
had been publishing a list of the annual holidays in the notice board at the 
beginning of each year (vide Ext, D series) and in 1954 a similar notice 
Ext. C was also published notifying the holidays. 1), W. 1 did not venture 
to say that there were fabricated documents. On the contrary, P. W. 1 
admitted that such notices were published by the Company but he denied 
that any such notice was published in 1954. O.P.W. 1 also proved that after 
publication of the notice, the Company grants holidays according to its 
terms and makes note thereof in the Attendance Register. Exhibit D shows 
that in 1954 the Attendance Register contained the note regarding holidays 
so declared by Ext. C. Actually for 1954 the Company did not grant holiday 
on the Dasahara day but granted holiday on some other day in lieu of it. 
If the employees were aggrieved on account of the fact that no holiday was 
declared on Dasahara day they ought to have moved the Company at once 
after the notice Ext. C waa published in the notice board. They were 
absolutely unjustified in taking the law in their hands and absenting them- 
selves on the llth of June 1954. That the Company has right to settle the 
days on which holidays are to be declared is clear from the fact that all 
that the standing order enjoins is hat the Company will have to publish 
the list of such holidays and it imposes no other reservation of their right. 
P,. W. 1 himself also practically admitted this when it admitted that the 
Company puts up such notices each year. They never said that the workers 
had any hand in the selection of the days or in fixing the number of days 
‘to be observed as holidays. So in consideration of all the circumstances 
T hold that the Company is justified in refusing to give a holiday on the 
Dasahara day afd the workers are not entitled to any relief on that score.

Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes

While the aforesuil dispute was pending, the present application under sec-

charji on the allegation that during the pendency of the said Tribunal the

Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 2737 


was Alegal, unjustified and capricious, that immediately atter his retrench-

{he petitioner prays for reinstatement and full wages for the period of

‘ 

Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the opposite

(fovernment order of reference, dated 2Uth September 1954, that in view of

The only points for decision are—

(2) bit the petitioner is entitled to reinstatement and/or any other

AWARD 


Point 1.—The order of reference referred to in the petition of com- 
plaint was regarding the following issues: 


(1) 1195 the revision of the old scales of pay of typists and steno- 
graphers by the management adversely affected the old entrants? 
What should be their scales of pay? 


(2) What should be the wages of Shri Kedar Nath Ahir? 


The petitioner, who 1s a clerk in the Head Office and is neither a steno- 
erapher nor a typist, 1s obviously a person who is not in any way concerned 
in the above issue. Although the dispute was between Karam Chand 
Thapar & Brothers, Ltd. and their workmen represented by Karam Chand 
Thapar & Brothers Ltd. Employees’ Association, my award in that case will 
not affect this workman in any way. I, therefore, hold that he is not a 
person concerned in the dispute and therefore he has n6 locus stand to 
apply under section J3A of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


Point 2.—Qn merits also it is found and the petitioner admitted that he 
signed and received the letter of appointment, Ext. A. He cannot be 
believed when he later tried to say that it was handed over to him in an 
envelope meaning thereby that he could not look to the contents. But the 
letter, Ext. A, contained his signature with the word ‘accepted’. So he 
cunnot be allowed to back out. Besides O.P.W. ۱, Company’s first assistant, 
proves that his appojintsnent was under Ext, A and was a temporary appéint- 
ment as stated therein. He was appointed to clear up some of arrears in 
respect of posting, some despatch of records and he worked as such. Here 
also he tried to invent a different story that he wus appointed in South 
India Department but he was forced to admit later on that he was appointed 
in Coal Sales Department as stated by O.P.W. 1. So no reliance can be 
placed on the prevaricating statements of O.P.W. 1. 


There is a clear provision in Ext. A that the service should be of a tem- 
porary nature for six months only and it further stipulates that the Com- 
pany has right to terminate his services during this period of six months 
without giving him any notice during the course of this period of six months, 
obviously if the purpose for which he was appointed is finished even before 


2738 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 [Parr ] 
وک سک‎ Se کت ھت ےس سا ھت‎ owe US EE Se 


expiry of ৪1৯ months. This has happened in this case. 0,1৮0, 1 sayé that 
the arrears which he had to make up hud been made good within six months 
and consequently Company was perfectly within its rights to discharge him 


without notice on that ground and the worker has no right,"to seas for 
wages after that (1953 K.L.J, page 62). 


Hence on merits also the petitioner has no case and he is not entitled to 
any relief.

90185011617 PRICE INDEX NUMBERS FOR WORKING CLASSES 
FOR’.THE DISTRICTS OF MIDNAPORE-BANKURA, NADIA- 
MURSHIDABAD, MALDA-WEST DINAJPUR, AND BIRBHUM. 


In connection with implementation of the Mintmum Wages Act, 
necessity has been felt for the preparation ,of Consumer Price Index 
Numbers for Working Classes for the different districts of West Bengal, 
hacause minimum wages enforced in the industries like Rice Mills, Oil 
Mills, Public Motor Transport, Buildings and Road Construction, etc., 
are in most cases linked with Consumer Price Index Numbers. The 
economy of Calcutta, and those of the districts are quite dissimilar and 
the দা পাশ Price Index Number prepared for Calcutta is not strictly 
‘applicable to the outlying districts. Separate series of auch Index Numbers 
have, therefore, been found to be necessary. 


In pursuance to the above principle, the following series of Consumer 
Price Index Numbers have been prepared :— 


(1) Maidnapore-Bankura,~ (2) Nudin-Murshidabad, (3) Malda-West 
Dinajpur and (4) Birbhum. ৪ 


The districts of Midnapur and Bankura, Nadia and Murshidubad and 
Malda and West Dinajpur have been taken together for preparing 
Consumer Price Index Numbers because of their geographical contiguity 
and economic homogeniety. The different Advisory Committees formed 1n 
connection with fixation of minimum wages in different industries have 
8150 recommended same rates for these pairs of districts. 


Base.—The period from January to December 1951 has been taken to 
be the base for these indices, because during that year a family budget 
survey was conducted in the above districts amongst the workers covered 
by the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. 


The annual average retail prices have been taken to be the basic quota- 
tions for the purpose of the indices. The annual averages have been 
001১1) in order to eliminate the effect of seasonal fluctuation in retail prices. 


The following centres have been selected as outlets for different series 
of Index Numbers: — 


Series of Index Numbors. Outlet. 
1. Midnapore-Bankura ve .» (1) Midnapore town. 
(2) Jhargram. 
(3) Bankura town. 
(4) Bishnupur 
2, Nadia-Murshidahad »» (1) Krishnanagar. 
(2) Berhampore. 
3. Malda-Wost Dinajpur_.. .» (1) Malda town (English Bazar). 
(2) Balurghat. 
4. Birbhum - 7 ...ےم‎ (1) Bolpur. 
(2) Saimthia. 
(3) Dubrajpur. 


N.B.—Kharagpur has not been selected, because the Working Classes 
in Kharagpur are most employed at Railway Workshops at Kharagpur and 
their composition and economic conditions differ materially from rest cf 
the Working Class families belonging to other parts of the two districts. 
Moreover, the Labour Bureau, Government of India, is preparing a 
separate Index series for Kharagpur. 


2740 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 [Pant I 


Price-collecting agents have been appointed in each of the?‘ above 
markets, and they collect retail prices once every week in the prescribed 
price schedules which indicate the commodity with their grades, varieties 
and units from two representative shops in each of the above markets, 
under the supervision of a Gazetted Officer. The price quotations reported 
by the agents are carefully scrutinised at the Head Office betore using 
them for tabulation and construction of the Index Numbers. 


Coverage (items covered and their weights).—Attempt has been made 
to include in the Index Numbers as many as possible of those representa- 
tive items on which consumption expenditure has been reported 1 the 
standard budgets and which tend to show characteristic price behaviours 
The items selected on this principle, for the different series of Index 
Numbers have been classified into five main groups, viz.,-(I) food, (TI) 
fuel and lighting, (III) clothing and footwear, (IV) house rent and (V). 
miscellaneous. 

The items included in the above main groups have been shown in 
Appendix II together with the weights worked out from the standard 
budgets as revealed in the family budget surveys held in 1951, with 
certain adjustments described below. 

In Appendix I may be found summaries of the items included in main 
classes together with percentages of expenditure of items 11008810901 to total 
expenditures on the group and also to total expenditures in the budget. 

It has not been possible to include in the Index seried' al® the items 
entering into the standard budgets, because either the base year prices ure 
not available, or the items are not priceable. Total weight thus lost hus 
been adjusted by adding the weights of the excluded items to those priced 
which have more or less a similar price movement as those of the excluded 
items. This procedure has been recommended by the Internatipnal 
Conference of Labour Statisticians in 1947 and has been adopted in prepura- 
tions of these indices. 

Certain items like, tomato, fowl, pork, etc., which do not appear to he 
common items of expenditure have been dropped and also in the case of 
items like ‘‘Other pulses’, ‘‘Other vegetables’, ‘Other fuel and other 
lighting’, which are not priceable, their weights have been distributed 
amongst the individual items of the same group in proportion to the 
weights of these items. 

n the clothing group, in view of the large number of grades, varieties 
and sizes of stitched garments used by the working class people, materials 
used for making these garments have been accepted for compilation of 
Index Numbers as price-fluctuation of ready-made garments are highly 
co-related with the materials from which they are made. Thus, shirting 
is taken to represent shirts, coating to represent coats, drill for trousers, 
longcloth for pyjamas, blouses and frocks have been retained as such 2৪ 
the base year price of printed cloth are not available. 


Averaging.—Simple price-relutives of each of the varieties of each of 
the constituent items are worked out in the first instance and 
then simple averages of these price-relatives ore calculated ا٥‎ 
obtain the average price fluctuation of the items over the base period. 
They were then multiplied by their respective weights and summuated. 
Group indexes were thus found out. These group indexes have been 
allotted their respective group weights as found in the Family Budzet 
Enquiry and the weighted average of the group indexes constitute the 
Consumer Price Indexes for the particular area. The figures have heen 
calculated for each of the months from January 1952 to March 1956 whiclt 
۲۰۹ mentioned in Appendix ITI. 

S. N. CHATTERJEE, 
Dy. Labour Commissioner

DECISION 


1 These two appéals are preferred ogainst one and the same award of 
the First Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, dated 13th March 1958, and 
published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 9thwApril 1953, under the order 
of the Government of West Bengal No 1084Dis./D/11L-56/58, dated Ist 
April 1958, one by the Management of Titaghur Paper Mills Co., Ltd. (No. 1 
Mill), and the other by thei: workmen represented by the Paper Mills 


286 


THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 


[Tarr TA 


صسوعپچپستتتحبتبتیت س1چ سس ےت سشجشبم‌ٴ‌۹_ةہب ۸4‏ ّْٔ۔ع۔رژٹ ‏ جب ژ ژچژںسسسپسبہہبسسووس۰اتسہےس۔بییپیسییےچجبڑبھھممٹڑسکس٢وٌسکصسھوووھسجت--ب-×وہ Fe‏

Employees’ Union, Titaghur. This the appellants in each appeal are the 
respondents in the other, Therefoxg, it will be convenient to deal with the 
two appeals together. 


2. The industrial dispute referred for adjudication to the Lower 
Tribunal was about the questions (a) whether the dismissal of 11 of the 
workmen of the Company by an order of the Manager, dated 23rd September 
1950, was justified and (b) whether the said 11 workmen were entitled to 
reinstatement and/or compensation. 


3. The undisputed facts are as follows:— 


In 1947, 1948 and 1949 the Company paid one month’s basic wage to 
each of the workers as advance before Durga 1৮110 recoverable in easy 
monthly instalments. By an award published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
dated lst December 1949, the workmen became entitled to production 
bonus. On 12th September 1950, the Company gave notice that the said 
production bonus would be paid to the workmen before Durga Puja but 
not the advance as was paid in previous years. The workmen got 
dissatisfied. 


4, On 19th September 1950, the incidents which led to the dismissal of 
11 workmen took place. The management’s version of the incidents 8 
as follows :— 


In the morning a large crowd of workmen gathered in front of the 
Manager’s office and clamoured that the Manager should have a talk 
with them. The Manuger expressed willingness to talk to a small 
delegation but not to the large crowd. The crowd gradually dispersed. 
The Manager and the Cost Accountant were proceeding from the office 
towards their houses, at about 1 p.m., to take lunch. While Hey were 
passing through the machine house, a large crowd of workmen led by 
the 11 dismissed workmen suddenly surrounded them and informed 
them that they would not be allowed to leave the place till their 
demands were conceded and barred their way so that the officers had to 
remain on the spot surrounded by the workmen till police, who were 
sent for, arrived by about 4-30 p.m., after which they were able to 
sroceed to their houses. On 20th September 1958 charge-sheets under 

tanding Orders ات‎ and 19(b)(5) were issued calling for explana- 
tion and enquiry was held on 23rd September 1950 after due notice and 
the orders of dismissal were passed on the same day, by the Manager. 


5. The police prosecuted the 11 workmen for offences under sections 
149 and 342 of the Indian Penal Code on the basis of the incident, dated 
19th September 1950, between 1 and 4-30 p.m., but the workmen were 
discharged by the Magistrate. 


6. The version of the workmen is that they in a batch merely 
approached the Manager in connection with payment of Puja advance which 
was delayed and that the Manager refused to talk to them and that after 
8 hours or so the police were sent for and false prosecution was launched 
and that after the men were discharged by the Magistrate, the Company 
refused to take them back into service and that this is a case of victimisation 
and unfair labour practice. 


7. Qn the materials placed before it, the Lower Tribunal came to the 
conclusion (i) that the version of the management was substantially correct 
as to the incident between 1 and 4-30 on 19th September 1950, (11) that 
the 11 dismissed men took active part in the incident and thus committed 
the offences of insubordination and disobedience under Standing Orders 
19(b)(5) and 19(b)(3), (151) that the requirements of natural justice were 
ام‎ complied with in the proceedings held by the Management culminating 
in the dismissal order and (iv) that there was no victimisation or unfair 
labour practice in taking disciplinary action against the men. The lower 
Tribunal next turned 1ta mind to the question of punishment and came 
to the conclusion that, in view of the fact that the men were misguided and 
did not use violence and that the Manager passed the order of dismissal 
in violation of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, during the 
pendency of conciliation proceedings, these 11 men should be discharged 
under Standing Order 18 on payment of 7 days’ wages in lieu of notice 
and on payment &1 gratuity at 15 days’ basic pay for each completed year 
of service subject ٠ a minimum of 3 months’ basic pay, within one month 
after the date on which the award came into operation. The workmen in 
their appeal challenged the ndings on the ments and the award approving 
disciplinary action and glaimed reinstatement. The Company in their 
appeal challenged the #®ard by which the lower ‘Tribunal substituted 
discharge accompanied by payment of a weck's wages in lieu of notice and 
gratuity, under Standing Order 18, for dismissal. * 


First turning our attention to the appeal hy the workmen it is 
conceded that it will not be maintainable unless if involves some substantial 
question of law within thesaneaning of section 7(1)(a) of the Industrial 
Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The learned Counsel for the 
workmen formulated the following four points as the substantial questions 
of law involved, vaz., (i) on the same set of facts (1,088. workmen were 


کو ے 


Part TA] 


THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 


287 


১১ 


prosecuted before a competenf criminal court and were discharged. 
Therefore, the Industrial Triburjal should not come to a different conclusion 
and should not substitute its different decision. (ii) The facts alleged by 
the Company and found to be true by the lower Tribunal, amount to a 
strike though short-lived. between 1 p.m. to 4-30 p.m. Therefore, Standing 
Orders have no application to those workmen who took part in the strike and 
hence they cannot be punished under Standing Orders 19(b)(3) and 
19(b)(6). (৫10) Acgording to the Company’s case the Manager was perso- 
nally involved in the incident and therefore he was a direct witness. He 
subsequently played the role of prosecutor and judge in framing charges, 
holding enquiry and deciding the case against the workmen and inflicting 
the punishment of dismissal. This combination of witness, prosecutor and 
judge in one person is opposed to law. (iv) The lower, Tribunal found the 
workmen guilty of the offence of ‘‘insubordination and disobedience of 
lawful and reasonable order of the superior’, but the charge framed by the 
Manager in the charge-sheet on the basis of which he dismissed these 
workmen does not contain the charge of the offence as found by the lower 
Tribunal. Thus thé lower Tribunal upheld disciplinary action taken by 
the Manager against the workmen on a charge which was not levelled 
against them by the Manager and against which they had no opportunity 
to defend themselves. 


9. In our opinion, point No. (i) raises no substantial question of ۰ 
To start with, the learned Counsel for the workmen conceded that he could 
not contend that the decision of the criminal court operated as res judicata. 
If so, nothing stands in the way of the Industrial Tribunal’s examining the 
evidence and facts and arriving at its own conclusion. This proposition 
receives support from the decision reported in 1952 II L.L., p. 36 
(Indian Copper Corporation Ltd. vs. Tripati). On such examination the 
Tribunal may come to the same conclusion as that arrived at by the 
criminal court or to a different conclusion. The point as formulated reads 
as if a substantial question of law will be involved only if the Industrial 
Tribunal comes to a conclusion different from the one arrived at by the 
criminal court. If there should be any bar, it should be against a second 
examination of the facts and evidence and not against arriving at a conclu- 
sion, one way. If it is a matter of mere advisability or otherwise of the 
Industrial Tribunal coming to a conclusion different from the conclusion 
arrived at by the criminal court, no question of law at all will be involved. 
There is no question of the Industrial Tribunal substituting its decision for 
the decision of the criminal court. Whatever the conclusion of the 
Industrial Tribunal may be the order of discharge passed by the 
Magistrate stands good. The fields of operation of the two Tribunals are 
different. The criminal court’s function is to punish people for acts which 
amount to offences against society, though a private individual might be the 
immediate victim. The function of the Industrial Tribunal in this case is 
only to uphold or set aside the disciplinary action taken by the management 
of a private concern against its own workmen who are alleged to have 
misconducted themselves in their behaviour towards a superior officer. 
Such conduct of the workmen may not amount to an offence under the 
Indian Penal Code but may be misconduct sufficient to deserve disciplinary 
action. Hence if the Industrial Tribunal upholds the disciplinary action 
taken by the Manager, it is, in no sense, a substitution for the decision of 
the criminal court. The two can exist independently of each other. 


10. According to the learned Counsel for the workmen, point No. ا‎ 
is of great general importance affecting all workmen in the industrial field. 
It may be so, but in our opinion that is not a test to determine whether the 
point raised is a substantial question of law. A substantial question of law 
will remain to be such even 11 a decision on it is going to affect one or two 
individuals. A point which does not raise a question of law or raises a 
question of law which is not substantial otherwise, cannot become a sub- 
stantial question of law for the reason that a decision thereon will affect a 
large number of people. 


11. Without deciding, we shall assume, for purposes of this point, 
that there was a strike by the workmen from 1 p.m. to 4-30 p.m. on 19th 
September 1950. The question is whether the Standing Orders cease to 
have operation, in the sense that none of the workmen who took part in the 
strike can be dealt with undér the Standing @rders for any misconduct 
defined and made punishable by the Standing Orders. The learned Counsel 
for the workmen ۹1۹4 not draw our attention to any provision of law or prece- 
dent on the strength of which Standing Orders ‘cease to have operation by 
virtue of a strike. Tet us see if there is any principle which can support 
the contention. Standing Orders are framed by the management in 
exercise of statutory powers under the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1946, and are submitted to the certifying authority constituted 
under the styye Act. That authority, after giving notice to the workmen 
and after heating them and the management, arrives at a decision whether 
or nol, the Standing Orders submitted to if comply with the provisions of 
the Act and the model Standing Orders as far as possible. He certifies the 
Standing Orders only if and when they satisfy the requirements of the Act, 
if necessary by suitable alterations. An appeal lies against such decision. 
Once ghey are certified the Standing Orders come into operation within the 


THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 12, 1956 


time prescribed by section 7 of the Act and become the terms of employment 
and contract of service between the management and the workmen. If the 
workmen are dissatisfied with the Standing Orders or any of them on the 
ground that they are unfair or unjust, an Industrial Dispute arises under 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Then the Standing Orders may be 
subjected to alteration or addition or modification as may be adjudicated 
upon by an Industrial Tribunal. Terms of employment and conditions of 
service are normally matters of bilateral contract. The Industrial Employ- 
ment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, has evolved an alternative statutory 
method of bringing into existence terms of employment and conditions of 
service in establishments of a certain size. Though Standing Orders are not 
the result of a bilateral contract, the characteristics of a bilateral] contract 
are not altogether absent, because the management are the authors thereof 
and the workmen have a say in the matter and can take steps before duly 
constituted authorities to alter them. Such being the case there can be no 
principle known to law underlying the proposition advanced before us that 
Standing Orders cease to be applicable to workmen who go on atrike by a 
unilateral decision. 


12. The whole basis for the contention raised on behalf of the work- 
men is that a strike is now recognised as lawful though it is a deliberate 
breach of contract of service and that therefore the terms of that contract 
in the shape of Standing Orders can no more be of any application to the 
strikers. A strike is recognised as lawful only to the extent of the cessation 
of work or refusal to continue to work though in breach of contract of 
service. Therefore, it is easy to understand a proposition that the cessa- 
tion of work or refusal ما‎ work cannot be punished os amounting to disobe- 
dience and if there is a Standing Order which makes cessation of work or 
refusal to work punishable, it will remain in suspension or abeyance during 
the strike. But to say. that Standing Orders as a whole cease to have 
operation on the commencement of a strike is not understandable. 


In our case there is a Standing Order providing for punishment for theft 
or damage to machinery. The argument, if accepted, will result in the 
proposition that if the strikers steal goods or damage machinery re a 
siete: no action under the Standing Orders can be taken. The absurdity 
of such a position 1s self-evident. There is nothing in law which deprives 
the statutory Standing Orders of all operations during a strike by the 
workmen. The Standing Orders remain in full operation irrespective of a 
strike but for the fact that the mere cessation of work or refusal to work 
cannot he dealt with as misconduct under the Standing Orders. If thereby 
acts of insubordination or disobedience of lawful orders otherwise than by 
mere cessation of work, the same can be dealt with under the Standing 
Orders, causing disturbance is no part of a strike. It is outside the lawful 
scope of a strike, though in practice disturbance accompany strikes. If 
disturbance was caused by the strikers on the mill premises, they can be 
dealt with under the Standing Orders. Whether there has been such 
causing disturbance or insubordination or disobedience, is a question of fact. 
We are of opinion that there is no substantial question of law involved in 
this appeal in consequence of the workmen having been dealt with under the 
Standing Orders for acts alleged to have been perpetrated during the 
incident in question, even if it amounts to a strike. 


13. Next coming to point (211) we have first to seé that Standing 
Order 19 provides that the Manager is the only authority who can dismiss 
an operative. Therefore, the Manager could not delegate the duty to some 
one else. As the Manager himself is alleged to be the vietim of the acts 
of the workmen, if the Manager deputed a subordinate to hold the enquiry, 
it is likely to be attached as hypocrisy on the ground that a subordinate 
cannot be expected to give a finding against the evidence of the Manager. 
It is inconceivable for the Manager to appoint an outsider for holding a 
disciplinary enquiry. Therefore, in this case, the Manager examined 
witnesses to the occurrence and tested the evidence with his own ‘personal 
knowledge. That was the best that could be done under the circumstances. 


14. Supposing for a moment that the fact that the Manager who was 
himself witness to the incident held the enquiry, makes the enquiry and 
findings and punishment unlawful, the consequence should not be to set 
aside the punishment infliged by the Manager, simply for that reason. As 
the matter has come up before an independent Tribunal, the correct course 
is for the Tribunal to satisfy itself on the materials placed before it by 
both sides, whether the punishment should be allowed to stand or not, on 
merits. In other words the Tribunal should do what it is expected to do, 
if there was no enquiry at all or jf the enquiry did not satisfy the require- 
ments of natural justice. This case cannot be worse than o case in which 
no charges are framed and no enquiry is held but punishment is awarded. 
In this case, though the lower Tribunal found as a matter of fact, that the 
enquiry satisfied the requirements of a natura] justice, “it thoroughly 
examined the facts and merits as disclosed in the voluminots evidence adduc- 
ed by both sides including the oral evidence of the Manager and then arrived 
at ita own conclusion. Hence no substantial question of law arises in this 
appeal, from the fact that the Manager who was a witness to the incident, 
held the enquiry.

15. Next coming to point (ii) iff is true that the clause ‘‘insubordination 
and disobedience of lawful and resonable order of the superior’ is not 
found in the charge-sheets. The ‘uctual wording of the charge-sheets is 
“‘whereas on 19th September 1950, you along with others wrongfully 
restrained and confined the undersigned against their will thus 
causing disturbance in the® Mill, you are required to show cause by 
2180 September 1950, why disciplinary action should not be taken against 
you under 19(b)(8) and ای‎ of Standing Orders’’. Henge we have to 
see whether, on the facts of this case, the lower Tribunal allowed the 
management to justify a punishment inflicted on the basis of one charge by 
proving a different charge to meet which the workmen had no opportunity. 
There could be absolutely no difficulty for the workmen who were charged 
to understand that the charges related to the incidents on 19th September 
1950 as the date was mentioned in the charge-sheets. According to the 
case of the workmen also, the Manager, on 19th September 1950 remained 
amidst the workmen for about 3 hours, till the police arrived, though he 
refused to talk to them on their demands. Therefore, when they were 
charged with having regtrained and confined the Manager against his will 
and were called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be 
taken under Standing Orders 19(b)(5) which describes the misconduct of 
wilful insubordination and disobedience, the only reasonable way of under- 
standing the charge is that the workmen were being charged with insubor- 
dination and disobedience by having wrongfully restrained and confined the 
Manager against his will. Whether wrongful confinement and restraint 
can amount to insubordination and disobedience or not is a different matter 
and it depends on the facts. If the Manager was wrongfully restrained or 
confined with a view to make him concede the demands of the workmen 
relating to the 1476 advance or production bonus or both, it should be the 
height of insubordination. All that is inconsistent with or opposed to 
subordination must be insubordination. Demands can be made by work- 
men on the Manager consistently with their subordinate position. If 
demands are made on the Manager coupled with the threat that he shall 
not be allowed to leave the place where the demands are made till he conceded 
them, it is just a reversal of their respective positions, the workmen 
assuming to themselves a position of authority mail reducing the Manager 
to the position of obedience on pain of being subjected to physical incon- 
venience, and amounts to an act of gross insubordination. Whether such 
facts are proved or not is quite a different matter. At this stage we are 
merely trying to making it clear that, on the facts of this case, it is impos- 
sible to conclude that the lower Tribunal] allowed the management to justify 
the punishment on the footing of a charge which was not levelled against 
the workmen and to defend against which they had no opportunity. 


16. We hold that the appeal of the workmen does not involve any 
substantial question of law and hence that it is not maintainable. 


17. Out of the eleven dismissed workmen one Ramesh Gupta alias 
Rameshwar Gupta did not wish to press his appeal before this Tribunal as 
he was satisfied with the award which gave him compensation and he stated 
that he did not want reinstatement. At the same time the management 
stated that they would not press their appeal in respect of compensation so 
far as the said workman was concerned. These statements were recorded 


by this Tribunal in an order, dated 10th June 1904. 


18. At the time of the hearing of these appeals the learned Counsel 
for the Mills produced a letter received by Messrs. Orr, Dignam & Co., 
Solicitors, 29 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta, purporting to have been 
signed by an Advocate called Shri Biswanath Ash, stating that on behalf 
of the workman Sarubani Chatterjee, he moved this Tribunal on 4th 
April 1965 for permission to withdraw the Appeal No. Cal.-40 of 1953 and 
that orders were passed striking out the name of the said workman from 
the appeal. No such application ang order are traced in the records. The 
Counsel for the workmen denied that the said workman withdrew his appeal. 
Hence his appeal was heard on the supposition that it was not withdrawn. 
In the result Appeal No. Cal.-40 of 1953 preferred by the workmen is 
dismissed. No costs. 


19. Next we come to the appeal preferred by the management of the 
Mills. The Company inflicted the punishment of dismissal for misconduct 
falling under Standing Orders 19(b)(3) and 19(b)(5) which 1s authorised by 
Standing Order 19(b). The lower Tribunal found that miscond under 
Standing Order বাতি! and 19(b)(5) was proved and that the Company 
was entitled to take disciplinary action, but that the punishment should be 
revised because, (1) the workmen used no violence, (2) the workmen were 
misguided and (3) the Company contravened the provisions of section 33 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as conciliation proceedings between the 
parties were pending on 29107. September 1950, and that the order of 
dismissal should not stand and then passed the award under appeal directing 
that the workmen shoyld be discharged under section 18 of the Standing 
Orders and that they sBould be paid 7 days’ wages in lieu of notice. Next 
the lower Tribunal procecded to grant the workmen gratuity at the rate of 
17 days’ basic pay for each completed year of service subject to a minimum 
of 3 months’ basic pay. The contention of the Company is that Standing 


290 


THE CAIXUTTA GAZETTH, JULY 12, 1956 


Order 18 does not at all apply to this cas}: where misconduct is accepted by 
the lower Tribunal as proved justifying(disciplinary action and that the 
workmen are not entitled to notice or wages in lieu of notice or gratuity. 
In so far as the contention relates to the applicability of Standing Order 
18, 1 involves a substantia] question of law within the meaning of section 
7(1)(a) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 10950, viz., 
interpretation of the Standing Orders us was held by this Tribunal] in the 
decision reported in 1953, 1] L.L.d., page 822 (Cawnpore Textiles, Ltd.). 
The award of a week’s wages in lieu of notice is based on Standing Order 
18 only. So far as gratuity is concernd it is not based on any Standing 
Order 18 only. So far as gratuity is concerned it is not based on any 
Order. Hence it can only be gratuity on discharge in which case it falls 
under section 7(1)(b)(v) of the said Act. Hence this appeal is main- 
tainable, in so far as it 1s against the award of gratuity. 


20. The word ‘‘discharge’’ used by the lower Tribunal is not used in 
Standing Order 18 at all. The words “dispense with’? are used in it and 
the title is ‘‘termination of employment’”’. Hence the lower Tribunal must 
be taken to have used the word ‘‘discharge’’ to convey the meaning of 
nothing more and nothing less than termination of employment عم‎ a 
measure of punishment. Dismissal also is nothing more and nothing less 
than termination of employment as a measure of punishment. Thus 
termination of the employment of the workmen as a measure of punishment 
hus been approved by the Jower Tribunal. Standing Order 19 is specially 
provided for terminating employment as a punishment for severul items of 
misconduct of workmen enumerated therein. Standing Order 18 provides 
for termination of employment by either party and unrelated to the conduct 
of the opposite side. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the idea 
underlying the framing of two separate Standing Orders, viz., 18 and 19, 
one for punishment and the other for mere termination unrelated to the 
conduct of the workmen must be that Standing Order 19 should be exclu- 
sively resorted to when punishing workmen and that Standing Order 18 
should be resorted to if the employment of workmen is to be terminated 
otherwise than as a measure of punishment. 


21. Standing Order 18 provides for a week’s notice or wages in lieu 
of notice whereas Standing Order 19 does not provide for notice or wages 
in lieu of notice. This is the obvious reason why the lower Tribunal 
substituted Standing Order 18 for Standing Order 19. We can understand 
the justice in giving notice or wages in heu of notice in the case of ter- 
mination of employment otherwise than by way of punishment because 
neither party should be taken by surprise and a party must be compen- 
sated if tuken by surprise and thus inconvenienced. But in the case of 
termination by way of punishment which is brought on the workmen by 
their own misconduct; there can be no principle of law or equity which should 
require notice of termination or wages in lieu of notice. That is why 
Standing Order 19 does not provide for notice or wages in lieu of notice. 
We are clearly of opinion that Standing Order 18 does not apply at all to 
termination of employment of workmen as a measure of punishment for any 
of the items of misconduct described in Standing Order 19(b). 


22. The award of gratuity is not supported by Standing Order 18 or 
any other Standing Order. If the award is of gratuity in the strict sense 
of the expression, viz., a variety of retiral benefit, the lower Tribunal had 
no jurisdiction to award it because there was no reference by the Govern- 
ment of any Industrial Dispute’ about gratuity between the parties nor is it 
an ijncrdental matter. If what the lower ‘Tribunal awarded is mere 
compensation for loss of employment, there can be no justification for 
granting compensation to workmen who are guilty of misconduct and who 
deserved termination of employment as a punishment as was held in the 
decision of this Tribunal reported in 1952 II L.L.J., page 648 (Punjab 
National Bank, Ltd., vs. Their workmen). Compensation for loss of 
einployment can be awarded only if teymination of employment by the 
Company is found to be unjust though reinstatement is found unsuitable 
and not in a case like ours where termination of employment is upheld but 
only under a name (discharge) different from the name used by the 
Company, viz., dismisyal. — 


23. The lower Pribunal wag free to choose a lower form of punishment 
to be inflicted on the workmen than that inflicted by the Company if it 
was so minded and if there be any extenuating circumstances. But to 
direct thag’ompany to pay compensation to the workmen for loss of employ- 
men isgfar from choosing a lesser form of punishment. It is in effect, 
ات‎ the Company for terminating the employment of the workmen, 

hile fading oie the workmen ےت‎ the termination. Even the lower 
form of punishment must make the guilty persons alone suffer or lose and 
must not make an innocent party to the proceedings share the suffering 
or loss caused to the guilty persons in consequence of the punishment, 
গা a Magistrate sentenced af accused person to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000 
and then asked the complginint to pay Rs. 500 out of it to the accused 
to meee the burden of the aecused bearable, it will not differ from the case 
on hand. 


4. Phe Tribunal below relied on 3 circumstances for its award, viz., 
(1) that the workmen did net use violence. (2) that they were misguided,

25. We are in agreement with the finding of the lower Tribunal that 
conciliation proceedings were pending between the parties on 2910 
September 1950) and that the Manager contravened the provisions of section 
43 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, in ordering dismissal of the workmen 
on 28rd September 1950 without the permission of the conciliation officer. But 
we fail to see how this contravention of section 33 by the Manager on 23rd 
September 1950 could be an extenuating circumstance or could have the 
effect of minimising the gravity of the misconduct of the workmen which 
took place on 19th September 1950. The two are absolutely independent 
of each other and wil] have independent consequences. Thus we find that 
none of the circumstances mentioned by the lower Tribunal is an extenuating 
circumstance which can minimise the gravity of the misconduct, 


26. Hence we hold that the award of gratuity to the workmen ordered 
by the lower Tribunal cannot be supported in any view. We are of opinion 
that nothing Jess than outright dismissal will satisfy the requirements of 
this case. But as the Manager should not have passed the orders of dis- 
missal on 25rd September 1959) the orders should be given effect to only from 
a date on which the orders could have been passed without contravening 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes’ Act, 1947, 


27. Appeal No. Cal.-37 of 1953 preferred by the Company is allowed 
except 58 against Ramesh Gupta alias Rameshwar Gupta. We set aside the 
order of discharge on payment of one week’s wages in lieu of notice and 
gratuity passed by the lower Tribunal on the other 10 workmen, and in its 
place we order that the punishment of dismissal inflicted by the Manager 
shall stand but that it shall take effect from the date on which conciliation 
proceedings found by the lower Tribunal to be pending on 23rd September 
1950 must be deemed to have concluded under section 20 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947. No costs.

PART IIl—Advertisements, Notices 


Procedure regarding sending Manuscripts for publication of Advertisements, Notices, oetc., in the 
“Calcutta Cazette’’ (Part 01), 


1, Manusoripts should be properly edited and complete in iteelf. 


2. Manuscripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. The name of the signatory should be type- 
written below the signature. 


3. Manuscripts Intended for advertisement In the next Issue of ‘Calcutta Gazette’’ shall be received by Publiloation 
sales Office at New Seoretariat Buildings, 1 Hastings Street, Caloutta, up to 11 a.m. on Saturday and at Wead Office 


‘at Alipore up to 12 noon on Monday. 
4. All costs shall be paid in advance and deposited along with the Manuscripts. 


§. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressed to SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING 
(PUBLICATION BRANCH), WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE. 


The Press shall not be held responsible for delay In publication of any advertisement due to the non-observance of the 
instructions detalied above. ;

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 
Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 28th June 1956. 


Summary.—During the weck under report thore was rainfall in thirty-five subdivisions. The weather conditions were unfavour- 
able in twelve subdivisions. Transplantation of Aman and Aus continuing in some subdivisions. The condition of the standing crop 
was on the whole fair. 


The fodder was reported to be insufficient in eighteon subdivisions and cettle-diseaso was reported from six subdivisions. 
The wages of the labourer varied from rupee one to rupees two and annas eight during the week under report.

much more than the notified wages, I do not consider that the claim for 
increase of wage is justified and this issue is accordingly answered.

The plea of the Union that permanent workers were laid off and casual 
workers recruited to continue the work of production and by this method 
the Company endeavours to drive out the old workers and replace them 
by new hands has not heen justified in evidence. Tt appeara that no case 
of lay-off of a permanent worker has been proved in evidence. At the 
time of the argument, the learned spokesman for the Union named some 
casual workers whose services had been terminated after some time. There 
ean be uo doubt that casual workers and temporary workers have to face 
termination of their jobs after the completion of the job or after the 
expiry of the period for which they were emnlovyed. This is not a case of 
lay-off or involuntary unemployment of a permanent worker requiring pay: 
ment of compensation under the Act. The plea that the Company 
haphazardly laid off workers to drive ont the old workers and replace them 
by new hands is unworthy of support. There is no substance In this 
contention. 


The Union praved for suitable free quarters. It was urged that 
Mesars. Bhagat Oil Mills in Caleutta were granting the benefit of free 
quarters to their workmen. It is in evidence that Messrs. Bhagat 01) 
Mills is the biggest unit in the industry and emplovs more than four times

house rent is made in caloulating the cost of living on which the minimum 


Part I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 06 1641 


wages u8 mentioned above were fixed by the Minimum Wages Advisory 
Committee. Normally, it is not the function of the Management to 
provide accommodation tor its employees, although the principle is subject 
to qualification in certain cases where the Company sets up an establish- 
meut in ৮ rural area (wde the case of penis. Cement Companies, 1953 
L.A.C., 677 at page 683). In the Jute Textile Mills in West Bengal or in 
the Textile Mills in Bombay, no separate house rent is paid and house rent 
is ordinarily considered to be an item which must be borne by the employees. 
The claim for free quarters or for house rent in lieu thereof is not worthy 
of support and is rejected, ; 


The Union claims for special allowance for the night shift workers 
on the ground that the workers working in night shift are to pay more 
energy and attention in order to accomplish their job. In the present 
case, the Company works the factory in three shifts of 8 hours each, and 
all the workers have to work in night shifts by rotation. In these cir- 
cumstances, the claim for additional allowance for the workers who work 
in the night shift is not justified. It has been decided in the case of Fire- 
stone Tyre & Rubber Co, of India Ltd,, reported in 1953 L.A.C., 509, at 
7986 211) that it is a common feature in all industries where there are 
three shifts that some of the workmen should have to work at night and 
in such cases the wage structure assumes that the workmen should be 
required to do night shifts in turn. The learned Tribunal decided that 
when 1 19 not suggested that any of the workmen is not permanent 
night shift worker, no special allowance should be given for work in the 
night shift. This decision was given following the decision of the same 
(0011 in the case of the Fertiliser and Chemicals Travancore Ltd., 
Alwave ]1951)11( 15150. ا‎ These decisions have been approved by 
“3 Full Bench of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribun@l of India in 

essrs. Asbestos Cement Ltd., reported in 1954 L.A.C., 1 at 4. It 18, 
therefore, clear that the claim for special allowance for the night shift 
workers 18 incompetent. This claim 1s, therefore, rejected.

do রি consider that any award on this question should be made by this 
Tribunal. 


1 do not consider that an additional retiring benefit in the form of a 
gratuity scheme should be introduced over and above the Provident Fund, 
which is going to be introduced by the Government soon. The claim 19 
uaworthy of support and is rejected.

While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application under 
section-33A ‘of the Industrial Disputes Act was filed by Shri Jhagru 
Jeswara stating that he was a permanent employee of Messrs. Dhur Tin 
Factory, that he had been dismissed on 4th May 1954, that there was no

petitioner prays that an award may be passed directing the employers 00 
reinstate him with full compensation for the period of idleness. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the ) 608 
Party, the Company filed its written statement in which it contended that 
the worker Jhagru Jeswara remained absent without leave for more than 
six months since 25th May 1953, that the workman hy his such long 
absence without leave lost all lien on his service and his place was duly 
filled in, that there was no justification whatsoever for his long absence, 
that the service of the said workman was terminated by his own action, 
that im the circumstances the Opposite Party submits that the application 
as such is not maintainable both in law and in equity and should be (11৯- 
missed as merely harassing and speculative, 


The only point which arises for decision is: 


Whether Jhagru was in the employ of the Company and was disniissed 
on 4th May 1954? What relief, if any, can he get? 


AWARD 


The case of the Union is based on Ext. D. It shows that in ceurse of 
conciliation before Miss R. Dutta, Labour Officer, West Bengal, on (۵ 
March 1954, it was agreed hy the parties that “Shagru Jeawara will be 


Part [] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 1956 1645 


reinatuted in service from 2nd Baisakh 1861 B.S. und the period of hin 
absence would be treated as leave without pay’’. The Union’s case 14 that 
after this order Jhagru was reappointed and he worked till 4th May 1954 
when he was again dismissed. সিন দা after that on 10th May 1954 
Union complained about it to the same Labour Officer Miss R. Dutta and 
they pushed the matter over there for some time but when the attempt 
for a settlement proved abortive they applied for a copy of the proceedings 
on lat June 1954 and the Labour Officer forwarded the copy of the proceed- 
ings by Ext. D in first part of August 1954 and on getting this copy the 
Union filed this complaint on behalf of the worker on 26th August 1954 
and hence this delay has been properly explained. 


Much was made by the learned Advocate for the Company regarding 
the letter Ext. C, dated 11th June 1954, in which the Labour Officer wanted 
to know the decision of the Company regarding the matter of reinstatement 
of Jhagru and from it the learned Advocate argued that this document 
shows that the conciliation was still going on, therefore, Ext. D is 
apparently a faked document. I have considered the matter in the light 
of the circumstances of the case but I am unable to subscribe to this 
interpretation on the language of the document. The document read in 
the above context obviously shows that the Labour Officer only wanted to 
know what was the reaction of the Company regarding complaint of the 
Union made to her by Ext. 6, dated 10th May 1954. In my opinion she 
referred to the joint discussion made on 27th May 1954 simply to remind the 
Company regarding the agreement, dated 30th May 1954, and she wanted 
to know if the Company wants to drag on with the matter any further or 
if they were minded to have the differences squared up even now. But
