AWARD 


This is a complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Shri Raghunath Prosad and Shri Rumbali Ahir. They alleged that 
although they were permanent workers in the Opposite Party Company, 
the, were discharged during the pendency of adjudication proceedings 
without permission. They, accordingly prayed for reinstatement as also 
payment of compensation for the period of unemployment. 


The Opposite Party Company opposed the application. It was stated 
that the application under section 338A was not maintainable. The Opposite 
Party denied that petitioner Shri Raghunath Prosad was an employee of 
the Company and pleaded that he was the personal driver of Shri D. Sinha, 
who happened to the Director of the Company; that petitioner Raghu- 
nath Prosad used to be paid his wages by Shri D. Sinha and not by the 
Opposite Party Company; that Shri D. Sinha disposed of his car and ۹ 
such services of Shri Raghunath Prosad were no longer required by him 
and that his due salary wus sent by said Shri D. Sinha by money order 
but Shri Raghunath Prosad refused to accept the same with mala fide 
intention, 


Regarding the petitioner Shri Rambali Ahir, the Opposite Party plead- 
০1 that he was a cooly employed purely on casual and temporary basis as 
and when required on “no work no pay” basis; that he (Shri Rambali Ahir) 
occasionally worked on casual and temporary basis for some time in 1954 
and 1966 and that the Opposite Party aid not discharge him. It was said 
that he was not available after he had last left Company’s work. 


1648 THE CAL, GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 1956 [Part 1 


The Opposite Party accordingly submitted that the complaint should 
be rejected. 


Decision 


Petitioner Shri Raghunath Prosad (P.W. 1) is a driver. He claimed 
to have joined service in the Opposite Party Compuny as a drive: m 
September 190১ and to have been discharged in August 1955. There is, 
however, no document or any other witness to support his case. The 
attendance register of the Opposite Party Company, Ext. C, on the con- 
trary shows thut P.W. 1 Shri Raghunath Prosad did not work in the 
Company during the period. 1.۴١۷. 1-Shri Raghunath Prosad admitted 
in his deposition that his name was not entered in the attendance register 
of the Opposite Party Company. In cross-examination }’.W. 1 said that 
he could not say whether in the wage-sheets in which the Company used 
to pay wages to the employees his name appeared. Exhibit D is the pay 
register in respect of monthly paid employees covering the period in which 
۲۰۷٢۷۰ ۱ claimed to have served. The said register, too, shows that he was 
never paid wages by the Company. The other wage registers, Exts. B and 
Bl, for payment of wages to the workers of the i are for the years 
1954 and 1955, Itkewise do not show payment by the Company to him. 
These therefore support Company’s case that P.W. 1 was not an employee 
of the Opposite Party Company. 


Though denied in examination-in-chief, Shri Raghunath Prosad had to 
adimit in cross-examination that Shri D. Sinha, Director of the Company, 
owned an old car. He further admitted that the said car was sold away 
2/°$ months before he was discharged and that the money order coupon 
shown to him was refused by him. LExhibit A is the said money order 
coupon. ا٢٢‎ was, however, sent by Shri D. Sinha to Shri Raghunath 
Prosad remitting his salary of Rs. 100 tor the month of July 195 less the 
money order commission of Rs, 1-14. It was stated therein that as hia car 
was sold ,ہد‎ services of Shri Raghunath Prosad were no longer required 
apd that as he was not taking his salary, though repeatedly asked to do so, 
it had to be sent by money order post less the money order commission. 
The said money order was sent long before the complaint under section : ۸ 
was filed. The allegations in the money order coupon that Shri Raghu- 
nath Prosad was in service under Shri J). Sinha and that he was being 
paid by him as revealed therein cannot be lightly brushed aside. From 
the evidence and circumstances, I believe the case of the Opposite Party 
Company that Shri Raghunath Prosad was in the employ of Shn 0). 
Sinha, Director of the Company, and not in the Opposite Party Company. 


No doubt the evidence disclosed that the petitioner Shri Raghunath 
Prosad did occasionally drive the van belonging to the Company but this 
fact cannot make him « employee of the Company. It appears that while 
holding employment under the Director, Shri D. Sinha, he did so casually 
on the contract basis with the tacit consent of his employer for earning 
extra money. Had Shri Raghunath Prosad been directly in the employ of 
the Company, his name would have been entered in the attendance register 
as well as in the wage register, and the money order would not have been 
sent by Shri D. Sinha. The allegation of Shri Raghunath ۲۶۱۸۵۹ that 
the Management became displeased with him as he joined the Union, as 
he was selected as witness of the Union in 0 case, 08 he demanded provi- 
dent fund and as he instituted a case for overtime, is afterthought and 
unreliable. The employment, it appears, was terminated as Shri D. Sinha 
had sold away his car in July 1955. Ramapati Dutta, it appears, ۸ not 


part I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 1956 1649 


a 7777585855555277---7--্প 
Opposite Party’s driver but of Shri Bhattacharya, the Engineer of the 
Cofipany. Complaint of Shri Raghunath Prosad is accordingly held to 
he without any foundation. 


The other petitioner Shri Rambali Ahir did not appear before the 
Tribunal to support his complaint. P.W. 1 Shri Raghunath Prosad, who 
deposed on his behalf, had to admit that he met Shri Rambali Ahir for 
the last time 2/3 months ago when Shri Rambali Ahir disclosed that he 
would not come to the Tribunal as he was not quite well. It would thus. 
appear that Shri Rambali Ahir was not at all serious about his complaint. 
The evidence of D.W. 1, Dhirendra Chandra Dutta, on the contrary, 
reveala that Shri Rambali Ahir wag a temporary cooly who used to be 
employed only for a term of three months at a time and that when hie. 
last term for three months expired in June or July 1955, his employment 
ceased. His evidence further discloses that as Shri Rambali Ahir did not 
thereafter turn up no question of pag him did arise. As he was ৪, 
temporary workman appointed for a fixed term, it 1s obvious that his 
employment ceased automatically on expiry of the fixed term and thus 
section 33 was not attracted. A casual and temporary worker appointed 
for a given time ceases to be a workman after the period is run out (vide 
1954 L..A.C., 329). Thus in his case, too, there was no contravention of 
section 33 of the Act. 


The petition under section 38۸ must therefore fail. 


It is awarded accordingly.

The Government of West Bengal, Jwbour Department, by order

the Sribunal in respect of the proceedings was made on 17th March ا‎ 
und the award has since been published in the Calcutta Gazette. 


AWARD 


During the pendency of the original dispute, the present complaint 
purporting to be under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 41 
was filed before this Tribunal on 19th March 1956 by the employee Asraf 
Ali on the allegation that while the origina] dispute was pending before 
this Tribunal, the Opposite Party, Empire Bone Mills, in contravention of 
the provisions of section 33 of the Act, dismissed him summarily with effect 


[7৮1] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 6 1651 


‘trom 27th February 1956 without taking permission from the Tribunal. 
the said order of dismissal has been characterised as unjustified and illegal. 
[815 alleged that the petitioner was victimised, simply because he happened 
to be a member 01 the Mmpire Bone Mills Mazdoor Union. So, reinstate- 
nent with back wages was claimed by the petitioner. 


The Opposite Party denied that there was any contravention by the 
Company of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It stated 
that on 24th February 1956 at about 11-10 a.m. while the Company’s 
Munager, Mr. 21. N. Ray, was going to his bungalow from the Mill’s 
(0009) a crowd of over 30 workmen bégan throwing stones and_ 10110100869 
and shoes at him, and that the present petitioner was one of those workmen. 
As a result of the above incident, the said Munager decided to dismiss the 
petitioner summarily, and by a letter, dated 27th February 1956, he 
unformed the petitioner accordingly. 


Admittedly the original dispute was pending before this Tribunal at 
the relevant time. Exhibit 1 is the letter that was issued by the Manager 
to the petitioner. It is dated 27th February 1956. This letter goes to 
show unmistakably that the petitioner was summarily dismissed from 27th 
February 1906. As the original dispute was pending before this Tribunal 
at the time, the Company had no right to dismiss the petitioner in this 
fushion, without the ily permission of the Tribunal. But obviously, 
no such permission of the Tribunal was taken before dismissing the _peti- 
tioner. So, there can be no manner of doubt that section 93 of the Act 
was contravened. My attention was drawn to the fact on behalf of the 
(ompany that in this letter (xt. 1), it is also stated at the end that 
pending decision from the Tribunal, the petitioner would remain suspended. 
ites on this, Mr. Manna, learned Counsel on behalf of the Company, 
hus argued before me that the petitioner was not actually dismissed, but 
he was kept under suspension 9ٍ8 permission from the Tribunal, and 
that this suspension was made by way of security measure. I must say 
straightway that 1 am unable to agree with Mr. Manna on this point, on 
a perusal of the letter itself (Ext. 1). The language used in that letter is 
that the petitioner is summarily dismissed from 27th February 1956. In 
the face of such clear and unequivocal expression, 1t cannot be held by any 
stretch of imagination that the petitioner was not actually dismissed, but 
was kept under suspension as a security measure pending decision from 
the Tribunal. In my view, the words ‘pending decision from the 
Tribunal you will remain suspended forthwith” as used in the aforesaid 
letter at the end, were put deliberately by the Manager with a view to avoid 
the application of section 33 of the Act. It is not capable of any other 
explanation or interpretation. The Tribunal, therefore, comes to the 
vonclusion that there was contravention of section 33 of the Act in the 
present case. So, the application under section 33A is competent. 


It is now well settled that where section 33 has been contravened, the 
Tribunal must enquire into the merita of the discharge or dismissal on a 
complaint being made under section 33A. As the complaint has to he 
investigated by the Tribunal, as if it were a dispute referred to or pending 
before it, the scope of investigation on the merits must exactly be the 
same where the subject-matter of the challenged discharge or dismissal had 
been the subject-mater of an independent reference under section 10 of 
the Act. The merita of the impugned dismissal are, therefore, to be 
considered by the Tribunal. This leads me necessarily to enter into the 
ا( ہہ‎ of the dismissal of the petitioner. The main charge as could be 
gathered from the letter of dismissal sent to the petitioner on 27th February 
1956 (vide Ext. 1), was that on 24th February 1956 at about 11-10 a.m. 
in front of the main gate of the mill, the petitioner along with other 


1662 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 1956 [Parr 1 


workers threw brickbats at the Manager, and abused him in filthy languages. 
Such a charge against a worker, if established us true, is indeed ao serious 
misconduct, which justifies summary dismissal. But the question 38 
whether the aforesaid charge is true, and has been substantiated by the 
materials on record. The petitioner himself has denied the charge levelled 
ngainst him. He has deposed before this Tribunal that he did not, along 
with others, throw brickbats at the Manager on 24th February 1956 at 
about 11-10 a.m. in front of the main gate of the mill, nor did he abuse 
him in filthy languages. He has stated that at that time, he was not in 
front of the main gate, but he was inside the mill taking his meal in the 
canteen. Shri H. N. Ray, the Manager, Shri নি. K. Mukherjee, Assistant 
Maintenance Engineer, Shri Padam Bahadur, a darwan of the mills, and 
Persia, a coolie sardar of the mills, have been examined on behalf of the 
Opposite Party to prove the alleged incident. 0 P. W. 1 Shri 1. 
Ray, the Manager, has no doubt spoken about the incident. He has also 
stated that the present petitioner was involved in that incident, and took 
:؛١‎ leading part. He has further said that he saw the present petitioner 
amongst the persons who shouted slogans and abused him im filthy 
languages, and that he was also one of the workers who threw brickbats 
and shoes at him. O. P. W. 2 Shri*S. .کا‎ Mukherjee, Assistant Maintenance 
Engineer, has also corroborated the Manager. 0. 1১ W. 3, Shri Padam 
Bahadur, darwan and 0, 1১, W. 4, Persia, a 00019 sardar, have also 
leposed in the same tone. But the point 15 whether the evidence of all 
these witnesses can be accepted, in view of what has transpired from the 
documentary evidence. Shri H. N. Ray, Manager, has admitted in 0018 
cross-exumination that he sent a letter to the se Officer about this 
incident, and he has proved a copy of that letter, which is Ext. A. It 
is interesting to note that in this letter, which is addressed to the Officer. 
in-Charge, Magra police-station, by a person no other than the Manager 
himself, no mention is made of the name of the present petitioner. This 
letter was written on the very date of the incident, that is, on 24th 
February 1956 by the Manager himself. It has transpired from his 
evidence that the petitioner took a leading part in the incident. If that 
was 80, how could the Manager omit to mention his name in the letter 
written to the Officer-in-Charge, Magra police-station, regarding the 
incident. It cannot be believed readily that the name of the petitioner 
escaped through inadvertence. According to him, the petitioner took a 
leading part in the incident. So, 16 was not likely for the Manager that 
he should forget so easily to mention his name in the report written to the 
police. This is 9 circumstance which points to the direction that the 
present petitioner did not take part in the alleged incident, if it at all 
took place on 24th February 1906 at 11-10 a.m. in front of the mill gate. 
This also fits in with the version of the petitioner that on that date at 
11-10 a.m. he was taking his meal in the canteen inside the mill. There 
is another document. It is also the Company's document, which makes 
the whole version of the incident doubtful. This document is Ext. B, 
and it is the charge-sheet which was served on the petitioner on 24th 
February 1956, that is on the date of the alleged incident. In this charge- 
sheet, it is specifically stated that the petitioner was found out of his post 
at 10-30 a.m. and that he was still sitting idle at 12-30 p.m. instead of 
doing the job allotted to him. The incident, for which the petitioner was 
summarily dismissed, is alleged to have taken place at 11-10 a.m. on 241 

February 1956. But it is curious that nowhere in this charge-sheet 
served on the petitioner on 24th February 1956, a whisper was made regard- 
ing this incident, although in the said charge-sheet what the petitioner did 
til] 12-30 p.m. was recorded. Had the incident as alleged really taken 
place on that date, at 11-10 a.m. under the circumstances as alleged, it 


would have been surely mentioned in the charge-sheet given to the

wditioner, because he is suid to have taken ao leading part in_ that

In view of what hag transpired from the documents, the oral evidence

BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT ; 
Shri G. P. Mukherjee, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal 


Appearances : 
For the employee: Shri Sunil Dhar, Advocate, 


For the Company: Shri 9.0. Sen, Advocate, and 
Shri 8. (0. Das Gupta, Advocate. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Dpeartment, by order 
No. 4669Dis./D/11]-207/55, dated 24th September 1955, referred the 
criginal dispute existing between Messrs. Khimjee Hunsraj, 165 Lower 
Chitpore Road, Calcutta, and their workmen represented hy the Federation 
of Mercantile Employees’ Union, 20/۸ Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-l, 
regarding the matters specified in the schedule to this Tribunal for adjudica- 
tion, The award of the Tribunal in respect of the proceeding was maie on 
سا‎ March 1956 and the award has since been published in the Calcutta 
razette.

‪۱ ۵ 


During the pendency of the original “dispute, the present complaint 
purporting to-he under section 38A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
was filed before this Tribunal on 10th February 1956 by the employee, 
Shri Nar Bahadur, on the allegation that while the original dispute was 
pending before this Tribunal, the Opposite Party Messrs. Khimjee Hunsraj, 
in contravention of the provisions of section 33 of the Act, dismissed him 
without taking permission from the Tribunal. The said order of dismissal 
hos been characterised as unjustified and illegal. So, reinstatement with 
hack wages was claimed by the petitioner. 


The Opposite Party has admitted that the petitioner was employed as a 
Motor Car Driver under the Company, but he was mainly employed for the 
personal service of the partner of the firm. The Opposite Party has further 
admitted that the petitioner was dismissed during the pendency of the 
original dispute before this Tribunal. But it wanted to say that it was 
under the impression that the petitioner being regularly employed for 
dumextic purpose and for personal use of the partner of the firm at 20 Theatre 
Road, Calcutta, was not concerned in the original dispute. Regarding 
11871018901) the Opposite Party assertedethat the order of dismissal of the 
petitioner was justified and proper in the circumstances, inasmuch as he 
was found on 4th December 1955 attempting to open the steel almirah in 
the room occupied by one of the partners named Shri V. J. Suratya alias 
Muljee Babu, during his temporary absence from that room in the afternoon. 
He was charge-sheeted for this misconduct, and an enquiry was held in 
which the petitioner was present, and statements of witnesses were also 
secorded in his presence. As a result of this enquiry, the charge levelled 

ainst him was proved, and accordingly he was dismissed from service 

ith effect from 16th December 1955. 


Tt appears from the evidence that the petitioner was employed as a 
Motor Car Driver in Messrs. Khimjee Hunsraj and that his salary was paid 
hy that Company. So, there can be no manner of doubt that he was an 
employee of Messrs. Khimjee Hunsraj. The fact that he used to reside at 
the house of the partners at 20 Theatre Road, Calcutta, and was solely 
employed for domestic purpose and for personal use of the partners of the 
firm, did not matter much to his being called an employee of the firm— 
Messrs. Khimjee Hunsraj. Admittedly, he being a workman of Messrs. 
Khimjee Hunsraj, was dismissed during the pendency of the original dispute 
16109 this Tribunal. So, undoubtedly there was violation of section 89 of 
the Act. Thus the Tribunal feels no hesitation in holding that in this case 
section 33 has been contravened. Where section 33 has heen contravened, 
the Tribunal must enquire into the merits of the discharge or dismissal on 
a complaint being made under section 88۸ of the Act. Each such com- 
plaint has to he investigated by the Tribunal as if ‘it were a dispute referred 
fo or pending before 16/, The scope of the investigation on the merits 
must he exactly the same, where the subject-matter of the challenged 
discharge or dismissal had heen the subject matter of an independent 
reference under section 10 of the Act. The principles laid down in the 
Buckingham & Karnatie Mills Co. os. its workmen [1981 11.7. (ii), 314] 
would equally apply, and the Tribunals would not be entitled to substitute 
their own judgments for the judgments of the Management except in four 
enses, namely, (1) where there was want of bona fides on the part of the 
Management, (2) in the case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or 
violation of the principles of natural justice. (8) or where there was basic 
error of facts, and (4) or a perverse finding by the Management on the 
materials, which it had before it at the time of the enquiry. 


1654(b) THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 12, 1956 (Parr ] 


Bearing the above principles in mind, let me now proceed to investigate 
the merits of the petitioner’s dismissal. The charge oY allegation against 
the petitioner is that on 4th December 1956 “he went into the room of 
Shri V. J. Suraiya alias Muljee Babu at 20 Theatre Road during his 
temporary absence, and attempted to open the steel almirah situated therein 
with the key, which the said partner inadvertently 161, behind. Tt appears 
that the said partner made preliminary enquiry from the persons, who saw 
the applicant trying to open the almirah, and finding that a prima facie case 
had been made out, issued the charge-sheet to the petitioner. 4 copy of 
the said charge-sheet has been proved in thia case, and it is Ext. C, dated 
211) December 1955. It 1s clear from that charge-sheet that the petitioner 
was charged with attempting to commit theft from the residence of the 
partner Shri V. J. Suraiya at 20 Theatre Road, Calcutta, on 4th December 
1955 at about 4 p.m., and that this fact was detected by the cook, Shi; 
Bhirulal, who saw him trying to open the steel almirah with the bunch ‘of 
keys. The petitioner has admitted in his evidence that he received such 
charge-sheet. Extracts C(1) is the reply sent by the petitioner. It is dated 
6th December 1955. In this letter, he no doubt denied the allegation made 
against him. Thereafter an enquiry was held on 14th December 1955 into 
the charge at 3 p.m., and this enquiry was conducted in the office hy Shri 
V. J. Suraiya. The petitioner has admitted in his cross-examination that 
he got a letter informing him that an enquiry would be held on 14th Decem- 
her 1955, where he was required to be present with his witnesses. He has 
further admitted that the enquiry was duly held on 14th December 1956 in 
the office at 3 p.m. and in that enquiry, witnesses were examined, and their 
statements recorded. He has also said that his statement too was taken down. 
Exhibit A is the proceedings of the said enquiry. So, it cannot be said 
that there was any violation of the principles of natural justice. The 
petitioner was asked to give his explanation, and an enquiry was held fn 
his presence. The statements of witnesses recorded at the time of enquiry 
have also been produced before this Tribunal. Shri V. J. Suraiya and Shri 
Bhirulal, the cook, who found the petitioner attempting to open the atecl 
olmirah with the key inside the room of Shri Suraiya, have deposed before 
this Tribunal. Their evidence cannot be lightly brushed aside or dis- 
helieved. There is no reason as to why they would depose falsely. No 
motive could be suggested or proved as to why this petitioner could be 
implicated falsely. So, the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the 
Management in dismissing the petitioner had acted bona fide. The finding 
of the Management on the materials, which it had before it at the time of 
enquiry, cannot be said to be perverse. Nor the matter can he brought 
within the second or third exception in Buckingham & Karnatic Mills’ ০৯৭6. 
So, the order of dismissal of the petitioner was perfectly justified, and the 
Management could take such a possible view on the materials before it. 
It is evident that the petitioner concerned ia afflicted with strong criminal 
propensity. He had attempted to open the steel almirah, and if he was not 
discovered in the act at the psychological moment hy the cook, he would 
have succeeded in helping himself to the valuable contents, if any. It is 
indeed unsafe to employ a man, who could do such a daring act. Therefore, 


the Management was perfectly justified in getting rid of him. It has 
transpired from the evidence that an information was lodged at the thana 
regarding the incident. This document has not been called for in this case. 
Naturally, the learned lawyer for the petitioner has commented much on 
this fact. But I may say straightway that nothing turns on the fact that 
the information lodged at the thana was not called for. The incident has 
been proved to demonstration by the materials already on the record.

The result.is thet the petitroner is not entitled to get any relief. The 
application 1f’accordingly rejected.

widermentioned personnel u Regional Allocation

Annapurna Cotton Mills 14077 Shyam-

Gangadhar Banerjee Lune—Member. 

(6) Shri Phanindra Nath Mukherjee, M.L.A., 
Mina Cinema Buildings, Panihati— 
Member. 


2 The functions of the Committee will be— 


(1) to convene meetings of the Committee at a 
place and time to be fixed in consultation 
with the Chairman and submit the appli- 
cations received in response to the adver- 
tisement for letting out the tenements 
issued by the Department of Housing of 
this Government. The Committee will 
consider the individual applications and 
draw up a list of candidates to whom the 
tencments, in their opinion, may be 
allotted. The list should be drawn up in 
order of preference and the number of 
candidates included in the list should be 
26 per cent. in exeess of the total number 
of tenements available for allotment. 


(11) In making the selection the Committee 
should take into consideration the follow- 
Ing factors as also such other factors as 
they consider necessary— 


(a) the size of the tamily of the candidate. 
(b) Monthly wages of the person. 


(c) Distance of the factory in which he works 
from the quarters to be allotted. 


(d) Recommendation of the employer. 


(iii) The proceedings of the meetings of the 
Committee together with the 46 
mentioned above and all the applications 
will thereafter be submitted by the 
Secretary to the Department of Housing 
of this Government. 


Allotment of tenements to individual workers 
will then be made by the Department of Housing 
on the basis of the recommendations of the Com- 
mittee. Government reserve the right to override 
the recommendations of the Committee in any 
individual case. 


Order. 


OrvereED that the above Resolution be published 
in the Calcutta Gazette, and copies thereof be 
forwarded to the Chairman and members of the 
Committee. 


OrneEreD also that a copy of the Resolution be 
forwarded to other departments of this Govern- 
ment and the Directorate of Housing.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, filed by Shri Parimal Bhattacharjee, an employee of Messrs. 
Bengal Immunity Co., Ltd., Baranagar, Calcutta-36. 


BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAI, 
PRESENT: 
Set M. C. BANERJEE, //strict Judge (Retared), Judge, First Industrial 


Tribunal. 
For the complainant: Shri Suprabhat Mukherji, Pleader. 


For the employer: Shri 8. C. Sen, Advocate, and Shri 8. K. Dhar 
Chowdhury, Pleader. 


AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by order 
No. 3700Dis./D/10L-7/53, dated 5th October 1958, referred, under sections 
Tand 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Bengal Immunity 00.) Ltd., Baranagore, 
Calcutta-36, and their workmen to this Tribunal for adjudication. The award 
of the Tribunal on this dispute was made on 17th November 1954 and was 
published in the Calcutta Gazette on 16th December 1954. 


On 24th December 1964 Shri Parimal Bhattacharjee, an employee of the 
Company, filed a complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, stating that the Company unlawfully denied him the bonus which fell 
due and which was a condition of service. It is stated that the Company 
terved a charge-sheet on the petitioner on 806) April 1954, and the Director- 


9794 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 [Parr I 


২ স্লিপ 
Manager passed orders that the petitioner was guilty of insubordinafon, 
and so he was warned and it was ordered that no bonus would be given to 
him. The petitioner, therefore, prays for an order directing the Company 
to pay him the bonus which has been withheld. 


The Company, in its written statement, states that the payment of 
bonus to the employees of this Company is not a condition of service, thut 
it is an ez-gratia payment made in consideration of efficiency and good 
work, It is stated that the Company has followed the following principle 
in making this eg-yratia payment :— 

(a) Bonus is paid to an individual workman at the absolute discretion 
of the Management in consideration of his work and efliciency. 


(b) Before payment of any honus, the Management scrutinises the 
service records and the reports of the Department-in-charge in 
respect of each of the workmen and then decides whether the 
workman concerned deserves to be paid or not and, in pursuance 
of the said decision, pays the same. 


Following the above principle, the Company paid bonus in May 1954 to the 
applicant at the rate of one month’s basic pay. In September 1954, the 
Company on considering his records and the reports of the Department-in- 
charge decided not to pay him bonus at that time. The applicant is not 
entitled to get any bonus, or the bonus in question as of right and aa a 
condition of service. Consequently, non-payment of bonus to the applicant 
is not a contravention of section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act, In 
the circumstances, the application should be dismissed. 


The points that arise for decision in this case are as follows :— 


Points 
= (1) Is the application under section 984 of the Act maintainable? 
(2) Is the applicant entitled to any relief in this case? 


DECISIONS 


Point No. 1.—The question for decision is if the application under 
section 934 is maintainable. It is the contravention by the employer of 
section 33 of the Act that gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the 
workmen to approach and move the Tribunal and this contravention is the 
condition precedent to the exercise by the ‘Tribunal concerned of the 
additional jurisdiction and powers conferred on it by section 88۸ (de the 
decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Automobile 
Products of India, Ltd., reported in 1955 14.4..0., 211). The question, there- 
fore, is if the Company in not paying the bonus in September 1954 to the 
petitioner violated section 33 of the Act. 


(0.1. 1 Shri Nihar Bindu Guha deposed on behalf of the Company. 
Documents Exts. A series and Ext. B were marked for the Company. No 
evidence was adduced for the applicant. It appears from the evidence of 
0.۲۰٢۲۲۰ 1 that the Company pays bonus usually three times in the financial 
year—once in May, again in September and again in the following January. 
The financial year of the Company is from May to the following April. 
On each of the three occasions, bonus corresponding to one month’s hasic 
wage is paid to the employees. The witness states that one out of the 
three bonuses is paid to all employees without exception, but the other two 
bonuses are paid according to efficiency of work of the individual employees 
and their conduct. In the case of the applicant, Parimal Bhattachagjee, he 
was given the bonus for May and January but was not allowed the bonus 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2705 


for September, on account of some adverse remarks about his work, which 
yas found to be justified on enyuiry. It is also stated that payment of 
none of these three bonuses is a condition of service for the workmen but it 
18 Customary 1n the Company to give at least one of these three bonuses, 
wndependent of the quality of work. 


There is nothing on record to show that the payment of bonus is a 
condition of service of the employees. ١0.۰۷۷۰ 1 in his cross-examination 
alates that 25 per cent. of the nett profit of every year 1s earmarked for 
payment as bonus to the employees and Ext. B shows the amount of bonus 
paid in the years 1952-53, 1953-54 and 1954-65 and also the profits during 
these years. O.P.W. 1 also states that Parimal Bhattacharjee was not 
deprived of the bonus in September 1954 by way of punishment. There 
1৪) therefore, nothing on record to show that it is a condition of service for 
the employees to get all the three bonuses. All that the witness states 
ig that it 1s customary for the Company to give only one out of the three 
bonuses in the year to all employees, independent of the quality of his 
work. In the present case, the applicant was given the bonus in May 1954 
and January 1955. He was deprived of only one bonus out of the three, 
1.6.) the bonus paid in September 1954. I do not find that the pay- 
ment of bonus in Septemher 1954 was a condition of service of tke 
applicant, Parimal Bhattacharjee. That being so, it cannot be claimed 
that the Company altered to the prejudice of the workman concerned 
condition of service applicable to him immediately before the commence- 
ment of the proceedings. Again, it also appears that in order to attract 
the operation of clause (a) of section 33 of the Act, the alteration of the 
condition of service should be in regard to a body of workmen and not an 
individual workman. This view has been held in the case of Hindusthan 
Development Corporation, reported in 1951(I) L.LJ., 37, by a State 
Tribunal of Calcutta. In any case, it appears that the fact that the 
applicant was not given the bonus in Séptember 1954 does not attract the 
operation of section 33(a) of the Act. 


It was also argued by the learned spokesman for the petitioner that uon- 
payment of honus in September 1954 to the petitioner was a punishment 
to him and was a conduct which was hit by section 33(b) of the Act. In 
view of the evidence of 0.P.W. 1 that one of the three bonuses is paid 
to all workmen and the other two bonuses are paid according to efficiency 
of work and conduct of the individual employees non-payment of one out of 
three bonuses after an enquiry on an adverse report by the departmental 
head cannot be considered to be a punishment that could attract the 
operation of section 8900) of the Act. In view of these circumstances, 
١۲ 18 decided that the conduct of the Company in not giving the applicant 
bonus in September 1954, was not a violation of section 33 of the Act and 
the present application under section 33A of the Act was not, therefore, 
competent. 


Point No. 2.—Even if the application under section 383A of the Act 
was competent, it would appear from the facts of the case and the evidence 
on record that the application of the petitioner cannot succeed on merits. 
Ext. A(4) is a report by the departmental head under whom the applicant 
worked, stating that the petitioner refused to work in the Distilled Water 
Section, as he was ordered by hia immediate superior. Ext. A(3) is the 
charge-sheet served on the petitioner for this alleged misconduct. Ext. A(2) 
is the explanation of the petitioner. Here he states that he only wanted 
to know what work he was to do in the 10190111901 Water Section, as he was 
afraid that he might otherwise cause damage to the interest of the Company, 


2796 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 [Parr [ 


and that he was prepared to work there even now. Ext. A is the state. 
ment of Shri A. K. Chowdhury, the departmental head and the petitioner 
to the enquiring officer, O.P. 1. In this statement to the enquiring 
officer, the petitioner states that he wanted to know the reasons for his 
transfer to the Distilled Water Section and the cause of his objection to 
work there was that the place was very hot. The explanation, Ext. A(2) 
to the charge-sheet, does not disclose this ground of objection. Ext. A is 
the report of the enquiring officer and the order of the Director-Manager 
appears at the back of the charge-sheet. It shows that the petitioner wag 
guilty of insubordination and disobejience. He was warned. 1٦ was also 
ordered that he should not be given the next bonus. This order was made 
on the 26th of May 1954. There is no evidence on record to justify the 
conclusion that the report, Ext. A(4), against the petitioner or the enquiry 
following it and the order of the Directur-Manager after the enquiry was 
not buna fide. It is, therefore, clear that the petitioner, Parimul Bhatta- 
charjee, was not given the bonus in September 1954 as a result of adverse 
report against him, which was found to be justified on a detailed enquiry 
in which the petitioner was examined and was given an opportunity of 
defending himself. As is was a rule for the Company to grant only one 
out of three bonuses to all employees, independent of the quality of their 
work, and to allow the order two bonuses in consideration of the efficiency 
and conduct of the workmen concerned, the Company was justified im 
refusing the bonus to the petitioner in September 1954, after the enquiry 
on his conduct, as reported in Ext. A(4). The petitioner is uot entitled 
to any relief even on merits. This point is accordingly answered. 


In the result, it is ordered that the application under section 33A of the 
Act be rejected and it is awarded accordingly. 


M. 0. BANERJI, 
Judge, First lndustrial Tribunal. 
The 214 June 1956.

D. S. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

ORDER 


No. 288Q@Dis./D/11L-164/55.—3rd July 1956.—Whereas under the 
Government .of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 492Dis./)D | 
11L-428/54, dated the 4th February 1955, read with its corrigendum 
No. 3962Dis./D/11L-164/55, dated the 24th August 1955, the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Kanehialal Lohia, 112 Chiltaranjan Avenue, 
Caleutta-7, and their senior mate Shri Subha Singh, C/o Messrs. Kanebiala! 
Lohia, on the one hand, and two of their workmen, namely, Ram Charan 
and Basanta, represented by Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ Union, 1 Joy 
Bhattacharjee Lane, Calcutta-2, on the other, regarding the matters

(1) Is the discharge of Ram Charan and Basanta justified? What

DECISION 


Shri Ram Charan and Shri Basanta were admittedly Khatawalas or 
Khatawala Mates in Messrs. Kanehialal Lohia. It was been, contended on 
{heir behalf that they were employees of the said Kanebialal Lohia and 
were discharged by them, whereas 1 has been contended on behalf of the 
latter that they were merely contractors who used to do work of assorting 
with the help of their own men paid on the basis of outturn of their work. 


In support of their case Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ Union (hereafter 
called the ‘‘Union’’) on behalf of the workmen has examined only P.W. ] 
Shri Ram Charan Dus while Messrs. Kanehialal Jiohia has examined its 
senior mate, D.W. 2 Shri Subha Singh, the Sarkar, D.W. 3 Shri Lakshmi 
Narayan, Khatawala, D.W. 4 Shri Kamdhar Singh and Manager, D.W. 9 
Shri Sitaram Sharma besides a formal witness in the Bench Clerk of the 
Qourt of Authority under the Payment of Wages Act, D.W. 1 Shri Durga 
Prasad Mandal and filing the documents, Exts. A to E. 


Messrs. Kuanehialal Lohia (hereafter called the ‘‘baler’’) carries among 
others the business of a jute baler. As such jute baler it purchases raw 
jutes from the markets and stacks thém in the godown situated in the 
premises of ‘Messrs. Lohia Jute Press, Lid., at 28 Barrackpore Trunk Road. 
The jute baler engages men for assorting raw jute according to the quality 
and then for pressing it into pucca bales in a jute press as also for extract- 
ing jute fibre from the jute sticks. For these two kinds of work payments 
unre made on the basis of output at fixed rates—Hs, 2-8 for each pucca bale 
and a different rate for extracting jute fibre from the jute sticks. 


‘These different items of work are done by the Khatawalas or Khatawala 
Mates through their own men whose number generally varies from 2 to 6. 
These men form a gang under the leadership of the Khatawala who happens 
to be the seniormost in the party (vide P.W. 1). 


Khatawala and Khatawala Mates, it appears, are interchangeable terms, 
for P.W. 1 Shri Ram Charan Das styled himself as simply Khatawala in his 
deposition before the Court of Authority under the Payment of Wages Act 
(Ext. A), and as Khatawala Mate before this Tribunal. The men who 
work under a Khatawala Mate are called Jachandars. The number of 
Jachandars in a gang under a Khatawala varies generally between 2 and 6. 
The number varies according to the requirement of work. If the work is 
heavy the number of men is more and if the amount of work is 1688 the 
number of men engaged is also less (vide P.W. 1). 


Formerly 3/4 years ago there were 60 to 70 Khatawalas in Messrs. 
Kanehiala] Lohia. The number of Khatawalas has come down since then 
and at the date of deposition the number has been 15 to 16 (wde D.W. 2). 


Besides Khatawalas and Jachandars as aforesaid, the jute baler has 
permanent monthly paid staff in his employ. P.W. 1 Shri Ram Charan 
Das admitted that the senior mate, D.W. 2 Shri Subha Singh, second mate 
and third mate under him and the Sarkar, D.W. 3 are such permanent 
staff. They are admittedly monthly paid employees of the baler. The 
senior mate (D.W. 2) and his two subordinate mates supervise and check 
the work of the Khatawalas and Jachandars after raw jute is sorted out and 
made into kutcha bale and before it is pressed into pucca bale. While a 
Khatawala supervises the work of Jachandars under him and teaches and 
guides them in the matter of sorting the jute up to the stage of making 
kutcha bale. The Sarkar (D.W. 3), on the other hand, keeps account 
regarding the quantity of pucca bales as produced by each of the Khata- 

alas and enters them in the khatas of the baler and simultaneously in the 


2800 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 [Parr 1 
== —————— 288 88588 
hatchittas said 06. be kept in the custody of Khatawalas. From the 
accounts so maintained the Khatawalas used to be formerly paid fortmyhtly 


and for some’ time past weekly. In this way the operation of jute baling 
18 carried on. 


According to the Union, Shri Ram Charan and Shri Basanta were 
workmen of Kanehialal Lohia and were discharged or dismissed as they 
protested against deductions from their remuneration by the employer 
Jt was said by Shri Ram Charan that the employer used to deduct one anna 
for pinjrapole, one anna per rupee ax profit and two annas per head for 
mate subscription out of the fixed rate of Rs. 2-8 payable to them for each 
pucca bale. ‘The employer’s men denied the allegations and stated that 
Shii Ram Charan and Shri Bayanta were not at all employees of Kanehialal 
Lohia but their contractors and that they left as the work of jute baling 
came down considerably leaving no scope for sufficient earnings. 


In the case of Cooke & Kelvey, 140.) and their employees reported in 
1955 L.L.J., Vol. II, page 582, the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India 
considered the test to determine whether a person is an independent 
contractor or an employee. It has been laid down therein as follows: 


‘Under section 2(5) of the Industrial Disputes Act, a workman 
must be an employee in the industry to do skilled or unskilled work 
for hire or reward, and the work might be manual or clerical. The 
designation together with the nature of the work done should be 
considered in ascertaining if a person is a workman or not. 


A servant is a person subject to the command of his master as to 
the manner in which he shall do his work. The independent contractor 
in one who undertakes to produce a given result but in the actual 
execution of work he is not under the control and order of the othe: 
party. In the case of an employee falling within the definition it is 
the person who is engaged to perform certain services on whom 
emphasis is laid while in the case of a contractor emphasis is not on 
his engagement but only on the work to be executed and _ performed 
by him according to the requirements or specifications. While in the 
case of the former personal service becomes essential, in the case of the 
latter the personal service becomes a secondary matter.’’ 


In Salmond’s Law of Torts, 11th edition, at pages 98 and 99, the 
distinction between a contract of service and contract for services 1: 
summarized : 


“What then is the test of this distinction between a servant and an 
independent contractor? The test is the existence of a right of control 
over the agent in respect of the manner in which his work is to be 
done. A servant is an agent who works under the supervision 90৫ 
direction of his employer; an independent contractor 1s one who 
ic his own master. A servant is a person engaged to obey 
his employer’s orders from time to time; an independent contractor 18 
a person engaged to do certain work; but to exercise his own discre- 
tion as to the mode and time of doing it—he is bound by his contract, 
but not by his employer’s orders. 


This may be put in another way by drawing a distinction between 
one employed under a contract of service (a servant) and one empfoyed 
under contract for services (an independent contractor). The distinc- 
tion between a contract for services and a contract of services can be 


Part J] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2801 


summarised in this way: In the one case the master can order or 
require what is to be done; while in the other case he cannot only 
order»er require what is to be done but how itself it shal] be done.’’ 


(01১67 marks of a contract of service are:— 
**(1) the master’s power of selection of his servant, 
(119 the payment of wages or other remuneration, 
(ii1)* the master’s right of suspension or dismissal.’’ 


In collins v. Ilertfordshire County Council (1947 1 K.B. 598), 
Hilbery, J., discussed this question at pages 614 and 616. At page 616 
is the observation: 


‘‘The proper test is whether or not the higher had had authority to 
control the manner of execution of the Act in question.”’ 


In this case there is no direct documentary evidence in support ot 
either of the conflicting versions. The question whether Shri Ram Charan 
and Shri Basanta were employees or contractors is, therefore, to be decided 
having regard to the test as laid down above and the attending circum- 
stances, such as entire picture of thefr engagement, method of work, 
conduct during work, mode of payment, etc. 


The outstanding feature is that the jute baling industry has no 
regularity of work. The requirements of a jute baler are guided hy duily 
jute markets and upon the orders as are received. So a Khatawala who 
18 tto execute certain work through Jachandars on the basis of fixed rate 
cart have necessarily no regularity in the work. A Khatawala is neither 
a daily-rated nor a monthly-rated worker: the more he can produce the 
11019 he can earn. When the work is completed and the assorted jute 1s 
preased into a pucca bale he is entitled to get remunerations at fixed rate 
and not before that. The number of Jachandars under him 1s never fixed 
but varies according to requirements. According to P.W. 1, Shri Ram 
Charan Das, it varies from 2 to 6 while according to the employer’s men, 
it varies from 2 to 10. Thus the number of Jachandars under a Khata- 
wala varies according to requirements and necessity. This system ot 
work, it is obvious, 1s more বা to be executed on the basis of contract 
than by means of permanent staff. 


Regarding remuneration, it appears that it is payable exclusively to the 
Khatawalas and not to the Jachandars under him. The baler pays the 
Khatawala calculated at fixed rate per bale according to quality on the 
total bales pressed from the jute sorted out by the Khatawala and_ the 
Jachandars under him. The register regarding payment of wages shows 
payment of total dues to the Khatawalas only on the basis of output of 
pucca bales by the gang comprising the Khatawala and the Jachandars 
under him. P.W. 1 admitted in his deposition in the Court of Authority 
under the Payment of Wages Act that he used to receive the whole amount 
as were due under his thumb impression (vtde Ext. A). Before this 
Tribunal, too, P.W. 1 admitted having affixed his thumb impression in the 
register of payment of wages in acknowledgment of payment of entire 
amount due. His allegation that after such thumb impression the employer 
was distributing the said amount to him and the Jachandars 18 ea hg 
Had the employer been under obligation to pay the stipulated amount both 
to the Khatawalas and the Jachandars under them, not only the names of 
the Khatawalas but also the names of the Jachandars under them would 
have been noted in the register of payment of wages by way of obtaining 
to, go from all of them. The fact that only the names of the Khata- 
walas are mentioned in the said register and acquittance is obtained from 


2802 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 [Part ] 


=a a ESL a a ১ এছ e- 
them goes to show that the baler had and has obligation ip pay the 
stipulated amount only to the Khatawalas and to none else. Had the 
amount been not so exclusively payable to the Khatawalas, the Khatawalas 
would not have complained about the alleged illegal and unauthorised 
deductions from the fixed rate and brought case No. 210 of 1954 in the 
Court of Authority under the Payment of Wages Act for recovery of such 
wages as were said to have been illegally deducted. P.W. 1 admitted in 
cross-examination that all the 29 Khatawalas including himself made the 
application in the Court of Authority under the Payment of Wages Act 
regarding such illegal deductions from their dues. The fact that only the 
Khatawalas and not the Jachandars along with them brought the case 
leaves no room for doubt that the amount on the basis of output was and 
is payable by the baler exclusively to the Khatawalas. I believe that the 
hatchittas are kept in the custody of Khatawalas showing the number of 
pucca bales as are produced by them. 


Regarding appointment, discharge and control, I prefer to accept the 
evidence that it is the Khatawala who appoints his Jachandars and who 
teaches and guides them (Jachandars) in their work of sorting os _ being 
more natural and probable. Had it heen otherwise, the baler would have 
made payment to the Jachandars as well. The evidence and circumstances 
as already referred to, however, leave no room for doubt that the 
Jachandars are paid hy the Khatawala and that the jute baler has no 
obligation or connection whatever in the matter of payment to them. | 
also believe that it is the Khatawalas who grant leave to the Jachandars 
and not the baler or his men. The fact that in case of going on leave they 
do not admittedly get pay shows that they are not also employees. 


Regarding working hours, P.W. 1 said that they were to work formerly 
from 6 in the morning to 9 in the night and after intervention of the 
Factory Inspector the hours of work were reduced to 8 hours a day. He 
also said that whether there was work or not they were required to atten 
the godown daily. From the evidence and circumstances I am unable to 
accept his version as fully correct. When a Khatawala is entitled to ne 
paid at fixed rates on completion of certain works, it 18 obvious that the 
baler can have no control over the time taken by him to complete the work 
which the Khatawala undertook to do for the specified remuneration. In 
the circumstances neither the Khatawalas nor the Jachandars under them 
were under any obligation to attend on any particular day or any particular 
hour. No doubt the attendance register is being maintained for some time 
past for the Khatawalas and the Jachandars by the men of the jute baler, 
but from this it cannot be said that the Khatawalas are workmen. lt 
rather appears that it is so as the godown in which the operation of jute 
baling is carried on is situated within the precincts of the jute press 
which is_a factory within the meaning of the Factories Act having been 
operated by electric current and having more than 20 men working there. 
As it is a factory the hours of work for men working in the baling 
operation in the godown situated in the compound of the jute press canuot 
but be regulated under the Factories Act. From this, it cannot be said 
that the Khatawala is a workman or that the baler has authority to control 
the manner of execution of work. Even during those hours the Khatawalas 
und the Jachandars appear to be their own master and can work in the 
manner as they please. The baler, it appears, is under no obligation to 
provide work to a Khatawala on any given day. These, I think, are only 
consistent with the position of contractors. The mere fact that the work 
is done within the godown and it is of late regulated by the hours of-work 
us prescribed for a factory would not show that the baler has coutrol over 
the time of the workers. The time spent on the work of sorting, 1 


part I] THE CALCUTPA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2808 


ممسسس۳سمپم٤عمدمسجدہ>‏ دہ جککیچھجد و পু পাতিল‏ 


appears, is uot at the disposal of or under the orders of the baler. , The 
fact that no overtime is admissible or payable to the Khatawalug’ and 
Jachandarg under him would also support this. Thus a Khatawala, in my 
opinion, 1188 his own time and cannot be 9810 to be bound to work tor fixed 
hours. So, from the evidence and circumstances I am unable to find that 
relation of employer and employee existed between Messrs. Kanehialal 
Lohia firm on one hand and Shri Ram Charan and Shri Basanta 07) the 
other. I rather believe that Shri Ram Charan and Shri Basanta were 
contractors. It is, therefore, obvious that the Tribunal cannot give any 
relief to them. 


Regarding charge of victimisation, P.W. 1 Shri Ram Charan stated in 
rross-examination that there were altogether 29 Khatawalas in Kanehialal 
Lohia firm at the time and that all of them were members of the Union. 
Why out of the said 29 Khatawalas only Shri Ram Charan and Shri Basanta 
were singled out for victimisation has not been satistactorily explained. 
Regarding Shri Basanta, nothing was said, while regarding Shri Ram 
(Sharan, it was said that Kanehialal Lohia had usked him to leave the 
Union and as he did not oblige he was driven out. The explanation is 
unconvincing. ‘The evidence, on the contrary, points that there was dearth 
of work for the Khatawalas. P.W. 1 admitted that before partition of the 
country in 1947 the work of jute baling was very heavy and that since the 
partition the work has been going down gradually. The evidence shows 
that the number of Khatawalas has come down to 16/17. It is, therefore, 
not unlikely that Shri Ram Charan and Shri Busanta had themselves left 
finding no prospect of sufficient earnings any longer. 


I award accordingly.

1. By order No. 3885Dis./D/11L-297/55, dated the 22nd August 1909, 
the Governor of West Bengal, in the labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputea Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Steel & Allied Products, Ltd., Temple Chambers, 6 Old 
Post Office Street, Calcutta-1, and their employee Shri Jatindra Nath Roy, 
8/74 Bojoygarh Colony, Calcutta-32, represented by himself, regarding the

constituted under section 7 of the Jndustrial Disputes Act, 1947, by 
notification No. 592Dis./D/12L-5/52, dated the 28rd February 19538, for 
adjudication. 

9 tSfter usual summons the parties entered appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 18th November 
1955. The parties were thereafter directed to file list of documents. Then 
the employer-Company filed additional written statement on 5th April 1906 
raising preliminary objection regarding the maintainability of the reference. 
The workman filed counter-statement to the same on 9th April 1956. Then 
after adjournments, the matter was heard on 7th June 1906. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 


reference is as follows: — 
Whether termination of services of Shri Jatindra Nath Roy was 
justifiedP What relief is he entitled to? 


Part V] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2807 


DECISION 


Shri Jatindra Nath Roy was admittedly in the employ of Messrs. Steel 
& Allied Products Ltd. (hereafter culled the Company). The Heag (01909 
of the Company is situated at 6 Old 1১98৮ Uffice Street, while the workshop 
at 2/1 Hossais Sha Road, Kidderpore. Shri Jatindra Nath Roy admittedly 
jomed as o clerk in the workshop of the Company on lst March 1954 on a 
salary of Rs. 75 per month and subsequently got two increments when his 
pulary rose to Its. 115 per month. 119 was admittedly discharged by ao 
notice, dated 20th January 1955 (Exts. 1 und la), trom that date without 
assigning any reason. Upon such ¢ermination of employment the present 
dispute arose. 


The Company by an additional written statement filed on 65th April 
1956 took preliminary objection that the diypute referred to was not an 
industrial dispute but an individual dispute and as such the reference was 
bad in law. It was, on the other hand, contended on behalf of Shri Jatindra 
Nath Roy that the individual dispute like the present one would come 
within the meaning of the ‘‘industria? dispute’’ ug defined in the Act and 
thus the reference was competent. Reliance in this respect was placed on 
the decision of the Full Bench of the Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case 
of Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company, Ltd., versus Shri Ram Baran reported 
in 1953, L.A.C., 189. 


It is not disputed that the workmen in the employ of the Company 
either in the 1190 Office or in its workshop had no Union for long even 
after termination of employment of Shri Jatindra Nath Roy. According 
lo P.W. 2 Shri Sunil Chandra Sarkar, a» Union of the name of Steel & Allied 
Products Ltd. Employees’ Congress was formed only 8 or 9 months after 
the discharge of Shri Jatindra Nath Roy. Shri Jatindra Nath Roy was 
discharged on 20th January 1955. So the Union, according to P.W. 2, was 
established some time in October or November 1955. The reference was, 
however, made by the Government long before—on 22nd August 1955. It is, 
therefore, obvious that the Union did not and could not have taken up his 
cause up to the date of reference. The evidence does not show that the 
workmen in the employ of the Company took up his cause either. 
According to the workman P.W. 1 Shri Jatindra Nath Roy, after termina- 
tion of his employment it was he who moved the Labour Directorate and 
none else. He also admitted that the employees of the Company did not 
make any demand in writing about his reinstatement up till now. It is, 
therefore, an individual dispute pure and simple which was ut no time prior 
to the reference espoused by the workmen in the employ of the Company or 
by any Union. The evidence of Shri Jatindra Nath Roy (P.W. 1) that 
the employees made verbal demand for his reinstatement before the 
Managing Director and the Works Manager before the Puja of 1955 (i.e., 
October 1966) is afterthought and unreliable. P.W. 2 Shri Sunil Chandra 
Sarkar, who claims to he the Assistant Secretary of the Union, admitted 
that they did not intervene on behalf of the workman at the time. His 
subsequent evidence that on application was made by the Union to the 
Labour Directorate for reinstatement of Shri Jatindra Nath Roy runs 
counter to the evidence of P.W. 1 and is not borne out by the records of 
conciliation proceedings and is apparently untrue. After the reference the 
workman himself filed his written statement. Only during hearing the 


2808 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 = [Parr I 


Assistant Secretary of the Union, P.W. 2 Shri Suml Chandra Sarkar, had 
been examined to say that the Union supports his cause. But his words 
of mouth would. not turn it into a collective dispute. Apart from a vague 
allegation that the workmen approached the management to roinstuate 
Shri Jatindra Nath Roy, bis additional written statement filed in reply to 
preliminary objection does not even contain a claim that the Union supports 
his cause. The case ay made out therein of his having ventilated the 
grievances of co-workers and acted in the interest of the workmen in the 
employ of the Company would not constitute a collective dispute. The 
dispute as referred to is pure and simple an individual dispute and it 
appears that it was at no time either ‘before or after the reference taken 
up by the workmen of the Company or any Union. 


Now the question is whether an individual dispute like the present one 
can be said to come within the language of the definition of ‘‘industrial 
dispute’ in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It has, of 
course, been so held by the Full Bench of the Labour Appellate Tribunal 
in the case already referred to, but then, on behalf of the Company, 
reliance has been placed on the two decisions of the Calcutta High Court 
reported, respectively, in 55 C.W.N., 256 and 57 C.W.N.,, 169, wherein 
it was held that an individual dispute was not an industrial dispute as 
defined in the Act. It was also pointed out to me that the Madras High 
Court as also the High Court at Patna had similarly held regarding the 
question (vide A.I.1. 1951, Madras, 616 and 1..1..J. 1954, Volume II, 21). 
As the decisions are not uniform, the question arises which is to be followed 
by the Stute Tribunal. Under article 227 of the Constitution, every 
টা in the State is subject to the judicial supervision of the State High 
Court. It being so, it is obvious that the law laid down by the High 
Court is the law as far as that State is concerned and every Tribunal in 
that State is bound to accept that law. His Lordship Chagla, C.J., of 
Bombay’ High Court also so observed in the case between Gambhirji 
Odharji and Labour Appellate Tribunal of India and others reported in 
1965 L.L.J., Volume II, page 202. In the circumstances following the 
decisions of the Calcutta High Court, T find that the dispute as it 1s, is not 
an industrial dispute and as such the reference is incompetent. The 
preliminary objection must therefore succeed. The Tribunal cannot, 
therefore, give any relief to the workman Shri Jatindra Nath Roy. 


Had it been otherwise, I would have found that the termination of 
employment of the workman without assiguing any reason was not justified. 
According to the written statement of the Company, the said Shri Jatindra 
Nath Roy was appointed in a post on probation for one year on lst March 
1954. سن‎ to both sides, the said Shri Jatindra Nath Roy had served 
at the date of termination of employment for about a year. The Company, 
according to both sides, has no standing orders. As per Model Standing 
Orders, a probationer is a workman who is provisionally employed to fill a 
permanent vacancy in a post and has not completed three months’ service 
therein. In the circumstances when the workmen had completed more than 
three months’ service, he censed to be a probationer and must be deemed 
to have been permanent and the Company had no right to discharge him 
in the way aa it did. He could not have heen treated as a temporary work- 
man either as it was not alleged or proved that he was engaged for work 
which was of an essentially temporary nature likely to be finished within 
a limited period. The Company’s case during hearing that he was surplus 
and as such was discharged cannot be sustained as the evidence of the 


Past 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2809 


Company's witness, D.W. 1 Shri Santosh Kumar Sen Gupta, shows -that 
after the dischayge of Shri Jntindra Nath Roy another clerk was appointed 
in the workshop. As, however, the preliminary objection succeeds, no 
relief can be afforded to the workman. 


It 1s awarded accordingly. 
Jictated and corrected by me. 


J. MAITRA, JITENDRA NATH MAITRA, 
Judge. Judge, Third Industrial Tribunol.

in the matter of a complaint under section ھ33‎ of the Industrial Disputes

= 


AWARD 


The contention of the employees is that they put in over 18 months’ 
continuous, satisfactory and effictent service in their respective capacities 
under this Municipality, but they were discharged with effect from 12th 
February 1956 by the Municipal authorities, without taking express 
permission in writing from the Tribunal, before which the main case was 
then pending. 


The Municipality, that is the opposite party, contended that the 
applicants were purely temporary employees, and as such no permission of 
the Tribunal under section 33 of the Act was necessary for discharging 
them. The Municipality has further stated that it did not require any 
longer the services of these employees, and accordingly terminated their 
services with effect from 12th February 1956 with one month’s notice. 
It may be stated in this connection that the Municipality filed a supple- 
mentary written statement at the time of hearing raising some legal 
objection as to the maintainability of the present complaint. 


1 shall disposo of the legal objection first. It is contended by the 
Municipality that notice on the Municipal Commissioners by ٥۹ 
complainants under section 68901) of the Bengal Municipal Act should 
have been served hefore filing the present complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act before the Tribunal. Section 535 of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1932, says that no suit or other legal proceedings shall he 
brought against the Commissioner of any Municipality for any 801 
purporting to be done under that Act, or any rule or by-law made there- 
under until expiration of one month next after notice in writing has been 
delivered or left at the office of such Commissioners. In my view, no such 
notice, as contemplated in section 535 was required for the present case, 
because the present case can neither strictly be deemed to be a suit nor 
other legal proceedings brought against the Commissioners of Hooghly- 
Chinsurah Municipality within the meaning of sectior 535 of the Bengal 
Municipal Act. The Act complained of in the present case, originated 
during the pendency of the main dispute before this Tribunal, in respect 
of which a reference waa already made by the Government for adjudication. 
So, the present application cannot be deemed to be a suit or independent 
legal proceedings—it is rather an offshoot of the original dispute. Further- 
more, J am not aware of any authority, in which it has been held that 
section 535 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932, applies also to industrial 
disputes between the Municipalities and their workmen, referred to the 
Tribunals by the Goverument for adjudication. So, section 535 of the 
Bengal Municipal Act can have no application to the present case. Section 
548(2) of the Bengal Municipal Act mentioned also in the supplementary 
written statement of the Municipality, does not obviously apply in the 
present case. Accordingly, the legal objection as raised in the supple- 
mentary written statement is overruled. 


Next point that is urged on behalf of the opposite party is that these 
employees, who have been discharged, happened to be temporary hands 
and they were not permanent employees of the Municipality. So, 1t was 
argued that the question of obtaining permission from the Tribunal under 
section 33 of the Act did not and could not arise. I may say straightway 
that there is no substance or merit in this argument. Section 33 can have 
no application where temporary emplovees are entertained for a specific 
purpose or for a specific period. In such an event, their employment comes 
to an end on the conclusion of that purpose or of that period. It cannot 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 2811‏ ۷۱ کترہ 


০ 77525555555 
pe denied that the appointment ‘of tentporary hands terminates when that 
riod is over and when that work is ftnished. Such termination is 
nutomatic more or Jess. In such a case, of dourse, no permission of the 
Tribunal is necessary. In the instant cuse, if the employees when enter- 
tained had been told that their services were for the temporary period for 
specific work or purpose, then their employments would cease, when that 
eriod 18 reached, or that purpose and the job are accomplished. But I do 
not find sufficient evidence on the record in the present case to justify the 
yiew that the employees knew that they were being entertained for a 
temporary perod for specific purpose and job. There is no such evidence 
وم‎ to the object or the period of their’employment. They were no doubt 
taken In a8 temporary clerks, but it is proved that they continued in their 
services for more than 18 months, and they got also increments. In the 
circumstances, they could not be discharged without the permission of the 
Tribunal, Admittedly, at the time when they were discharged, the main 
dispute was pending before this Tribunal. Yet no permission of the 
fribunal was taken while discharging them. In my view, prior permission 
1 the Tribunal was necessary, even though these employees happened to 
he temporary hands. I may say in this connection that section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act is not confined to permanent employees only—it 
applies to all workmen. So, the termination of services of these four 
petitioners without the permission of this Tribunal, was contravention of 
section 99. In the circumstances, the Tribunal holds that the present 
application under section 88۸ is competent. If any authority is needed for 
such ty view, 1 would refer to the decisions reported in 1954 1.1.4. (i), 809 
ind 1963 L.L.J. (ii), 882. 


It ia. now well settled that where section 33 has been contravened, the 
Tribunal mut enquire into the merits of the discharge or dismissal on ao 
complaint being made-under section 33A. As the complaint has to be 
investigated by the Tribunal, as if it were a dispute referrd to or pending 
hefore it, the scope of investigation on the merits must exactly he the same 
where the subject matter of the challenged discharge or dismissal had 
heen the subject matter of an independent reference under section 10 of 
the Act. The merits of the impugned discharge are, therefore, to be 
considered by the Tribunal. This leads me necessarily to enter into the 
merits of the discharge of the petitioners. Of the four employees, Shri 
Muralidhar Palit, though he signed the petition of complaint under section 
۵۸۸ did not appear hefore the Tribunal at the time of hearing to depose. 
The lawyer and also the Secretary of the Union said that they had no 
instruction on his behalf. The other three employees did not say anything 
material regarding Shri Palit. In the circumstances, the Tribunal refrains 
from adjudicating upon his case, which ia kept open. Regarding the other 
three petitioners—Shri Gobinda Kinkar Dutta, Shri Amiya Kumar 
Majumdar and Shri Lakshmi Narayan Modak—they have all deposed before 
this Tribunal. It appears from the evidence that Shri Gobinda Kainkar 
Dutta was appointed as a clerk in the Tax Department of the Hooghly- 
Chinsurah Municipality on 3lst March 1954 and worked till 11th February 
1956, and the other two clerks, that 1s Shri Amiya Kumar Majumdar and 
Shri Lakshmi Narayan Modak joined their appointment in the said 
Municipality on 2nd June 1954 and worked till 11th February 1956. They 
got increments in course of their employment. There 1s nothing to show 
that they were found inefficient, or their work was _ unsatisfactory. 
PW. 2 Shri Amiya Kumar Majumdar has deposed that four persons were 


2812 THE CALCUTTA UAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 = [Parr ] 


taken in by the Municipality after their diacharge, and they were appointed 
on 29th March 1956. So, it eannot be believed that the services of thegg 
three employees had to be terminatgd for faucity of work, and this state. 
nent of Shri Amiya Kumar “Majewhdar stood unchallenged and 
uncontradicted. The Municipality has adduced no evidence to show that 
since the discharge of these three employees, they did not take new clerkg. 
O.P.W. 1 Shri Nitya Gopal Bose, Accountant, who deposed on behalf of 
the opposite party, has not said a word about -% in his evidence. Sp» 
it appears that the Municipality could not satisfy the Tribunal as to the 
real reason why the three employees mentioned abdWe were discharged fron 
12th February 1956, although they jsut in about two years service under the 
Municipality. The very fact that new hands were taken in immediately 
after the discharge of these three employees, indicates that they were not 
really discharged for paucity or want of work for them in the Municipality, 
but they were discharged with some ulterior motive. For reasons best 
known to the Municipality, the authorities wanted to getrid of them. The 
fact remains that though the appointments of these three employees were 
temporary, their appointments were for an indefinite period, and __ the 
employees continued in their service for a pretty Jong time. Therefore, the 
Municipality could not take shelter behind the plea that their appoint. 
ments automatically came to an end without any action on its part. So, 
the order of discharge in respect of these three employees should he set 
aside, because they were discharged without the permission of the Tribunal 
and also without good reasons. The application, therefore, succeeds ৪0 
far as it relates to these three employees. 


Accordingly, it is ordered that these three employees—Shnri Gobinda 
Kinkar Dutta, Shri Lakshmi Narayan Modak and Shri Amiya Kumar 
Majumdar—be reinstated in their former posts or in posts equivalent 
thereto carrying similar pay and other emoluments within 15 days from 
the date of publication of this award in the Calcutta Gazette. Shri 
Lakshmi Narayan Modak and Shri Amivya Kumar Majumdar shall get back 
pay and dearness allowance at the rates last drawn for the entire period 
from the date of their discharge till reinstatement. As regards Shri 
Gobinda Kinkar Dutta, he will get such back pay and dearness allowance 
for the period from the date of his discharge till 4th May 1956, because it 
appears from his evidence that he has been working in the School Board 
in a leave vacancy since 5th May 1956. The payments as directed above 
should be made also within the period mentioned above. 


No adjudication is made regarding the complaint of Shri Muralidhar 
Palit for the reasons stated already. Huis case is kept open. 


This is the award of the Tribunal.

(Food and Supplies) 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 6786F.8.—30th June 1956.—In exercise of the powers conferred 
by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India, the Governor 
| pleased to make the following rules to regulate the pay of the staff in 
the Food, Relief and Supplies (Food and Supplies) Department, viz. :— 


RULES 


1, With effect from 186 April 1956, every member of the staff in the 
Food, Relief and Supplies (Food and Supplies) Department who holds a 
post specified in column 2 of the annexed Schedule shall draw pay in the 
revised scule shown in column 4 thereof: 


Provided that if he was in service in the department on dist March 
1966 and has been continuing in the départment since then he may, at 
hie option— 


(৫) draw pay in the revised scale, with effect from the day following 
the date of increment, if any, falling due after the Jlst March 
1956 in the present pay of the post held by him on the 3lst 
March 1956, or 


(by) retain the present pay in the post held by him on 818۲ March 
1956 as well as in the post or posts to which he has been or may 
hereafter be promoted or transferred within Food, Relief and 
Supplies (Food and Supplies) Department.

eave. 


(b) The option exercised under this rule shall be final and cannot be 
modified at any subsequent date. 


8. The initial pay of a person who is liable to draw pay in the revised 
scal® shall be fixed as follows:— 


(৫) Where the aggregate of the present pay and the ad-interim 
increases in pay as admissible on 3lst March 1956 is less than 
the minimum of the revised scale, the initial pay shall be fixed 
at such minimum.

Increases in pny as admissible on 918 March 1956 is equal to 
or higher than the maximum of the revised acale, the initial

DECISION 


This is an appeul trom an award of the Third Industrial Tribunal, West 
Bengal. The issue reterred to the Tribunal by Order No. 2671Dis./D/111- 
129/54, dated the 25th May 1954, was ‘“‘whether the workmen are entitled 
to have any bonus tor the year 1953۲ What should be the amount thereof?’ 


2. The learned Tribunal rejected the claim. Hence this appeal by 
the workmen. 

3. At the hearing of the appeal, an application was moved on behalf 
of the Company tor adjournment on the ground that Shr: Manna, Bar.-at-Law, 
engaged for the Company had to go out of Calcutta and would not 
return before the 8th April 1956 and that the Managing LTurtner was 
indisposed. We rejected the application. 

4. The workimen’s representative argued thot bonus for the year 1925: 
was payable as customary Puja bonus which had become a condition of their 
service. ‘he Company has been in existence for 80 to 90 years. It has 
paia bonus only m two years. During the year 1949, it paid Puja 00705 
equal to seven days’ wages while in the year 1950, it paid Puja bonus equal 
to nine daya’ wages. No honus was paid either prior to 1949 or in [1 
and 1952. It was not even claimed in the years 1951 and 1952, though it 
hud been paid in the two previous years. 


5. Appellanf’s:case is that in 1951 and 1952, there was no Union and, 
therefore, no demand could be made. Conceding only for the sake of argu- 
ment that aheence of a Umon may be a 8990 reason for the workmen’s 
inubility to, make or press a demand for bonus, still for a claim to Puja 


296 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 (Parr TA 
٢ 
সা پت لس ٹج چچجچچچجچ جس سج جچت تس ےت چس -سجچیسسسےٌ.یسپشکسیسبیپیٹتٹ بب--ے-‎ ০০০০ 


bonus as a condition of service it has to be shown that it has been paid durmy 
17111) good number of years from which a custom may reasonably be 
widersed. The number of years may differ according to the facts of each 
مت‎ it is not the workmen’s case that bonus was a condition of service 
as uo result of any agreement. They asked the Tribunal to infer it from 
the employer’s conduct of paying it during the years 1940 and 1950, which 
wie said to be years of loss. Non-payment 01 Puja bonus during 1951 and 
1952 mdicates that the employer did not like to continue the practice 
stated by him in 1949. Even assuming that the Company paid Jdurga 
Puja bonus in spite of losses in 1949 and 1940, can it be said in this case 
that bonus had been paid during a sufficiently large number of years, in 
order to lead to the inference that it had hecome a condition of service? 
We answer the question in the negative. 


Next, it was agued alternatively that the Company had not proved‏ ۔نا 
any loss in the year 1953 and therefore, bonus should be ordered to be paid‏

It is clear from this that the workmen did not like to avail of the opportu-‏
