For the Respondent: Shri M. Mazumdar, Factory Manager, 


State: West Bengal. 
Industry: Kngineering. 


DECISION 


This appeal is preferred against the award of the Second Industrial 
Tribunal, West Bengal, dated 26th July 1954 and published in the 
Caleutta Gazette, dated 19th August 1954, under the orders of the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal No. 3809])is, /D/10L-162/54, dated 31d August 1954, 
by which retrenchment of 95 workmen, dated Jdth May 1953 and lay. cft 
of some other workmen in two batches on Ist June 1903 and Ist July 1903 
made by the Company were found to be justified. At the time of hearing 
of the appeal the appellant gave up the appeal in so far as it ghallenged 
the finding of the lower Tribunal in respect of the lay off and confined fhe 
arguments only against the finding in respect of the retrenghment. 


2. ‘The lower Tribunal examined in detail the finanojal and trading 
position of the Company as disclosed in the oral evidence of the Manager 
and in the documentary evidence produced by the Company and came to 
the conclusion that there was general decline in the business and fall in 
the production of this Company which manufactures to orders vil containers 
and drums and supphes them to dealers in oil and vegetable ghee aud that 
there was nominal profit of Rs. 47 in the year 1902 and وط‎ 1088 of 


[art TA] 


THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 


کس ہے ے جح ہم مس ہے موہ ٹمکسکجسوسوسبسسجے سس cr ললঙ‏ 


Rs. 74,325 in 1953 and that production fell heavily by May 1953 and that 
there was dearth of orders. There is no evidence on the side of the 
appellant to meet the oral and documentary evidence offered by the 
Company. The curious argument advanced by the appellant is that no 
evidence was adduced because the burden of proof was on the Company. 
But the Company adduced evidence to discharge its burden and the effent 
of that evidence will stand unless تی‎ by counter-evidence. The 
learned representative of the appellant had practically nothing mote 10 
suy against the above finding of the lower Tribunal. 


3. The learned representative of the appellant submitted that im 
making the retrenchment, the Company was actuated by ulterior motives 
und that his case stands or falls by 1 and submitted that the Union came 
into existance on 10th December 1952, submitted its charter of demands 
on 3rd March 1953, a joint meeting was convened by the Labour Comnnis- 
sioner on 5th May 1958 and that the retrenchment took place on 911 May 
1953 and the meeting did not take place and that the Manager brought 
about the retrenchment without notice and without the previous sanction 
of the Directors of the Cempany and that these facts show that the 
retrenchment was not bona fide and was made to punish the workmen for 
having formed a Union and put torward demands, 


4. If the decline in business and fall in production and lack of profit 
in 1952 and loss in 1953 be not true, the above facts urged by the 
appellant may be useful to show that the Company might be actuated ۷ 
ulterior motives. But in view of the unchallenged proof of that decline 
in business, and fall in production due to dearth of orders, and loss, it can 
only be concluded that there was un unfortunate coincidence of the bad 
days on which the Company fell and the time chosen by the Union to ۶ 
forward its charter of demands. So far as the lack of previous sunction 
of the Directors is concerned, we cannot see liow it affects the nghis اہ‎ 
the workmen one way or the other. So fur as workers are concerned 
subsequent approval of the retrenchment is as fateful to them as a previous 
sanction for retrenchinent. Hence there cun be no_ difference Mateo 
previous sanction and subsequent approval in so tar &9 bona fides of the 
Company are concerned. We are not able to find that the Company was 
actuated by ulterior motives in eftecting the retrenchment. 


§. It is satisfactorily proved by documentary evidence that all the 
retrenched men were temporary hands with o short service of about turee 
months. Still the Company voluntarily paid four days’ wages 28 
retrenchment compensation and workmen willingly received the same and 
passed receipts. The lower Tribunal ordered 15 days wages in lieu of 
notice to be paid to the retrenched workmen, but the Company has not 
chosen to appeal. These circuinstances also indicate the bona fides of the 
workmen. 

6. We are in entire agreement with the lower Tribunal in holding 
that the retrenchment was necessitated by bona fide trade reasons, the 
business having been on the decline und loss having been suffered. There 
has been no challenge in this appeal on the number of men retrenched or 
selection of particular persons for retrenchment, Originally 60 persons 
were proposed to be retrenched but five persons were cut out from that 
list. The remaining strength of the establishment has remained constunt 
from May 1958 till now showing that the retrenchment could nov be 
excessive. Under these circumstances ithe lower Tribunal was _ perfectly 
correct in not awarding reinstatement or more compensation tu the 
retrenched men. Hence this appeal is dismissed. We award no costs 1.8 
the appeal is on behalf of retrenched and unemployed workmen.

IN THE HONOURABLE DORA لان تا‎ TRIBUNAL OF INDIA, 


UTTA 
Appeal No. Cal.-203 of 1954 
Gulf O11 Workers’ Union, Calcutta ... Appellant, 
ig VETSUSs 
Messrs. Gulf Oil (India), Ltd., Calcutta we dtespondent. 


In the matter of an appeal against the award of Shri M. .ا‎ Chakravartti, 
Judge, Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, made on 2nd June 1954 in 
respect of an industrial dispute between the above parties. 


Dated the 27th January 1956.

Mr. V. N. DIKSHITULU, Aember. 
Appearances : 
Kor the Appellant: Shri J. Pandey, Officer of the Union. 
For the Respondent: Shri 8S. .کا‎ Mullick, Solicitor, Sanderson & Morgan, 
Calcutta. 

State: West Bengal 
Industry : 


DECISION 


This appeal is preferred by the workmen of Messrs. Gulf Oil (India), 
Ltd. (to be hereinafter referred to as the Company), represented by Gult 
Oil Workers’ Union, Calcutta (to be hereinafter referred to us the Union) 
against the award of the Sixth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, dated 
Od June 1954, and published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 191 July 1954, 
under the orders of the Government of West Bengal, No. 3048))is./D/5)- 
11/54, dated 19th June 1994, Two issues were referred to the lower 
Tribunal for adjudication, viz., (1) bonus, (2) whether the Compauy was 
justified in terminating the services of Shri T. C. Mehta. What relief 1s 
i entitled to? Both the issues are subject matter of this appeal and will 
be dealt with one after the other in the above order. 


2. fssue No. 1.—The workmen claimed one month’s wages 7৭ bonus 
for the years 1951 and 1952 in addition to one month’s wages paid as Puja 
bonus in each of the said two years voluntarily by the Company. The 
lower Tribunal rejected the claim for 1901 on the ground that it was 
belated having been made only towards the end of 1902 and rejected the 
claim for bonus for 1952 on the ground that the Company suffered huge loss 
in that year. It is conceded that in the year 1902 there was loss. Hence, 
there can be no valid claim for bonus by way of participation in the 
prosperity of the concern in that year. In 1951, there was a net profit 01 
Rs, 63,609 for a period of 14 months according to the balance-sheet. 
Hence, for 12 months the proportionate profit should be Rs. 56,022. Tasn- 
tion thereon comes to Rs. 23,684 as shown in the memorunduim of caleulation 
filed by the Company before this Tribunal. Sia per cent. return on nine 
lakhs of rupees which is the paid-up capital of the Calcutta branch of the 
Company to which the present dispute relates, comes to Ks. 64,000. 10591) 
without taking into account any other pnor charges, there will he no 
aviuulable surplus left over according to the Full Bench formula of the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal. Hence, there can be no valid cluim for bonus 
by way of participation in the prosperity of the concern in 1951 also, even 
if the cluim be held not belated as held by the lower Tribunal. 


۹. Obviously for above reason, the appellant’s learned representative 
before this Tribunal urged that the claim to bonus in this case is not by 
way of profit sharing but that it has been a condition of service of the 
workmen of this Company to be paid bonus represented by two months’ 
Wages per annum and that half of it is payable in September before Pujas 
and the other half in April irrespective of profit or loss. This is a clear 
atter-thought and a variation of the Union’s case. In paragraph 10 of the 
written statement of the Union filed betore the lower Tribunal, it was 
urged that one month’s wages were paid as bonus at the time of Puja and 
another month’s wages were paid as bonus out of profit every year and that 
in 1951 and 1952, no bonus out of profit was paid. Lower down in the 
same paragraph it was mentioned that bonus was u part of the wage and 
mere a condition of service than extra paymeut in consideration of profit 
vecruable, This statement reads like enunciation of the theory of the 
Union upon which the bonus has been granted in the past and does 701 
read as a statement of fact that bonus of two months’ wages was 10010 
irrespective of profit or loss. In any event, there is no evidence of —pav- 
ment of bonus in April consisting of one month’s wages in any year in which 
the Company suffered loss. Admittedly, the amount of bonus paid in 
April was not uniformly one month’s wages. There is no dispute now about 
bonus payable before Pujas in 195] and 1952, For these reasons, we hold 
that the Union has not made out a condition of service that honus of ০৪ 
month's wages should be paid irrespective of profit or loss in April of 
Abt | year. Hence, the claim to bonus as now advanced by the Union is 
hereby rejected, in agreement with the lower Tribunal, though for slightly 
different reasons. 


_ 4. Issue No. 2.—The services of Shri T. C. Mehta who was entertained 
in service on 1061) December 1948 were terminated with effect from 14 
November 1951. The lower Tribunal found that the termination was 
unjustified and awarded compensation of four months’ basic pay of Rs. 100 
and dearness allowance of Rs. 100. The Company has not preferred any 
appeal. The Union only appealed and contends that Shri T. C. Mehta 
should have been reinstated and that his claim to Rs. 27,490 under various 
heads detailed in the written statement should have been allowed. 


® As Industrial Tribunal, unlike a Court of law governed by the law 
of master and servant, has jurisdiction to reinstate a = workman whose 
services ure terminated without justification; but, it does not mean — that 
in all such cases reinstatement should be ordered. The object of Industrtal 
adjudication in to settle disputes in such a manner as to bring about or 
restore peace and harmony مز‎ the employer and employee — relatiens. 
Whether reinstatement is conducive to such a purpose or not depends oa 
the facts of cach case. THlence, it should be a matter of discretion to be 
exercised by the Industrial ‘Tribunal judicially with reference to the facts 
and circumstances of each case. This is the law as laid down by the 
Calcutta High Court in 1955 11 L.L.J. 214 (Bank of India vs, Labour 


298 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 19, 1956 [Part TA 
এলাচ مجح سے‎ ্)্শ্লশশ্গট 58897859৯৯৪. 


nant TA] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JOLY 19, 1956 209 
এল শল্য 


Appellate Tribunal of India & Ors.). If the decision is so exercised, the 
Appellute Tribunal should be reluctant to interfere with the way in which 
the «discretion is exercised by the trial Tribunal. Therefore, the point is 
whether the lower Tribunal has exercised the discretion judicially and not 
arbitrarily or perversely. In this case the Company proved to the satis- 
faction of the lower Tribunal that Shri T. ©. Mehta played a dirty trick 
in trying ما‎ prove and in relying upon a document, dated 12th May 1950 
said to have been executed by Mr. Hempson at Calcutta whereas سا‎ fact 
Mr. Hempson was at Bombay on that day. Such being the case the 
Company can no more he expected to repose confidence in Shri Mehta ond 
Shri Mehta also may not be happy in service with the Company, _ if 
reinstated. In view of this circumstance, the lower Tribunal held 0171 
compensation was the proper relief in this case and not reinstatement. We 
have no hesitation in saying that the lower Tribunal has correctly exercised 
its judicial discretion and no interference with it is called for. Shri Mehta 
served the Company only for a little over three years. The award of four 
months’ basic allowance as compensation, if at all, errs on the generoua 
side. The other claims advanced on behalf of Shri Mehta are amounts 
alleged to he due to him Gnder the terms and conditions of his service while 
he was in employment. Such claims have not been referred to the lower 
Tribunal for adjudication. Only relief arising out of the termination 01 
his service, it found 10 be unjustifiable, has been referred to the lower 
Tribunal. Proper forms of relief in such a case are reinstatement or, in 
the alternative, compensation for loss of employment. Claims to money 
alleged ہا‎ be due under terms of employment while in employment cannot 
participate in the characteristics of compensation for loss of employment 
as they should be due irrespective of the termination or retention § in 
service. Hence, none of the several claims advanced can come under the 
category of compensation for loss of employment nor can they be considered 
as incidental thereto. Hence, the Union cannot successfully urge in these 
proceedings such of the cluims of Shri Mehta os have not been awarded by 
the lower Tribunal. 


In the result, the appeal is dismissed. No costs.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND 7٤8 


In most of the advanced countries, the hours of work 
for industrial workers have been reduced from 48 hours to 
44 Hours and even less, The workers in thoy countries are 
now demanding a 40-hour week. This demand arises 
primarily becatse of the intensification of work that has 
recently. Jeen introduced in almost all industries causing 
excessive exertion. 


This Amendment to the Factories Act, 1948, seeks to 
reduce the hours of work from 48 hours to 44 hours a week 
in all factories.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health 


NOTIFICATION 
No, BLT. /2647/2R-37/56.—18th July 1956.—Whereas the Governor is 
batished that the municipal area of Ranaghat is threatened with an out- 
break of cholera; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of 
section 2 of the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (11] of 1897), the (dovernor 
is pleased to prescribe the following temporary regulations for the preven- 
tion and control of cholera, and for the medical inspection, isolation, 
observation and surveillance of persons suffering from, or suspected of 
being infected with, cholera in the said municipal area for a period of 
three months : — 


TEMPORARY REGULATIONS FOR THE PREVENTION AND 
CONTROL OF CHOLERA. 


1. In these regulations, unless there 28 anything repugnant in the 
subject or context— 


(৫) ‘‘Health Officer’? means the Health Officer of the municipality; 


(b) “Sanitary Inspector’? means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
municipality ; 


(c) ‘Suspected cholera” means any disease accompanied by vomiting 
and diarrhoea; 


(d) ‘‘Patient’’ means a person suffering from or suspected to be suffering 
from cholera; 


(6) ‘Medical practitioner’? means any person practising the medical 
profession. 


1677 


1678 THE CAL, GAZ. EXTRY., JUPY 20, 1996 [Parr ] 


2. Whenever any land is held jointly by two or more persons, whether 
as owners or occupiers of that land, such persons shall be held jomtly and 
severally liable for carrying 6ut any measure ordered in o notice under these 
regulations, and the names of any ome or more of such joint-holders may he 
entered upon such notice at the discretion of the Health Officer or a Sanitar 
Inspector and the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector shall not be bound 
to enter the names of all the joint-holdera in the notice. 


Notices. 


38. If in any case the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers 
that the issue of a notice under these regulations is likely to lead te such 
an amount of delay as might facilitate the spread of cholera he may forth- 
with take such steps as he may think fit for carrying out the work, and shal! 
thereafter, as soon as possible, issue a notice on the person concerned stating 
the reason why such work has been carried out. 


4, If any measure which the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector has, 
by a notice issued under these regulations, required to be carried out 
he not carried out to his satisfaction within the time stated in the notice, 
the Health Officer or a Sanitary Jnspector shall be entitled to carry out 
the measure. 


Costs and compensation. 


5. (1) All expenses incurred in carrying out any work in pursuance of 
un order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the municipality 
except in any case where the order directs a person to carry out any work in 
relation to property in his possession, in which case the expenses shall be 
puid by that person: 


Provided that where the conditions, which led the Health Officer or a 
Sanitary Inspector to pass such an order, are not attributable to any act or 
default of the persons in possession of the property, the municipality may 
pay to such person the whole or a part of the expenses incurred by him in 
carrying out the order. 


(2) The municipality may recover all expenses incurred by the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector in carrying out the measure under regulation 
4 from the person or persons to whom the notice was originally issued. 


0. The municipality shall pay adequate compensation to any person who 
hos sustained substantial loss or damage by reason of anything done under 
these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall receive any compensation for anything 
done, or suffered under these regulations, if he has failed to carry out an 
order “issued under these regulations within the time specified in the order 
and to the satisfaction of the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector. 


Location of disease. 


7. When a case of cholera or suspected cholera occurs in a house, the 
nearest male relative in attendance upon the patient, or in the absence of 
auy such relative the occupier of the house, or if the occupier be the patient. 
some male inmate of the house shall, within twenty-four hours of the onset 
of the disease, give information regarding the ovcurrence of such case eithe 
personally or in writing to the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector.

‘municipality shall forthwith give notice of any case of cholera brought to

9. Registrars of births and deaths shall supply to the Health Officer or

trom -time to time call upon them to furnish. 


10. The Health Officer or o Sanitary Inspector may examine any 
person who is, or suspected to be, suffering from cholera or who, in his 
opinion, may be infected with or likely to spread cholera. 


Isolation of patients and evacuation of houses, etc, 


11. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers 
that the isolation of any patient is a precaution necessary for the protection 
of the neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe 
isolation and may order the nearest relative in attendance on the patient, or 
the occupier of the house in which the patient is staying to arrange for the 
\solation of the patient in such a manner and for such a time as may be 
approved by the Health Officer or the Sanitary Inspector. 


He 81701] not direct the patient to be removed from the house unless it is 
m his opinion impossible to make proper arrangements for his isolation 
therein. 


12, The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that 
১100 person, who has in his opinion been exposed to infection from cholera, 
shall take such drugs in such quantities as may be specified by the Health 
(Officer or 0 Sanitary Inspector or shall submit himself to anti-cholera 
inoculation within a time to be specified in the order. 


13. No person shall enter any place wherein a patient is isolated under 
نا ات‎ 11 without the permission of the Health Officer or a Sanitary 
007. | 1 


14. The municipality shall provide free of charge suitable places, with 
nevessary attendants, medicine, diet nnd other necessaries for persons 
isolated under regulation 11: provided that a private individual may 
provide places certified by the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector as 
heing fit for the purpose of such isolation. 


16. If it is not possible for the Municipal Commissioners to provide 
suitable places with necessary attendants, diet and other necessaries for 
isolation of the patient or if satisfactory arrangement for such isolation is 
not also possible in the house where the patient is staying, the patient shall 
he aent, under proper sanitary precautions, to the hospital within or outside 
the nearest municipality where there is suitable arrangement for isolation. 


16. No person, who is or has been suffering from cholera shal] have 
the place where he has been ataving until he har received from the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Tospector written permission to do so.

17. The Health Officer or 0 Sanitary Inspector may require any 
person to allow to be curried out by such agency, and within such time ag 
may be specified in the order, such measures for the disinfection or evacua- 
tion of any premises in the occupation of such persons or for the disinfec. 
tion or destruction of any of his personal effects, as the said officer or

18. The Health Officer or oa Sanitary Inspector may direct the 
owner or occupier of any premises to cause to be inoculated with anti-cholerg 
vaccine within o time specified in the order any person residing on such 
uremises and under the control of such owner or occupier if the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector is of opinion that such person has been 
exposed to infection from cholera. 


19. The Health Officer or ao Sanitary Inspector may forbid any 
person who has been a patient or who hus, to his knowledge, been in contuct 
with a patient to act as vendor of any article for such period as may be 
specified in the order. 


20. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
n patient except in the case where a patient is carried with proper 
precautions to a hospital. 


21. No person shall sell any article which has been in contact with a 
patient until it has been disinfected to the satisfaction of the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector. 


22. No person shall expose in any street, shop, bazar, or any public 
place any clothing, bedding or other article which has been in contact with 
n patient or shall cause or suffer such articles to be carried in any public 
conveyance. but nothing in this regulation shall apply to a person who 
transmits with proper precautions against spreading the disease any such 
article for the purpose of having the same disinfected. 


23. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
the dead body of any person who has died of cholera without the previous 
written permission of the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector and 
without taking proper precautions against spreading the said disease. 


Water-supply. 


24. (1) When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector is of 
opinion that the water in any well, tank, pool or other possible source of 
water-supply is contaminated or is likely to be contaminated, he may at 
once-take such steps as he deems necessary to close such well, tank, pool or 
other source of water-supply, or may require the owner or occupier of Jand 
upon which such well, tank, pool or source of water-supply is situated, to 
take steps to close the same to the satisfaction of the Health Officer 
or the Sanitary Inspector as the case may be, within such time as may be 
specified in the order. 


(2) The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may require such 
owner or occupier to keep during such a period as shall e specified 
in the order any well, tank, pool or other sources of water-supply closed 
under paragraph (1) of this regulation. 


Ezplanation.—In this regulation, ہا“‎ close’ includes the placing of 
watchman to prevent access to the well, tank, pool or other sources of water:

25. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector is of opinion 
that the water in any well, tank, pool or source of water-supply is cOn- 
taminated he may disinfect it or order 168 owner or occupier to disinfect it 


with such disinfectants us he may specify in such quantities and at such 
times a8 he may think fit. 


06. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may prohibit persons 
from entering into or using for drinking, bathing, or any other purpose, 
during such period as may be specified in the order, the water in any well, 
(2100) pool or other possible source of water-supply, which, in his opinion, 1s 
contaminated or likely to be contaminated. 


27. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may, by an order pub- 
lished at such places as he may think fit, set apart any well, tank, part 
of a river, stream or channel not being private property, or being private 
property with the consent of the owner, for the supply of water for drinking 
or culinary purposes and may prohibit therein or within a distance therefrom 
to be stated in the order all bathing, washing of clothes or animals, or other 
acts calculated to pollute the water; and may similarly set apart any well, 
tank, part of a river, stream or channel for the purpose of bathing or for the 
purpose of washing animals or clothes or for any other purpose connected 
with the health and cleanliness of the people using such water-supply. 


28. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may prohibit

29. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may (1) prohibit the

Ezplanatton.—In this regulation ‘‘nuisance’’ means anything which in 
the opinion of the Health Officer or Sanitary Inepector is likely to spread 
or to cause the outbreak of cholera. 


30. Whenever the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector is satisfied 
that the condition of any privy, urinal, drain, sewer, or cesspool is such 
as to cause risk of spreading cholera to the inhabitants of the neighbourhood 
he may order the occupier of the land in which such privy, urinal, drain, 
sewer or cesspool is situated to disinfect, or to allow an officer of the 
municipality to disinfect, the same with such disinfectants in such 
quantities and at such time as the said officer or inspector shall think fit.

such land or to remove any such drain, sewer, privy, or urinal or close any 


such cesspool within such time as may be fixed by the said officer or 
(nspector.

dispute between 101 specified Jute Mills and their workmen regarding some 
matters specified in a schedule to this Tribunal for adjudication. The award 
of this Tribunal in respect of this proceeding was published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated 6th October 1935. 


While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application under 
section 9:34 of the Industrial Disputes Act in case No. 218 of 1955, was 
filed by Shri Nagendra Nath Das on the allegation that he was an employee 
of the opposite party and he used to work as a sardar of the Mixing Depart- 
ment of the Mill, that on 2nd April 1954 the petitioner received a serious 
injury on his left hand in course of his duty for which he had to remain 
absent with the permission of the opposite party for his treatment, that 
the petitioner's left hand has been permanently injured and useless, that 
as it was nmpossible for the petitioner to work, the petitioner approached the 
Company and asked for the payment of gratuity, ات‎ wages due, 
Provident Fund money credited on both accounts and also for the leave 
wagey due, that the opposite party refused to pay the legal dues to the 
petitioner, that the opposite party oe contravened the provisions of section 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act by refusing to pay off the normal benefits 
during the pendency of the Tribunal and without taking permission from 
the Tribunal, that in the circumstances the petitioner prays for an award 
directing the Company to pay the petitioner the earned wages due for 19 
days, the leave wages due for the statutory period, Provident Fund mone\ 
including the employer’s contribution, gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ 
pay for each year of service for service of 14 years. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the opposite 
party, the Company filed its written statement in which it contended that 
the petitioner was a line sardar in the Webbing Department and not in the 
Mixing Department, that the opposite party admits the accident but denies

DECISTON 


We had not to enter into the merits of this case as the petitioner on 5th 
June 1956 filed a petition praying for permission to withdraw his petition 
for complaint under section 33A of the fndustrial Disputes Act. We have 
read and considered the petition and we grant the petitioner permission to

form a part of this award. As the petition of complaint under section 37۸ 
is withdrawn, there will be a ‘‘no dispute’? award in this case.

While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present upplication under‏ پ 
১101) SIA of the Industrial Disputes Act in case No. 15 of 1955, was‏ 
fled by Shri Pundeo Singh on the allegation that he had been working in‏ 
the said Mill as a durwan for about last 7 years, that the charge-sheet, was‏ 
served on the petitioner on the allegation that the petitioner‏ 
was found = sleeping while on duty, that neither any proper‏ 
enquiry was held nor the petitioner was given any hearing in person‏ 
vor any opportunity was given to the petitioner to prove his innocence, that‏ 
the petitioner was suspended before the employers filed any application for‏ 
permission before the Tribunal under section 83 of the Industrial Disputes‏ 
Act to dismiss lim, that the suspension and/or dismissal of the petitioner‏ 
was illegal and ultra vires, that the motive behind this victimisation is that‏ 
the petitioner retused to pay the usual bribe 00 Mr. ٢. 11. Pathankar, the‏ 
durwan-in-clrarge who is in the habit of accepting the same regularly from‏ 
the durwan for a long time, that as such the petitioner should be reinstated‏ 
to hia previous post, that the petitioner is also entitled to get full compensa-‏ 
tion for the period kept out of employment, that in the circumstances the‏ 
petitioner prays that the employers should he directed to reinstate him to‏ 
his previous post and 10 pay full compensation for the period he was kept‏ 
out of employment.‏ 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having heen served on the opposite 
party, the Company filed its written statement on Jrd March 1955 contend- 
ing that the application of the complainant Pundeo Singh is not maintain- 
uble as 1 does not reveal any violation of section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, that an application under section 33 of the Industrial J)isputes 
Act seeking permission of the Honourable Tribunal for the dismissal of 
Pundeo Singh has already been filed by the Company, that the application 
of the complainant contains various vague, misleading and false allegations, 
that the complainant was found sleeping on duty by the departmental-in- 
charge at 11-45 p.m. on 20th December 1954 and between 12-30 a.m. to 
12-45 a.m. on 21st December 1954, that as a serious theft of mill properties 
had occurred on the preceding night a warning had been issued to all 
durwans to be vigilant, that the complainant’s serious negligence of duty 
constituted a misconduct and a charge-sheet was issued to him on 218 
December 1954, calling upon him to explain his conduct, that after receiving 
his explanation, o full enquiry was held, that as a result of the enquiry 
the Manager found that Pundeo Singh was guilty of gross negligence of 
duty and accordingly decided that he should be dismissed but would remain 
suspended pending permission of the Tribunal, that in the circumstances 
the complainant is not entitled to reinstatement and/or any compensation as 
claimed by him and the the application of the complainant should be 
rejected on the preliminary point of law and/or on merits. 


NECISION 


Although a petition of complaint alleging violation of condition of 
service for failure to apply under section 33 for permission of this Tribunal 
has heen filed, it has now been proved by the employers that actually this is 
not the case. In fact they applied under section 88 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act for permission of the Tribunal. We have perused the 
applications under section 83 and under section 33A of the Industrial 

isputes Act and we find that the petition under section 88 covers the 
ground which forms the subject matter of the complaint under section ۸ 
of the Tndustrial Disputes Act and which has since been struck off as the 


a became functus officio after one month of the publication of the 
ard, 


1704 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 [Parr 1 


It has now been held by the Supreme Court in the case of رکا ون‎ 
Products of India Ltd. (1955 1[:.1۰,[., Vol. I, page 346) that it is the con- 
travention by the employer of the provision of section 88 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act or section 23 of the Appellate Tribunal Act which gives rise 
to a cause of action in favour of the workman to approach and move the 
respertive authority concerned of the additional jurisdiction and powers 
conferred on it by the section. The authority referred to in the section 
is a Court of Limited Jurisdiction and must accordingly he strictly confined 
to the exercise of functions and powers actually conferred on it by the Act 
which constituted it. 


In the present case it being proved that a petition seeking permission of 
the Tribunal was actually on the self-same grounds, we hold that the 
petition of complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act is not 
maintainable and we award accordingly.

parr I] THE CAL, GAZ, EXTRY., JULY 24, 6 1715 


refggred under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
ا‎ of 1947), the industrial dispute between 101 specified Jute Mills and 
their workmen regarding some matters specified in a schedule to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. The award of this Tribunal in respect of this 
proceeding was published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 6th October 5۰ 


While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application under 
section 38A of the Industrial Disputes Act in case No. 369 of 1965, was 
fled by Shri Gouri Shankar Roy on the allegation that he was a permanent 
workman having about 6 years of service, that the opposite party has kept 
the petitioner without work since 27th December 1954, that the opposite 
party filed an application under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
seeking permission to retrench the petitioner before the Tribunal, that the 
petitioner submits that there was no reason for the Company to bring up 
an application under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, that the 
petitioner feels that the Company has contravened section 33 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act by keeping the petitioner out of work without wages and 
as such the petitioner prays for relief under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, that under the circumstances the petitioner prays for an 
award directing the opposite party to reinstate the petitioner with full 
compensation for the period of forced unemployment. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the opposite 
party, the Company filed its written statement in which it contended that 
the application under section 33A filed by Shri Gouri Shankar Roy is mis- 
conceived and not maintainable in law as the Company has not violated 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, that the Company has already 
filed an application under section 33 on 13th December 1954 seeking permis- 
sion of the Tribunal to retrench the workman concerned, that the application 
under section 33A filed by the said workman contains various vague, mis- 
leading and incorrect allegations and the Company denies the same, that 
the Company prays that the application under section 33A filed by the 
complainant should be rejected on the preliminary point of law. 


DECISION 


Although a petition of complaint under section 33A alleging violation 
of condition of service for failure te apply under section 33 for permission 
of this Tribunal has been filed, it has now been proved by the employers that 
actually this is not the case. In fact they applied under section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act for permission of the Tribunal. We have perused 
the application under section 38 and under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act and we find that the petition under section 33 covers the 
ground which forms the subject-matter of the complaint under section ۸ 
of the Industrial Disputes Act and which has since been struck off as the 
tee became functus oficto after one month of the publication of the 

ward, 


It has now been held by the Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Treducts of India Ltd. (1955 L.L.J., Vol. I, page 346) that it is the contra- 
vention hy the employer of the provisian of section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act or section 29 of the Appellate Tribunal Act which gives rise 
to a cause of action in favour of the workman to approach and move the 
respective authority concerned of the additional jurisdiction and powers 
conferred on it by the section. The Authority referred to in the section is 
a Court of Limited Jurisdiction and must accordingly be strictly confined to 
the exercise of functions and powers actually conferred on it by the Act 
which constituted it. 


1716 171] CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1906 [Panr 1 


In the present case it being proved that u petition seeking permissiow of 
the Tribunal was actually filed on the self-same grounds, we hold that the 
petition of complaint under section J3A of the Industrial Disputes Act 18 
not maintainable and we award accordingly.

AWARD 


The Government of West HKengal, in the Department of Jabour, by 
order No. 3700Dis./D/10L-7/53, dated 5th October 1969, referred, under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Bengal Immunity Co., Ltd., Baranagore, 
Calcutta-d6 and their workmen to this Tribunal for adjudication. The 
award of the Tribunal on this dispute was made on 17th November 1954 
and was published in the Calcutta Gazette on 16th December 1954. | 


On 24th December 1954 Shri Monmohan Dutta, a workman in the 
employment of the Company, filed a complaint under section 833A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, complaining as follows :— 


The Company unlawfully denied bonus to him, which was a condition of 
service of the petitioner. The Company served a charge-sheet, dated 24th 
May 1954 on the petitioner, and the Director-Manager passed orders that 
the petitioner was guilty of attempt at sabotage, and he was warned and 
bonus was denied to him. This action of the Company amounted to a 
punishment and/or change of service condition, and since it was effected 
without prior permission of the Tribunal, it has come under the mischief 
of section 33 of the Industrial Disputess Act. The Tribunal should, therefore, 
order the Company to pay bonus to the petitioner which has been withheld. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows: 


The application under section 383A of the Act is not maintainable, in- 
as much as, it does not disclose any contravention of section 33 of the Act. 
The payment of bonus-is not a condition of service. It is an ex gratia pay- 
meut made in consideration of efficiency and good work. Bonus is paid to 
an individual workman at the absolute discretion of the Management in 
consideration of his work and efficiency. Before payment of any bonus, the 
Management scrutinises the service records and the reports of the Depart- 
ment-in-chaurge in respect of each of the workmen and then decides whether 
the workman concerned should be paid any bonous or not, and in pursuance 
of the said decision, the bonus ia paid or withheld. The Company paid 
bonus to the petitioner in May 1954 at the rate of one month’s basic pay. 
In September 1954, the Company, on considering his records and the reports 
of the T)epartment-in-charge, decided not to pay him bonus. The non- 
payment of bonus to the applicant is not a contravention of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. 


The points that arise for decision in the case are as follows: — 


(1) Is the application under section 838۸ of the Act maintainable? 
(2) Is the applicant entitled to any relief in this case? 


DECISIONS 


Point No. 1.—The question for decision is if the application under 
section 838۸ is maintainable. It is the contravention by the employer 01 
section 33 of the Act that gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the 
workmen to approach and move the Tribunal and this contravention is the 
condition precedent to the exercise by the Tribunal concerned of the 
additional jurisdiction and powers conferred on it by section 38۸ (vide the 

ecision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Automobile 

Products of India, J.td., reported in 1955 L.A.C., 211). The question, 
therefore, is if the Commpany in not paying the bonus in September 1954, 
to the petitioner violated section 33 of the Act. 


1718 THH CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 [Paur 1 


QO. 1১, W. 1 Shri Nihar Bindu Guha deposed on behalf of the Company, 
Documents Ext. A series and Ext. B were marked for the Company. No 
evidence was adduced for the applicant. 16 appears from the evidence of 
QO. 1), W. 1 that the Company puys bonus usually three times in the 
finaucial year—once in May, aguin in September and again in the 
following January. The financial year of the Company is trom May to the 
following April. On each of the three occasions, bonus corresponding to 
one month’s basic wage is paid to the employces. ‘the witness states that 
one out of the three bonuses is paid to all employees without exception, 
but the other two bonuses are paid according to efficiency of work of the 
individual employees and their conduct. In the case of the applicant, 
Manmohan Dutta, he was given the bonus for May 1954 and January 1956, 
but was not allowed the bonus for September 1954, on account of sume 
adverse remarks about his work, which was found to be justified on enquiry, 
It is also stated that the payment of none of these three bonuses is a 
condition of service for the workmen, but it is customary in the Company 
to 80 atleast one of these three bonuses, independent of the quality of 
work. 


There is nothing on record to show that the payment of bonus 28 a 
condition of service of the employeys. O.P.W. 1 in his cross-examination 
states that 25 per cent. of the nett profit of every year is earmarked for 
payment as bonus to the employees, and Ext. B shows the amount of bonus 
paid in the year 1952-53, 1968-54 and 1954-55 and also the profits during 
these years. O.P.W. 1 also states that Manmohan Dutta was not deprived 
of the bonus in September 1954 by way of punishment. There is nothing 
on record to show that it is a condition of service for the employees to 
get all the three bonuses. 41] that the witness states’is that it is customary 
for the Company to give only one out of the three bonuses in the year, 
independent of the quality of his work. In the present case, the applicant 
was given the bonus in May 1954, and January 1955. He was deprived 
of the 1১078 paid in September 1954 I do not find that the payment 
of bonus in September 1954 was a condition of service of the applicant, 
Manmohan Jutta. That being so, it cannot be claimed that the Company 
altered to the prejudice of the workman concerned condition of service 
applicable to him immediately before the commencement of the proceedings. 
Again, it also appears that in order to attract the operation of 
clause (a) of section 88 of the Act, the alteration of the condi- 
tion of service should be in regard to a body of workmen and not an 
individual workman. This view has been held in the case of Hindusthan 
Development Corporation, reported in 1951(1) L.I..J., 37, by a State 
Tribunal of Calcutta. In any case, it appears that the fact that the 
applicant was not given the bonus in September 1954, does not attract the 
operation of section 33A of the Act. 


Tf was also argued by the learned spokesman for the petitioner that 
non-payment of bonus in September 1954 to the petitioner was a punish- 
ment to him and was a conduct which was hit by section 33(b) of the Act. 
In view of the evidence of 0.P.W. 1 that one of the three bonuses is paid 
to all workmen and the other two bonuses are paid according to efficiency of 
work and conduct of the individual employees non-payment of one out of 
three bonuses after an enquiry on an adverse report by the departmental 
head cannot be considered to be a punishment that could attract ۶ 
operation of section 33(b) of the Act. In view of these circumstances, 11 
is decided that the conduct of the Company in not giving the applicant 
bonus in September 1954, was not a violation of section 33 of the Act, and 
the present application under section 894 of the Act was not, therefore, 
competent.

competent, it would appear from the facts of the case and the evidence on

Ext. A(4) is the report by the departmental head under whom the appli- 
cant worked, stating that the petitioner was guilty of negligence in his

petitioner, Manmohan Dutta, was not given the bonus in September 1954, 
as a result of an adverse report against him, which was found to be justified 
on a detailed enquiry, in which the petitioner was examined and was given 
an opportunity of defending himself. The Company was Justified in refus- 
ing bonus to the petitioner in September 1954, and the petitioner is not 
entitled to any relief even on merits This point is accordingly answered. 


In the result, it is ordered that the application under section 33A of 
the Act be rejected and it is uwarded accordingly.

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by 
Order No. 3700Dis. /D/10.-7/53, dated the 5th October 1953, referred, under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Bengal Immunity Co., Ltd., Baranagore, 
Calcutta-d6 and their workmen to this Tribunal for adjudication. ‘I'he 
award of the Tribunal on this dispute was made on 17th November 1954 and 
was published in the Calcutta Gazette on 16th December 1954. 


On 24th December 1954, Shri Jitendra Nath Biswas, a workman in the 
employment of the Company, applied under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, stating as follows: Bonus is a condition of service of the 
workmen in this Company, and this bonus was denied by the Company. 
The Company served a charge-sheet, dated the 17th August 1954, against 
the petitioner and the Director-Manager passed an order that the petitioner 
was guilty of disobedience and he was warned and bonus was denied to 
him. The action of the Company, as mentioned above, amounts to 4 
punishment and a change of service condition of the workmen, and as it 
was effected without prior permission of the Tribunal, it has come under 
the mischief of section 99 of the Act. The petitioner, therefore, prays 
that the Tribunal should order the Company to pay him the bonus which 
has been withheld. 


The Company, in its written statement, states us follows: 


The application under section 383A of the Act filed by the applicant 1s 
not maintainable inasmuch as it does not disclose any contravention ০1 
section 33 of the Act. The payment of bonus is not a condition of service 
It is an ex gratia payment made in consideration of efficiency and good 
work. The bonus is paid to the individual workman at the absolute 
discretion of the Management in consideration of his work and efficiency. 
Before payment of bonus, the Management scrutinises the service records 
and the reports of the Department-in-charge in respect of each of the work- 
men and then decides whether the workman concerned deserves to be paid 


part J] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 1721 
০০০৮-০৮-৮০ 
ض‎ not and in pursuance of such decision, the Company paid bonus to the 
applicant in May, 1954, at the rate of one month's basic pay. In September 
1954, the Company considering the record of the petitioner and the reports 
of the Department-in-charge decided not to pay him bonus. The applicant 
18 not entitled to get this bonus and the petition under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act should be rejected. 


The points that arise for decision in this case are as follows: 


POINTS 
(1) Is the petition under section 994 of the Act maintainable? 
(2) Is the petitioner entitled to any relief, as prayed for? 


DECISION 


Point No. 1.—The question for decision is if the application under 
section 894 is maintainable. It is the contravention by the employer of 
section 33 of the Act that gives rise to a cause of action in favour ot the 
workmen to approach and move the Tribunal and this contravention is the 
condition precedent to the exercise by the Tribunal concerned of the 
additional jurisdiction and powers conferred on it by section 33A (vide 
the decision of the Hon’ble Suprente Court of India in the case of 
Automobile Products of India, Ltd., reported in 1955 L.A.C., 211). The 
question, therefore, is 1f the Company in not paying the bonus in September 
1934, to the petitioner violated section 33 of the Act. 


O.P.W. 1 Shri Nihar Bindu Guha deposed on behalf of the Company. 
Documents, Ext. A series were marked for the Company. No evidence 
was adduced for the applicant. I1t appears from the evidence of 0.P.W, 1 
that the Company pays bonus usuully three times in the financial] year — 
once in May, again in September and again in the following January. The 
fnancial year of the Company is from May to the following April. 
The witness states that the applicant, Jiten Biswas, was given the bonus 
tor May 1954 and January 1955, but was not allowed the bonus for 
September 1954, on account of some adverse remarks about his work, 
which was found justified on enquiry. It is also stated that the payment 
of none of these three bonuses was a condition of service. The witness also 
states that Jiten Biswas was not deprived of the bonus in September by 
way of punishment. I do not find that the payment of bonus in September 
1954 was a condition of service of the applicant, Jiten Biswas. That being 
su, it cannot be claimed that the Company ultered to the prejudice 
of the workman concerned condition of service applicable to him 
immediately before the commencement of the proceedings. It appears, 
therefore, that the fact that the applicant was not given the bonus in 
September 1954 does not attract the operation of section 33(a) of the Act. 
It was also argued by the learned spokesman for the petitioner that non- 
payment of bonus in September 1954 was a punishment and was a conduct 
which was hit by section 33(b) of the Act. In view of the fact that Jiten 
Hiswas was given two bonuses in May and January and was not given the 
bonus in September 1954, because as the witness states, he did not 
deserve it by his work, it cannot be claimed that in view of these 
circumstances, it is decided that the conduct of the Company in not giving 
the applicant the bonus in September 1954 was not a contravention of 
section 33 of the Act and the present application under section 33A of the 
Act was not, therefore, competent. 


Point No. 2.—Even if the application under section 33A of the Act was 
competent, it would appear from the facts of the case and the evidence 
on record that the application of the petitioner cannot succeed on merits.

that Jiten Biswas stopped doing any work since 8-830 a.m. in the morning 
on 17th August 1954 in spite of repeated requests from the supervisor and

that no next bonus would be given to him. ‘There is nothing on record to

enquiry following it and the order’ of the Director-Manager after the 
rag were not bona fide. It 1s, therefore, clear that the petitioner, 
Jiten Biswas, was not given the bonus in September 1954, as a result ot 
an adverse report against him, which was found to be justified on a 
detailed enquiry in which the petitioner was examined and was given 
opportunity to defend himself. The Company, therefore, was justified in 
refusing the bonus in September, 1954, after the enquiry into his conduct. 
The petitioner is not entitled to any relief even on merits. This point is 
accordingly answered. 


In the result, it is ordered that the application under section 383A of the 
Act Be rejected and it is awarded accordingly.

AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by 
order No. 38700Dis./D/10L-7/53, dated 5th October 1953, referred, under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), 
the industrial dispute between Messrs. Bengal Immunity Co., .6اا‎ 
Baranagore, Calcutta-36, and their workmen to this Tribunal for adjudi- 
cation. The award of the Tribunal on this dispute was made on _ 17th 
November 1954 and was published in the Calcutta Gazette on 16th 
Devember 1954. 


Qn 23rd June 1954 Shri Parimal Bhadra and 18 other employees of 
the company, filed n complaint under section 383A of the Industrial 
Jisputes, Act stating that the Company unlawfully denied them bonus, 
which was a condition of service. It is stated that the 14 employees 
have not been paid bonus, which was due to them in May 1954. The 
petitioners, therefore, pray for an order directing the Company to pay 
the bonus which has been withheld. 


The Company, in its written stutement, states that the application under 
section 338A of the Act filed by the applicants is not maintainable, 
Masmuch as it does not disclose any contravention of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. It is also stated that the payment of bonus is 
not a condition of service and that it 1g an er gratia payment made im 
consideration of efficiency and good work. Three bonuses of varying 
Amounts are given in a year at the absolute discretion of the Management. 
It is stated that before payment of each bonus, the Management 
scrutinises the service records and the reports of the Department-in- 
charge in respect of each 01 the workmen and then decides whether the 
workmen concerned deserves to be paid or not and in pursuance vf the 
suid decision pays the same. ‘Following the above principle, the 
Company paid bonuses in October 1953, and January 1954, to the

14 persans at the rate of one month’s basic pay. In May 1954, tae 
Company on considering their records and the reports of the Department. 
in-charge, decided not to puy them the third bonus. The workers in 
question are not entitled to get any bonus or the third bonus in question 
as of right and as a condition of service, and the application should bp 
dismissed with costs. 


The points that arise for decision in this case ure as follows :— 


Points 
(1) Is the application under section 383A of the Act maintainable? 
(2) Are the applicants entitled to any relief in this case? 


DECISIONS. 


Point No. 1.—The question for decision is if the application under 
section 338A 19 maintainable. It is the contravention by the employer 
of section 83 of the Act that gives rise to a cause of action in favour of 
the workmen to approach and move the Tribunal, and this contravention 
is the condition precedent to the exercise by the Tribunal concerned of 
the additional jurisdiction and powers conferred on it by section ۸ 
(vide the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case 
of Automobile Products of India bid., reported in 1955 J..A.C., 211). 
The question, therefore, is if the Company, in not paying the bonus in 
May 1954, to the petitioners, violated section 33 of the Act. 


O. P. W. 1 Shri Nihar Bindu Guha, deposed on behalf of the 
Company. Documents Exts. A series to N series were marked for the 
Company. Affidavit, Ext. 1, was marked for the applicants. 1 appeurs 
trom the evidence of O. P. W. 1 that the Company ear-marked 25 per 
cent. of the net profit for the payment of bonus in the year in question 
us in other years, and bonus is paid up to three months’ basic wages 
payable respectively in May, September and January next. The 
financial-~ear of the Company is from May to the following April. On 
euch of the three occasions, bonus corresponding to one month’s 1)2810 
wage is paid to the employees. The witness states that one out of (119 
three bonuses is paid to all employees without exception, but the other 
two bonuses are paid according to efficiency of work of the individual 
employees and their conduct. In the case of the applicants, VParimal 
Bhadra and 18 others, they were paid bonus for September 1954 and 
January 1955, but were not paid the bonus for May 1954, on account of 
adverse remarks about their work from the departments. There was an 
enquiry over each report and they were all warned by way of punishment. 
The petitioners were not also given the bonus for May 1954. Nxt. A 
series to N series are the papers relating to the enquiry against these 
14 persons. It is also stated that the payment of none of these three 
bonuses in the year is a condition of service for the workmen, although 
it mf customary for the Company to give at least one of these three 
bonuses, independent of the quality of work. O. P. W. 1 also states that 
{he petitioners were not deprived of bonus in May 1964, by way of 
punishment. There‘is nothing on record to show that it was a condition 
of service for the employees to get all the three bonuses. 


Ext. A is an affidavit sworn by Shri N. B. Guha _ before the Hon’b't 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India at Calcutta, in connection with the 
case of Amritalal Bhadra and the Company. In this affidavit, 
Q, P. W. 1, Shri Nihar Bindu Guha, states that bonus is not a condition 
of the service of the workmen employed in the Company, that tue 
Company pays bonus as an ez gratia payment in consideration 61 
efficiency und good work, and the principle followed in making such 
payments is as follows.

gu) Thiee bonuses of varying amounts are given ina year at the

and the third bonuses sre usually paid in each year in October ond in 
January following respectively. Before payment of the second and the 
third bonuses, Management scrutinises the service records and reports of

In view of statement of the affidavit, it is clear that the payment of 
bonus for the May instalinent, 1.e., the rst bonus of the year, is a condi- 
tion of service for the workmen, and the act of the Company im depriving 
the workmen of this bonus may also be considered to be a sort of punish- 
ment, 11 is, therefore, clear that the Company, in not paying the bonus 
for May 1954 to the petitioners, violated section 33 of the Act und = the 
present application under section 383A is, therefore, competent. 


Point No. 2.—Fven if the application under section 383A is competent, 
the Tribunal has to adjudicate upon the complaint as if it were a dispute 
eterred to or pending before it and decide on the merits of the act and 
the order of the employer (ride decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of 
India in the case of Automobile Products of India Ltd., reported im 
1955 L.A.C., 211). The claim of the employer that in the case of every 
one of the 14 employees petitioners, there was an adverse report by the 
Department-in-charge, which was followed by an enquiry, and that on 
the results of the enquiry each of these petitioners was warned and 
deprived of the bonus has to be considered on merits. The case cf 
the individual employees will be considered below:

Qn a consideration of the matter, it appears to me that in every .۰ک‎ 
the Company served charge-sheets on the employee concerned and |,ع‎ 
him an opportunity of explaining his conduct. Thereafter the Company 
held a detailed enquiry in which witnesses were examined in the preseng, 
of the employee concerned, and it appears that in every vase, the dicisigy 
of the Munagement was a possible view of the matter on the evidence 
before it. ‘‘In such a case, the Tribunal should refraim from substitucng 
its own judgment for the judgment of the Management, of 11) sigh 
matters the Tribunal does not act like a court of appeal but rather y, , 
supervisory body exercising what would ordinanly he regardsd نو‎ 
powers of revision for correction of basic errors which go to the rwt of 
the matter and of perverse findings.’’ I do not consider that in ihe 
decision of the Management in relation to the charges against the 
employees mentioned above, there was want of bona fides, or there wag 
any case of victimisation or unfair labour practice, or violation (4 the 
principles of natural justice, or there was basic error of facts im any 
case, or there has been a perverse finding on the materials in any 19৮, 
It is, therefore, decided that the decision of the Management in relatioy 
to the charges against the employees mentioned above should 11171] 
oO) the case of Buckingham & Carnatic Ltd., reported in 1982 L.A.C., 
490). 

The 14 employees mentioned above are not, therefore, entitled 1) 10 
the next bonus, as ordered by the J)irector-Manager. It has been stated 
above that in the affidavit, Ext. 1, O.P.W. 1 Shri N. B. Guha admitted 
that the bonus payable in May 18 usually paid to every one of the 
en:ployees without any consideration, aa. that the other {wo bonuses, i.e., 
those that are payable in October (or اسنا ےت‎ and January following 
are paid in consideration of the quality of work and conduct of the 
individual employees. It is, therefore, clear thut all the employees are 
entitled to get the bonus in May, but the other two bonuses, 1.e., those 
payable in September or October and January following, are to be paid 
in consideration of the quality of work and the conduct of the employees. 
In the present cases, all the 14 employees were deprived of the bonus 
payable in May 1954, by the order of the Director-Manager as ٭<‎ result 
of enquiries on the conduct of the employees. It was argued by the 
learned spokesman for the employees that the Company was bound to 
puy them the bonus in May 1954. That is correct. <All the employees, 
however, got both the other two bonuses, 1.6.) those which were ور"‎ ٥ 
in September and January following. The employees should have been 
deprived of one bonus, 1.e., the bonus in September 1954, instead of the 
bonus in May 1954, in view of the order of the Director-Manager in a 
result of the enquiries on the charge-sheets against them. The Company 
instead of paying the bonus in May and depriving the 14 emplovees of 
the bonus in September, deprived them of the bonus payable in May, 
1954, and paid them the other two bonuses in the year. I do not .« nsuler 
that in these circumstances, any loss has been caused to the employees 
on account of their having been derpived of the bonus in May 11). 
The evidence on record suggests that all the bonuses were of the sume

AWARD 


The present complaints purporting to be under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, were filed before this Tribunal by the 6ء‎ 
complainants on the allegation that while the original dispute was pending 
before this Tribunal, the opposite party—Empuire Bone Mille—in contraven- 
1100 of the provisions of section 38 of the Act dismissed them summarily 
with effect from 27th February 1956 without taking permission from the 


1732 THH CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 [Panr | 


Tribunal. The said order of dismissal hus been characterised as Uj WH. 
fied and illegal. It is alleged that the petitioners were victimised, simply 
because they happened to be members of the Empire Bone Mills Mazdoo; 
Union. So, reinstatement with back wages was claimed by the petitioners 


The opposite party denied that there was any contravention by the 
Company of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Tt stated that 
on 24th February 1956 at about 11-10 a.m. while the Company’s Manager 
Mr. H. N. Ray was going to his bungalow from the Mill Office, a crow, 
of over 30 workmen began throwing stones and brickbats and shoes at him 
and that the present petitioners were the persons who were in that crowd 
As a result of the above incident, the said Mannger decided to dismiss th, 
petitioners summaiily, and by lettets, dated 27th February 1956, he 
infcrmed the petitioners accordingly. 


These three cases were taken up together for hearing at the instance of 
the parties and also for the sake of convenience, as the-evidence in all the 
cases is the same. : 


Admittedly, the original dispute was pending before this Tribunal at 
the relevant time. Ext. A-series are the [লও issucd hy the Manager to 
the petitioners, and they are dated 27th February 1956. These letters وج‎ 
to show unmistakably that these petitioners were summerily dismissed from 
27th February 1956. As the original dispute was pending before this 
Tribunal at the time, the Company had no right to dismiss the petitioners 
in this fashion without the express permission of the Tribunal, because such 
dismissal constituted punishment. But obviously, no such permission of 
the Tribunal was taken before dismissing the petitioners. So, there can be 
no manner of doubt that section 33 of the Act was contravened. Mr 
Manna, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the Company invited my 
attention to the fact that in those lettera (Ext. A-series), it is also atated 
at the end that pending decision from the Tribunal, the petitioners would 
remuin OE A Relying on this, Mr. Manna has argued before me that 
the petitioners were not actually dismissed, but they were kept under sus 
pension pending permission from the Tribunal, and that such suspension 
was made by way of security measure. I may say straightway, on و‎ 
perusal of the letters (Ext. A-series), that I am unable to agree with 
Mr. Manna on this point. The language used in those letters is that the 
petitioners were summarily dismissed from 27th February 1956. ہ1‎ the 
face of such clear and unequivocal expression, it cannot be held by any 
stretch of imagination that the petitioners were not actually dismissed, but 
were kept under suspension as a security measure pending derision from 
the Tribunal. In my view, the words “pending decision from the Tribunal 
you will remain suspended forthwith’’ as used in the aforesaid letters at 
the end, were put deliberately by the Manager with a view to avoid appli- 
cation of section 33 of the Act. It is not capable of any other explanation 
or interpretation. There can be no manner of doubt that what had _ heen 
done by the Management in these cases was virtually dismissal in the garb 
of suspension, avowedly to skip over the ban imposed under section 3 
The Tribunal, therefore, comes to the conclusion that there was clear co- 
travention of section 33 of the Act in the present three cases. So, the 
present applications under section 333A are competent. 


It is now well-settled that where section 33 has been contravened, the 
Tribunal must enquire into the merits of the discharge or disrmiasal on 4 
complaint being made under section 383A. As the complaint has to be 
investigated hy the Tribunal. as if it were a dispute referred to, or pending 
before it, the scope of investigation on the merits must be exaoily the ۸6 
where the subject-matter of the challenged discharge or dismissal had heen 


THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 6 1733‏ ا 


ss ST 
রা subject-matter of an independent Teference under section 10 of the 
act. The merits of the impugned dismissal are, therefore, to be considered 
hy the Tribunal. In these cases, unother fact emerges, which needs consi- 
deration also. The petitioners were summarily dismissed, and the Manage- 
ment before dismissing them did not give them any charge-sheet, or hold 
any enquiry. So, a grievance was made on behalf of the petitioners that 
they were wrongfully dismissed by the Management without any enquiry 
into the alleged charge made against them, which is against the principles 
of natural justice. 11 has been laid down in a series of cases that where 
‘he rule of natural justice is not followed, the Tribunal is to go into the 
merits and to critically examine the propriety of the Management’s order 
of 01151701450] or discharge. Though the principle of natuial justice does 
demand enquiry against a worker before disciplinary action is taken against 
him, such principle would reduce itself to a mere technicality, if the charge 
is (lear, and the facts constituting the charge are known to the worker, and 
do not admit of being explained away by him. The fact that no charge- 
sheet was delivered or no regular enquiry was held by the Management, 1৭ 
of no consequence in this case. Necessary evidence has been tendered before 
the Tribunal. JT may observe that the petitioners do not appear to have 
been prejudiced in any way for want of any charge-sheet or for not holding 
any regular enquiry against them, befare their dismissal. In view of what 
has been stated above, it becomes necessary for the Tribunal to enter into 
the merits of the dismisaul of the petitioners. The main charge, as could 
he gathered from the letters of dismissal sent to the petitioners on 27th Ieb- 
ruary 1956 (wide Ext. A-series) was that on 24th February 1956 at about 
11-10 am, in front of the main gate of the Mill, the present petititoners 
dlong wilh other workers threw brick-bats at the Manager, and abused him 
1 filthy languages. Such a charge against a worker, if established, 08 true, 
A indeed a grave misconduct, which might justify summary dismissal in the 
interests of discipline and smooth working of the Mill. But the question 
is whether the aforesaid charge is true, and has been substantiated hy the 
materials on record, One of the petitioners Shri Pashupati Ghosh (P.W. 1) 
nas deposed on behalf of the workers, and he has denied the charge levelled 
against them. He has deposed before Tribunal that they did not along

Maintenanee Engineer, Shri Padam Bahadur, a darwan of the Mill. and 
Persia, a Coolie Sardar of the Mill, have been examined te prove the alleged 
incident. O.P.W. 1 Mr. H. N. Ray has spoken about the incident. He 
has deposed clearly and unequivocally that the present petitioners took 
part im that incident. He has further said that he saw the present peti- 
tioners amongst the persons, who were throwing brick-bais and shoes at 
lim. 116০ stated that he could identify these petitioners, as he knew them 
by name and face, Before this Tribunal. he also identified most of them. 
He xppears to be a respectable ond responsible person. He holds also 
foreign degrees. It cannot he believed for a moment that a man of his 
st tus and position would depose falsely, nor can it be conceived thai he 
would concoct a false story against these workers in order to 6 
them. TI had the opportunity of seeing this witness in box and hearing his 
evidence. T must say that I was impressed by his evidence. He deposed 
In a very straight-forward manner. In the circumstances, I hold that his 
evidence bears the stamp of truth. Accordingly, the Tribunal accepts his 
evidence regarding the incident that took place on 24th February 1956 at 
11-10 a.m. The Tribunal is convinced from his evidence that these workers 
along with others threw brick-bats and shoes at him and also abused him in 
filthy languages, while he was going to his bungalow from the Mill Office.

: Dae ہچ‎ aay a ee برک کت ہے دہ‎ a cae ae ہے سے رہہ ہے کے ہہ کیہ مہہ ہے‎ ee rere

or hesitation in saying that the action of the Management war justified, not. 
withstanding the absence of charge-sheet or proper enquiry into the matter. 
No Management can afford to tolerate such insubordination, insolence and 
vross nusconduct on the part of the workers. This sort of misconduct and 
insubordination undermines discipline, and the gravity of such action رر‎ 
not be under-rated. The view taken by the Management 11) dismis-ing

the decision of the Management is called for. The Tribunal, theretore, 
holds that these petitioners have heen rightly dismissed and none of thew 
is entitled to uny relief. Jt 1s also a salutary principle of law and equity 
that in case of grave misconduct, a worker could be summarily dismissed, 
particularly when such workers insult and try to assault a Manager in this 
fashion. In such cases, the Management would be amply justified ىا‎ 
forthwith dismissing such impertinent and insubordinate workers. ‘The 
Tribunal is unable to believe that that these workers were victimised, 
simply because they happened (9 be members of the Empire Bone Mills 

Mazdoor Union. 


The result is that the applications filed by these petitioners under section 
9348 are rejected.
