The original reference, out of which this case has arisen, was made under 
Government order No. 4045Dis./1)/11L-53/55, dated 915৮ August 1955 
The award of the Tribunal in respect of the original reference was made op 
17৮) March 1956, and the award has since been published in the Caleuttg 
0266০, 


AWARD 


The present complaint purporting to be under section 338A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed before this Tribunal by the above 
complainant on the allegation that while the original dispute was pending 
before this Tribunal, the opposite party—Empire Bone Mills—in contravep. 
tion of the provisions of section 33 of the Act dismissed him from service from 
10th March 1956 without taking permission from the Tribunal. The 8816 
order of dismissal has been characterised as unjustified and illegal. It is 
alleged that the petitioner was so victimised, simply because he happened to 
be a member of the Empire Bone Mills Mazdoor Union. So reinstatement 
with back wages was claimed by the petitioner. 


The opposite party denied that there was any contravention of section 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It stated that on 9th March 1956, 
at about 11-50 p.m. before the expiry of the second shift of the workers at 
the Empire Bone Mills, the petitioner wrongfully assaulted one Kedar 
Bhattacharjee, an employee of the Mills working in the Godown Department. 
The said assault was committed in presence of Mr. Nat Amroon, the 
Supervisor, who personally prevented the petitioner from committing further 
assault and further breach of discipline. For this misconduct on the part of 
the petitioner, a charge-sheet was issued to him on 10th March 1956, and on 
ط118‎ March 1956, the petitioner submitted his explanation, in which he 
admitted the assault. The petitioner was suspended on and from 10th March 
1956 pending enquiry. Thereafter, an enquiry was held on 12th March 1956 
by Mr. S. Mukherjee, an officer of the Company. (Qn enquiry, it was found 
and proved that the petitioner was guilty of wrongful assault. Consequently, 
the Management decided to dismiss the petitioner subject to the permission 
of the Tribunal heing obtained. 


The first question for consideration is whether there has been contraven- 
tion of section 33 by the Management. Admittedly, the original dispute 
was pending before this Tribunal at the relevant time. Annexure “‘C”’ of 
the written statement of the Company is the copy of the letter issued by 
the Manager to the present petitioner, and it is dated 13th March 1956. 
The petitioner has also filed a copy of this letter as Annexure to his applica 
tion. This letter goes to show clearly that the petitioner was dismissed 
from the service of the Company from 10th March 1956, as the charge against 
him for the incident, which is alleged to have taken place on 9th March 
1956, was duly proved as a result of the enquiry held on 12th March 1956. 
There can be no manner of doubt that such dismissal was a punishment. 
As the original dispute was pending before this Tribunal at the time, the 
Company had no right to dismiss the petitioner in this way without the 
express permission of the Tribunal. But obviously, no such permission of 
the Tribunal was taken before dismissing the petitioner. So, I am of the 
view that section 33 of the Act was contravened. Mr. Ginwalla, learned 


I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 1739‏ ىیہ 


CS سوسحم‎ AR a A aa a 

vnnsel appearing on behalf of the Company, invited my attention to the 
‘ait that i the said letter it 1s also atated at the end that pending decision 
om the Tribunal, the petitioner would remain suspended. Relying on this, 
‘ir, Ginwalla has argued before me that the petitioner was not actually 
vigmissed, but he was kept under suspension pending permission from the 
Tribunal, and that such suspension was made by way of security measure. 
[ may say straightway that on a perusal of the letter with care, I om 
ماما‎ to agree with Mr. Ginwalla on this point. The language used in the 
aid letter is that the petitioner was dismissed from the service of the 
Nompany on and from 10th March 1956. In the face of such clear and 
inequivocal expression, it cannot be held by any stretch of imagination 
hat the petitioner was not actually dismissed, but was kept under suspension 
as n security measure pending decision from the Tribunal. In my view, the 
words ‘pending decision from the Tribunal you will remain suspended”’ as 
used in the aforesaid letter at the end, were deliberately put by the Manager 
و‎ order to avoid application of section 33 of the Act. It 1s not capable of 
any other explanation or interpretation. What Management did in this 
ease was nothing, but dismissal] in the garb of suspension, with a view to 
akip over the bar or ban imposed under section 33. The Tribunal, therefore, 
comes to the conclusion that there was clear contravention of section 33 of 
the Act in this case. So, the present application under section 33A 1s 
competent. 


It is now well settled that where section 33 has been contravened, the 
Tribunal must enquire into the merits of the discharge or dismissal on a 
complaint being made under section 094১. As the complaint has got to be 
investigated by the Tribunal, as if it were a dispute referred to or pending 
before it, the scope of investigation on the merits must be exactly the same, 
where the subject-matter of the challenged discharge or dismissal had been 
the subject-matter of an independent reference under section 10 of the Act. 
The merits of the impugned dismissal are, therefore, to be considered by the 
Tribunal. This necessarily leads the Tribunal to go into the merits and 
to critically examine the propriety of the Management’s order of dismissal 
or discharge of the petitioner. In this case, the principles of natural justice 
were not violated. A charge-sheet was delivered to the petitioner for the 
incident on 10th March 1956, and the petitioner was also given an oppor- 
tunity to explain his position. The petitioner did offer explanation. This 
will be evident from Ext. A. The petitioner has also admitted before this 
Tribunal that he got charge-sheet, and he submitted his explanation. From 
the explanation, 1t appears that the petitioner admitted that he assaulted 
Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee inside the Mill premises on 9th March 1956 at 
11-50 p.m. and that he also used his slipper on him. He wanted to say, 
however, that he abused and assaulted Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee in this 
way, simply because he lost his temper. It appears from the materials 
placed before this Tribunal that even after this explanation, a regular 
enquiry was held by the Management in presence of the petitioner, and 
that in that enquiry witnesses were examined. So, it cannot be said that 
in the present case there was any violation of the principles of natural 
justice. Before this Tribunal, the petitioner made a grievance that he was 
not allowed to examine his witnesses in the enquiry. But this cannot be 
believed, in view of what has transpired from the report of the Enquiring 
Officer (Ext. B) and also from his evidence. The report of the Enquiring 
Officer shows that Md. [88016 and Md. Rafique were examined on behalf 
of the petitioner Sakaldip. O.P.W. 2 Shri 9. K. Mukherjee is the Officer, 
who held that enquiry. He has deposed on oath that the petitioner 
Sakaldip examined two witnesses, who were Md. Isaque and Md. Rafique. 


1740 THY CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., JULY 24, 1966. [Parr] 


سے RT A ee rw‏ سس 


Tt is interesting to note in this connection that the petitioner himself he. 
stated before this Tribunal that he does not remember the names of person, 
whom he wanted to examine as his witnesses in the enquiry. This indicate 
that the version of the petitioner that he was not allowed to examune witni ہیں‎ 
in the enquiry, 1s not worthy of credit. J{ cannot be believed 601 a INOment 
that the Enquiring Officer, who is the Assistant Maintenance Enginee, 
would depose falsely and incorporate in his report something which did uo 
represent the actual state of things. 


Now I shall enter into the merits of the case. The charge against th, 
petitioner, as could be gathered, was that on 9th March 1956 at 11-50 p.m. 
he mishandled with the help of a slipper a worker, Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee 
inside the Mill. As stated already, the petitioner admitted the incident 
while giving his explanation to the charge-sheet on 11th March 1956. By 
before this Tribunal he had the temerity of saying that he did not assay 
Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee on 9th March 1956 at about 11-50 p.m. In viey 
of his unequivocal admission in his explanation, it is now idle and tutile 
for him to say before the Tribunal that he did not assault Shri Keda, 
Bhattacharjee on 9th March 1956 at about 11-50 p.m. Such denial ور‎ 
meaningless, and cannot be believed in view of his previous statement, and 
also in the face of the evidence adduced on behalf of the Company. (8 
appears that the charge-sheet against the petitioner for the incident of 00 
March 1956 was issued by Mr. Nat Amroon, who was at that time workin, 
as Overseer of the Kmpire Bone Mills at Bansberia. He was an eye-witness 
to the inrident. He has deposed before this Tribunal at O.P.W. 1, Ile 
has said that on 9th March 1956 while he was in the B shift from 3-0 p.m, 
to 12 o’clock midnight, he at about 11-50 p.m. heard a noise outside the 
office where he was at that time, and came out. He saw the petitioner and 
Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee, another employee engaged in struggle. This 
petitioner had his arm round the neck of Kedar, and in his right hand he 
had a slipper with which he was beating Kedar at random. Mr. Amroon 
has further stated that he at once proceeded to the spot, and succeeded m 
separating them. He hus deposed also that the incident took place in«de 
the Mill compound a few yards off from the office. The Tribunal 108 
considered the evidence of Mr. Nat Amroon. His evidence bears the stamp 
of truth. He deposed before the Tribunal in a straight-forward manner 
So, the Tribunal accepts his evidence in its entirety. That this petitioner 
assaulted Shri Kedar Bhattacharjee, another employee, inside the Mull 
during the working hours, is amply proved by the evidence of Mr. Amnoon 
and also from the other materials on record. The Tribunal is unable to 
hold that the petitioner has been falsely implicated or that the action of 
the Management was influenced by mala fides. The circumstances do not 
show that any attempt was made on the part of the Management to victimuse 
him fax his being a member of the Empire Bone Mills Mazdoor Union 50, 
the petitioner was found nightly guilty of misconduct by the Management, 
because his conduct was subversive of discipline. What he did, clearly 
amounted to misconduct. So, the Tribunal feels no doubt or hesitation im 
saying that the action of the Management was justified. No Management 
can afford to tolerate such gross misconduct on the part of a worker inside 
the Mill during working hours. An employer is certainly concerned with 
the peace and good order in the factory or Mill, and any act on the part of 
the worker having tendency or effect to disturb peace and good order should 
be regarded as subversive of discipline. The act complained ot had 
undoubtedly material bearing on the smooth and efficient working of the 
concern, and had a direct connection with the contentment or ء۷٥‎ 
the men at work. That being so, the Tribunal feels no hesitation in holding 


part I] THE CAL. GAZ, EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 1741 


aca 
ft the Management was perfectly justified in dismissing the petitioner. 
Jo, 0 interference with the decision of the Management is called for. 
Hence, the petitioner is not entitled to any relief. 


The result is that the present application under section 338A is rejected.

Issue NO. 1.—Grades and scales : pay.—The Company has no 80199 
or grades of pay for the clerical staff, but it allows increments to individual

Commerce scule, which is a generous and lavish one, The second ground 
put forward on behalt of the Company is that, regard being had to its 
nature of business, and in view of is financial position which has been 
gradually deteriorating year by year, it waa not in a position to introduce 
grades und scales of pay for the present. Both parties have filed chartg. 
In the chart filed by the Union, the dearness allowance that each employee 
gets is not mentioned. But in the chart filed by the Company, basic salary 
and dearness allowance are shown separately. In that chart also, the total 
emoluments that each employee gets has also been shown. On a perusal 
of the charts, it 18 manifestly clear that the total emoluments of each 
employee are reasonable and adequate. It further appears from those 
charts that increments from time to time are given by the Company to itg 
employees. The minimum total emoluments of an employee are not below 
Rs. 172-3. This cannot by any means be said to be inadequate or low ag to 
justify any increase, regard being had to the length of service. The total] 
emoluments paid to the employees of this Company are indeed decent and 
handsome, and compare favourably with similar concerns in the locality. 
The Company has produced balance-sheets for the years from 1951 to 1955 
(Ext. B-series). It appears from these balance-sheets that the financial 
position of the Company has been gradually deteriorating year by year, 
The net profit in the year 196] was Rs. 2,08,325, but it came down to 
Rs. 2,056,578 in 1962. In 1953, it reached Rs. 1,64,489 and in 1954 it stood 
at Rs. 1,59,867. But in the year 1955, the net profit came down to a

& Lewes, Chartered Accountants, a reputed firm. Though some comments 
were made by the learned representative on behalf of the Union on these 
balance-sheets, I must say that he could not show me anything tangible, 
as a result of which these balance-sheets could be deemed to be incorrect. 
So, regard being had to the financial position of the Company, which has 
been gradually deteriorating, I am ot the view that this is not an opportune 
time for introduction of grades and scales of pay for the employees. In the 
case of Messrs. Union Drug Company, Ltd. versus their workmen reported 
in 1953 ہا‎ A. C. 714, it has 22 held by their Lordships ‘‘Before incremental 
scales can be imposed by adjudication, it is essential to see whether the 
employer would be able to bear its burden. The financial condition of the 
Company must be such as to Jead to the condition that it would be able to 
pay increments year by year for an appreciable number of years, for wage

19 not propose to introduce grades and pay-seales at the present time, 
the employees would do well to co-operate with the Company for some 
me more, With a view to improve its condition and to renew their claims 
hereatter. Another reason, which makes me unable to concede to the 
‘nron’s demand for introduction of grades and pay-scales at the present 
me, 18 that the total emoluments, which are being paid to the clerks, do 
10 at any rate fall short ot the minimum, The total emoluments of the 
lerka of this Company are not only fair and adequate, but are substantially 
par with the prevailing rates and consistent with the concept of fair 
minimum کا‎ I am mindful of the fact that in the Mercantile Tribunal 
(ward and also in the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme, grades and

ered that the award of the Mercantile Tribunal or the scheme of Bengal 
‘hamber of Commerce in 81] respects related to big firms, and was unsui-

mports 011] certain goods from abroad, The nature of its business 7৪ also 
yeculiar, and on account of competition there is also risk for this Company 
oosing much of ita business. learned representative appearing on behalf of 
the Union has argued much on the question of balanced diet, in order to 
yonvince the Tribunal that in this concern the total emoluments for the 
lowest paid employees consisting of their busic wages and deurness allowance, 
dhat is their pay packet, were inadequate and unfair. But TI must say that 
] was not impressed in this respect by his argument. He could not convince 
me that the total emoluments be the lowest paid workmen in this Company 
jn any case fell below the minimum, and compared unfavourably with the 
wage rates paid to other employees in other industries. After all, the 
elementary requirements of an employee are the same, whether he is work- 
ing in the Jute or an Isngineering Industry. The Union has failed also to 
establish that the majority of the employees are rotting. From the charts 
filed, it appears that many of the employees are getting increments and 
decent salary within a reasonable period of time. In al] literatures on the 
subject of balanced and satisfactory diet, the authorities tried to lay down 
certain principles only, which they considered to be ideal or satisfactory 
for a certain class of people. The primary difficulty about the realisation 
of that ideal is that there igs no enough such protective foods available for 
all of us, nor they are within the competence of al] to have them. The 
truth about it is that there is no enough such food to go round for every 
body in the country. Another contention urged by the learned represen- 
tative appearing on behalf of the Union is that the cost of living has gone 
up, Rise in the averaye cost of living index, eVen if it be accepted to be 
a0, does not justify any increment in the scale of pay or any fixation of scale 
and grades of pay. A rise in the cost of living index prima facie supports 
a case for revision of dearness allowance, But in the present case, the 
dearnesa allowance which is given to the employees, is indeed very generous 
and lavish, aa auch allowance is given according to the Bengal Chamber 
of Commerce Scheme. So, considering the matter in all its bearings, I 
do not find my way to introduce grades and scales of pay for the clerical 
staff of the Company at present. This issue is decided accordingly.

Issue No, 3.—Gretuty.—The Union has demanded one month’s pay as 


gratuity tor each year of service in, the Company. This is resisted by the 
(Gmpuny on the tollowing grounds :— 


(a) That the Company has a Provident Fund scheme in operation, which 
ig considered to be fair and adequate as the ratiral benefit; 


(b) that the double retiral benefits by way of both Provident Fund 
and graduity, are not prevalent in a Commercial Establishment 
of similar nature; and 


(c) that gratuity, being a long-term commitment, the Company's 
financial position and the uncertainty of its business do not allow 
it to undertake any such long-term commitment. 


I quite agree that pratuity is a long-term commitment. It is not correct 
that double retiral benefits by way of both Provident Fund and gratuity are 
uot prevalent in Commercial Estublishments. There are lots of decisions, 
where such double retiral benefits were given by the Tribunals. But the 
question 18 whether any scheme or provision for gratuity in this Company 
should be -made tor the clerical staft. Admittedly, there is Provident Fund 
scheme for the clerical staff in this Company. The current rate of contri- 
bution to the Provident Fund 1s 71 per cent. on basic pay and dearneas 
allowance on either side. This rate of contribution was started from Ist 
January 1956. Prior to that, the contribution was at the rate of 74 per cent 
on the basic pay only on either side, and it continued from Ist January 1948 
Before that, the rate of contribution to the Provident Fund wag 5 per cent. 
on either side on the basic pay, and this scheme continued from January 
1934 to 3lst December 1947. Prior to 1933, there was no scheme for 
Provident Fund in this Company, but there was a Pension Scheme known as 
‘Babcock Staft Pension Fund’’, in which both the employees and_ the 
employer contributed. But with the introduction of the Provident Fund 
scheme, the contributions made by the employer and the employees under 
the Pension scheme, were transferred to the scheme of Provident Fund 
including“interest. Thus, it is evident that the Provident Fund scheme was 
only introduced in this Company from January 1934, and in the Pension 
scheme that was introduced in 1929, only 5 per cent. of the workmen’s 
basic pay was deposited by deducting from their monthly pay. Naturally, 
the clerks who have rendered long service in this Company and who will 
have to retire soon, will not be much benefited by the amount available to 
them under the Provident Fund scheme. The clerks, who joined this 
Company after 1934, will get benefits of the Provident Fund scheme that 
was introduced in the year 1934. They will no doubt get sufficient money 
from their Provident Fund to fall back upon in their old age on retirement, 
hut such will not be the case with the clerks, who joined this Company 
before 1954. Accordingly, I direcct that only the members of the clerical 
staff, who joined the Company’s service prior to the introduction of the 


p xt 1[ THE CAL, GAZ, EXTRY., JULY 24, 1956 1747 
55455555554 
1%,810616 Fund, shall be পা benefit of gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ 
hasic wages for each completed year of service, subject to a maximum of 
10 months’ wages between the period of their joining and the date, when the 
Provident Fund scheme was introduced. Such gratuity would not be 
payable to them for the period after the introduction of the Provident Fuud 
scheme. So to be precise, ۱1 provide gratuity of those employees for the 
uncovered period only, This benefit 01 gratuity will not extend to other 
clerical staif, as the retiral benefit by way of Provident Fund scheme, which 
ig in operation in this Company, is considered to be fair and adequate for 
them. I hope, the Company will not grudge to pay, in spite of its present 
jnuncial position, such gratuity as directed ubove to the clerical staff, whose 
number perhaps will be very small. This issue is answered accordingly. 


issue NO. 4.—/2fin allowance.—The Union claims Re. 1 per head per 
working day as tiffin allowance for the clerical staff. It is resisted by the 
Company. It is contended that the tiffin allowance is not a condition of 
service, and that the tiffin allowance is a mere concession, for which there 
cannot be ahy compulsion. At present, the Company does not grant any 
tifin allowance, but 2 cups of tea nnd 2 pieces of eae in a day are 
served free of cost to the clerical staff on every working day at their deaks, 
in the absence of any space for tiffin room in the office buildings. In my 
view, the existing arrangement for tiffin will continue. J do not think that 
the Company should be asked to pay any tiffin allowance to the clerical 
8101. The Tribunal interferes in the matter of tiffin in two cases, viz., ۷ 
if the ouncern is located at a place where tiffin cannot be had or procurec 
and (11) where the salary of the staff is such as it does not permit them to 
spend for tiffin, But in the present case, both the elements are absent. The 
08100 of the Company is located near about Dulhousie Square, where there 
are 8) any restaurants and tea stalls. The sulary paid to the clerical staff 
is not such as cannot permit them buying their tiffin out of it. Accordingly, 
the claim of the Union on this score is turned down. 


Issue No. 5.—Afedical facilities.—Admittedly, the Company has no 
arrangements for medical aid to the clerical staff. The demand of the Union 
18 that the employees and their dependants should be allowed free medical aid, 
free medicine and free medical diet, or in the alternative, one mouth’s wages 
in the year ag medical allowance. In my view, the demand of the Union 
appears to be rather unreasonable. 1 have given my due consideration to 
this matter. The employees must share with the 0 equally in enjoying 
medical benefits. The employer may rightly refuse to contribute for the 
special advantage, unless it be proved that the income of the employee 
is less than the national income per capita. It is, therefore, against the 
principles of social justice that the persons entering any Company, shall 
get any preferential treatment. In the present case, the income of the 
employees ia not less than the national income per camta. It is evident 
that the employees get decent and handsome emoluments from the Com- 
pany. That being so, they like other citizens of the State, can spend money 
out of their ھ0‎ for their own ‘medical treatment and also for the 
treatment of their family and dependants. In my view arrangement for 
free medical treatment is a» matter for the State, and no individual employer 
can be compelled to undertake this. The State may take contributions from 
the individual employer. Furthermore, the Employees’ State Insurance 
Scheme is very soon goins to cover the clerical staff of this Company in such 
matters, So, 1 refrain from giving any direction to the Company regarding 
medical facilities. This issue is disposed of thus.

NOTIFICATION 


No. 4707J., dated the 24th July 1956.—In exercise of 
the powers conferred by section 17 of the Mahajati Sadan 
Act, 1949 (West Bengal Act XVI of 1949), the Governor is 
pleased to make the following rules ;— 


Rules 
Short 1. These rules may be called the Mahajati Sadan Rules, 
title. 1956. 
ار‎ 2. In these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in 


the subject or context,— 


(1) ‘‘Chairman’’ means the Chairman of the Board; 
(2) ‘‘form’’ means a form appended to these rules; 
(3) ‘Secretary’? means the Secretary to the Board; 
(4) ‘‘section’’ means a section of the Act; and 

(5) ‘‘the Act’? means the Mahajati Sadan Act, 1949. 


Trustees. 3 (1) The Board shall be constituted by the State 
Government by notification in the Calcutta Gazette and shall 
consist of eleven trustees, of whom— 


(a) four shall be ez-oficio trustees, namely :— 


(2) the Speaker, West Bengal Legislative Assembly, 
(87) the Mayor of Calcutta, 
(at) the Sheriff of Calcutta, 

(1%) the Vice-Chancellor of the Calcutta University, and 


(b) seven shall be appointed by the State Government. 


(2)(a) A trustee, other than an er-oficio trustee, shall, 
unless he resigns or is removed from office earlier, hold office 
for five years from the date of his appointment and shall be 
eligible for reappointment: 


Provided that on the expiration of the term of office of 
such a trustee, he shall continue to act as a trustee until his 
successor is appointed und the appointment is notified in the 
Calcutta Gazette. 


(b) An ez-oficig trustee shall hold office as’such trustee 
so long as he holds the office by virtue of which he is such 
trustee. 


(3) If a trustee, other than an es-oficio trustee, gives 
notice in writing to the Board that he desires to resign his 
office, the Board shall cause such notice to be recorded in its 
proceedings and he shall thereupon cease to be a trustee. 


Removal 4. ‘he State Government may, by notification in the 
of Calcutta Gazette, remove from office any trustee, other than 
Trustec®. an روس‎ ×٦ trustee, who— 


(a) is convicted of any offence invol-:ng moral turpitude; 
or 


(b) is declared an insolvent; or 


(c) wilfully commits any breach of the duties or obliga- 
tions of his office or wilfully violates any of the 
provisions of the Act or persistently acta in a 
manner prejudicial to the interests of the Board 
or the objects and purposes of the Act; or 


(d) has, without the permission of the Board, been absent 
from all meetings of the Board for a continuous 
period of at least one year; or 


(e) has directly or indirectly any interest in any con- 
tract with the Board by which he may derive any 
benefit or financial gain without fully disclosing 
‘9 the Board his interest in such contract; or 


(f) refuses or becomes unfit or incapable to act as a 
trustee

(2) When a trustee dies, or resigns, or is removed 
from office before the expiry of his term of office, his successor 
shall hold office for the unexpired portion of the term. 


Mootings. 6. The minimum number of meetings to be held by the 
Board in any year shall be four and at least one meeting 
shall be held every three months. 


oe 7. (1) The trustees shall, at a meeting held within one 
Board. month of the constitution of the Board, elect one from amongst 
themselves as the Chairman of the Board. The Chairman 


shall hold office till the expiry of his term as a trustee: 


Provided that the Chairman may at any time resign his 
office as Chairman by a letter in writing oddressed to the 
Board. 


(2) In the case of a vacancy in the office of the Chairman, 
a new Chairman shall be elected at a meeting of the Board 
held within one month of the occurrence of the vacancy. 


(3) 18۶ the Board fails to elect a Chairman according to 
these rules, the State Government shall within one month of 
the expiry of the period mentioned in sub-rule (Z) or sub- 
rule (2) appoint one of the trustees as the Chairman. 


(4) The Chairman shall preside over the meetings of the 
Board and in case of his absence from any particular meet- 
ing, the trustees present shall elect one from amongst them- 
selves to preside over the meeting. 


(5) The office of the Chairman shall be honorary. 


দা of 8. (7) Every matter which requires decision of the 
سا‎ Board ৪1199 considered either at a meeting of the Board 
af ihe or, if the Chairman so directs, by circulation of the neces- 
trustees. sary papers for opinion to every trustee who is present in 


India at the time: 


Provided that any trustee may request that the matter may 
be considered at a meeting of the Board and thereupon the 
Chairman may, and if the request is made by three or more 
trustees shall, direct that it is to be so considered. 


(2) All questions in a meeting of the Board shall be 

decided by a majority of votes. In case of equality of votes 

~the Chairman or the trustee presiding at the meeting shall 
have a casting vote. 


(3) Every matter circulated to the trustees for opinion 
under sub-rule (7) shall, unless the Chairman in pursuance 
of the proviso to that sub-rule directs it to be considered at 
a meeting, be decided in accordance with the opinion of the 
majority of the trustees, recording opinion within the time 
allowed for 14.

10. The Board shall be responsible to the State Govern- 
ment for the proper maintenance and management of the 
Mahajati Sadan and the Mahajati Sadan Fund. 


11. The Board shall use the Mahajati Sadan and its 
equipments for the purposes set out in the Second Schedule 
to the Act and objects connected therewith subject to such 
terms and conditions as may be approved of by the State 
Government. 


12. (Z) The Board shal) keep clear and correct account 
of all receipts into and disbursements out of the Mahajati 
Sadan Fund. 


(2) The Secretary to the Board shall be responsible for-— 


(a) 1 item of receipt into and expenditure out of the 
ahajati Sadan Fund, 


(৮) the custody of all articles of stock and stores vested 
in ا‎ oard and all issues and receipts thereof, 
an 


(c) maintaining records of all properties vested in the 
Board including lands, buildings, and investments. 


(3) All the account books and registers of the Board shall 
be bound and paged before being brought into use and all 
entries therein shall be made in English. All such books and 
registers shall be kept in the office of the Board and shall not 
be removed therefrom. 


(4) All corrections and alterations in accounts shall be 
neatly made in ink and attested by the initials of the Secre- 
tary. All corrections and alterations in vouchers shall be 
attested by the payee. No erasure shall be permitted in 
any account register, statement, voucher or book. Every 
سا‎ on the payment side of the cash book except in respect 
of charges not exceeding Rs.20, shall be supported by 
vouchers which shall be kept in a guard file and numbered 
consecutively in order of payment in each year. 


(5) As soon as any loss of money, stock or stores by 
embezzlement, theft or otherwise is discovered, the fact shall 
he reported by the Secretary to the Chairman. The Secretary 
shall with all possible despatch submit a further and com- 
plete report after full enquiry showing the total extent of 
the loss, the manner in which it occurred, and the steps taken 
to recover the amount or article lost and to punish those 
responsible for the loss. The Chairman shall submit the 
report to the State Government. 


(6) The amount of loss hy embezzlenrent, theft or other- 
wise shal] not be written off from the accounts without the 
sanction of the Board, provided that when the amount of 
losa exceeds Rs. 500 the sanction of the State Government 
shall also be necessary for writing it off. 


(7) The Board in consultation with the State Government 
shall decide upon the number and forms of account books to 
be maintained by the Secretary for the purpose of keeping 
accounts of the Moahajati Sadan Fund. The Secretary shall 
maintain a cash book in such form as may be prescribed by 
the State Government. At the end of each day the Secre- 
tary shal] verify the cash in hand and shall cause a memo- 
randum to be recorded showing the total expenditure and 
the bulance in hand, in cash and in the bank. 


(8) The Secretary shall prepare the annual accounts of 
the Mahajati Sadan Fund for every financial year beginning 
on the Ist day of April as 805১৮ as possible after the 6) 
March following in Form A. He shall also prepare a 
balance sheet showing the asseta and liabilities of the Fund 
at the end ofthe year. 

(9) The annual accounts of the Mahajati Sadan Fund 
shall be examined and audited by an auditor appointed by 
the State Government. The cost of audit shall te paid out 
of the Fund. 

(10) The auditor shall send copies of his report to the 
Chairman and the State Government. The State Government 
shall examine the report and may call for the explanation 
of any person concerned in regard to any matter therein, and 
shal] pass such orders on the report as it thinks fit. 

(77) An abstract of the annual accounts together with 
the auditor’s certificate thereon shall be published in the 
Calcutta Gazette for general information.

RESOLUTION No. 4288J. (ii) in item No. ‘(bh)’, under the heading

The Governor is pleased to decide that the Law 
Revision Committee appointed by the State Govern- 
ment in 1962 for revision of West Benga! Laws be 
redesignated as the State Law Commission to con- 
sist of the following existing members, namely :— 


(1) Sir Arthur Trevor Harries, ex-Chief Justice, 
Caleutta High Court—Chairman. 


(2) Shri M. N. Ghose, Barrister-at-Law. 


2. ShriS. K. Maitra, Assistant Secretary, 
Legislative Department, will act as Secretary to 
the State Law Commission. 


3. The functions of the State Law Commission 
will be— 


(a) to examine all Acts, Rules and Regulations 
affecting West Bengal except Central Acts 
relating to matters in the concurrent list 
and to suggest such amendments as may 
be found necessary to bring them into 
conformity with the Constitution, 10 
remove the difficulties experienced by the 
Administrative Departments concerned in 
udministering the Acts, and to eliminate 
the defects pointed out by judicial deci- 
sions; and چا‎ 

(9) to deal with such departmental requisitions 
of the Administrative Departments in con- 
nection with legislation matters as may be 
referred to it by the Judicial Department 
and to undertake any other allied func- 
tions which may be entrusted to it by the 
State Government in the Judicial Depart- 


ment. 
Order 


OrnEren that the resolution be published in the 
Calcutta Gazette and that a copy thereof be for- 
warded to the members of the State Law Commis- 
sion. کی‎ 

2. ORvERED also that a copy of the resolution 
be forwarded to all departments of Government 
and the Accountant-General, West Bengal, for 
information. 

By order of the Governor, 


K. K. HAJARA, Secy.

No. 6328M.2M-4/55.—20th July 1956.—In exercise of the powers con- 
ferred by sub-section (1) of section 4 of the Local Authorities Loans Act, 
1914 (IX of 1914), the Governor is pleased to make the following amend- 


ment in the Local Authorities Loans Rules, 1915, 


published with the 


(tovernment of India notification No. 1020A, dated the 10th November 1914, 


namely:— - 


Amendment. 


After rule 9 of the said rules, imsert the following rule, namely :— 


“9A. Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules, the State 
Government may grant loan to a local authority on such terms 
and conditions und in accordance with such procedure, as it may 
deem fit, consistent with the provisions of the Act if it is satia- 
fied that the loan is required for the carrying out of any works 
referred to in clause (1) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the 
Act, which, in its opinion, are necessary in any area where there 
has been heavy concentration of displaced persons from East 
Pakistan, within the local limits, and subject to the control, 


of such local authority. 


Ezplanation.—In this rule, a “displaced person’? means a person, who 
was ordinarily resident in the territories now comprised in Kast 


Pakistan, but who, on account of civil 


disturbances or on 


account of the partition of India, has migrated— 


(a) in the case of persons migrating from the district of Noakhali 
or the district of Tipperah, now forming part of East Pakistan, 
on or after the lst October 1946, and 


(b) in the case of persons migratin 


from any other area in Kast 


Pakistan, on or after the lst June 1947, 


to the territories now included in the Union of India, with the intention of 
taking up permanent residence within such territories.”

Midnapore.—No. 65808/M.3R-14/56.—5th July 1956.—Whereas the 
provisions of Schedule VI to the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act 
XV of 1932), have not been extended under section 312 of the said Act to 
the Ghatal Municipality in the district of Midnapore; 


And whereas the Commissioners of the said শি having heen 
so required by the State Government, have made the following by laws 
under sub-section (1) of section 328 of the said Act; 


Aud whereas the Commissioners of the said municipality have applied 
to the State Government for the confirmation of the said by-laws under 
section 506 of the said Act; 


And whereas— 


(a) a notice of the intention to apply for such confirmation of the said 
by-laws has been duly given one month before the making of the 
application for confirmation ag required by clause (1) of sub- 
section (2) of section 506 of the said Act, and 


(b) for one month before making of the application a copy of the said 
by-laws has been kept at the office of the Commissioners of the 
said municipality and has been open during office hours thereat 
to the inspection of the inhabitants of the said municipality, 
without fee, as required by clause (11) of sub-section (2) of 
section 506 of the said Act; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 506 of the 
anid Act, the Governor is pleased to confirm the following by-laws, namely :— 


BY-LAWS 


By-laws framed for the control of the erection of buildings and material 
alterations and additions to buildings within the Chatal Municipality as 
required by the Covernor of West Bengal under order No. 1030/M 3R- 
17/54, dated 8th February 1955, issued in exercise of the powers 
conferred by sub-section (1) of section 328 of the Bengal Municipal 
Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), 


1. Particulars to accompany application of erecting or re-erecting a 
masonry building.—Every person who intends to erect or re-erect a masonry 
building shall forward to the Chairman an application with a plan and 
specification of the building and a site plan of the land on which he pro- 
poses to make the erection or re-erection. In the said application he shall 
give a description of the building and its dimensions, and shall indicate the 
position of the site, the number assigned to it in the assessment book, its 
dimensions and such other particulars as may be required by the 
Commissioners. 


2. Floor of building used for manufacture and storage of articles for 
human consumption.—The floor of every masonry building intended to be 
used for the manufacture or storage of articles for human consumption shall 
be constructed of some impermeable materia] approved by the Commissioners, 


8. Building over muntctpal drain.—A masonry building shall امھ‎ 
extend over any municipal drain. 


4, Level of foor.—The lowest floor of every masonry building erected 
or re-erected from the ground shall be constructed at such level as will 
admit of the construction of a drain sufficient for the effectual drainage of 
the building, and placed at such level as will admit of the drainage heing 
led into an existing or projected municipal drain. 


5. Foundation.—Except with the sanction of the Commissioners, the 
foundation of a masonry building shall rest on natural ground. 


6. Plinth.—The plinth of a masonry building shall be at least two feet 
above the level of the centre of the nearest street; provided that the plinth 
of stables and cow-sheds need not be more than one foot above such level. 


٠٣. Walls in butlding exceeding one storey in height.—(1) If a masonry 
building exceeds one storey in height— 


(a) no part of any wall, other than a cornice or a moulding, shall over 
hang any part of a wall underneath it; and 


(b) every wall shall be of such thickness as the Commissioners may 
consider necessary to ensure safety, regard being had to the 
height of the building, the materials of which it is constructed 
a the purpose for which it is intended. 


(2) Nothing contained in sub-rule (1) shall prevent the erection of a 
second storey upon an existing masonry building, the walls of which are 
certified by the Commissioners as being able to bear the load proposed to 
be put upon them. 


2860 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 


8. Interior courtyards and open spaces to be raised.—Every interior 
courtyard and every open space shall be raised at least one foot above the 
level of the centre of the nearest street so as to admit of easy drainage. 


9. Herght.—No masonry building exceeding fifty feet in height shall 
be erected without the special permission of the Commissioners. 


10. Stte-plan.—The site-plan sent to the Chairman under rule 1 shall 
be drawn to a scale of not less than one-fiftieth of an inch to a foot, shal] be 
sent in duplicate and shall show:— 

(a) the boundaries of the site and of any contiguous land belonging to 
the owner thereof; 

(0) the position, form and dimensions of privies, urinals, drains, cess- 
pools, stables, cattle-sheds, cow-sheds, wells and other appur- 
tenances of the building; 

(c) the space which it is proposed to leave about the building to secure 
the free circulation of air, the admission of light and access for 
scavengering purposes; and 

(৫) such particulars as may be required by the Commissioners, 


11. Building plan.—The plan of the building (and the elevations and 
sections, whenever necessary), sent to the Commissioners under rule 1, shall 
be neatly and accurately drawn to a scale of not less than one-eighth of an 
inch to a foot shall be sent in duplicate and shall show— 

(a) the depth and width of the foundation of the building; 

(b) the level of the lowest floor of the building; and 

(c) the level of all courtyards and open spaces in the building or 
premises and the plinth level of the building with reference to 
the level of the centre of the nearest street, 


12. Specifications.—The specifications sent to the Chairman with any 
such plan shall comprise full information as to the following particulars :— 
(8) the manner in which roof and house drainage and the surface 
drainage of the land will be disposed of; 
(iz) the means of access to service privies that will be available to 
acavengers; 


(£2) the means of ingress and egress if the building is intended to he used 
as a dwelling house for two or more families or as a place for 
carrying on any trade or business in which more than 20 peuple 
may be employed, or as a place of public resort; and 


(tv) such other particulars as may be required by the Commissioners, 


13. Signature of plans, elevations and sections.—The plan, elevations 
and sections referred to in rules 10 and 11 shall be signed clearly and in a 
prominent place by the ower of the وھ‎ or if he ig illiterate, by any 
other person authorised by him to sign in his behalf, in which case they 
shall be marked with the owner’s thumb impression. 


14. Chairman to sign approved plans.—The Chairman shall sign all 
passed plans in token of the approval of the Commissioners. 


16. Restriction on 21৮71500601 of certain rules.—Rules 1, 10, 11, 12, 19 
and 14 shall not-be applied in the case of any alteration of, or addition to, 
a masonry building, unless one or more of the following works is under- 
taken, namely سے‎ 


(a) the construction of a roof or an external or party-wall ; 


(b) any repairs to the building which involve the reconstruction of a 
masonry wall after the same has been entirely or in a great part 
demolished ; 


(c) the closing of any door or window in an external wall; 
(0) the construction or removal of an internal wall or partition ; 


(6) any other alteration of the internal arrangements of a building 
which affects its courtyard or courtyards, or its drainage, venti- 
lation or sanitary arrangements or which affects its security ; 


(f) the addition of any building, room, outhouse or other structure ; 

(9) the roofing of any space adjoining a wall or building; and 

(h) the alteration of a building for the purpose of effecting a partition. 

16. The penalty for the infringement of any of the by-law Nos. 2 to 
9 shall be— 

(a) a fine not exceeding Rs. 60, and 


(b) in the case of a continuing infringement, a و‎ fine not exceedin 
Ra. 56 for each day after written notice of the offence is serve 


by the Commissioners,

Office of the Accountant-General, West Bengal 


NOTIFICATION 


Subject :—Small Savings Scheme—Lodging of 
National Savings Certificates in 019 068. 
suries. 


No. TM/566.—6th July 1956.—It has been 
decided by the National Savings Commissioner 
that there is no objection to an authorised agent 
depositing National Savings Certificates in the 
treasury in case of the death of the investor in 
the intervening period of collection of the amount 
and delivery of certificates. In such cases, the 
entry to be made by the Treasury Officer in the 
space provided on the reverse of the authorised 
agents’ official receipt book for the purchaser's 
receipt will be to the following effect :— 


“The purchaser feing dead, certified that the 
certificate has been duly lodged for safe 
custody at this treasury.” 


All Treasury and Sub-treasury Officers in West 
Bengal are requested to note the above instructions. 


P. KHANNA, Dy. Accountant-General.‏ .لا

ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Jagannath Prosad 
Khettry & Sons, 20 Umesh Dutta Lane, Calcutta-6, and one of their 
employees, Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya, C/o Shri Sankar K. Paridya, 
59 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1. 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. 


PRESENT : 
Sori J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Third Industrial Trebunal. 


For the employee: The employee in person. 
For the Company: Shri N. C. Das Gupta, Advocate. 


AWARD 


٠١ By order No. 5832Dis. /D/11L-406/55, dated the 10th December 1955, 
the Government of West Bengal in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Tnsputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Messers. Jaganuath Prosad Khettry & Sons, 20 Umesh Dutta Lane, 
Calcutta-6, and one of their employees, Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya, C/o 
Shri Sankar .کا‎ Paridya, 59 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1, regarding the 
matter specified in the schedule, to the Third Industrial Tribunal consti- 
tited under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification 
No, 592Dis./D/121-5/52, dated the 28rd February 1953, for adjudication. 


8 After usual summons the parties entered appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 21st February 1956. 
[he parties were thereafter directed to file list of documents. The dispute 
wa: then heard on 28th June, 1956. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows: — 


To what amount of compensation is Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya 
entitled for dismissal from service? 


DECISION 


٠ Mesars. Jagannath Prosad Khettry & Sons (hereafter called the ‘“employ- 
]ঃ ) are dealers of rickshaw parts. They have a shop at 20 Umesh J)utta 
‘ane, Calcutta, in which they have about 14 employees. Shri Rajendra 


2900 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 [Darr 1 


a SS 
Prosad Khettry, the eldest son of Shri Jagannath Prosad Khettry, manages 
the business. 


The employee Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya was a general assistant in 
the said shop on a pay of Rs. 65 per month. His work was mainly to pack 
up the articles and to book them in the railway station. According to the 
employee Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya, he was discharged on and from 
29nd January, 1965, while according to the employer he had left service on 
that day as the employer could not agree to give him advance up to Rs, 500. 


Before entering into the merits, let me first deal with the preliminary 
objection taken by the employer regarding maintainability of the reference. 
1t was contended on behalf of the employer that the dispute was an indivi- 
dual dispute and would not come within the language of the definition of 
৫1170081710] dispute’ in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
and as such the reference was incompetent. 1 agree that it is so. In the 
‘resent case, none of the workmen in the employ of Messers. Jagannath 
مسا‎ Khettry & Sons or any Union took up cause of Shri Narayan Chandra 
Paridya either leading to or after the present reference. So the dispute as 
referred to is purely an individual dispute which has never been taken up 
by any other workmen or Union. No doubt in the case of Swadeshi Cotton 
Mills Co., Ltd., versus Shri Ram Baran reported in 1953 1..A.C., 189, the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal held that an individual dispute like the present 
one would come within the meaning of the ‘‘industrial dispute’’ as defined 
in the Act, but on the other hand the Calcutta High Court held in the cases 
reported in 55 C.W.N., 256 and 57 C.W.N., 169 that an individual dispute 
was not an industrial dispute as defined in the Act. As the decisions are 
not uniform, the question arises which 1s to be followed by the State Tribu- 
nal. Under Article 227 of the Constitution, every Tribunal in the State در‎ 
subject to the judicial supervision of the State High Court. It being ৪০, 
it is obvious that the law laid down by the High Court is the law as far as 
that State 1s concerned and every Tribunal in the State is bound to accept 
the same. His Lordship Chagla 0. J. of Bombay High Court also so held 
in the case between Gambhirji Odharji and Labour Appellate Tribunal of 
India and others reported in 1955 L.L.J., Volume II, page 202. In the 
circumstances following the decisions of the Calcutta High Court, I find 
that the dispute raised in the present case is not an industrial dispute and as 
such the reference 1s incompetent. 


In view of the above findings no decision is necessary on merits. Had 
it, however, been necessary, I would have also found against the workman 
The case as made out by the employee Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya in his 
written statement of claim is as follows. On 22nd January 1955 when the 
workman approached Shri Rajendra Prasad Khettry for leave of one month 
to go home in connection with his marriage and for an advance of Rs. 600 
for the purpose to be recoverable from his salary in instalments, said Shri 
Rajendra Stoel Khettry told him that under مھ‎ circumstances 
they would give him leave far less advance of Rs. 500, and when the workman 
insisted for the same, he turned him out from the shop with threats of heat- 
ing. Before so doing the employer made him to sign the salary book for 
his outstanding duse of Rs. 9-10-6 but eventually refused to pay him the 
amount. His employment was thus terminated wrongfully. The workman 
accordingly سا‎ for payment of gratuity for 8 months at the rate of Re 
65 per month for his 8 years’ service under the employer as also 3 months’ 
pay in lien of notice besides arrears of salary of Rs. 9-10-6 up to- the 
date of termination of employment. 


parr رآ‎ THE CAJLUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 6 2901 


020 that he had himself quitted the service in the circumstances as 


below : 

Qn 22nd January 1955 when the workman prayed for leave and an 
advance of Rs. 500, Shri Rajendra Prosad Khettry said that he had no ob- 
jection to his going home for a month but he would not be able to pay him 
Its, 600 as advance as the condition of business was not good and as auch 
huge sum was never advanced to any of the employees at any time. But 
the employee would not listen to this. He became angry and quarrelled 
wiih the employers and said that if Rs. 500 were not paid to him as advance 
he would not continue his service under the firm any longer and he 
demanded that his up to date dues of salary should at once be paid. There- 
upon his up to date dues amounting to Rs. 9-10-6 were paid to him forth- 
with for which he made an endorsement on the salary book and signed his 
name. Thereafter the workman told Shri Rajendra Prasad Khettry that he 
would not work in their firm any more and went away without leaving 
any address of the place he was going to. After this the workman never 
came back to the shop. As the workman left his service of his own accord, 
no question of payment of gratuity or compensation did arise. 


In support of his case the workman Shri Narayan Chandra Paridya has 
alone deposed. He is P.W.1. The employer, on the other hand, has 
exumined Shri Rajendra Prasad Khettry hesides proving documents 
Exts. A to J). 


Qn giving careful consideration to the evidence and circumstances, T 
accept employer’s version of the case, which is more probable and natural. 
Qn 22nd January 1965 the workman, according to both sides, approached 
Shri: Rajendra Prosad Khettry for leave for one month as also for an 
advance of Rs. 600 in connection with his marriage. The case of the 
workman that Shri Rajendra Prosad Khettry flatly refused to 156 leave and 
also the advance has been given direct 116 by the workman himself in his 
deposition before this Tribunal. He admitted that Shri Rajendra Prosad 
Khettry granted him the leave prayed for and also agreed to give him an 
advance up to Rs. 100. In his written application before the Labour Direc- 
(01916, 1/%1.4, the workman also so admitted. So the allegation that the 
employer hecame angry because he wanted leave and advance cannot stand. 
On the contrary, it appears that there was cause for the workman to be dis- 
satisfied as Shri Rajendra Prasad Khettry could not agree to give him 
advance beyond Rs. 100. Jn the circumstances, it was more natural that 
the workman flared up and said that he would no Jonger serve if Rs. 500 
were not paid to him as advance. The demand for payment of up to date 
dues also points more in favour of workman's expressing unwillingness to 
continue service under the firm any longer. The workman admittedly made 
endorsement and signed in the salary hook (Ext.C) acknowledging receipt 
of the outstanding dues of Rs. 9-10-6 till then. His allegation that he did 
not receive the said sum is unreliable. If the employer could have agreed 
to give him an advance up to Rs. 100, it is not natural and probable that 
such employer after taking signed acknowledgment would refuse to pay a 
paltry sum of Rs. 9-10-6 which was outstanding till then. The emplover’s 
ease that on their unwillingnesa to grant him an advance of Rs, 500 the 
workman hecame angry and said that he would no longer work and accord- 
ingly he demanded payment of his dues till then is more natural and 
probable. From the evidence, I believe that the workman received his 
outstanding dues of Rs. 9-10-6 till then. IT also believe that after having 
reveived the snid amount he left the job and did not come back. It appears 
that the workman was offered re-employment during conciliation proceed- 
ings by the employer but he refused to accept. Before this Tribunal, too, 


2902 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 [Parry 


the workman expressed his unwillingness to rejoin. These would SU Wort’ 
that he had left the employment lumself. After having done so, it ;, 
obvious, the workman cannot claim either gratuity or notice pay. 

So both in law and on merits, Shri Narayan Chandra Varidya is entitle 
to no relief. 


I award accordingly.

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour by 
order No. 1988Dis. /D/7L-48(A)/53, dated 7th April 7954, order No. 2329- 
Dis. /D/7L-47/54, dated Oth May 1954, order No. 3398Dis./D/3A-10/54, 
dated 12th July 1954, order No. 3537D1s./D/7L-47/54, dated 21st July 
1954, and order No. 41360Dis./D/70-47/54, dated 26th August 1954, 
referred, under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), the industrial dispute between 101 specified Jute Mills 
and their workmen regarding some matters specified in a schedule to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. The award of this Tribunal in respect of this 
proceeding was published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 6th October 1955. 


While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application 
under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act in case No. 402 of 1955, 
was filed by Jhunkun Bhor and two others on the allegation that the 
petitioners have served the Company for long eight years, that Shri Bibhuti 
Bhusan Chatterji, bead issue clerk had some urgent necessity of money 
for his daughter’s marriage and as such requested the petitioners to make 
some immediate arrangement of money, further romising to pay the 
money on the next date, that realising the urgency, ۳ petitioners on their 
own risk took loan of Rs. 300 from mahajan on terms of high interest and 
ay the head clerk, that the head clerk failed to pay on the next date, 
ut promised to pay on the date of receiving the salary, that the peti- 
tioners on 2nd May 1955 after closing hours requested the head clerk out- 
side the Mill premises to return the money but the head clerk denied 
everything and there was altercation, that the head clerk made a false 
teport to the Manager against the petitioners but the Manager issued a 
false charge-sheets and suspended the petitioners in violation of the 
standing orders and for this a criminal case was started against the head 
clerk, that the order of suspension is illegal, that the petitioners have 
been thrown out of employment, that under the circumstances the 
petitioners pray that the Tribunal may be pleased to pass an award for 
reinstatement with compensation for the period of unemployment. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the opposite 
party, the Company filed its written statement in which it contended that 


2912 THE CAIXCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 [Panr [ 


the application filed by the petitioners is misconceived and not 10181706610. 
able in law as the Company has not violated section 33 of the Industria 
Disputes Act, that the Company has already filed separate application under 
section 33 on 17th May 1955 seeking permission of the Tribunal to dismiag 
the workmen concerned, that the application under section 838A filed by 
the said workmen contains various vague, misleading and incorrect allegy. 
tions and the Compuny denies the same, that the ss ey prays that the 
application under section 383A filed by the complainants should be 
rejected on the preliminary point of law. 


DECISION 


Although a petition of complaint under section 33A alleging violation 
of condition of service for failure to apply under section 33 for permission 
of the Tribunal has been filed, it has now been found by the employers 
that actually this was not the case. They have in fact applied under 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for permission of the Tribunal]. 
We have perused the three applications under section 33 and under section 
83۸ of the Industrial Disputes Act and we find that the petition under 
section 33 covers the ground which forms the subject matter of the com. 
plaint under section 394. of the Industria) Disputes Act and which has since 
been unfortunately struck off as this Tribunal became functus 017০০ after 
one month of the publication of the award. 


It has now been held by the Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Products of India, Ltd. (1955 1515 1৮01. I, page 346), that it is the 
contravention by the employer of the provision of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act or section 23 of the Appellate Tribunal Act which 
gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the workmen to approach and 
move the respective authority concerned of the additional jurisdiction and 
powers conterred on it by the section. The authority referred to in the 
section is a Court of Limited Jurisdiction and must accordingly be strictly 
confined to the exercise of functions and powers actually conferred on it 
by the Act which constituted it. 


In the present case it being proved that a petition seeking pemnission 
of the Tribunal was actually filed on the self-same ground, we hold that 
the petition of complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
is not maintamable and we award accordingly.

2924 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 [Part | 


(XIV of 1947), the industrial dispute between 101 specified Jute Mills aud 
their workmen regarding some matters specified in a schedule to tly 
Tribunal for adjudication. The award of this Tribunal in respoct of this 
proceeding was published in the Calcutta Gazette, duted Gth October 1955. 


While the aforesaid dispute was pending, the present application under 
section 383A was filed by the complainant Ramjan stating that he 1s im service 
under the Company for about 80 years without any fault, that there was a 
strike of the workers on account of some dispute between the Company and 
the workers regarding working hours, and this was followed by a lock-out 
declared by the Management, that thereafter on 12th July 1954 during 
lock-out the Company got some workers arrested from inside the Mill 
premises, that though the petitioner was quite innocent of the matter of 
strike, he was arrested by the police on mere suspicion and was sent to jail 
at Dum Dum and Barrackpore, that the Company has filed a petition under 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act on incorrect and false grounds, 
that in the circumstances the petitioner prays for an order of the Tribunal 
to allow him to continue in service pending decision of the application under 
section J3 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


Notice of the aforesaid complaint having been served on the opposite 
party, the Company filed its written statement on 26th April 1955 statin, 
that the application of the complainant Ramjan contains various 1160711 
and misleading allegations, that on 12th July 1954 at about 7 a.m. workers 
of almost all the departments resorted to an illegal stay-in strike. that those 
workers who resorted to violence and lawlessness were arrested by the 
police, that Ramjan was also arrested on 12th July 1954 for indulging in 
similar activities, that a charge-sheet was issued to him and after enquiry 
he was found guilty of charges which amounted to misconduct and he was 
suspended pending the permission from the Tribunal for his dismissal, that 
in the circumstances the opposite party submits that the application of the 
complainant Ramjan under section 994 should be rejected. 


DECISION 


Although a petition of complaint alleging violation of condition of 
service for failure to apply under section 33 for permission of this Tribunai 
has been filed, it has now heen proved by the employers that actually this 
is not the case. In fact they applied under section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act for permission of the Tribunal. We have perused the two 
applications under section 33 and under section 338A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act and we find that the petition under section 88 covers the 
ground which forms the subject matter of the complaint under section 334 
of the Indestrial Disputes Act and which has since been struck off as the 
oo became functus oficto after one month of the publication of the 
award. 


It has now been held by the Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Products of India Ltd. (1955 L.I..J., Vol. I, page 346) that it is the 
contravention by the employer of the provision of section 88 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act or section 28 of the Appellate Tribunal Act which gives 1186 
to a cause of action in favour of the workman to approach and move the 
respective authority concerned of the additional jurisdiction and powers 
conferred on it by the section. The authority referred to in the section 
is a court of Limited Jurisdiction and must accordingly be strictly conftned 
to the exercise of functions and powers actually conferred on it by the Act 
which constituted it. 


part 11 THE 04140010014 GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 2925 


In the present case it being proved that a petition seeking permission 
ot the Tribunal was actually on the self-same grounds, we hold that the 
ition of complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act is Lut 


maintainable aud we award accordingly.

9 12th October 1955 seeking permission to dismiss the workman concerned 
and pending such permission he was suspended, that in the circumstances

ihe company prays “that the application under section 8304 filed by phe 
ক should be rejected on “the preliminary point of law and dy 
merits. 


For the sake of convenience ‘of decision these two cases are taken up 
together and hence this Award will govern both the cases. 


DECISION 


Although a petition of complaint alleging violation of condition of 
service for failure to apply under section 33 for permission of this Tribunal 
has been filed, it has now been proved by the employers that actually this 
is not the case. In fact they applied under section 33 of the Industria] 
Disputes Act for permission of the Tribunal. We have perused the two 
applications under section 33 and under section 388A of the Industria] 
Disputes Act and we find that the petition under section 383 covers the 
ground which forms the subject-matter of the complaint under section ৭) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act in each case and which has since heen struok 
off as the Tribunal became functus officio after one month of the publication 
of the Award. 


It has now been held by the Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Products of India Ltd. (1955 L.L.J., Vol. I, page 346) that it 18 the 
contravention of the employer of the provision of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act or section 28 of the Appellate Tribunal Act which 
gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the workman to approach and 
move the respective authority concerned of the additional jurisdiction and 
power conferred on it by the section. The authority referred to in the 
section is a Court of Limited Jurisdiction and must accordingly be stgictly 
confined to the exercise of functions and powers actually conferred on itwby 
the Act which constituted it. 


In the present case it being proved that a petition seeking permission 
of the Tribunal was actually on the self-same grounds, we hold that the 
petition of complaint under section 894. of the Industrial Disputes Act in 
each of these cases Nos. 92 of 1955 and 365 of 1955 is not maintainable and 


we award accordingly.

DECISION 


This appeal is against an award of ihe First Industrial Tribunal, West 
Bengal, dated 27th May 1955, and published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 
24th June 1955. By order No. 2869 Dis./D);7L-15/54, dated 4th June 1954, 


two issues were referred to the Tribunal— 


* (1) Whether the Company was justified in terminating the services 
of Shri Sreeman Chandra Basu on grounds of superannuation? 


(2) What relief Shri Basu is entitled to? 


Issue No. 1 was decided against Shri Basu. Hence this appeal by him. 


Shri Basu, a cashier in the Respondent 7 was retired by order, 
dated 380th November 1958, with effect from Ist December 1958, on the 
رد‎ of having reached the age of superannuation with an offer to get 

is dues per Jute Award. He denied having reached that age and 
imputed bad faith to the Company. When he demanded his pay and other 
dues, Company made a deduction of Rs. 2,932-0-6 from his dues. Con- 
ciliation failing, this reference was made. He denied Company’s claim 
for outstandings against him. The Adjudicator found against him on this 
matter as ell and awarded him only the balance, after calculating his 
gratuity uccording to the provisions of Chapter VA of Industrial Disputes 
Act and deducting therefrom the amount due to the Company. 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 1956 


Regarding the rule of retirement, the workmen’s Union whose 
registered office is in the appellant’s house, served a charter of demands on 
the Company on 29th January 1953, one of the demands being that ‘“‘a 
man shall retire after completing 55 years of age and in exceptional cases 
where parties agree extension may be granted’’. Company says it accepted 
this demand. Appellant’s contention 1s that the Company did not accept 
any of the demands, never intimated to the Union its acceptance of any 
demand and that it could not accept one demand out of many, some of 
which were inter-related to the matter of retirement, e.g., rate of gratuity. 
The Adjudicator has believed the Company’s case that it had accepted 
this demand of the Union, as the junior section of the employees was getting 
restore. This is a finding of fact and there being evidence in support of 
it, it cannot be disturbed in appeal. 


As to the appellant’s age, a statement marked A showing the age of 
different employees, was enclosed with the said charter of demands, in 
which the appellant’s age was shown as 54 years, on Ist December 1952. 
The Company got the ages of different employees ascertained. In a slip 
Ext. E, 1897 is given as the year of appellant’s birth and this entry is 
initialled by him. Appellant denied this initial. Shri Panchanan Chanda, 
O.P.W. 1, assistant cashier proved this initial. The Adjudicator believed 
him. Appellant was cashier. Shri Chanda was assistant cashier. He 
knew appellant’s initial. We find no reason to disagree with the learned 
Adjudicator. Born in 1897, the appellant was over 55 on Ist December 
1963. He was rightly retired. 


Regarding deductions from the amount due to the appellant, he pleaded 
in paragraphs 32 and 33 of his claim statement that being cashier he had 
to maintain suspence cash account of sundry payments and receipts and 
this account need not have appeared in the original cash book and had to 
be kept in kutcha cash book. The Company purchased several shares in 
different companies in the appellant’s name all of which are not known to 
him and Shri Dayaram Babu used to pay Rs. 50 per month in the 
appellant’s name from his own funds for reasons best known to him. As 
a faithful servant he has done many things in the interest of the Company 
details of which shall be furnished at the time of hearing, these being 
business secrets. Company replied that these allegations are distortions of 
facts and on checking accounts a balance of Rs. 3,315-0-6 was found against 
him. Though he had admitted his guilt, still due to his long service, the 
management allow him to pay Rs. 50 per month from his salary. A 
further sum of Rs. 1,017 was lying to his debit in the Company’s books. 
Out of this total of Rs. 4,300 and odd he paid Rs. 1,400 leaving a balance 
of Rs. 2,932-0-6 against him. In his examination-in-chief the appellant 
did not say a word relating to their matter. In cross-examination, he 
denied that he had defalcated any money, but admitted signing the 
vouchers which fasten Tiability on him. Shri Panchanan Chanda deposed 
to the balance outstanding against the appellant and the alleged under- 
standing against the appellant that the appellant would pay 
Rs. 50 per month out of his monthly salary. He denied in cross- 
examination that this money was not taken by the appellant and 
was kept for the Company’s business. The Company tendered in evi- 
dence the vouchers signed by the appellant. The Adjudicator believed 
Company’s case. In appeal, Shri D. L. Sen Gupta argued for the appel- 
lant that Shri Daya Ram Poddar purchased shares in the appellant’s name 
to avoid payment of income-tax and when appellant was assessed to tax on 
that account, he approached Shri Daya Ram Poddar who teld him that he 
(Poddar) weuld pay the amount of income-tax. This explanation was 
neither given in these words in the claim statement nor in the appellant’s 
statement nor was it put to Shri Chanda, 0.P.W. 1. Therefore, it can- 
not be accepted in appeal, when there is no evidence in support of it. 
Shri D. L. Sen Gupta argued that Shri Poddar must have entered the 
witness box and denied this version of the appellant. But it was not put 
forth by the appellant in his pleadings or سا ا‎ therefore, Shri Poddar 
need pat have appeared in evidence. We uphold this part of the award 
as well. 


Lastly, it was contended, that it is a case of victimization and unfair 
discremination due to trade Union activities of the appellant, as imme- 
diately after the formation of the Union the Secretary was discharged and 
then the appellant, as the office of the Union is undoubtedly in the appel- 
lant’s house and others who have exceeded the aforesaid age of super- 
annuation are still in the service of the Company. The Secretary’s age was 
68. The appellant had exceeded 55. It is true that there are others still 
in service who are over 55. The Company’s reply is that it is retiring 
them as permitted by the requirements of the business. Those others are 
৪190 in key positions. All work cannot be disturbed at once. These expla- 
nations are reasonable. There is no force in this contention as well. 


ORDER. 
The appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs. 


A. DAS GUPTA, 
President. 


S. B. SINGH, 
Member.

In the matter of an appeal against the award of Shri J. N, Moitra, Judge, 
Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, made on 2nd September 1955, in 
respect of an industrial dispute between the above parties.

Appearances: 


For the Appellants: Shri Panchanan Bhattacharjee. 
For the Respondents: Shri S. B. Roy, Law Officer. 


State : West Bengal. 
Industry : Miscellaneous. 


DECISION 


This appeal is directed against an award of the Third Industrial 
Tribunal, West Bengal, dated 2nd September 1955, and published in the’ 
£ andl Gazette, dated September 29, 1955. The only issue referred to the 

ribunal was :— 


“Introduction of grades and scales.’’ 


In view of the precarious financial condition of the Company and the 
nature of the Industry, the learned Adjudicator did not consider proper 
to introduce grades cnd scales, but in view of the fact that bonus paid in 
the past had ceased and the rate of Puja bonus had been reduced since the 
award of Shri Palit, he awarded a general increment of Rs. 3 per month 
in the basic pay of all the 51 workmen concerned with this dispule. Being 
disatisfied with the award the workmen have preferred this appeal. Only 
two grounds have been taken in the Memorandum of grounds of appeal: 


(1) That the learned Judge erred in disallowing retrospective effect 
in respect of increments. 


(2) He did not suggest any grade or scale. 


The Company,*as its name suggests, manufactures medicinal preparations 
and injections which are very vital for all common people. Its invested 
capital is less than 1.50 lakhs. It runs on a small scale. Since 1948-49, it 
paid dividend at 6 per cent. in the first {wo years, none in 1950-51 and 
1954-55 and 3 per cent. between in 1951-52, 1952-53, 1953-64. It paid 
bonus amounting to Rs. 14,752 in 1948-49, none in the following three 
years and a little over Rs. 3,000 in each of the last three years ending 
with 1954-55. Its balance sheet, profit and loss account are duly audited. 
Tt is clear that its financial conditioa is not very sound. There is a reason 
for it. During war-time, being afraid of bombing it opened branches out- 
side which had to be closed down resulting in loss to the Company. 


The workmen’s contention is that it is paying high salaries, commis- 
sion and bonus to its high paid employees at top men. But the work 1s of 
such a technical nature that only highly skilled persons can do substantial 
work in it. Other workmen can shy work according to their directions. 
It is, therefore, not surprising that high emoluments are paid to its to 
employees. It is further urged that some of the employees are employe 
unnecessarily, e.g.,, a Law Officr in such ao small concern and some of the 
highly paid employees are relatives of the Directors of the Company. 
There is no such evidence on record. We reject this contention. 


When once it is established that financial position of the Company is 
not sound, the learned Adjudicator was fully justified in refusing to fix 
grades and time-scale. Besides this grades can be fixed when categories of 
workmen can be fairly ascertained. That may be possible only in those 
industries which are well established, the number of which are not many. 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 26, 6 


In an industry like the present one, this is not possible and wages can be 
fixed only having regurd to efficiency and experience of the workers. No 
doubt some of the 51 workmen are of the commonly known categories, e.g., 
sweeper, typist clerk, durwan, etc., ete. Annexure A to the Company's writteu 
statement is a list of ull the 51 workmen. It indicates the occupation of 
each and payments made to each of them. It was conceded on behalf of 
the appellants that the employees whose basic pay exceeds Rs. 150 are not 
concerned in this appeal. We have examined the basic wage and dearness 
allowance of each of these employees. We think that in view of the 
financial condition of the Company the wages of none except three are 
below the minimum and if we add Rs. 3 as awarded by the Tribunal, that 
will be quite fair in view of the financial condition of the concern. The 
existing wage of none of the employees is below Rs. 30 and now it has 
pene Rs. 33 for the lowest paid workmen. The three employees are as 
ollows : 


(1) Mir Errudat Hossain, duftary and despatch clerk. His existing 
basic pay Rs. 45 and dearness allowance Rs. 30. We fix his basic pay at 
Rs. 55, because a duftary’s job is somewhat inferior to that of a werk 


(2) D. Bose, clerk, gets Rs. 30 basic wage. No clerk in Calcutta gets 
less than Rs. 60 as basic wage. The Company must pay the minimum basic 
wage at least. Similarly is the case of (3) K. Chatterjee, a despatch clerk

whose basic pay is Rs. 39. We fix the basic pay of these two clerks at 


Rs. 60 


The wage of all the other employees is satisfactory ufter addition of

The increase of Rs. 3 shall
