2096 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1956 {Part 1 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAI, TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
۱ PRESENT: | 
Suri G. 1১. MUKHERJEE, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances : 
For the employee: Shri Potit Paban Pathak. 
For the Company: Shri N. M. Das Gupta, Advocate. 


The original reference, out of which this complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, has arisen, was made to this Tribunal 
لصا‎ Government order No. 4013Dis.//111-90/55, dated 30th August, 
1955. 


AWARD 


This is a complaint under section 83۸ of the Industrial Disputes Act 
filed by Shri Anil Kumar Chatterjee, a workman of Ganges Valley Bone 
Mill. His case is that during the pendency of the original reference, the 
Opposite Party, Ganges Valley Bone Mill, dismissed him on 6th June 19656, 
on a false and baseless charge, without the permission of the Tribunal, and 
as such section 33 of the Act has been contravened. 


The application was contested by the gh ae Valley Bone Mill, the 
Opposite Party. It is urged on its hehalf that the application is not 
maintainable in law. The Opposite Party further wanted to say that the 
Management was quite justified in dismissing the petitioner. 


An objection has been taken on behalf of the Opposite Party that the 
present application under section 33A 1s not competent on the ground that 
this very question was the subject matter of another complaint under 
section o8A, which the petitioner himself did not like to pursue ultimately, 
as a result of which a ‘‘no dispute’? award was made in the case. 
Accordingly, the Opposite Party has contended that the petitioner cannot 
raise نت‎ dispute in respect of the matter, which ended in a ‘‘no 4٠٥٥” 
award. 


In order to appreciate the contention of the Opposite Party on this 
point, I called for the file of the case, in which this particular workman, 
Shri Anil Kumar Chatterjee, made the previous complaint under section 
934 of the Act. It 1s case No. 340 of 1955 under section 33A. I have 
perused the said file, and it appears that this petitioner made similar 
complaint under section 338A in the aforesaid case, as has been done in the 

resent case. The allegation in both the complaints is exactly the same. 
he previous complaint, as the record of the case goes to show, was allowed 
to be withdrawn, as the petitioner filed a petition stating that in pursuance 
of a talk he had with Mr. Pyane, Manager of the Company, he did not like 
to proceed with this complaint under section 33A of the Act. The Tribunal 
acting on this petition allowed the complaint to be withdrawn as prayed 
for, and gave an award accordingly on 6th February 1956. The petition 
filed by the petitioner was made part of the award as Annexure ‘‘A”’. 
The present complaint was filed only a few days after this. So, the 
question is whether the present complaint is maintainable on the same 
facts, in view of the withdrawl of the previous complaint, which culmi- 
nated in an award by this Tribunal. I have given my careful and anxious 


Part T | THE CAIOUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1956 2997 
———— ০ ৯ ২ 
coysideration — to the matter, and I am of the view thut the present 
cumplaint is not maintainable, mm view of what hap ened as regards the 
previous complaint as stated above. J have already observed that the 
allegation as made in this complaint is the same, as was made in the 
previous one. There has been no further cause of action since the previous 
complaint was made by the present petitioner. The grievance of the 
petitioner in the হল complaint was that the Opposite Party 0151019860 
him by a notice dated 6th June 1955 on false and baseless charges of gross 
insubordination, ete., during the pendency of the original reference, and 
without the permission of the Tribunal. Similar is the grievance of the 
petitioner in the present complaint. There is no addition of any new 
cause or grievance in the present complaint. If that be so, I wonder how 
the petitioner can reagitate the same matter, which was finally concluded 
between the parties by the order passed by this Tribunal on 6th February 
1956 on the basis of an application made by this very petitioner to the 
effect that he did not like to proceed with the case. The Tribunal in 
pursuance of that application made an award. That award has the bind- 
ing effect on the parties, and continues to he binding on the parties still. 
The matter involved in the present case, waa the matter directly and 
suhatantially raised in the previous complaint. Admittedly, there has 
heen no further cause of action. That being so, a party cannot be allowed 
10 agitate again before a Tribunal the same cause, nor is it desirable that 
the Tribunal should be vexed twice over the same cause. If such a 
thing 18 allowed to go on, the work of the Tribunal would he stultified. 
The rule of finality should be observed in Industrial Courts in appropriate 
cases, otherwise the harmonious relations between capital and labour may 
be disturbed, and the defeated party may be encouraged to raise the same 
point over and over again in the hope of ultimate success. I am mindful 
of the fact that the rule of res judicata, as understood in Civil Law, does 
not strictly apply to industrial disputes, for in view of the provisions of 
section 18 of the Act, the rule of res judicata if applied to industrial 
disputes, would lead to stagnation and a feeling of frustration, and so 
would create more unrest in the industrial sphere. But the recognition 
of the doctrine of finality of a judgment between the same parties cannot 
be ruled out altogether. even when the matter involved is raised before an 
Industrial Court, if the matter directly and substantially raised and 
adjudicated upon in the previous proceedings be directly and substantially 
in issue in the aubsequent proceedings. My view ia that such o rule of 
finality should, therefore, apply to awards given in respect of industrial 
disputes, when the facts and circumstances existing at the time of the 
prior award continue to remain the same. Even if the provisions of 
section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot in terms apply to the 
industrial disputes, the principle embodied in that section is applicable 
to appropriate cases, If the matter has once been directly raised before 
an Industrial Tribunal and adjudicated upon fairly without fraud or 
collusion, the adjudication must be held to he binding on the parties, if 
the same question is directly ond substantially raised in the subsequent 
proceedings. Even if it be conceded that ordinarily the principle of res 
judicata 1s not strictly applicable to industrial matters, still it will not be 
open to a workman to reagitate a matter, which has already been dealt 
with by the Industrial Tribunal previously in a proceeding, except when 
there is no material change in the circumstances or some other sufficient 
cause. Judged by this test, it can be safely said that such element is 
absent in the present complaint. 


For the reasons stated above, the Tribunal finally holds that the present 
application under section 33A is not maintainable in law. In this view 


of the matter, the Tribunal refrains from entering into the merits of the 
case, which might be kept open.

‘The result, therefore, is that the present application under section ڈ0‎ 


of the Act be rejected, |

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour. hy

— ‌‌۶ the matters described in a schedule to this Tribunal for adjudi- 
cation. 


part 1ر‎ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1956 299? 
————————————————————————————————— عست‎ 


Notices were issued on both parties, who filed written statements 
setting’ forth their respective cases. 


Qn 19th June 1966 the Company filed an application and raised the 
preliminary objection that, inasmuch as, the Company carried on an 
industry in the manufacture or production of glass and ceramics, it was & 
controlled industry within the meaning of the term in the Industries 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 (IXV of 1961) and that, there- 
fore, the appropriate Government under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947, was the Central Government (the (tovernment of 
India) and not the State Government (the Government of West Bengal). 
li is, therefore, stated that (i) the Order of reference made by the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal is without authority and jurisdiction and is invalid 
and otherwise bad in law. 


(ii) There is no proper, legal or valid reference to this Tribunal. 


(ii) This Tribunal has no jurisdiction to take seisin of matters relating 
to a “scheduled and ০0100011607) industry. 


(iv) This Tribunal should desist or refrain from adjudication of the 
sasues in the achedule mentioned in the order of reference. 


The petitioner Company prays that before proceeding further into the 
adjudication of the case, a decision of the preliminary objections as 
mentioned above should be made. A copy of the petition was served on 
ihe Union and the Union opposed the application. The parties were heard 
at length on 19th June 1956 and 27th June 1956. 


The learned Advocate for the Company pointed out that the present 
Company carried on an industry engaged in the manufacture or production 
of glass and ceramies and that such an industry was covered by item No. 
97 of the first schedule of The Industries (Development and Regulation) 
Act of 1951. Clause (ee) of section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act was 
inserted by section 32 of the [Industries (Development and Regulation) 
Act of 1951. Under that clause ‘‘a controlled industrv’’ means on industry 
the control of which by the Tnion has been declared by anv Central Act 
to he expedient in the public interest. Section 2 of The Industries 
(Development and Regulation) Act of 1951 declares that it is expedient 
in the public interest that the Union should take under its control the 
industries specified in the First Schedule of the Act. The industry of the 
present Company is, therefore, a controlled industry within the meaning of 
the term in section 2(ee) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The learned 
Advocate, therefore, pressed that, inasmuch as, the industry of the 
Company was a controlled industry, it was the Central Government who 
had the power to contro) the industry in various matters as mentioned in 
the Industries (Development ond Regulation) Act, 1951 (LXV of 1951) 
and the State Government did not possess the powers to interfere with this 
industry in any manner. It is urged that the “‘appropriate Government”’ 
in relation to an industrial dispute concerning this Hh oni is, therefore, 
the (entral Government and not the State Government. The learned 
Advocate referred to sections 25, 26, and 307 of the Act LXV of 1951 and 
pointed out that the Central Government had not delegated its powers 
regarding the control of any of the controlled industries mentioned in 
the First Schedule of the Act to the State Government, that the Central 
(fovernment also did not give any direction to the State Government as to 
the carrying into execution in the State of any provisions of this Act or of 


3000 THE CAICTTTA GAZETTE, AUGUSTD 2, 0 | Part | 


el 


any oider or any direction made thereunder or that the Central Govern. 
nent did not exempt the industry of the present company from the 
operation of all or any of the provisions of this Act or of any rule or order, 
made thereunder and that, therefore, the State Government had no 
authority to refer an industrial dispute in relation to this industry to the 
Tribunal aa it had done. Act LXV of 1951 lays down the mode in which 
the control of the scheduled industries is to be exercised by the Central 
Government. These are mentioned in Chapters Tl, ITT, 111۸, and 7 
and IV of the Act. Chapter II relates to the establishment of Central 
Advisory Council and Development Councils, principally to advise the 
Central Government on matters concerning the development and regulation 
of scheduled industries. Chapter IIT relates to regulation of scheduled 
industries, licensing of new industrial undertakings, etc. Chapter IITA 
relates to the direct management or control of industrial undertakings by 
Central Government in certain cases. Chapter ITIB relates to the control ' 
of supply, distribution, price, ete., of certain articles. Chapter IV lays 
down some miscellaneous provisions regarding the powers of inspection 
of scheduled industries, etc., for any person authorised by the Central 
Government in this behalf and other provisions. Section 26 lays down that 
the Central Government may by a notified order direct that any power 
exercisable by it under this Act [other than the power given to it by section 
16 and 18(a)], shall be exercisable by such officer or authority which will 
include in the said expression any Development Council, State Government 
or Officer or Authority subordinate to the Central Government os may be 
specified in the direction. Section 26 lays down that the Central Government 
may give directions to any State Government as to the carrying into 
execution in the State of any of the provisions of this Act or of any order or 
direction made thereunder. Section 201) lavs down that if the Central Gov- 
ernment is of opinion having regard to the smallness of the number of 
workers employed or to the amount invested in any industrial undertaking 
or to the desirability of encouraging small undertaking generally or to the 
stage of development of any scheduled industry that it would not he in the 
public interest to apply all or any of the provisions of this Act thereto, it may 
by notification in the official Gazette exempt, suhject to such conditions as 
1 may think fit to impose, any industrial undertaking or any clasa of 
industrial undertaking or class of scheduled industries as may be specified 
from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this Act or of any rule or 
order made thereunder. It is, therefore, clear that the delegation of power 
laid down in section 25 or the power to issue directions as mentioned in 
section 26 or the power to exempt in special cases some scheduled industries 
all relate to powers exercisable by the Central Government under this Act in 
regard to the controlled industries. There is nothing in this Act and in the 
definition of the great variety of powers mentioned in varioun section of 
the Act to show that the Central Government has been vested by this Act the 
power to refer industrial disputes concerning any controlled industry to the 
Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. In other words, these variety of 
powers do not make the Central Government the appropriate Government 
for industrial disputes in relation to the scheduled or the controlled indus- 
tries. Section 32 of this Act amends section 2 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act in the definition of the appropriate Government in relation to the 
reference of an industrial dispute to the Tribunal. Section 2(a) has heen ২০ 
amended as to show that an “appropriate Government” means the Central 
Government in relation to an industrial dispute “concerning any such con- 
trolled industry as may be specified in this hehalf by the Central Govern- 
ment’’. In relation to any other dispute, the appropriate Government is 
the State Government. Section 32 also inserts clause (ee) defining what is 
meant by “‘controlled industry”? in section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1956 3001 


aI EI Cm ARI ge ১১১22৬০১০38 সার এ RE TED +۰۳ نہ وو‎ জি 


t ix, therefore, clear that although the industry carried on by the present 
Company is a controlled industry, in relation to the industrial dispute 
concerning this industry, the Central Government will be the “‘appropriate 
(0০171167067 only if this controlled industry was specified in this behalf by 
the Central (tovernment, and in the absence of such specification, the State 
Government will be the “‘appropriate Government’ in relation to such an 
industrial dispute. There is nothing on record to show, nor 1s it suggested 
by the learned Advocate for the Company that the Central Government has 
ever specified itself to be the “‘appropriate Government’’ in relation to the 
present industry. It is, therefore, abundantly clear that the Central 
(Government is not the appropriate Government in relation to the industrial 
dispute in the present case, and the State Government is the approprtate 
Government in accordance with section 2(a) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
The reference by the Government of West Bengal of the industrial dispute 
in question is, therefore, competent. 


The learned Advocate for the Company cited the decision of the Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in the case of Bhowra Coke Plant, 
reported in 1966(1) L.I.J., 195. In this case it was decided that the 
definition of ‘‘mine” in section 2(j)(vi) of the Mines Act, 1952, included a 
coke plant manufacturing tar and industrial coke from coal purchased from 
outside. It was further decided that such industry is an industrial under- 
taking pertaining to one of the industries included in the First Schedule to 
Industrial Development and Regulation Act, 1951. Hence it being an 
industry carried on under the authority of the Central Government, the 
appropriate Government for the purpose of section 2(a) must be held to he 
the Central Government and not the State in which it is situated. The 
Hon’ble Tribunal decided that the reference made by the Bihar Govern- 
ment in relation to an industrial dispute concerning the Bhowra Coke Plant 
was ultra vires of the Act and, therefore, incompetant, inasmuch as, for 
reasons mentioned above the Central Government was the appropriate (Gov- 
ernment in relation to the industrial dispute in question. The Bhowra Coke 
Plant was considered by the Hon’ble Tribunal to be a Mine under section 
4(})(vi), of the Mines Act, 1952. Under section 2(a) of the Industrial 
Iisputes Act, this decision alone was sufficient to make the Central Govern- 
ment the appropriate Government in relation to the diapute concerning the 
Bhowra Coke Plant. The other decision of the Hon’ble Tribunal that 
hecnuse this industrial undertaking was one in relation to a controlled 
industry, it was an industry carried on under the authority of the Central 
(fovernment and the appropriate Government for the purpose of section 2(a) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act was the Central Government does not appear 
to be at all necessary. With great respect for the decision of the Hon’ble 
Tribunal, it appears to me that hecause an industry is a controlled industry, 
it was not necessarily one which was carried on by or under the authority 
of the Central Government. Jf that were so, the legislature would have 
found it necessary to enact section 32(a) and (b) of the Industries (Develop- 
ment and Regulation) Act, 1951, for amendment of section 2 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act in respect of controlled industries. In the present case, 
the Bharat Glass Works was not an industry which was carried on by or 
under the authority of the Central Government, although it was a controlled 
industry. The Central Government only exercised the power of control as 
mentioned in Act LXV of 1961 and not otherwise. 


It is, therefore, decided that the order of reference made by the West 
Bengal Government as mentioned ahove was with authority and jurisdiction 
of the Government and is valid in all respects. Tt is also decided that the 
reference to this Tribunal of the industrial dispute in question ia lawful and

valid and the Tribunal has jurisdiction to entertain the reference and is 
competent and even obliged to adjudicate on it. The preliminary objection 
raised hy the Company is, therefore, rejected.

AWARD 


This is a complaint under section 9:34 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by the workman Shri Ajit Kumar Samanta. The petitioner alleged that 
after he submitted explanation to the charges he was suspended during the 
pendency of the adjudication proceedings without obtaining permission 
from the Tribunal and thus the Opposite party contravened section 33 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act. Ilence, the complaint. 


The Opposite party denied having contravened section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act and contended that the complaint was not maintainable. 


DECISION 

The parties filed a joint petition of compromise on 26th June 06 
stating that they had settled the dispute outside the Court and did not 
wish to proceed with the case. There was also an application under section 
33 by the Upposite party Company. The parties prayed in the petition of 
compromise that both the petitions under sections 33 and 994 should be 
dismissed. The petition of compromise is accepted and given effect to. 
The complaint under section 338A is accordingly dismissed. It is awarded 
accordingly. The petition of compromise is made a part of the award.

Appearances: 
For the Petitioner: Shn J. N. Chakraborty.

This is an application under section 33A of the [Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, filed by the workman Shri Mayadhar Bera on 15th of May 1956. 


It is the contention of the petitioner that while the original reference as 
mentioned above was pending before this Tribunal, the Opposite party, 
Company, charge-sheeted and suspended him on 1161) May 1956 without 
taking permission from the Tribunal and as such the provisions of section 
33 of the Act were contravened. 


The Company denied having contravened the provisions of section 3: 
and pleaded that charge-sheet was issued to the workman on the ground of 
misconduct and pending enquiry into this charge, he was suspended. It 
thus contended that the application under section 388A was not maintainable. 


Having heard Shri N. K. Mookherjee, learned Advocate for the 
Company and also Shri Jatin Chakraborty, Jearned representative who 
appeared on behalf of the worker and on perusal of the record, I am of the 
view that section 33 has not been violated and consequently the application 
under section 338A is not competent. 


The workman concerned admittedly received a charge-sheet on 1110) May 
1956 and pending completion of that enquiry he was suspended. In the 
circumstances the suspension caunot be regarded as punishment. Section 
89 15 attracted only when the suspension is by way of punishment. In the 
present case it is not so. Suspension was made as a security measure pend- 
ing completion of the enquiry. So it cannot be said that section 33 has been 
violated. That being so, the application under section 383A is not maintain- 
able. I award accordingly.

as mentioned above was pending before this Tribunal, the Opposite party— 
Company, charge-sheeted and suspended him on 1161) May 1956 without 
taking permission from the Tribunal and as such the provisions of section 33 
of the Act were contravened. 


The Company denied having contravened the provisions of section 33 
und pleaded that the charge-sheet was issued to the workman on the ground 
of misconduct and pending enquiry into this charge, he was suspended. 


0 on contended that the application under section 338A was not maintain- 
able. 


Having heard Shri N. K. Mukherjee, learned Advocate for the Com- 
pany, and also Shri Jatin Chakraborty, learned representative who appeared 
on behalf of the worker, and on perusal of the record, I am of the view 


that section 33 has not been violated and consequently the application under 
section 3.4 18 not competent. 


3010 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1966 [Parr I 


The workman concerned admittedly received a charge-sheet on 1161) May 
1956 and pending completion of that enquiry he was suspended. In ‘the 
circumstances the suspension cannot be regarded as punishment. Section 33 
is attracted only when the suspension 18 by way of punishment. In the 
present case it 18 not so. Suspension was made as a security measure 
fag ee completion of the enquiry. So it cannot be said that section 33 

as been violated. That being so, the application under section 3838۸ is not 
maintainable. 


I award accordingly. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

Schedule to the order of reference 


Whether the termination of services of Shri G. D. Roy and Shri J. R. 
Bhattacharjee was justified? What relief are they entitled ۶ 


Part 11 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1956 3011 


سے سے سیہمسمسسچج ججچمسسہسسیں سس سس تسس سے س”تپتےجچمسىپچےم٭سيےمجچت سے جج سج تی٣‏ ڈیڈ رشں سس سس سس سے سس سسستۓ ‏ 
AWARD‏ 


Fa 

The present dispute relates to the termination of services of Shri G. J). 
Roy and Shri J. R. Bhattacharjee who were employed at the relevant time 
in the Calcutta Chromotype Limited as supervisors. Their services were 
terminated with effect from 2nd November 1955. The case of these two 
employees in short is that the alleged termination of their services was 
unjustified and mala fide. So, they claim reinstatement with back wages. 


In reply, the Company has contended that there were sufficient grounds 
for termination of their services. As a result of enquiry held hy the 
management they were found guilty of negligence and inefficiency in the 
discharge of duties. Hence they had to be dismissed. 


A preliminary objection has been raised also on behalf of the Company 
and it is that these two employees who were employed as supervisors were 
not workmen within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
and were not, therefore, entitled to any relief under the said Act. 


This leads the Tribunal necessarily to take up the preliminary objection 
first. Obviously this objection touches the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. 
If the two employees who are concerned in the present case are found ٥ 
be not workmen, the dispute under reference ceases to be an _ industrial 
dispute. In such an event the employees cannot get the aid of the Act, 
nor can the Tribunal adjudicate upon the dispute, despite the reference 
mude hy the Government. It has been repeatedly kala. that in deciding 
whether a particular employee is a workman or not, designation does not 
matter and is not of great moment. What is of importance is the nature 
of his duties. The relevant question is whether he performs clerical or 
manual work so as to place him under category of “workman” under the 
Act. The approach should, therefore, be not from the angle of testing 
whether the employee is an officer but from that of examining the duties 
to be performed by the employee and deciding whether they are in the 
main clerical or manual. This is ultimately a question of fact. At hest 
it is one of mixed facts and law. Now let me approach the question froin 
the standpoint of the duties of these two employees. Admittedly they 
are employed as supervisors of two departments of this Company. In_ 9 
connection I am to observe that the question whether an employer is a 
supervisor Or exercises directional or controlling power, supplies a 
negative test of a workman which cannot be conclusive. I shall now 
discuss the duties and responsibilities which have emerged from the 
evidence. Both the employees have examined themselves in this case. 
(m the side of the Company the Managing Director has deposed and some 
documents have been admitted in evidence. ] have সি scrutinised 
the evidence. On the evidence it is clear that these two employees were 
supervisors in two separate departments of the Company and their main 
duties were of supervisory nature. Not only they had to inspect the 
works of the workers but had to see also that the works were done properly 
and according to specification. The evidence further indicates that they 
had to make complaints if the work of any workman employed under them 
was found to be defective. So, on a careful consideration of the materials 
placed before it and bearing in mind the test laid down ina_ series of 
cases, the Tribunal holds that these two employees cannot be considered 
to be workmen within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. They 
were responsible for supervision and proper administration of the depart- 
ments under their charge. They had under them a set of workers whose 
works they not only supervised but whom they controlled and directed 
also. Certainly they had duties and responsibilities of a much higher 
order than that of a workman. Of course, it has transpired from the 
evidence that in course of supervision and inspection the employee 


3012 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST’, 1956 [Part } 
|. ৯৯ 


Shri G. D. Roy was required to demonstrate to the workers %111)10700. under 
him hew the ‘work was to be executed and that the employer Shri ,۰ 
Bhattacharjee had to mix up somelimes the colours for preparing different 
shades therefrom. ‘The learned lawyer for the employees relying on the 
same has voiced an argument that this clearly showed that these two 
employees had to do also manual work and as such they came within the 
meaning of ‘‘workman”’. But it js extremely difficult to accept this 
argument. It might be that in course of supervision and inspection they 
had to do such work. But it was only part of their duties as supervisors 
to see that the work was properly done and done by the workers 8601 011) 

to specification. JX does not mean that they had to do manual work 
themselves. If im the course of supervision and inspection they had _ 10 
do anything by their own hands by way of testing or demonstrating, ا‎ 
cannot be said to be manual work. It was a part of their duties as 
supervisors. Next it was argued that these employees had to do clerical 
duties also as they had to write requisition repotts for materials and 0১1৭0 
reports of daily outturn and production, etc. It is true no doubt that 
they had to write such reports daily. But in the view of the Tribunal, 
the clerical duties which they performed were insignificant as compared 
with the importance of their works and was only ancillary to their main 
duties as supervisors. Then again, it has transpired from the evidence of 
the Managing Director that for such clerical duties half an hou® was 
required daily. Lastly, it was contended that as these two employees had 
no power to dismiss any worker employed under them, they cannot be 
deemed to be invested with the powers of supervision and control in the 
day-to-day works of the departments in which they were employed. It is 
now well settled that non-conferment of powers to appoint, suspend and 
dismiss any worker does not detract from the supervisory powers the 
employees had over the workers in the departments. If any authority 2১ 
needed for this I may cite the cases reported in 1954(11) L.L.J. 457 nd 
1955(11) L.L.J. 595. The preliminary objection raised on behalf of the 
Company therefore succeeds. 


In- the result the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that these two 
employees concerned cannot be considered to be workmen within the 
meaning of the Act, the nature of their duties in the main being neither 
clerical nor manual. That being so, the present dispute between the 
parties does not fall within the ambit of the expression ‘‘industrial dispute” 
as defined in section 2(k) of the Act. Accordingly the employees concerned 
are not entitled to invoke the aid of the Act nor has the Tribunal jurisdic- 
tion to adjudicate on the issue referred to it, despite the reference made by 
the Government. In this view of the matter, it is not necessary for the 
Tribunal to enter into the merits of the case or to express any opinion 
regarding the termination of services of these two employees. 


This is my award. 


Dretated and corrected by me. 
G. P. MUKHERJEHK, Judge.

DECISION 


This is an appeal from on award of the Third Industrial Tribunal, West 
Bengal, dated the 17th March 1954, published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 
April 8, 1954. By Government order No. 592Dis./D/12L-5/52, dated the 
23rd February 1953, the following 9 issues were referred for adjudication to 
the Third Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal :— 

(1) To what relief the workers are entitled for the period of their 
unemployment between 26th September 1952 to 9th November 
1962? 


(2) Pay and dearness allowance. 
(3) Leave. 

(4) Permanency. 

(5) Retiring benefits. 

(6) Abolition of contract system. 
(7} Bonus for 1962-63. 


306 


THE CALCUTPA GAZETTE, AUGUST 2, 1966 


(8) 10 what relief the workers mentioned, in attached list ure entitled 
for their non-employment hy the’ management? 


(9) To what relief the workers are entitled for forced idleness for two 
days in a weekP 


The appeal is by the employers and is directed only against the findings on 
issues Nos. two and eight. Issue No. two was ‘‘pay and dearness allowance’, 
and issue No. eight was ‘‘to what relief the workers mentioned im attached 
list are entitled tor their non-employment by the management’. 


This Company pays consolidated wages to its workers. Prior to the 
dispute the consolidated wage (pay and dearness allowance) of the unskilled 
category of workmen was Rs. 2 per day and that of the skilled category of 
workmen Rs. 2-4 per day. The learned Tribunal increased the rate of each 
category by annas 4. To the cight workmen mentioned in the award out 
of 44 workmen named in the order of reference, the learned Tribunal below 
has granted three months’ consolidated wages as retrenchment compensation. 
The Company has challenged only these parts of the award. Therefore, it 
ig unnecessary to refer to the other issues. 

The first question tor decision is whether the increase of annas 4) in the 
40050110980. wage of each category was justified. The appellant is an 
Engineering concern. The learned Tribunal relied upon the observations ot 
the Central Pay Commission and also on the findings of Major Engineering 
Tribunal. For an unskilled worker in the Engineering Industries in West 
Bengal, a minimum basic wage of Ks. 30 per month or Rs. 1-2-6 per day 
was fixed by Major Engineering Tribunal, while dearness allowance at 
Ks. ۵1 per mensem was fixed by the Second Engineering Tribunal. The 
total wages of an unskilled worker thus came to 118. 61 per month. In a 
month of 26 working days the daily wage would amount to nearly 
Rs. 2-5-3. Against this the learned ‘Tribunal below has fixed the con- 
solidated daily wage of Rs. 2-4 only and certainly it was not wrong in doing 
so. This new wage comes to Rs. 58-8 per month of 26 working days and is 
still Jess by Rs. 2-8 than the minimum wage fixed by the two Tribunals. 
The difference of annas 4 in the rate of unskilled and skilled categories can 
by no means be said to be at all high. These wages are, rather, lower than 
the minimum basic wages payable for the two categories of workmen in the 
industrial concerns generally in the region. 


The only argument advanced by the appellant’s learned lawyer is that 
the cost of living index in 1950, ashen the Second Industrial Tribunal fixed 
the dearness allowance of the unskilled category at Rs. 31 was 350 and now 
it is J10. But, he could not place any material before us to prove that it 
was 80. This dispute as appears irom the order of reference arose in 1952. 
The appellant should have placed before us the cost of living index figures for 
the years 1950, 1952 and ate for year 1954, when this award was made. On 
the material on record before us no case for interference with the award has 


been made out. 


Regarding compensation to the eight retrenched employees who had 
not been taken in by the Company, the only point urged on behalf of the 
employer is that an award of retrenchment compensation at an ad hoc rate 
of three months’ pay to each of the workmen irrespective of the length of 
service of each is against the well recognised principles. The learned Counsel 
concedes that there is no material on record from which the length of 
service of each of these eight workmen could be ascertained. He contended 
himself by simply saying that none of these eight workmen had put in 
more than four years of service. Continuing the Counsel argued that the 
retrenchment in question had taken place prior to the passing of Act No. 43 
of 1953 and that the Act had no application He had to concede that in 
addition to compensation for their past services workmen were entitled to 
some compensation for future unemployment, according to well recognised, 
pringiples of retrenchment compensation. Moreover, added thé Counsel, 
even under the said Act a retrenched workman was only entitled to com- 
peneation relief equivalent to 15 days’ wages for each year of completed 
service. We may at once say that the said Act only recognises the 
principles which governed the grant of retrenchment compensation laid 
down in a number of decisions of this Tribunal ج2‎ to their incorporation 
in the Act, vide 1955, II LLJ. 280, where it has been observed that the 
Act has not fixed a ceiling. In these circumstances, even if we attach any 


,mportance to the oral statement made at the bar on behalf of the employer 


that the length of service of none of the eight workmen was more than four 
years, we are of the opinion that three months’ pay by way of compensation 
for future unemployment is by no means high. And, if length of servicé, 
whatever it be, were taken into account, this amount could not be said to 
be excessive by way of retrenchment compensation which included compen- 


sation for past service along with compensation for " future unemploy- ° 


ment. Tastly, the learned. Congel for the appellant pleaded that the. 
arned lower Tribunal could not’ award the respondents relief-gn ad hoc 
889 1n an arbitrary way’ gs had been doné by it. He was unable to*hatiafy 
us that‘ any injustice or prejudice had been caused te the apptllant. In

Eee 


Part [A]

777৮-৮২-৮০, EE eee 


these circumstances, we find ae reason to interfere with the award-of the 
ic 


learned Tribunal below, w 


we,gonfirm. The appeal is, therefore, din- 


missed with costs to the Respondent Union which is fixed at Rs. 60.

COVERNMENT OF INDIA 


Ministry of Law 


The following Act of Parliament received the assent of 
the President on the 2181: May, 1956, and is hereby published 
for general information :— 


ACT NO. XXIII OF 1956 
THE 7 APPROPRIATION ACT, 
1956. 
[215 May, 1956. ] 
An Act to provide for the withdrawal of certain swms from 


and out of the Consolidated Fund of the State of 
Travancore-Coclun for the service of the financial year 


1956-57, 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Seventh Year of the 
Republic of India as follows :— 


1. This Act may be called the Travancore-Cochin Appro- 
priation Act, 1956. 


2. From and out of the Consolidated Fund of the State of 
Travancore-Cochin there may be paid and applied sums not 
exceeding those specified in column 3 of the Sehedule amount- 
ing in the aggregate [inclusive of the sums _ specified in 
column 3 of the Schedule (0 the Travancore-Cochin Appro- 
priation (Vote on Account) Act, 1956] to the sum of forty-one 
crores, eighty-one lakhs and ninety-four thousand rupees 
towards defraying the several charges which will come in 
course of payment during the financial year 1956-57, in 
respect of the services specified in column 2 of the Schedule. 


3. The sums authorised to be paid and applied from and 
out of the Consolidated Fund of the State of’ Travancore- 
Cochin by this Act shall be appropriated for the services and 
purposes expressed in the Schedule in relation to the said 
year.

Briefly stated the facta involved are that Mesars. Western India Theatres 
Limited which was engaged in distribution and exhibition of films transferred 
the management of the Elite Cinema to the 20th Century Fox Corporation 
(India) Limited on Ist June 1954. At the instance of the transferor the 
90th Century دہ"(‎ Corporation (India) Limited engaged the services of 
the employees who has hitherto served Messrs. Western India Theatres 
Limited. While dealing with the issues submitted to this Tribunal arising 
out of the dispute between the employees and the two employers aforesaid 
this Tribunal came to the conclusion that on ground of equity the workers 
should not suffer loss of benefits which they might claim on account of 
their past services rendered to the Western India Theatres Jimited. The 
Tribunal decided that Western India Theatres Limited had an obligation to 
provide them the amenities or reliefs which their services entitled them 
to. The relief in the estimation of the Tribunal was gratuity calculated at 
the rate of 15 days’ basic wages for each year of completed service, subject 
to a maximum of 15 months’ salary. 


Disputes have arisen between the employees and the Western India 
Theatres Limited as to quantum of gratuity. The focal point is the length 
of service. According to the Wnion the period of service réndered before 
the Western India Theatres Limited came into یم‎ must also be com- 
uted, It is necessary to mention here that originally, the business was 
see run by the Western India Theatres Tumited as a private Limited 
Company. it went into voluntary liquidation in 1946. An agreement 
was entered into on the 26th of September 1946 between the Limited Com- 
pany and the Western India Theatres Limited, a Joint Stock Company, 
incorporated under the Indian Companies Act VIT of 1918. By the agree- 
ment which has been produced before me as an Annexure to an affidavit 
aworn on behalf of the Comnpany, the Limited Company transferred its good 
will, assets, and properties and henefita of pending contracts and all hiabi- 
lities to the Joint Stock Company. According te the Union representative 
the employees who were in service under the Jamited Company werd 
entitled to Jook to the transferor Company for the benefits accruing to 
them for service already rendered. The new Company had taken over the 
business with all its liabilities ond obligations towards the employees. 
When this reference was made the dispute was in respect of the claim of 78 
employees. At the hearing the learned Union representative informed the 
Tribunal that at present the claim of 22 employees only as per hst submitted 
with the affidavit sworn require consideration, The Union is prepared to 
accept the amount offered by the Company by way of gratuity for the rest. 
The claim of the 22 employees named in the Union affidavit is کا‎ taken 
up for consideration. To prove their respective contentions regarding the 
length of service the Union and the Company produced their charts showing 
the date of appointment as well as the date of termination. Ext, 1 is the 
Union chart and Ext. 0 is the chart of the Company. The Company did 
not include the period of service, if any, under the Limited Company. 
The Union did not call for the service records or registers to prove beyond 
all shadow of doubt that the particulars supplied in chart Ext. 1 are correct 
in all respects, The evidence of P. W. 1 and P. W. 2 is that the chart 
was prepared on the verbal statements of the employees themselves. No 
Tegisters or authentic documents were drawn upon for preparation of the 
chart, It is very difficult therefore for the Tribunal to accept the chart and 


1920 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUG. 2, 1956 (Paar I 


use it as the basis for computation of the relief due. The Company’s chart 
was prepared with reference to service records lying 1n the Bombay office. 
It is unfortunate that the records themselves were not produced before the 
Tribunal for verification of the chart. As between the Union chart and the 
chart of the Company, the Tribunal is compelled to give preference to. 
the latter since it is allegedly based upon records and registers. The 
Tribunal has no other alternative but to act upon the Company’s chart. 
Regarding the Union agrument that the period of service before the transfer 
to the Joint Stock Company must also come into the equation, the learned 
lawyer for the Company লা that there is nothing to show that the private 
Limited: Company had not satisfied the claims of the employees at the time 
of the transfer. Since the agreement which is annexed to the Company’s 
affidavit shows that the liabilities of the business were taken over by the 
Joint Stock Company and there is nothing in the document that any parti- 
cular liability had been discharged, no conclusion can be drawn that the 
claim of the employees had been settled. 


The Company’s chart shows that of the 22 employees whose case is now 
under consideration as many as 10, viz., P. K. Bacchi Homi Muncharji, 
D. R. Chaman, B. J. Hossain, Baithnath, Drijadhan, Md. Monir, Md. 
Hossain, and Motahar entered service under the Western India Theatres 
Limited in 1948. The transfer had taken place in 1946. Even if they had 
put in service under the private Limited Company they lost the benetits 
of the said period since there was a break and re-employment commenced 
in 1948. One employee, Jal Bhasania by name entered service in 1949. So 
far as he is concerned, the position is the same as he cannot claim the 
earlier period, if any, to be tacked because of the break. Serial numbers 
(11) K. Prasad, (19) A. M. Roy, (17) D. L. Braham, (19) Sultan Ahmed, 
(34) Yusuf Mystry, (95) Bholanath Das and (61) Rambisen Singh, of Ext. C 
also had break of service. They had therefore forfeited the advantage of 
tacking on the service rendered prior to the break. Haridas, Imad Hussain 
and Ramoog Khan are shown 11) the Company’s chart as having entered 
service on 26th September 1946. That is the date on which the agreement 
of transfer of the business was entered into. Since the date of commence- 
ment of service synchronizes with the date of the contract rt is a fair 
inference that they were in the employ of the private Vimited Com- 
pany and were taken over by the transferee Company. With regard to 
these three employees the Tribunal has got to accept the particulars supplied 
by the Union in the chart Ext. 1, inasmuch as the Company has not 
produced earlier records. According to Ext. 1 Hari Dass and Imdad Hussain 
joined in 1939 and had been in service for 14 years six months and 15 years 
five months, respectively. Ramooz Khan joined in 1945 and was in service 
for eight years 10 months. Gratuity due to them must be calculated on the 
basis of these data. As regards the rest the length of service as shown 
in the Company’s chart must prevail. Gratuity will be computed accord- 


ingly.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
HOME DEPARTMENT

NOTIFICATIONS 
No. 21388H.J.—4th August 1956.—In exercise of the powers conferred by 
sub-section (1) of section JLA of the Prisoners Act, 1900 (III of 1900), the 
Governor is pleased to empower the Inspector-General of Prisons, ۲ے‎ ۹ 


Bengal, to exercise the powers to release prisoners temporarily under that 
section. 


No. 2139H.J.—4th August 1966.—In exercise of the powers conferred by 
section 310) of the Prisoners Act, 1900 (I11 of 1900), the Governor 18 pleased 
to make the following rules, namely سے‎ 


lI. Definttions.—(1) These rules may be called the West Bengal 
Prisoners (Temporary Release) Rules, 1956. 


(2) They shall come into force at once. 


(3) In those rules— 

(a) ‘““Inspector-General’’? means the Inspector-General of Prisons, West 

engal. 

(b) ‘‘Superintendent”’ means the Superintendent of the jail in which 
the prisoner, whose release under these rules is under considera- 
tion, is confined. 

(c) ‘The 4১0৮7 means the Prisoners Act, 1900 (III of 1900), as in force 
in West Bengal. 


“2. Application for tempurary release.—An application from a prisoner 
for temporary release under section 31A of the Act shall be made in the 
prescribed Form ۱ (Appendis I) in duplicate by the prisoner and submitted 
to the Superintendent. 


3. NSerutiny of application for temporary release. —The Superintendent 
shall personally examine the records of the prisoner making the application 
for temporary release and satisfy 14 that the prisoner is eligible for 
temporary release under sub-sections (7) and (8) of section 814 of the Act. 
He shall 9150 satisfy himself that the conduct of the prisoner has been good. 
11 so satisfied, he shall furnish a certificate to that effect under clause (c) 
of sub-section (2) of section 381A of the Act. 


4. Presumption of good conduct.—A prisoner who has become entitled 
to full ordinary remission under the rules for the time being in force made 
under the Prisons Act, 1894 (TX of 1894), for the twelve months previous 
10 the date of the application for temporary release, shall be deemed to have 
been of good conduct in prison for the purpose of clause (c) of sub-section 


(2) of section 914 of the Act. ٠

1924 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 4, 1956 [Parr ا‎ 
লি کے‎ 


6. Reference to the District Magistrate or the Commissioner of Police 
—If the examination of the records of the prisoner shows that he is 
eligible for temporary release, the Superintendent shall record the fact and 
forward the prisoner’s petition with his remarks, if any, to the District 
Magistrate of the district in which the prisoner was convicted. If the 
prisoner was convicted by a Court in Calcutta, the Superintendent shall send 
the application to the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta. The District 
Magistrate shall consult the Superintendent of Police and, if he considers 
necessary, the District Magistrate of the district where the prisoner 
ordinarily resided before conviction or wants to reside during the period of 
temporary release, if granted. The District Magistrate, or the Comumis- 
sioner of Police, Calcutta, as the case may be, shall then forward the peti- 
tion with his report to the Inspector-General under intimation 60 the 
Superintendent stating whether the prisoner can be anted temporary 
release without detriment to public interest and adding his grounds in sup- 
port. If he recommends temporary release of the prisoner he may suggest 
at the same time special restrictions on his movements, 1 deemed necessary. 
He shall also indicate the amount and number of sureties for the bond 
which the prisoner must execute in the prescribed Form II 
(Appendix II) before he is released. He shall also indicate the number of 
days that will be required for the journeys by the shortest practicable route 
to and from the place at which the prisoner proposes to reside during his 
temporary release or if the prisoner proposes to visit more than one place, 
the farthest place from the jail which the prisoner proposes to visit. 


6. Final order by the inspector-General.—lf, on receipt of the report 
of the District Magistrate or the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, as the 
case may be, the Inspector-General considers that the temporary release of 
the prisoner is undesirable in the ناس‎ interest, he shall intimate his 
decision to the Superintendent who shall inform the prisoner that his appli- 
cation has been rejected. If, on the ofher hand, the Inspector-General con- 
siders that the application can be allowed without detriment to public 
interest, he shall issue an order of temporary release of the prisoner in the 
prescribed Form 111 (Appendix III). While ordering temporary release 
the Inspector-General may impose such conditions, as he may consider 
necessary, including the condition that the prisoner shall, during the period 
of his temporary release, be under the supervision of a Probation Officer. 
He shall send the order to the Superintendent with copies to the District 
Magistrates of the districts wherein the places to be visited by the prisoner 
are located, as also of the district in which the prisoner was convicted. 4 
copy of the same order shall also be sent to the Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta, 1f the prisoner was convicted by a Court in Calcutta or proposes 
to reside there during his temporary release.

7. Date of release.—On receipt of the order of temporary release, the 
Superintendent shall fix in consultation with the prisoner, the date of his 
temporary release which shall ordinarily be not later than ten days from 
the date of receipt of the order. In the case of a female prisoner, the 
date of her temporary release shall be so fixed as to allow time for her 
transfer to the jail nearest to the place where she intends to reside during 
her temporary release and from which she is to be released. If a prisoner 
in respect of whom a temporary release order has been issued is ill, the 
Superintendent may postpone the date of his temporary release for such 
time as the Medical Officer of the jail considers to be necessary for the 
prisoner's recavery from illness. 


8. Cancellation of the order of temporary release.—If the prisoner 
commits a jail offence other than that pattie by a formal warning 
between the date of application for release and the Jate fixed for his tem- 
an release under rule 7, the Superintendent shall report the fact to 
the Inspector-General who may thereupon cancel the order for temporary 
release. On such cancellation further requests from the prisoner for tem- 
porary release shall not be entertained during a period of six months from 
the date of commission of the offence. 


9. Intvmation of release to the District Magistrate or the Commissioner 
of Police.—When a prisoner is released temporarily, the Superintendent 
shall report to the Inspector-General and the District Magistrate concerned 
or the Commissioner of Police, as the case may be, the date of the prisoner’s 
leaving the jail and the due date of his return to jail. 


10. Release Certtficate.—At the time the prisoner leaves the jail, he 
shall be furnished by the Superintendent with a temporary release certificate 
in the prescribed Form IV (Appendix IV), which shall be returned by the 
prisoner on his return to jail. A duplicate copy of the said certificate shall 
be kept in the jail records. 


li. Travelling and subsistence allowance tluring journey.—When ao 
ane is released temporarily under section 31A of the Act, he shall not 
e paid any diet money for the period of his temporary release. If such a 


Past J] , 


wt THE CALOUTTA GAZETTE EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 4, 1956 


prisoner has not got sufficient private cash or wages earned to his credit to 
pay for the journeys from and to the jail, he shall be supplied with— 


(7) a free puss of the lowest class to and from the railway or steamer 
station nearest to the place of his residence on the credit note 
syatem, 


(2) boat hire or bus hire or boat and bus hire, as the case may be, from 
and to the jail if the journey or ah of the journey has to be 
performed by boat or bus or by boat and bus, 


(3) subsistence allowance for the journey from the jail to the residence 
of such prisoner at the rate of twelve annas for every fifteen miles 
or part thereof to be travelled by road, for which no conveyunce 
hire is paid, and 


(4) subsistence allowance at the same rate in respect of every day’s or 
part of duy’s journey by rail, steamer, boat or bus. 


The subsistence allowance mentioned in clauses (3) and (4) above shall not 
be payable where the prisoner’s home is situated within five miles of the 
jail or where the prisoner has private cash or wages amounting to more than 
three rupees to his credit. 


12. Loan of 9৫21 articles.—A prisoner, who has no private clothing and 
bedding and is unable to purchase them, shall be supplied on loan with 
a blanket and unmarked prison clothing. These articles shall be entered in 
his Temporary Release Certificate (Form IV) and shall be brought back 
by the prisoner on his return to jail, 


13. Condition of release to be explained to the prisoner.—RBefore the 
prisoner leaves the jail, the conditions of his release shall be explained to 
him in the presence of the Superintendent. He shall be informed at the 
sume time of the date on which he has to return to jail, that if he fails to 
do so, he can be arrested without a warrant by dny Police Officer and that 
besides being committed to jail to undergo the unexpired period of his 
sentence (the period of temporary release not being counted towards the total 
period of his sentence) he shall be punishable as if he had committed a 
prison offence under the Prisons Act, 1894 (IX of 1894). 


14. Report to local police.x—An order for temporary release under the 
Act shall specify the চি or places which the prisoner shall be allowed 
to visit or where he may reside during the period of temporary release. The 
prisoner shall not be at liberty to visit other places. On arrival at the place 
where he intends to reside, the prisoner shall within twenty-four hours 
inform the Officer-in-charge of the local police-station of the fact of his 
arrival. He shall similarly notify his departure. 


15. Procedure when prisoner does not return.—A prisoner, who does 
not return to the jail before the evening lock-up of the date fixed for his 
return, shall be deemed to have escaped. Intimation of such escape with 
a descriptive roll of the prisoner, his usual address and the addresses of the 
places which he intended to visit during his temporary release and such 
other available information as will facilitate his capture, shall be given by 
the Superintendent immediately to the District Magistrates concerned or the 
Commisaioner of Police, Calcutta, as the case may be, with a copy thereof 
to the Inspector-General. 


16. If the prisoner returns to the jail of his own accord after the date 
fixed for his return, he shall be admitted to the jail and the prisoner’s return 
and the reasons for the delay shall be reported immediately to the 
authorities to whom his escape was notified and to the Inspector-General 
who will give such directions, as he considers necessary, as to how the 
prisoner shall be dealt with. 


17. Release of female prisoners.—When it is intended to release a 
female prisoner temporarily, she shall, in the first instance, be transferred 
10 the jail which is neareat to the place where she intends to reside during 
her temporary release. She shall be released from the jail where she is so 
transferred and she shall return to that jail. The Superintendent of the 
jail from which she is trensferred, shall forthwith intimate to her home 
address or to such relative or friend aa ahe may nominate, the date of her 
release and the jail from which she is to be released. In the event of no 
relative appearing to receive her, and if she be under 25 years of age or 
likely to be led astray, she should be sent to her home in charge of the 
female warder, if there is one attached to the jail, or of 4 respectable 
woman entrusted to escort her. The female escort shall be paid travelling 
allowance as for journeys on tour if she is a Government servant and-if not 
n Government servant, she shall be entitled to actual expenses for the 
journeys from and to the jail. If this escort is not considered necessary, 
ihe prisoner shall be given free pass, conveyance hire and subsistence 
allowance as prescribed in Rule 1.

NOTIFICATIONS 


No. 2457A. R.—8th August, 1956.—The following 
document is published for general information :— 


“Whereas consequent upon the death of Dr, Harendro 
Coumar Mookerjee, it has become necessary to make 
tenporary provision for the discharge of the functions 
of the Governor of West Bengal : 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by 
Article 160 of the Constitution and all the powers 
enabling me in that behalf, I, Rajendra Prasad, 
President of India, hereby appdint Shri Phani Bhusan 
Chakravartti to discharge the functions of the Governor 
of West Bengal until the person permanently appointed 
under Article 155 of the Constitution of India enters 
upon his office.

3. General.—lLvery employee shall at all times maintain absolute

4. Taking part in politics and elections.—{1) No employee shall be a 
member of, or be otherwise associated with, any political party or any 
organisation which takes part in politica nor shall he take part in, 


subscribe in aid of, or assist in any other manner, any political movement

(4) No employee shall canvass or otherwise interfere or 039 his

No. 48141 ,-3011 July 1956.—In exercise ot the powers conferred b 
section 22, sub-section (#4) of section 22A and sub-section (7) of section 21) 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), the Governor is 
pleased to make the following rules reluting to the appointment, powers 
and duties of the Justice of the Peace, namely :— 


Rules 
1. These rules may be called the Justice of the Peace Rules, 1956. 


2, (1) The qualifications of the person to be appointed a Justice of the 
Peace shall be as follows: سس‎ 
(£) he should be normally resident in the local area for which he is 
appointed ; 
(8) he should not, before such appointment, be less than 20 years and 
more than 60 years of age; 
(৮28) he should be literate and a person of some education; 


(tv) he should be a person of integrity and of some local standing and 
should be otherwise suitable tor appointment; 


(৮) he should be a person who has not been declared an insolvent, or 
convicted of an offence which, in the opinion of the State Gov- 
ernment, renders him unsuitable for such appointment. 


(2) A Justice of the Peace shall have a seal of office to be supplied by 
the State Government. The sea) shall contain the words ‘‘Justice of the 
Peace’ and the name of the local area for which he has been appointed. 
The seal shall be returned by him, when he vacates his office, to such officer 
as may be specified by the State Government. 


(3) Ou his appointment a Justice of the Peace shall be furnished by 
the State Government with a copy of the order of appointment. Such copy 
shall be returned by him, when he vacates his office, to such officer as may 
be specified by the State Government. 


(4) A Justice of the Peace shall not be entitled to any remuneration for 
his services. 


(5) The term of office of a Justice of the Peace, unless terminated 
earlier, shall on first appointment be one year and such term may _ be 
renewed for such period or periods as the State Government deems fit. 


(6) A Justice of the Peace may be removed by the State Government 
from office 11 
(2) he ceases to reside in the local area, or remains absent from that 

area, 10৫ a continuous period of six months without the permission 
of the State Government; or 

(2) he is declared an insolvent or accused of or convicted of an offence 
which, in the opinion of the State Government, renders him unfit 
to be retained in his appointment; or 

(882) his conduct appears to be unsatisfactory or he is found to be other- 
wise unsuitable by the State Government. 


3. (1) A Justice of the Peace may issue a certificate of identity to any 
person residing in the local area if he knows the latter personally or 1s 
otherwise satisfied as to his identity. 


(2) Such certificate of identity shall show the name of the holder, his 
father’s name, his place of residence and address, his profession or occupa- 
tion and any other particulars which may be necessary for the purpose for 
which the certificate is issued. There shall be affixed to the certificate a 
passport-size photograph of the holder. It shall be signed by the Justice 
of the Peace issuing it and shall bear the seal of his office. 


4. (1) When an origina] document is brought before a Justice of the 
Peace by a person residing within his local area for verification or attesta- 
tion either in respect of the particulars contained therein or in respect of 
the signature of the executant, the Justice of the Peace may, after such 
enquiry, if any, a8 may be necessary, endorse the verification or attestation 
on the document and affix his signature and seal thereto. 


(2) When a copy of such a document requires verification or attestation, 
the Justice of the Peace may, after comparing the copy with the original, 
endorse the verification or attestation on such copy and affix his signature 
and seal thereto. 


6. (1) In the case of an incident involving breach of the peace or of 
the commission of an offence in the local area, the Justice of the Peace 
shal 

(2) visit the place of occurrence immediately on receipt of informa- 
tion; 

(1) record the statement of the eye-witness and others having 
knowledge of the incident or of the commission of the offience, 
noting their names and addresses;

interest requires that the Inland Water ‘Transport

poses of the said Act for a period of six months 
with effect from the 20th August 1956.

Dated Calcutta, the 16th July 1956.

mittee, to be known as the West Bengal Spices 
and Cashewnut Committee, with the following 
members :—

(1) Shri Bisheswar Lall Kajuria of Messrs.

(8) The Special Officer (Potatoes), West Bengal 
(er officio). 


2. The Special Officer (Potatees), West Bengal, 
will act as Seeretary to the Committee. 


3. The members will hold office for a period 
of 6 years or until further orders. 


4. (Government reserve the power to add to 
the number of members, if necessary. 


5. The Committee shall have the power to 
appoint Sub-Committees for dealing with special 
problems or special matters and to appoint to such 
Committees persons who may not be members of 
the Committee. 


6. The Chairman shall have powers of invitiu 
persons with expert knowledge or eave 
experience to attend meetings of the Comumnittee 
and participate in its deliberations, 


7. The functions of the Committee will be— 


(a) to advise Government on all matters relat- 
ing to research and development work on 
Spices and Cashewnuts, 

(9) to prepare research and development 
schemes far increasing the production of 
Spices and Cashewnuts, 


(c) to ensure that the funds provided for the 
execution of the schemes are properly 
utilised, 

(৫) to secure that the local resources are fully 
exploited for increasing the production, 
etc., of the Spices and Cashewnuts, and 


(৫) to ‘enlist the public co-operation to the 
fullest possible extent for the execution 
of schemes for research and development 


works on Spices and Cashewnuts.

forwarded to all members of the Committee and 
the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for

September 1955, I required all persons interested 
in the waste lands specified therein to show cause 
withim the prescribed time why the waste lands 
should not be requisitioned ;

and after making further enquiry, I am satisfied 
that the waste lands as mentioned in the schedule

In exercise of the powers eonferted by section 0 
of the West Bengal Security Act, 1950, and 
delegated to me by Government order No. 2170P. | 


30-9/50, dated 116) April 1950, of the Home 
(Political) Jepartment, Government of West 
Bengal, under section 38 of the said Act, I do 


hereby order that the Hat at Newajkhana in 
Mekliganj subdivision, will continue to remain 
closed as ordered on 30th April 1955. 


I further order that the Dewanganj Hat in 
Mekliganj subdivision and the Hats and shops at 
Tharaikhana alias Kursha, Karala alias Natkabari 
and Chowhduryhat in Dinhata subdivision shall 
complete all transactions before sunset and shop- 
keepers,” vendors and customers attending the Hats 
and shops shall leave by that time.

three months, with effect from Ist August 1956. 
Any person contravening the said order shall be 
punishable aceording to the provisions of law.

Whereas [I ain © satisfied from information 
received that smuggling of foodgrains, parti- 
ularly of rice and paddy, is going on along the 
Indo-Pak ‘border in this distriet resulting in a 
rapid drainage of these commodities from the 
district, and whereas it is immediately necessary. 
in the interest of maintaining supphes of food- 
‘vrains essential for the lite of the community, 
to prevent -such smuggling, and whereas ] am of 
opinion that this can effectively he done only by 
restricting the movement of the said commo- 
dities within a helt of two miles along the 
ventire Indo-Pak border in this district, 1, Shri 
K. P. Sen, District Magistrate and Deputy Com- 
missioner, Cooch Behar, in exercise of the powers 
conferred on me by order No. 2170-P/30-9/50, 
dated 11th April 1950, issued by the Government 
of West Bengal, Home (Political) Depart nent, do, 
by this order under sub-section (1) of section 0 
of the West Bengal Security Act, 1950, prohibit 
the movement of foodgraina ineluding 1006 
paddy. pulses, oilseeds, wheat, gram, ete., in any 
form in quantities in excess of one maund at a 
time within a belt of two miles along the East 
Pakistan-Cooch Behar border in this district 
except the movement of such commodities in 
excess of one maund at a time by hona fide 
dealers and consumers under permits issued by 
the Subdivisional Controller of Food and Sup- 
plies, (€ooch Behar, or by the Subdivisional 
Officer of the subdivision concerned. 


This order will remain in foree for a period of 
three months from the Ist August 1956 to 31st 
October 1956 (77061) days inclusive). 


GFiven under my hand and seal this day the 
ط80‎ July 1956.
