ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between the Upper Fagu Tea 
Estate, P.O. Fagu, Darjeeling, and their workmen represented by the 
West Bengal Cha-Sramik Union, Jalpaiguri, 


BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 
Snr G. PALIT, Judge, Industrial Tribunal (Fifth), West Bengal. 


For the Company: Shri T. Sen Gupta, General Adviser of the Company. 
For the Union: Shri D. L. Sen Gupta, Advocate. 


1. By Government order No. 2586Dis. /D/9L-27/55, dated the 8th June 
1955, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal, 
resided over by me, for adjudication under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth Industrial Tribunal was 
cfustituted under section 7 of the Act by the notification No. .ناہ85811‎ 
dated the 9th June 1951. 


2. The reference was received here on 15th June 1955. The Union filed 
written statement on 8th July 1955, and the Company filed written objection 
on 22nd August 1955. After severa] adjournments the case was taken up 
for hearing on 1111) June 1956, and it continued till 14th June 1956 when 
the oe including the argument was concluded. The award was 
reserved. 


3. The issue contained in the schedule to the order of reference stands 
as follows سے‎ 


Whether the Upper Fagu Tea Estate under the management of Messrs. 
“ Padma, Ltd., from 6th March 1955 should be treated as a 
Darjeeling Hill Garden or Dooars Garden? What should be the 

rates of wages.of the workers of the garden from 6th March 1955? 


AWARD 


4. Before I discuss the issue specifically, I should like to preface it by 
a short history of the dispute. Originally the Fagu Tea Estate comprised 
both the Upper Fagu and the Lower Fagu. It is as ancient as 100 years, 
and it partly fell in the district of Darjeeling and partly in Jalpaiguri. 
It was under the management of British planters, and continued as such till 
6th March 1955 when it changed hands and the present management came 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 95 1956 3077 
a 
(9 own the Upper Magu Tea Estate. Though the Upper Fagu fell in the 
district of Darjeeling, still it was classified and treated as a Dooars Tea 
Garden. The rates of wages which were given in the Upper Fagu Tea 
state wore the rates in Dooars Tea Gardens. The Minimum Wages Com- 
miliee, West Bengal, in the year 1902 divided the whole plantation area. 
‘nto three divisions, and fixed the rates thereof. Those three divisions were, 
vit 

(a) the hilly area of the Darjeeling district, 

(v) Terai area in the plains of Darjeeling district in the Siliguri and 

Kurseong subdivisions, and 
(c) the Dooars area in the Jalpaiguri district, 


{Though the Dooars area was limited to the eastern side of the river Teesta, 
yet the Dooars Tea Crardens comprised also the tea gardens in the ‘‘non- 
hilly’ areas of Darjeeling, gardens in the plantation area in the district 
of Cooch Behar, and also gardens in the plantation area in the district of 
Jalpaiguri lying on the west of the river Teesta. So, according to the 
Union, Dooars Tea Gardens were comprehensive enough and practically 
comprised the residuary plantation area, barring the aforesaid three divisions 
as mentioned in the report of the Minimum Wages Committee, West Bengal. 
In this concept the Upper Fagu Tea Estate fell within the class of Dooars 
Tea Gardens, though وھ حم‎ in the Kalimpong subdivision of the 
Darjeeling district. But the present management, as soon as they took over 
the ten garden on 6th March 195d, supplanted the Dooars rates of wages 
by the Darjeeling hilly area rates of wages which were much less. This 
resulted in a dispute which was referred to conciliation, but the Company 
lid,not abide by the decision of the said conciliation proceeding, and 
intrbduced the Darjeeling rates of wages. Hence has arisen the present 


diapute. 


he Company contends that the Upper Fagu Tea Estate was situated 
in the hilly area of Kalimpong subdivision within the Darjeeling district. 
The previous management by mistake or inadvertence kept up the Dooars 
rates of wages in this Tea Estate. The present management did rectify this 
mistake with the result that the present dispute came into being. The 
present management, says the Company, cannot afford to pay or continue 
to pay the Dooars rates of wages because it proved to be an unprofitable Tea 
Estate. Its production is very small, and that is why the Government 
referred the dispute for decision with the idea that the Darjeeling Garden 
rates might be introduced here. 


During the hearing the Union made an amendment of their written state- 
ment by saying that the Lower T'agu Tea Hstate is also mn the district of 
Darjeeling, and not in the district of Jalpaiguri as originally stated. The 
other side, however, objected to it after the amendment was passed by the 
Tribunal. The Union could not produce any documentary evidence to 
show that really the Lower IFagu Tea Estate fell within the district of 
Darjeeling. Its motive to make this amendment is not far to seek. It is 
almitted that the Dooars rates of wages are still in vogue as before in the 
Lower Fagu Tea Estate under the European management. So, if the Dooars 
rates of wages are still being given in respect of a garden which falls within 
the ambit of Darjeeling district, then there can hardly be any point in 
denying the said privilege 10 the workmen of another garden which is 
geographically within the ambit of the said district. But both from the 
points of view of delay in moving this amendment, as also of want of 
evidence to substantiate it, I cannot attach much importance to this 
argument of the Union under the said amendment. So the dispute over the 
amendment should be at rest. 


3078 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 [Parr I 


The Union tried to. rely on tho three divisions adopted by the Minimum 
Wages Committee of West Bengal in 1982. The re evant portion of thy. 
report: occurs at page 7, and it runs thus: ‘The Committee has further 
decided with reference to section 8(3)(a)(iv) that minimuin wages should 
be fixed in respect of three zones or loralities, viz., (a) the Dooars area in 
Jalpaiguri district, (b) the Terai area in the plains of Darjecling 01800 
in the Siliguri and the Kurseong subdivisions, and (c) the hilly areas of 
Darjeeling district, these three areas boing described ordinarily as Dooars, 
Terai and Darjeeling, respectively, according to the prevailiug practice.”’ 


Now, the Company may argue that these were the divisions which the 
Minimum Wages Committee might have adopted for their work or for 
convenience, but that can never be accepted as a conventional classification 
of these three classes of gardens, viz., Dooars, Terai and Darjeeling. True 
enough. But in the said report it is mentioned that this was in conformity 
with the prevailing practice. The said Committee which met not only the 
planters, but also the Employees’ Unions, and toured through the area 
concerned, came to aC a that this was the practice current there. So, 
te say that it was not the prevailing practice, the onus is certainly heavy on 
the employer to displace the said Committee’s report on the point by clear 
and cogent evidence. Such evidence is, however, wanting, So I cannot 
but attach importance to this classification as adopted by the Minimum 
Wages Committee. Darjeeling gardens must be limited to hilly areas of 
the Darjeeling district. Unless such position can be shown it is difficult 10 
include the present Tea Estate in the class of Darjeeling gardens. It ig 
nobody’s case that the Upper Fagu Tea Kstate is in the Terai area as also 
in the Siliguri and Kurseong subdivisions. In this connection I have also 
to consider the fact that the European management had so long been 
treating the entire Upper Fagu and the Lower Fagu 1169, Estates as Dooars 
Tea Gardens. To brush it aside as the Company tried merely by saying 
that it was a mistake, or a piece of inadvertence, would be unconvincing. 
Secondly, 1-1 refer to the Assam Directory and Tea Areas Hand Book, 
1954, I find the Fagu Division being mentioned as ‘‘JJooars Gardens’’ at 
page 225. The Darjeeling Tea Companies are also mentioned in a separate 
chapter, but Fagu is conspicuous by its absence. So it is clear that Fagu 
was treated as a Dooars Tea Garden even in 1954. Then if I refer to the 
Calcutta Tea Market Report filed by the Union (Ext. 1), I find at page 7 
of it that the Fagu Tea Garden 1s mentioned there as a Dooars Tea Garden. 
Darjeeling Tea Gardens are mentioned under 0, separate heading, but Fagu 
is conspicuous by its absence there. This Calcutta Tea Market Report dates 
April and May 1956. So it is an up-to-date document to show that even in 
1956 May, the Fagu Garden was treated as a Dooars Tea Garden. So, it is 
abundantly clear that Fagu was all along treated as a Dooars Tea Garden, 
and not as a Durjeeling Tea Garden, and it is so right up to the present 
time. Now, what is the evidence that the Company has placed before me to 
displacé this accepted position of the Fagu Tea Garden? I should say, the 
evidence that has been produced is merely tentative, and hardly sufficient. 
The Company, by oral evidence, has wanted to show the elevation of the 
Upper Fagu Tea Estate thereby trying to show that it must be treated as a 
Darjeeling hill garden. But in the Assam Jirectory aforesaid which 
mentions the elevation of tea gardens in some cases, does not mention the 
elevation of the Fagu Division. That leads ine io think that its elevation 
is not such as is worth mentioning. Besides, I have got in evidence that 
only in some small spaces of the Upper Fagu there is some elevation, but 
the rest of the garden is more or Jess on level ground. So, mere elevation 
11) portions, unless there is average, will not go far enough. 


part 1] ']1[ CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 3079 
oe ee ee ne A ee a are 

Net, the Company has shown that production in the Upper Fagu Tea 
state is much less than that in Dooars Gardens. Its production compares 
and likens to the production im Darjeeling hill gardens. That may or may 
not be, but it does not prove anything. The climate of this garden may 
very well be as that of other Darjeeling gardens because it is in the same 
rygion. So, the point of production can never be decisive in this matter. 
qhen it is said that the culling of tea leaves of the Upper Fagu Gardens is 
more like the tea leaves culling of Darjeeling Gardens than that of Dooars 
Gardens. But this also can never be the criterion of classification for being 
q Darjeeling hill garden. So I must say that the Company has bent its 
energies in a wrong direction in its attempt to displace the established 
conclusion in the matter which the Union has proved by reference to docu- 
mentary evidence and age-long custom. In view of this, ] am clearly of 
opinion that the Upper Fagu Tea Estate should be treated as a ‘‘Dooars 
Garden’’ and not as a ‘‘)arjeeling Garden’’. 


Regarding the rates of wages, I can at once say that the Dooars rates 
of wages must be granted here ay before because 1t 1s a Dooars Carden 
Fiven if it be ussumed for the sake of argument that the Upper Fagu Tea 
Estate is a Darjeeling hill garden, even then there are রনির which 
would lead me to grant Dooars rates of wages here, and those are as 
follows: 


7 These workmen had so long been enjoying the Dooars rates of wages. 
Simply because there has been a change of ownership, to which the work- 
men were no consenting purty, their rates of wages are not liable to be 
reduced. If it was a mistake to grant them Dooars rates of wages originally, 
this Jong lapse of 100 years has taken away the basis of the mistake, and 
hag converted it into a substantial right. Such right cannot be so easily 
taken away. 


(2) The Lower Fagu Tea Kstate is still granting Dooars rates of wages. 
Becduse a portion has been carved out of the parent tea estate, that cannot 
entitle the present Company to introduce a eae rate here. That would 
never produce industrial peace or harmony. It will rather be the reverse 
of it. So as an Industrial Tribunal I can never approve of it. 


(3) I have shown above that the workmen’s right to have the Dooars 
rates of wages is more broad-based than the above considerations, which I 
need not repeat here. 


(4) If I look to the conduct of the present employer, 1 must say that it 

is bent on reducing the wages under some plea or other. Jt 1s well-known 
that Government, through the Minimum Wages Committee, granted some 
increment of wages in the case of workmen of the Darjeeling hilly area tea 
ardens, Theo workmen of the Upper Fagu Tea Mstate also claimed at 
লি this benefit granted by the Minimum Wages Committee, West Bengal. 
But the present management refused to concede even that claim of the 
workmen. The management had an injunction in a suit filed in the 
Kalimpong Court preventing the workmen from claiming the benefit under 
this move of (iovernment through the Minimum Wages Committee. So 
it ia clear that the employer is not prepared ما‎ extend even the privileges 
admiasible to Darjeeling hill garden workers to the workers of the Upper 
Fagu Tea Estate, though it wants to classify this garden under the category 
of Darjeeling hilly area tea gardens. That shows the mala fide of the 
present ا‎ সি wis-d-vis the workmen of the Upper Fagu Tea -Kstate. 


The representative of the employer wanted to make much of the fact 
that if the Dooars rates of wages are allowed to continue, the Upper Fagu 
Tea Kstate will be a lability. That cannot be helped. The management 


3080 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 {Panr [ 
ক trees 


itself made the bargain. Now if it does not prove to be a profitable hgrgain 
because of its being carved out from the parent tea estate, no justice wil] 
make the workmen pay for the same. So in any view of the matter, J 
cannot persuade myself to allow the Darjeeling hill garden rates of wages 
to supplant the Dooars rates of wages in the Upper Fagu Tea Estate with 
effect from 6th March 1955. This is my award, 


But the point is, should I grant any specific relicf to the workmen ip 
the present case? I have evidence before me that Darjeeling rates of wages 
ure already an accomplished fact in the Upper Fagu Tea Estate by the force 
of the employer. If that is so, the employer must make that good and pay 
the balance of wages which falls short of the Dooars rates of wages right 
from 6th March 1955 up to the date of reference, i.e., 8th June 1955. 1ڑ‎ 
cannot give any ascertained amount because there is no evidence before 
me specitic on the point. As an Industrial Tribunal, [ think, I am entitled 
to grant this individual relief which follows directly from my decision, and 
I do not think I am exceeding my jurisdiction in granting this very legi- 
timate relief io the workmen of the Upper Fagu Tea Estate in the present 
case. The Dooars rates of wages are given in the Appendix and this is not 
disputed as such.

AWARD 
1. By order No. 2266Dis./D/111-133(A)/56, dated the 28th May 


1956, the Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. General Dealers, Jitd., and Messrs. 
Ramsahaimull More, Ltd., both of 5 Clive Row, Calcutta, and their 
employee Shri Gour Chandra Dhar represented by the Federation 
of Mercantile Employees’ Union, 238A Netaji Subhas Road (top floor), 
regarding the matters specified in the schedule, to the Third Industrial 
Tribunal constituted under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
by notification No. 692Dis./D/12L-6/52, dated the 28rd February 19938, for 
adjudication. 


2. Summons was duly served on the Federation of Mercantile 
Kmployees’ Union representing the employee Shri Gour Chandra Dhar. It 
did not put in appearance. The employers Messrs. (teneral Dealers, Ltd., 
and Messrs. Ramsahaimull More, Ltd., put in appearance and filed their 
written: statements. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows: — 


Is the discharge of Shri Gour Chandra Dhar justified? To what relief 
is he entitled ? 


DECISION 


As neither the employee Shri Gour Chandra Dhar nor the Federation 
of the Mercantile Employees’ Union representing him put in appearance, it 
is presumed that they have no outstanding dispute for adjudication. The 
employers Messrs. General Dealers, Ltd., and Messrs. Ramsahaimull More, 
Lid., on the other hand, filed a joint written statement stating that the 
dispute has been amicably settled. In support of the statement, the 
emplovers have filed a copy of the application addressed by the workman 
to the Assistant Labour Commissioner Shri A. R. Ghosh. In the cir- 
cumstantes, it is abundantly clear that the dispute referred to has been 
settled and needs no adjudication. It is ا‎ accordingly.

ডি রি রতি 

By Government order No, 5868Dis./D/11L-228/55, dated 13th 
December 1955, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to this Tribunal “for 
adjudication regarding the matter specified in the schedule, 


issue as contained in the schedule to the order of reference is as‏ تا 
سس ollows‏ 


Is the termination of services of the workmen, as per list attached, 
justified? What relief are they entitled to? 


AWARD 


It is the version of the workmen that on 4th July 1955, the Shiva Glass 
Works Co., Lid. (Factory No. 1), declared lock-out in the whole factory 
from 6 p.m. without justification, and only to crush the Shiva Glass 
Mazdoor Union. The Labour Directorate was moved in the matter, and 
as a result of a series of conciliation proceedings conducted by the Labour 
Officer, the Munagement was directed to take back all the workmen, who 
had been working in the factory before the lock-out. The Management 
took back majority of the workers, but the present workmen, who are 
mentioned in the attached list and who are 195 in number, were not 
allowed to join their duties by the Management. Hence, they claimed to 
be allowed to join their services with full compensation including salary 
and allowances for the period of their forced unemployment. The action 
of the Company is stigmatised to be unjustified and mala fide. 


The Company’s version is that the number of workers employed ا‎ 
Factory No. 1 was about 425, and the work of this factory was going on 
smoothly for several years, but the workmen being misguided by the 
R.8.P. leaders, adopted go-slow policy, as a result of which there was 
considerable fall in production in the month of June 1955. The Company 
gave several notices to the workmen in the month of June 1955 requesting 
them to give up go-slow policy, but still the workers continued that policy 
and resorted to sit-down strike on several days in the factory thereby 
hampering the production. On 4th July 1985, the workers, all on a 
sudden, launched a sit-down strike. The Management apprehending danger 
considered it expedient, as a measure of security, to close down the factory 
on that very day at 6 p.m., and the matter was reported to the Labour 
Commissioner. The Company further contends that as a result of a series 
of conciliation proceedings with the representatives of the workers and the 
Management, an agreement was at last reached, and the lock-out was lifted 
from Gth August 1955 when the factory was reopened. The Management 
issued a notice on that date to the workers requesting them to rejoin their 
work by the 8th August 1955. The Company issued further notices on 8th 
August, 9th August and 10th August 1955 requesting the workers, who 
had not reported for duties, to report for duties at the factory within three 
days. The Company issued a further notice on 13th August 1995 imform- 
ing the workmen that the work in the production section would start on 
or about 18th August 1955, and that the workmen of this section should 
report at The factory by 18৮1) August 1955 without fail. This notice was 
also advertised in several newspapers. As in spite of all these notices 
several workers did not join their duties, the Company gave another notice 
on 20th August 1955, and in this notice the Management clearly mention- 
ed that if the workers did not join their duties by 22nd August 1950, it 
would be considered that the defaulting workers have left their services. 
At the suggestion and request of Shri N. C. Kundu, Labour Officer, the 
date of joining of such workers, who did not till then report for duties, 
was extended by the Management to 29th August 1955. But even in spite 
of this, only a few workers reported for duties. At last, the Management 


part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 3087 


০০০০০ 55০০ উপ স্কট সা 


was compelled to appoint fresh hauds from 18٦ September 1955 to run the 
factory. Accordingly, the Company contends that it did not at all 
fenminate the services of the workers, who are mentioned in the list 
attached to the order of reference, but these workers of their own accord 
had left the service of the Company. The Company further submits that 
the issue regarding termination of service is not maintainable in law in the 
present case, as the lock-out was, lifted with full knowledge of the workers, 
and that us the workers in question did not turn up in spite of notices, 
there was no cause for them to complain that there was termination of 


service. Accordingly, the Company contends that the workers are not 
entitled to any remedy. 


The contention of the workers, as could be gathered, is that the 
Yompany refused to allow these 195 workmen, as per list attached to the 
order of reference, to join their duties, although they had gone to join, 
und that the action of the Company was unjustified and mala fide. It is 
urged on behalf of the workers that this was an instance of unfair labour 
practice and victimisation on the part of the Management. The Company 
denied this contention of the workers. Its version, on the other hand, is 
that the Company did not terminate the services of these workers, but the 
workers themselves did not turn up to join their duties in spite of several 
notices issued by the Management from time to time, extending their 
joining time. Accordingly, it 1s urged on behalf of the Company that 
there was no termination of services of these workers by any order of 
dismissal, It further wanted to say that it could not keep the factory 
gute indefinitely open for any length of time in expectation of the workers 
‘goming or stepping in, as they pleased. 


So, the point in the instant case boils down to this. Whether the 

anagement refused: to allow these workers to join their duties, or whether 

these workers did not turn up of their own accord in spite of several notices 
issued by the Management 7 


At the very outset, I may say that in this dispute I am not concerned 
with any question of lock-out. The issue in the order of reference is 
regarding the termination of services of these workers. The Government 
in the order of reference has specified only one point for adjudication, and 
it is whether the termination of services of the workmen as per list attach- 
ed to the order of reference justified. That being so, the Tribunal shall 
confine its adjudication to that point only. The Tribunal cannot go 
beyond the strict terms of reference. Accordingly, the Tribunal cannot 
enter into the question whether the lock-out was justified or not. It may 
be stated in this connection that the discharge of workers or termination 
of their services does not amount to lock-out, and it has been held so by 
the Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of the Presidency Jute Mills 
Company, Ltd., and their workmen reported in 1952 ..A.C. 62. That lock- 
out in this factory was declared on 4th July 1955 18 admitted by both the 
parties. It has transpired from evidence that the said lock-out was lifted 
on 6th August 1955, as a result of conciliation proceedings held by the 
Labour Officer with the Management and the representatives of the workers. 
It has also been satisfactorily proved by the evidence, as furnished by the 
Company, that notices were issued by the Management asking all the 
workers to join their duties after the lock-out was lifted, and such date 
of joining was extended up to 29th August 1955. These notices have been 
proved (wide Ext. E-series). A copy of such notice was also published in 
five local newspapers (vide Ext. F-series). It has come out from the 


3088... THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 196 [0] 


Caine, Crete, 
سس‎ 


evidence of Shr ৩, 1১, Modi (O.P.W. 1), who is one of the Directors of 
Messrs. Shiva Glass Works Company, Ltd., and who manages the affairs 
of the Company, that the notices, which were issued on 8th, 9th, 10+ 
18th and 20th August 1955 were pasted on the Notice Board inside the 
factory and also outside the gate of the factory. He has denied the 
allegation that such workers, who belong to the Mazdoor Union, were not 
allowed to join by the Management. He has made wu positive statement 
that at tho request of the Labour Commissioner, the Management invited 
all the workers to join their duties, and that no discrimination was made 
in this respect. In this connection, it may be stated that out of 195 
workers us mentioned in the list attached to the order of reference, 111 
were taken in by the Company after the order of reference was made leav- 
ing behind only 84 workers. The very fact that out of about 500 workers 
who were in the factory at the tume of lock-out, more than 400 were allowed 
to join their duties leaving behind a fraction of such workers only, 
negatives the contention of the Union that the Management victimised 
them out of malice. In my view, this rather shows that the Management 
was exceedingly considerate, and must have weighed the conduct of every 
worker who came forward to 1010) by the dates prescribed by it. According 
to the evidence of the Secretary, Shiva Glass Muazdoor Union, this Union 
represents 85 per cent. of the workers. But the fact remains that 
majority of the workers was absorbed by the Company after the lock-out 
was lifted. So, the argument of the Union that these 84 workmen were 
not taken in simply because they belonged to the Mazdoor Union, does not 
hold good. P.W. 1 Secretary of the Union has stated no doubt that 
{these workmen approached the Management for resumption of their duties 
after the lock-out was lifted, but the Management refused to take them 
in. This is emphatically denied by O.P.W. 1 Shri 8S. ط‎ Modi, the 
Director of the Company. He has made a clear and positive statement 
that these 84 workmen did not at all report for duties. He has further 
deposed on oath that even after the last date fixed in the notice, dated 20th 
August 1955, they took those workers who came and reported for duties. 
He has denied with emphasis’ the suggestion that they did not allow these 
workers to join, in order to victimise the Unton, to which they belonged. 
It is interesting to note that in this case none of the workers has been 
examined. In the circumstances, no reliance can be placed on the un- 
corroborated testimony of the Secretary of the Union, im the face 01 
emphatic denial and positive testimony of Shri S$. P. Modi, who is one of 
the Directors of the Company and manages its affairs. After giving ٥۴۷ 
careful and anxious consideration to the evidence, facts and circumstances, 
I am of the view that all these workers did not at all report for duties in 
the factory in spite of several notices issued by the Management from time 
to time, and I am not prepared to believe that they presented themselves 
at the gate of the factory, but were not allowed by the Management to join 
their duties. Nor am I prepared to hold that such notices that have heen 
proved inethis case by the Management, were not issued in“a manner ×۸ 
deposed to hy O.P.W. 1 Shri S, P. Modi. All these workmen, in my view, 
had knowledge of these notices, and it cannot be held that they were 
totally ignorant of the same. These workers were members of a Union, 
and the said Union was acting on their behalf. So, such Union must have 
kept information as to what was going on in the factory, or what was 
being done by the Management. The lock-out was lifted on 6th August 
1955. The Management virtually kept the doors for re-entry open 1111 
28th August 1955 by issuing notices one after another. Tn spite of this, 
only a small fraction of the workers did not join. Thot is a thing for 
which the Management cannot be held responsible. The doors for such 


re-entry cannot be kept open for an indefinite time to enable the workers 


parr 11 TITH CALOUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 3089 


می شس pny‏ 


سی 


to join their services. They were in duty bound to come back within a 
reasonable time, and if they could not, they ought to have given satis- 
jactory explanation for the same. But here in the present case, no such 
explanation was given. The only explanation that was sought to be offered 
on their behalf before the Tribunal is that the Management did not sllow 
them te join, although they reported for duties at the gate of the factory. 
But such explanation has been found to be unacceptable for the reasons 
stated already. In view of what lras been stated above, it cannot be said by 
any means that the Management terminated the services of all these workers 
barring Sinhasan Jadal (serial No. 8 of the list attached to the order of 
reference). In my view, those workers must be deemed to have voluntarily 
loft the service of the Company by not turning up in spite of notices is used 
by the Management. Hence, it is not a case of termination of service by 
the Management as 73810171160 in the issue framed by the Government. in the 
order of reference. In its true essence, this is a case for voluntary relin- 
quishment or resignation of service by these men. Such a case is out of 
bounds of the Industrial Disputes Act. Hence, all the workers, save end 
except Sinhasan Jadab, are not entitled to any relief. In this connection, 
1 may observe that the Management was perfectly justified in recruiting 
new hands for running its business, as all the workers did not turn up to 
join after the lock-out was lifted. 


Regarding Sinhasan Jadab, his case, however, stands on a_ different 
footing. According to the Union, he was victimised on 18th June 1955. 
The matter was taken to the Labour Directorate. Although the labour 
Oticer requested the Management to reinstate him, the Management did 
it accede to it. The Company has denied the alleged victimisation ot 
نما‎ Jadab. The Company’s version is that he used to work as a 
yack-maker, but he was absent from duties for several days without leave 
abd intimation, and as such he was discharged. I called for the Labour 
119 in this case, and have perused the same. O.P.W. 1 Shri 8S. P. Mod 
haa also stated before this Tribunal that as Sinhasan Jadah was absent from 
duties for several days without leave and intimation, he was discharged. 
But in his cross-examination, he was constrained to admit that no written 
notice was given to Sinhusan Jadab when he was discharged, nor was any 
explanation called for from him before his discharge. Even 20 charge- 
sheet was issued to him, nor was any enquiry held before his discharge. 
Thus there can be no room for doubt that the principles of natural justice 
were violated in his case. It cannot be held that a worker will lose his 
service without having any opportunity to meet the charge levelled against 
him, and at the sweet will and pleasure of the Management. Sinhasan 
Jadab should have been given an opportunity to explain his position before 
being discharged. But the stubborn fact remains that no charge-sheet was 
delivered to him, nor was any enguiry held by the Management in order 
to ascertain what he had got to say by way of explanation for his alleged 
absence. The termination of service of Sinhasan Jadab cannot accordingly 
be justified. In such cases, the employer cannot be said to have acted with 
an honest purpose. That heing so, the termination of service of Sinhasan 
Jadab (serial No. 3 of the list attached to the order of reference) was not 
only wrongful, but illegal and unjustified. The action of the Management 
was rather arbitrary. In my view, this is a fit case, in which reinstate- 
ment should be ordered. Accordingly, the Tribunal directs that Sinhasan 
Jadab (serial No. 3 of the list attached to the order of reference) be 
reinstated. He must come back to duty and join as soon as this award 
becomes operative. He shall get back wages and allowance, if any, for 
the entire period from the date of his termination of service till reinstate- 
ment within one month of the award becoming effective. Be it further

noted that the period of his forced unemployment should not be regarded 
as a break in his ھ٥٠‎ 


This is the award of the Tribunal.

This reference made by the Government of West Bengal by order 
No. 2683Dis./D/101,-96/55, dated Calcutta, the 15th June 1955, was

on the ex parte evidence produced by the Union representing the workers. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1986 3093 


The Company had filed written statement in opposition but failed to appear 
on the date fixed for hearing. The Union offered evidence and the case 
was decided on the materials supplied by it. The Company went up in 
appeal and drew the attention of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal, 
pointedly to the order passed by the Tribunal on 22th September 1956 
settling 3rd November 1955 as the date for hearing. There wus a direction 
in the order to inform the parties. In conformity with established usage 
information was given by affixing notice in the Notice Board. Somehow 
or other the Labour Labour Appellate Tribunal was not apprised of the 
fact or was not convinced that the normal procedure for +4 i parties 
was by publication in the Notice Board. Under the general law the duty 
is cast upon parties to keep themselves acquainted with the proceedings 
and the orders passed therein. Courts and Tribunals are not required 
under the law to give information to parties. Be that as it may, in the 
view that the Company had no notice of the hearing date, the Jearned 
Appellate Tribunal remanded the case for fresh hearing and _ disposal 
according to law. That is how the matter has been reopened. 


The dispute is concerned with the dismissal of four employees and the 
issues formulated by Government are os follows :— 


issues 


(1) Whether the dismissal of Shri Krishna Chandra  Santra, 
Shri Sudhir Bhowmick, Shri Kalipada Dalui and Shri Balai 
Santra is justified ? 


(2) What relief including reinstatement are they entitled to? 


The written statement lodged by the Union is a model of brevity. No 
particulars are furnished as to the date and the circumstances in which 
the services of these employees came to an end. The bare statement 
appears that they were dischurged without any reason whatsoever and no 
payment of wages already due and compensation for abrupt termination of 
service had been made, 


The Company’s reply is that in September 1954, Krishna Chandra 
Santra, on whom the Proprietor relied to a large extent, conceived the idea of 
assuming leadership and dictate terms to the management. Forming a 
sort of “resistance group’? these employees started » mischievous campaign 
calculated to cause injury to the concern. Production was slowed down 
and the actual execution of work was performed perfunctonly. They 
became insubordinate and defied the Proprietor. On the 17th of December 
1954, these employees were given verbal notice that on the expiry of a 
month from date their services would terminate. On such notice beiag 
given there was an aggravation of the malpractices and costly machines 
and tools were wilfully dumaged or broken. Om the 15th of January 1995, 
they were reminded of the notice of dismissal and were asked to be 
present on the 17th to receive their dues. On the date thus appointed 
only Sudhir Bhowmick appeared but the other three remained absent. 
On the 18th morning all و‎ appeared but refused to accept payment of 
the dues offered by the Proprietor. Thereafter they left the workshop on 
being asked by the Proprietor to clear out. As these employees were 
dismissed on grounds of misconduct and insubordination, they are sot 
entitled to any relief 


The two issues are dealt with jointly. 


The written statement submitted on behalf of the employees does not 
disclose the relevant facts. In evidence the omissions were made ৫০০.

diarrhoea on Saturday the 15th January 1955. As he was too ill to do

J have considered the circumstances as stated by the employees. The 
waclusion I have arrived at is that they had taken false pleas in justifica-

four workers had banded themselves into a group and had started creating

the bit between their teeth they were riding rough-shod over discipline. 
There are ample grounds for believing the testimony of the Proprietor 
that the services of all these men were dispensed with because of calculated 
insolence and perfunctory execution of work causing Joss to the concern. 
It is true that no charge-sheets were served and no enquiry was_ held. 
The facts were to the knowledge of the Proprietor himself. The Tribunal! 
on independent consideration of the facts and circumstances comes to the

AWARD 


Qn 26th August 1954 the Company issued a notice laying off these 84 
workmen with effect from 30th August 1954. The notice stated inter alia: 
‘The employees thus laid-off will be entitled to get the benefits of laid-off 
compensation as provided under the Industrial Disputes Amendment Act of 
1953 on the conditions laid down therein’’. Pursuant to this notice, these 
84 workmen who are mentioned therein, were laid-off from 30th August 
1954. The Company in spite of the assurance given in the aforesaid notice, 
has not paid any lay-off compensation to any of these workmen. The 
Labour Directorate was moved in the matter, and there the Company also 
promised to pay the lay-off compensation to these workers, but the promise 
was not kept by the Company. Hence, the Government made this reference. 
ra پت‎ concerned accordingly 01811) compensation for the period of 
lay-off.

{he €ompany admits that these 84 workmen were laid-off from 380th 
August 1954, but it contests the claim for compensation as put forward cn 
pehalf of these workmen. It contends that among the workmen mentioned 
in the list, 14 [ Nos. (70), (71), (72), (73), 014), (75), (76), (77), (78), 
(80), Bl), (82), (83) and (84)] were recalled to duties on different dates, and 
have been working since then. It further contends that the workers 
00010611590 were engaged in employment elsewhere during the period of 
lay-off, and that none of them fulfilled the conditions mentioned in section 
290) of the Industrial Disputes Act. In the circumstances, it is urged 
on behalf of the Company that the workmen concerned are-not entitled to 
any lay-off compensation. 


There is no dispute or controversy between the parties that these 84 
workmen were laid-off by the Company from 30th August 1954 pursuant 
(0 a notice issued on 26th August 1954. Admittedly, that lay-off still 
continues, so far as most of the workmen of the het attached to the order 
of reference are concerned. The Company has adduced evidence that only 
14 among 84 workmen of the list, whose Nos. are (70), (71), (72), (73), (74), 
(75), (76), (77), (78), (80), (81), (82), (83) and (84) were subsequently 
recalled for duties on different dates, and are still working. The evidence on 
the side of the Company in this respect stands unchallenged and uncontra- 
dicted. There was no cross-examination on this point by the Union, nor has 
the Union furnished any evidence to the contrary. Shri Pathak appearing on 
behalf of the Union fairly accepted this position at the time of hearing. 


As stated already, one of the contentions of the Company is that the 
workmen concerned are not entitled to get lay-off compensation, as none of 
them fulfilled the conditions mentioned in section 20K of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. In this respect, the Company presumably relied on condi- 
tion 48 laid down in clause (ii) of section 25K, which runs as follows:— 


No compensation shall be paid to a workman, if he does not present 
himself for work at the establishment at the appointed time 
: during normal working hours at least once a day.’’ 


But I may say straightway that the workmen, who were thus laid-off 
in the present case, were not required to fulfil the condition as laid down in 
clause (11) of section 20H. In the notice issued by the Company for lay-off, 
it was not stated anywhere that the workers laid-off were to present them- 
selves for work at the establishment during normal working hours at least 
once a day. Furthermore, according to the written statement of ‘the 
Company (vide paragraph 2), the Company had to close down its work and 
to lay-off the workmen concerned, as there was no business, If the Company 
had to close down the work and business, then where was the scope for the 
workmen concerned to present themselves during normal working hours at 
least once a day? Possibly, there could be no such scope. Then again, the 
Company has further stated in paragraph 3 of its written statement that 
after the closure there was a distinct understanding that the workmen 
would be taken back, in case the Company was in a position to restart 
work, and that in pursuance of this understanding, they were not required 
to present themselves for their attendance as required under the Industrial 
Ihsputes Act to become eligible for the lay-off compensation. In view of 
this averment in the written statement, the Company cannot be allowed to 
raise an objection that the workmen concerned were not entitled to get any 
lay-off compensation, simply because they failed to present themselves for 
attendance at least once a day. This attitude of the Company to defeat the 
rights of the workmen concerned to compensation, is anything but satis- 
factory, and cannot be approved. The Company cannot blow hot and cold 
ai the same time, nor can it approbate and reprobate. Accordingly, this

چہچچچچ چس رش‎ সি 
contention of the Company is repelled. Next, 1١ was contended ow راودا‎ 
of the Company that as the workmen concerned were employed elsewhere 
during the period of lay-off, they were not entitled to any compensation, 
But the Company has not adduced any evidence to show that the workers 
concerned were so employed. Hence, this contention does not stand. 


The Tribunal, on a consideration of the facts and circumstances, feels 
no doubt or hesitation in holding that the workmen mentioned in the attached 
list, who were admittedly laid-off, by the Company, are entitled to benefit 
by way of compensation, mm accordance with section 250 of the Industrig] 
Disputes Act. It is interesting to note in this connection that these work. 
men were informed also by the very notice, dated 26th August 1954, under 
which they were laid-off, that they would get the benefit of lay-off compen. 
sation as provided under the Industrial রক Amendment Act, 1953. 
The Company, therefore, cannot dispute the rights of the workmen con. 
cerned to lay-off compensation. 


Now the question is what would be the quantum of compensation pay. 
able to these 84 workers under section 2580 of the Act. I shall take up 011 
the case of 14 workers, who were recalled for duties after lay-off. O.P.W. |

Adordingly, in accordance with ৮102) 25C of the Act, the workers 
Nos. (72), (74), (75), (77), (80) and (82) shall get lay-off compensation for 
10 days, workers Nos, (70), (76) and (81) for 17 days, worker No, (73) for 
18 days and worker No. (71) for 24 days. Such compensation they ehall 
get at the rate as provided in the body of section 260, that is 50 per cent. 
of the total of the basic wages and dearness allowance. 


Regarding the remaining 3 workers Nos, (78), (83) and (84) and 70 other 
workers in the dwt, the point is whether they ure entitled to get such lay-oft 
compensation only for the first 45 days, or for the entire period of lay-off, 
which admittedly varied from 216 to about 567 days. It is contended by 
the Company that in accordance with proviso (a) to section 25C, those workers 
were entitled to compensation for the first 45 days and for the rest of the 
period, no compensation was payable. According to the Company, proviso 
(b) to section 200 cannot apply to the present case. In short, the argument 
advanced on behalf of the Company is that the workmen in the instant case 
could be granted compensation only for the first 45 days of the lay-off, and 
not for any period thereafter. On behalf of the Union, it is agreed that 
proviso (a) io section 25C applies to the first period of 45 days. But its 
contention is that for the remaining period of the lay-off, the governing 
provision is proviso (b) to section 25C, and as such the workers in the 
present case are entitled to get compensation for the remaining period alsv. 


So, the point for consideration is that whether proviso (b) to section نار‎ 
would apply to the instant case. On a careful reading of section 2901, the 
Tribunal is of the definite view that proviso (b) to section 26C would not 
apply when there was a single continuous period of lay-off over 45 days. 
That proviso applies only, if the workmen had been paid compensation tor 
10 days, and were again laid-off for a further period of more than one week 
atta tine. In the present case, there was one continuous lay-off for the 
entire period. It could not be disputed and denied. That being so, 
praviso (b) to section 26C could have no application. By no straining of 
the language of that proviso, the present luy-off can be brought within its 
purview. The word ‘‘again’’ as used in proviso (b) to section 26C is very 
important and significant. That contemplates a second order of lay-oh, 
that is a separate and subsequent period of lay-off. In the present case, 
there was no such subsequent lay-off, but the origina] lay-off continues. 11 
any authority is needed for the view taken above, I may profitably cite 
the recent decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Modi Food 
Products & Co., Ltd., vs. Maquir Chand Sharma and others [1956Q) L.L.J., 
page 749]. In this case, their Lordships did not approve of the contrary 
view taken by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. 


In the result, the Tribunal holds that al] the workers barring Nos. (70), 
(71), (72), (73), (74), (7), (76), (77), (80), (81) and (82) shall get compen- 
sation’ only for 45 days as provided in proviso (a) to section 25C, and that 
they will get such compensation at the rate as provided in the body of 
section 26C, that is 90 per cent. of the total of the basic wages and dearness 
allowance. As regards workers Nos. (70), (71), (72), (73), (74), (75), (76), 
(77), (80), (81) und (82), direction has already been given as to what 
amount they will get as lay-off compensation. 


So, to be precise, it is awarded that the workers Nos. (72), (74), (75),

DECISION 


The Government of West Rengal in its order No. 21961)15.11))101,-1101

Bengal, for udjudication an industrial dispute between Messrs. Associated 
Electrical Industries (India), Ltd. (hereinafter to be referred to as the

787 and, their employees represented by Associated Electrical Indus- 
tries (India), Ltd. Employees’ Welfare Assaciation (hereafter to be referred 
to as the Union) regarding (1) additional benefit of gratuity, (2) tiffin 
allowance, and (3) bonus for the years 1950 and 1951. The Tribunal by its 
award, dated 1161) November 1954, and published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
dated 9th December 1954, under the orders of the Government of West 
Bengal No. 5574Dis./D/10L/1380/54, dated 27th November 1954, granted 
(1) gratuity payable at the rate of 15 days’ salary for each completed year 
of service up to a maximum of 16 months, in cases of retirement or term1- 
nation of service except on grounds of misconduct; (2) disallowed the claim 
to tiffin allowance; and (3) granted three months’ salary or } of the year’s 
earnings as bonus for the year 1951 and refused to grant any bonus for 1950 
on the ground that the claim was a belated one. Against that award Appeal 
No. Cal. 4 of 1955 is preferred by the Company contending that gratuity 
and bonus for 1951 নি not to be awarded and Appeal No. Cal. 5 of 1955 
is preferred by the employees represented by the Union contending that 
gratuity at the rate of one month’s salary per each completed year of service 
should have been awarded and that the misconduct disentitling an employee 
to gratuity should have been specificed as one involving moral turpitude, 
that tiffin allowance ought to have been awarded in view of their ule dae 
being below fair wage level and that bonus ought to have been awarded 
for both 1950 and 1951 at 6 months’ basic pay per year though the claim 
10,1950 was made a bit late because the employees did not know the profit 
position of the Company earlier. 


2. IsSue 1 (Gratuity).—There is one retirement benefit of Provident 
Fund available to the employees of the Company and gratuity is claimed 
as a second or additional retirement benefit. It has been repeatedly held 
by this Tribunal (one among several decisions was referred to by the lower 
Tribunal), that there is nothing wrong in awarding two retirement benefits 
and that such an award is even desirable in the interests of social justice 
ہا‎ enable the employees ৮০- have something to fall back upon during old 
age or incapacity for further work on account of any other causes to which 
human body is heir to and that the only limitation subject to which the 
award should be made is the capacity of the concern to bear the financial 
burden involved and that in view of the fact that retirement benefits are 
long range arrangements, the test of capacity should depend upon the 
past and present prosperity of the concern and stability so as to ensure 
possibilities of future prosperity too. 


3. This is a private limited Company which has been doing its business 
successfully ever since 1924. There has been not even an allegation of loss 
having been suffered in any year during this more than quarter of a 
century. Reserves amounting to many times the amount contributed b 
the share-holders in cash were capitalised by way of bonus shares and still 
there are reserves. 0.۱۷۰. 2 swore that in 1945 and 1947 dividends were 
declared at 25 per cent. and in 1950 and 1951 at 10 per cent. including 
bonus shares. Actua] profits in 1950 and 1951 according to profit and loss 
account indicate much greater prosperity than can be indicated by the 
dividends of 10 per cent. spoken to by O.P.W. 2. The Company contends 
that since 1949 operating expenses have been rising and that the value of 
orders received in recent years dropped. However, Ext. B shows that the 
rise and drop are not so alarming as to tell on the stability of the concern, 
{The main business of the Company is installation of heavy electrical 
machinery in pursuance of orders secured from al] over the country, for 
which business there ‘is a great future in this country which has undertaken 
systematised and planned economy towards industrialisation with the help 
of all sources of power including electricity. The biggest customer of the 
Company has been the Government of India. The fears expressed by the 
learned representative for the Company are based more upon possible 
changes in Governmental policies in regard to imports of heavy electrical 
machinery from foreign countries rather than upon what is inherent in the 
nature of the business of the concern and its future possibilities. It will 
take a long, long time before this country can produce its own heavy 
electrical machinery without which no Government can change its import 
policies. Hence we are not in a position to share his fears which are, 
at present at any rate, unfounded. Thus the Company has been and is 
prosperous and all indications are in favour of its future prosperity, and the 
prosperity has stabilised itself for over a quarter of a century. 31008 we 
agree with the lower Tribunal that there is justification for introducing 
2 second retirement benefit to the employees, 


The employees of this very Company serving at its Bombay office‏ ,4 ے 
have secured, by an award, dated 29th December 1950, and published in‏ 
the Bombay Gazette of that Government, dated 25th January 1951, under‏ 
the orders of the Bombay Government No. 1026148, dated 17th J anuary‏ 
gratuity at one month’s salary;for each year of completed service.‏ ,1951 
This fact does not appear to have been drawn to the attention of the lower‏ 
Tribunal. If it was drawn, a discrimination between the employees of‏ 
the Company at Bombay and Calcutta would not have been possible in the‏ 
matter of the rate of gratuity. There ought not to he any difference‏ 
between retired servants of the Company at Bombay and at Calcutta. On‏ 
behalf of the Company it was contended that gratuity at one month’s pay‏ 
per each completed year of service would involve the Company in an‏

ee eee a: 


additional expenditure of Rs. 44,000 a year. The total wage bill itself, 
even taking all branches of the Company into consideration, is much less. 
It is doubtful whether at any time, even in the future, the gratuity bill 
can come to so much as the monthly wage bill. Hence we believe that 
gratuity even at one month’s pay per completed year will not involve a 
burden too much for the Company to bear. Hence we raise the rate of 
gratuity awarded by the lower Tribunal to one month’s wages per each 
completed year of service. 


6. The lower Tribunal excluded employees who 7 to be dismissed 
for misconduct from the benefit of gratuity. The employees contend that 
those dismissed for misconduct involving moral turpitude alone should be | 
excluded. Moral turpitude is a vague thing which may not be easy to 
define in actual practice. The better thing will be to exclude employees 
whose services are terminated for misconduct involving the کت‎ in 
pecuniary loss, from the benefit of gratuity. We introduce this alteration 
in the award of the lower Tribunal. 


6 IsSue 2 (Tiffin allowance).—The first question is whether the appeal 
in this respect is maintainable under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 (hereafter referred to as the said Act). It 
is contended on behalf of the employees that the claim is described by, the 
Company in its written statement as one for additional salury and hence 
the claim relates to ‘‘wages’’ and that hence the appeal is one contemplated 
by section 7(1)(b)(i) of the said Act. As against how the Company 
described the claim, we find that the employees described it in their 
written statement as an allowance and not as wages. But we cannot decide 
the matter merely on the strength of how either party described thé claim. 
We must analyse the nature of the claim and see if it falls within the 
definition of ‘‘wages’’ in the said Act. ‘‘Wages’’ means remuneration 
payable in respect of the employment or of the work done in the employ- 
ment, whereas an allowance, which is not defined in the Act, means a 
stated quantity of money to meet expenses. The two are essentially 
different as an sallowance cannot be remuneration. Hence it became 
necessary for Parliament to expressly include allowances within the defini- 
tion of ‘‘wages’’; but, this is done under stated circumstances, viz., that 
the allowance should be such as the workman is for the time being, 
entitled to, so that an allowance which is merely claimed but rejected by the 
lower Tribunal cannot be ‘‘wages’’ for purposes of the said Act, as work- 
men are not entitled to it for the time being, 1.e., at the time when the 
appeal is preferred. Tiffin allowance claimed by the employees not being 
remuneration payable in respect of employment, or of work in the employ 
ment, the justification for the allowance should be based upon the fact that 
tifin has to be eaten during working hours at or near the place of work 
and away from home and hence is likely to cost more than what it would 
cost the employee at home and hence it should be a compensator 
allowance like daily allowance usually granted when an employee is 
outside headquarters on duty. Hence we find that the claim is not for 
“‘wages’’ as defined in the said Act and hence this appeal does not lie 
under section 7(1)(b)(i) of the said Act. 


7. The learned representative for the employees argued in the alter- 
native that this appeal is maintainable by virtue of section 7(1)(a) of the 
suid Act as there is a substantial question of law involved in it. The 
Jower Tribunal expressed the opinion that tiffin allowance can be only an 
ex-gratia payment which cannot be claimed as of right. It igs contended 
that this opinion raises a substantial question of law, viz., whether it is 
ex-gratua payment. But the lower Tribunal] did not entirely base its 
decision on such opinion. It also held that the allowance could not be 
claimed by these employees as a condition of their service for neither a 
contract nor valid custom to pay tiffin allowance is proved which is a pure 
question of fact. If the decision of the lower Tribunal can be supported 
on this finding of fact, the alternative opinion that the claim is to an 
et-gratia payment cannot raise a substantial question of law, even 
assuming that it raises some sort of a question of law, for the simple 
reason that the decision of the lower Tribunal can be maintained even 
if this opinion is held to be wrong. The employees did not seek to rest 
their claim on the footing of compensatory allowance and no ewdence 
was ۵۲ا‎ in on that footing. Hence no finding on such footing was called 
for atid the finding that no contract or custom is proved is sufficient to 
support the decision of the lower Tribunal. We are of opinion that there 
is no substantial question of law involved and that this appeal in relation 
to issue 2 is not maintainable. 


8. Issue 3 (Bonus for 1950).—In 1950, the Company’s account ytar 
closed on 81۸۲ October and its accounts were audited and auditors’ report 

‘ was dated 2nd February 1951. Thé@ Company informed the Union on 3rd 
June 1951, of its decision to pay a bonus of one month’s basic pay for 
the irading year ending October 1950. The Union, on 6th August 1951, 
expressed the grateful thanks of the members for what was done. The 
bonus was paid and received admittedly without any demur at the time. 
Nothing happened till 28rd July 1952. Meanwhile an Industrial 
Tribunal of Bombay awarded bonus consisting of the basic earnings of 
the year 1900 to the employees of this Company in its Bombay branch 


312 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 [Parr TA 


পিস হস 
eS 


and it was publishgd in the Bombay Government Gazette, dated 24th 
April 1952. The Union at Calcutta got at a copy of that Gazette and on 
23rd July 1952 sentsthe letter Mx. 1(a) claiming bonus of two months’ pay 
for the Calcutta employees. The Company refused this demand. The 
lower Tribunal rejected this claim on the ground that it was belated and 
made long after accounts of the year 1950 were closed, thus necessitating 
the reopening of the accounts especially after payment of bonus consisting 
of one month’s wage was accepted without protest at the time. It is 
contended, on behalf of the Union, (1) that the bonus which the Company 
voluntarily paid was customary Puja bonus payment of which hus become 
a condition of service and that its acceptance by the employees does not 
estop the employees from cluiming profit تا‎ (2) that profit bonus can be 
claimed only after profit or loss is known and that it can be known only 
after the closing of the accounts and hence there must be reopening of 
accounts if enough provision is not made therein for bonus and that in 
this case the profit or loss could not be known except through the award 
of the Bombay Tribunal as the Company would not publish its profit and 
loss accounts and that their claim should not be rejected as belated as 
there is no period of limitation. 


9. We are not impressed with the contention that the employees are 
entitled to two varieties of bonus, viz., Puja bonus as a condition of service 
and another profit bonus. 1 is common case that no bonus was ever paid 
to thege employees prior to 1947. Thereafter varying amounts were paid 
as bonis year after year, before the Puja holidays. We fail to see how 
a custom or condition of service to pay bonus of one month’s wages could 
develop in this fashion by 1950. Therefore, we cannot believe that what 
was admittedly paid in 1951 for the trading year ending October 1950 and 
was received with gratefulness was in no sense a customary bonus which 
became a condition of service. The lower Tribunal did not base its award 
on grounds of estoppel or on any bar of limitation of time nor are we going 
te 00 so. But we are of opinion that the delay in this case has come about 
under circumstances which make it a right step in the interests of 
industrial peace and harmony to refuse the claim. Industrial Tribunals 
are created under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for investigation and 
settlement of industrial disputes. If investigation and settlement of an 
industrial dispute by one Industrial Tribunal is used as a spring board for 

rojectiny another industrial dispute into an otherwise peaceful atmosphere 
it should be a most undesirable use of the Act which cannot be encouraged. 
When investigation into the history of an industrial dispute discloses that 
such was the case a legitimate way of settling that dispute is by rejecting 
‘the claim. In our case the Company voluntarily paid bonus consisting of 
one month’s wages for 1950 and it was accepted with grateful thanks. 
Long after that, a Bombay Tribunal presided over by Shri Sen awarded 
bonus consisting of 1/6%h of the year’s basic earnings after reducing 
therefrom the amount of one month’s wages already paid, to the employees 
of Bombay branch of the Company for 1950. On coming to know of it 
and after perusing the award the employees of Calcutta branch started 
the claim for more bonus for the same year 1950 for the reason that 
Bombay employees were given more. In the award of the Bombay 
Tribunal, claim for bonus for the year 1949 was rejected for the reason 
that the claim thereto was made after a delay of 15 months. The 
employees in our case should have realised that their demand on 23rd July 
1952 was being made after a delay of more than 20 months. If the Bombay 
award acted as an incentive for the demand made by the present employees 
on 28rd July 1952, the same award should have acted as a deterrent against 
advancing the claim after such a delay; but it did not deter them from 
making the demand and pressing it hard. The obvious reasoning of these 
employees must have been something like this: ‘‘Our brethren at Bombay 
have by raising a dispute secured an advantage beyond that we have got. 
Let us also raise a dispute and see what happens. Better lute than never. 
As to delay, let us hope for better luck than our Bombay brethren, before 
a different Tribunal’. The contention that the state of profit or loss of 
the Company was not known till the Bombay award was available as an 
excuse for the delay is only a convenient pretext in our opinion. Even 
after seeing the Bombay award, these employees could not have had 
knowledge of the exact amount of profit as it was not disclosed in that 
award. 17010 that award it could have been gathered only that there was 
enough profit to justify a bonus of 1/6th of the year’s basic edrnings 
reduced by one month’s wages already paid. Still, these Calcutta employees 
advanced their claim for bonus consisting of two months’ wages without 
reducing it by one month’s wage, already paid and accepted. It is clear 
ffom this also that the mentality of spreading the net wide and taking a 
chance was at the root and such knowledge as was acquired by a perusal 
of the Bombay award made them no wider for it. That being so, why | 
should Jack of knowledge of actual profit have prevented their claiming 
im August 1951 itself more than what was voluntarily offered by the- 
Company? It is cléar that this is a case of projecting a dispute in a 
speculative mood into an otherwise peaceful atmosphere thereby reopening 
a matter in which there was acceptance by one party to it with grateful 
thanks of what was voluntarily offered by the other and absolute peace 
following for 20 months thereafter, It is this circumstance that weighs 
with us more than any difficulty in reopening of closed accounts of 1950.

10. Frantic efforts ৮6161080600 convince ys that the demand on

the efforts fail just as they fuiled before the lower Tribupal for the simple

presided over by Shri Merchant referred to in the award of Shri Sen, for, 
Shri Merchant’s award was available before the date of Ext. I, whereas 
the later award of Shri Sen was not passed by the date of Ext. 1. 
Shri Merchant’s award covered bonus for the year 1947-48 and not the 
bonus for 1950. Hence Ext. 1 cannot be considered as containing a demand 
for bonus for 1950 though the expression ‘‘with retrospective effect from 
1947’? was used in it which, under other circumstances, may perhaps be 
used to cover demands up to the date of the letter. 


11. Under all the above circumstances, we are of opinion that the 
claim for bonus for 1950, beyond what was already paid, was rightly 
rejected by the lower Tribunal. 


12. 85588 3 (bonus for 1951).—The empolyees started their demand 
with a claim for bonus for 1951 at three months’ pay; but, during the 
roceedings before the Tribunal, they raised it to six months’ pay. The 
aoe Tribunal awarded three months’ pay as bonus on the footing that 
the available surplus on working out the formula of the Full Bench of this 
Tribunal would come to Rs. 3,00,000. The Company supplied the audited 
profit and loss account and balance-sheet for 1951 ‘‘pledged to secrecy” in 
the language of the lower Tribunal. The records disclose that the Company 
claimed that the document must be dealt with as confidential and the lower 
Tribunal agreed to do so, in which case section 21 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947, provides that information obtained from such docu- 
ments shall not be included in the award. The lower Tribunal somehow 
referred to various figures that can be obtained from the said document 
alone. We ascertained from the learned advocate appearing for the 
Company that the claim under section 21 was never given up by the 
Company and that it is there even now. Hence we cannot include, in this 
decision, figures that can be got only from that document. We can only 
discuss 1n general terms the necessary and prior charges to be deducted 
from gross profit in order to arrive at the available surplus in terms of the 
Full Bench formula and arrive at our own conclusion whether any bonus 
can be awarded and if 960১১ how much. 


13. The first item of charge is statutory depreciation about which no 
serious objection was urged on behalf of the employees. 


14. The next item is the income-tax. It is contended on behalf of 
the employees that income-tax is not payable on the amount of bonus and 
that hence deduction on account of imcome-tax must be made only after 
ascertaining the amount of bonus. There is no purpose to be served in 
deducting or not deducting income-tax after bonus is ascertained. It is 
true that income-tux is not payable on that part of profit which is paid as 
bonus; but, the amount of bonus can be determined only from the surplus 
available after deducting necessary charges. .Income-tax is undoubtedly 
a necessary charge after deducting which alone the measure of the pros- 
perity of the concern in which the employees are entitled to participate 
can be ascertained. It is true that the concern will later get refund of 
income-tax on that part of the profit which is paid as bonus. Therefore, 
this circumstance can ما‎ taken into consideration in distributing the 
available surplus between the employees and the concern. But income-tax 
cannot be held back till after the ascertainment of available surplus which 
course, if foJlowed, will give a wrong picture of the prosperity of the 
concern. 


15. On behalf of the Company, a chart of calculation according to 
the Full Bench formula was submitted before the lower Tribunal. In it 
no reserve for rehabilitation, replacement and modernisation was deducted 


expressly. In its place deduction of 20 per cent. for general reserves was‏ ۔ 


claimed. It js argued that the Full Bench formula was primarily intended 
for textile industry and that the same should be applied to other industries 
with suitable modifications and that, as in this case there 1s no manu- 
facturing plant and machinery, general reserves should be allowed to be 
built”up for financial stability of the concern. There is no objection to 
the Company's building up any amoynt of reserves actually from its 
profita. The Full Bench formula is intended only for a specific purpose 
and adopted certuin prior and necessary charges as deductable from gross 
profits for the specific purpose of ascertaining available surplus which 19 
supposed to supply the measure of the 000 in which the employees 
ate entitled to participate and get bonus. Such being the case, it is not 
permissible to add items of prior charges not found in the Full Bench 
formula. Reserve for rehabilitation was provided in the formula because 
when plant and machinery are actually getting depreciated in value far 
beyond the depreciation allowed by the Income-tax Act, by constant use 
in the industry, it will not be possible to maaaure the prosperity of the 
industry. without providing for such depregggamm from profits accruing

fram the industry. Therefore it is a matter of taking into consideration, 
the actual need for rehabilitation of machinery used in the industry and 
not a matter for setting by sufficient reserves in the interest of the stability 
of an industry. On behalf of the Company it is next contended that, if so, 
value of buildings, motor cars, fares, etc., available from the balance-sheet 
should be multiplied by 2.25 and 2.7 to get at the value necessary for 
rehabilitation, etc., and that the balance, after deducting total deprecia- 
tion, should be spread over 30 years and 15 years as was done in some 
decisions. Decisions are given on facts of the particular cases. The 
multiple has to be ascertained on the basis of the date of purchase of the 
assets and the time when rehabilitation may become necessary. In _ this 
(8৮36 no evidence was adduced on these points. Why should anybody 
assume that buildings or machinery will cost 2.25 or 2.7 times, at some 
unknown future time, more than what they cost at an unknown past time? 
fience no deduction on account of rehabilitation, etc., can be made and 
the deduction of 20 per cent. towards General reserves 1s not permissible 
for purposes of না bonus. 


16. The next item is return on capital. The capital of this Company 
consists partly of shares for which cash was paid and partly of bonus 
shares. The Company claimed return of 10 per cent. on the former and 
5 per cent. on the latter. The Jower Tribunal allowed 6 per cent. on both. 
The first objection on behalf of the employees is that the lower Tribunal 
allowed return on bonus shares more than what the Company itself claimed. 
This, in our opinion, is a valid objection. We are of opinion that the 
refurn should have been limited to 5 per cent. It is next contended by 
the employees that the return on bonus shares should be only as much as 
the return on reserves used as working capital and no more. We do not 
agree. Reserves when converted into bonus shares cease to be liquid 
assets and cannot be withdrawn. But on the other hand bonus shares 
represent not exclusively capital resources of share-holders but only past 
rofits earned with the help of the labour of employees also. Hence on 
onus shares, return .shotld be allowed at a rate less than that allowed on 
shares issued for cash but more than what is usually allowed on reserves 
used as working capital. We consider that 5 per cent. is the proper rate 
in this case. The Company repeats its claim for return at 10 per cent. on 
the capital consisting of shares issued for cash on the ground that the 
concern is running a risky trade in which the annual turnover runs into 
crores of rupees whereas the capital is a few lakhs of rupees and that hence 
a return higher than 6 per cent. allowed in the Full Bench formula must 
be allowed. On carefully considering the matter we do not see any 
reason to differ from the lower Tribunal in holding that 6 per cent. is a 
reasonable return in this case. 


17. The next deduction claimed is return of 4 per cent. on reserves 
used as working capital. It was allowed by the lower Tribunal against 
the opposition of the employees whose point of view is that it is not proved 
that reserves were at all used as working capital and at any rate for the 
entire year and that in any event only 2 per cent. return should be allowed. 
We are of opinion that there can be no hard and fast rule with regard 
to the rate. The principle is that on such reserves a reasonable rate of 
return should be allowed. The reasonable rate in our opinion 
should be in the vicinity of loan market rate. Four per cent. has been 
the usual rate allowed in awards passed in recent years and it approximates 
to loan market rate. As to Pree of user of reserves as working capital, 
we accept the evidence of the accountant of the Company (O.P.W. 2). 
His saying that it was ‘‘difficult’”’ to show with reference to documents that 
reserves were used in the business 17011) time to time does not mean that 
the point has not been proved at all. Tle made the necessary calculations 
and gave evidence. ©0.P.W. 1 also swore that reserves were used as work- 
ing capital. This oral evidence can be safely accepted. 2ھ‎ this Company 
took heavy loans, it can be safely assumed that it must have utilised all its 
reserves for working capital اج‎ then borrowed for excess needs. 


18. Then the next item claimed by the Company as a prior charge is 
interest at the rate of 4 per cent. on interest-free loan secured by the 
Company for use in the business. The employees strongly opposed. this 
claim of the Company on the ground that thane should be no such prior 
chuige because the concern paid no interest on the loan and no return can 
be expected by the Company on such moneys. <A_ close perusal of the 
balarice-sheet shows that there were sundry unsecured debts due to the 
Company extending over more than the amount of interest-free loan. If, 
the Company wants pro forma interest on the loan for which no interest 
was payable, then they must و‎ pro forma interest on the sundry debts 
on which admittedly no interest was realised. Interest-free loans obtained 
hy the Company would have helped the business just as much as the interest- 
free advances to subsidiary Companies and others would have done. 
Interest-free loans were secured from A.E.]. Finance which is a subsidiary 
Company of A.K.I., London, which i4a shareholder of this Company. 
Therefore, the claim of the Company that 4 per cent. interest on interest- 
free loans should be allowed as a prior charge cannot be accepted. 


19. The last item glajmed us a prior charge is interest at 4 per cent. 
on working capital sr@jjded by some special facilities secured from 


(Parr 1A 


Part TA] THE CATAMITTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 16 


Companies 7010 whom this Company purchased machinery. It is said that 
normally two months’ credit is allowed for payment in respect of goods 
imported but that a special facility wus secured by this Company of paying 
4 months after date of shipment. We are not able to accede to the claim 
that this facility should first be valued in money and that a return of 4 
per cent. on it should be allowed as a prior charge. Theoritically at least, 
prices of goods sold on short credit must be so fixed as to include interest 
also. ‘Therefore, though interest as such is not separately charged, it 
must be deemed to have been included in the price paid. Also, it 29 
admitted that this Company is not charging interest under similar cir- 
cumstances from its customers chief among whom is the Government ‘of 
India, For reasons similar to those discussed in the previous paragraph, 


we agree with the lower Tribunal in holding that this item cannot be 
allowed. 


0. Not being able to refer to actual figures is a handicap, but there is 
no help against it as even charts of calculation were claimed to be 
confidential and sent by the lower Tribunal in a special cover. The wage 
bill of these employees per month is Its. 37,000, so that bonus awarded 
by the lower Tribunal amounts to Rs. 1,11,000 which works at about one- 
third of the available surplus which will be arrived at if calculated takin: 
into consideration the above items. The needs of the Compan ile 
from the nature of the business carried on by it involving annual turnover 
running into 2 or 3 crores of rupees whereas the paid up capital is a few 
lakhs of rupees justify, in our opinion, distribution of available surplus 
in the ratio of 2:1 between the Company and its employees. The number 
of employees is said to be less than 400. Rs. 37,000 spread over them 
gives a rough idea of the average wage level, viz., just less than Rs. 100 
per month. At such a wage level, we consider that three months’ wages 
us bonus are fair to the employees. 6ء116‎ we confirm the rate of bonus 
awarded for 1951 by the lower Tribunal. We neither increase it as desired 
by the employees nor decrease as desired by the Company. 


21. In the result the employees’ appeal succeeds and the Company’s 
appeal fails on issue No. 11; the employees’ appeal fails on issue No. 2 and 


appeals of both fail on issue No. 8. Under the circumstances each party 
shall bear its own costs. 


M. N. GAN, President. 
V. N. DIKSHITULU, Member.
