PRESS NOTE. 


THE Finance Commission have to make recommenda- 
tions to the President on the following matters:— 


(1) the distribution’ of the net proceeds of income-tax 
between the Union amd the States and the alloca- 
tion of the States’ share among the States; 


(11) the distribution of other divisible Central taxos 
like Union excise duties; 


(111) the amounts to be paid to the States of Assam, 
Bihar, Orissa and West Bengal in lieu of the 
assignment of any share of the export duty on 
jute and jnte products; 


(iv) the principles which should govern the grants-in- 
aid of the revenues of tho States out of the 
Consolidated Fund of India;. 


(৮) the States which are in need of assistance by way 
of grants-in-aid of the revenues of those States 
and the sums to be paid to those States, having 
regard, among other considerations, to the 
requirements of the Second Five-Year Plan and 
the efforts made by those States to raise additional 
revenue from the sources available to them; 


(vi) the principles which should govern the distribution 
of the not proceeds of the oxstate duty in respect 
of property other than agricultural land; 


(vii) the modifications, if any, in the rates of interest 
and the terms of repayment of the loans made to 
the various States by the Government of India 
between the 15th August 1947 and the 3181 
March 1956. 


2. At present 55 per cent. of the divisible net proceeds 
of income-tax (other than Corporation Tax) is assigned to 
the States and distributed among them in the following 
percentage ratios:—

The shares of the States have to be rofixed as a result of 
the জি reorganization and new percentage recom- 
mended for the reorganized States. 


The share to be retained by the Centre also has to be 
determined. 


The present allocation is broadly worked out on the 
basis of 80 per cent. by population and 20 per cent. by 
collection. 


The basis of distribution of income-tax has always been 
a matter of controversy. Various bases have been suggest- 
ed for allocating income-tax— 


(i) the collection of income-tax in the various States; 


(21) the amount of income-tax realised in respect of 
income, wherever earned, of individuals resitjent in 
the different States ; 


(111) the collection of income-tax in the various States 
adjusted with reference to ,the origin of the 
income; 


(iv) the relative population of each State; 


(v) the relative volume of industrial labour im each 
State; 


(vi) the needs of the different States according to 
various qriteria; and 


(vii) different*tombinations of the ahove factors. 


3. Three Union dutios of oxcise, namely, those on 
matches, tobacco and vegetable products, gre now divisible 
between the Centre and the States and 40 per cent. of the 
net proceeds are distributed among the States on the basis

of population. The quantum of the taxes to be transferred 
to the States, the excises to be continued or made divisible 
and the basis of distribution all fall to be considered by 


the Commission, 


4. The first Finance Commission recommended that the 
rants-in-aid of Rs. 75 lakhs each to Assam and Bihar 
Its. 15 lwkhs to Orissa and Rs, 160 lakhs to West Bengal 
he paid each year in lieu of the assignment of a share of 
the export duty on jute. This Commission have to 
consider whether any change in the 0 suggested by 
ihe firat Commission and accepted by Government is 


necessary. 


5, In Chapter VII of their report the last Commission 
formulated certain principles to govern the payment of 
grants-in-aid to the States which they themselves had 
applied in making their recommendations. This Commis- 
aon Will re-examine these পপ in the light of 
subsequent developments and the changes in the practice 
in other countries and indicate any changes necessary in 


them. 


6. The Commission have to make recommendations 
regarding the States in need of assistance and the sums 
io be prescribed as grants-in-aid of the revenues of such 
States, At present Assam, Mysore, Orissa, Punjab, 
Saurashtra, Travancore-Cochin and West Bengal are in 
receipt of general grants-in-aid as a result of the recom- 
mendations of the Jast Commission. This Commission will 
re-oxanine the financial position of all the States and make 
recommendations to the President regarding the States in 
need of assistance and the sums to be prescribed as grants- 
in-wid of the revenues of such States. A large variety of 
aorriderations may enter into the determination of the 
1018 of the States and these may differ from State to 
Stata. The Commission will also consider the nature of 


the rants-in-aid, such as whether they should be fixed or 
progressive, general or specific, conditional or uncondi- 
tional. 


In addition to the genoral grants-in-aid which some of 
them may be receiving, Bihar, Hyderabad, Madhya Bharat, 
Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Patiala and East Punjab States 
Union, Punjab and Rajasthan are in receipt of special 
grants-in-aid for the expansion of primary education. The 
Commission will assess the results achieved by the specific 
grants given to these States. 


7. The net proceeds of the Estate duty on property 
other than on agricultural land is now being provisionally 
distributed among the States in the same way as_ the 
States’ share of the net proceeds of taxes on income other 
than Corporation Tex. In other words, it is being 
distributed by the percentage ratios fixed for the States for 
income-tax except that the Centre does not retain any 
portion of the receipts except those attributable to the 
Part ‘°C’? States. A more permanent basis of distribution 
has to be formulated by law of Parhament. An import- 
ant issue, in this connection, would be whether the duty 
should bo distributed on the basis of percentage ratios, 
whether arrived at on the basis of the percentage ratios 
prescribed for the distribution of income-tax or otherwise, 
or the distribution should be on the basis of assessments, 
the location of the property taxed, the residence of 
assessee, etc. 


8. Central loans have been given to the States for a 
variety of purposes ranging from the construction of big 
11020101100 multi-purpose projects to the construction 
of minor irrigation works, g¢row-more-food schemes, famine 
works, rehabilitation of displaced persons, etc. Some 901 
them have also been given loans to cover budgetary 
deficits. The terms of interests and repayment of these 
loans vary tor different categories of loans. These will be 
Tfeviewed and any changes necessary in the interest of 
Sound finance indicated. 


9, The Finance Commission would welcome the views 
of those who are interested in and have made a etudy of 
these questions. They would be glad if such views could 
٥ embodied in a self-contained memorandum and sent to 
the Secretary, Finance Commission, to reach him on or 
before the 30th November 1956. 


Dated New Dolhi, July 12, 1956.

Corrupt Practices 


123. The following shall be deemed to be corrupt prac- 
tices for the purposes of this Act:— 


(1) Bribery, that is to suy, any gift, offer or promise 
by a candidate or his agent or by any other person, 
of any gratification to any person whomsoever, 
with the object, directly or indirectly of induc- 
ing— 


(a) a person to stand or not to stand as, or to with- 
draw from being, a candidate, or to retire from 
contest, at an election; 


(b) an elector to vote or refrain from voting at an 
election, 


or as a reward to— 


(1) a ধা for having so stood or not stood, or for 
aving withdrawn his candidature, or for hav- 
ing retired from contest; or 


(12) an elector for having voted or refrained from 
voting. 


سپ 


Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause the term 
“gratification”? ig not restricted to pecuniary gratifications 
or gratifications estimable in money and it includes all forms 
of entertainment and all forms of employment for reward; 
but it does not include the payment of any expenses bona 
fide incurred at, or for the purpose of, any election and 
duly entered in the account of election expenses referred 
to in section 78. 


(2) Undue influence, that is to say, any direct or indirect 
interference or attempt to interfere on the part of the candi- 
date gr his agent, or of any other person, with the free exer- 
cise of any electoral mght: 


Provided that— 


(a) without prejudice to the generality of the pro- 
visions of this clause any such person as is referred 
to therein who— 


(t) threatens any candidate, or any elector, or any 
person in whom a candidate or an elector is 
interested, with injury of any kind including 


Part V) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 9, 1956 219 


...ےس ———————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————— 


social ostracism and excommunication or 
expulsion from any caste or community; or 


(17) induces or attempts to induce a candidate or an 
elector to believe that he, or any person in 
whom he is interested, wil] become or will be 
rendered an object of divine displeasure or 
spiritual censure, 


shall be deemed to interfere with the 26৪ 
exercise of the electoral right of such candidate 
or elector within the meaning of this clause; 


(6) a declaration of public policy, or a promise of 
public action, or the mere exercise of a legal 
right without intent to interfere with an elec- 
tora] right, shall not be deemed to be interference 
within the meaning of this clause. 


(3) The systematic appeal by a candidate or his agent or 
by any other person, to vote or refrain from voting on 
grounds of caste, race, community or religion or the use of, 
or appeal to, religious symbols or the use of, or appeal to, 
national symbols, such as the national flag or the national 
emblem, for the furtherance of the prospects of that candi- 
date’s election. 


(4) The publication by a candidate or his agent or by 
any other person, of any statement of fact which is false, 
and which he either believes to be false or does not believe 
to be true, in relation to the personal character or conduct 
of any candidate, or in relation to the candidature, or 
withdrawal, or retirement from contest, of any candidate, 
being a statement reasonably calculated to prejudice the 
prospects of that candidate’s election. 


(5) The hiring or procuring, whether on payment or 
otherwise, of any vehicle or 6889] by a candidate or his 
agent or by any other person, for the conveyance of any 
elector (other than the candidate himself, the members of 
his family or his agent) to or from any polling station pro- 
vided under section 26 or a place fixed under sub-section (1) 
of section 29 for the poll: 


Provided that the hiring of a vehicle or vessel by an 
elector or by several electors at their joint costs for the 
purpose of conveying him or them to and from any such 
polling station or place fixed for the poll shall not be deem- 
ed to 2 a corrupt practice under this clause if the vehicle 
or vessel so hired 18 0 vehicle or vessel not propelled by 
mechanical power: 


Provided further that the use of any public transport 
vehicle or vessel or any tramcar or railway carriage by any 
elector at his own cost for the purpose of going to or 
coming from any such polling station or place fixed for the 
ie shall not be deemed to be a Corrupt practice under this 
clause.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


Doubt has been raised whether retrenchment compensation under the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, becomes payable by reason merely of the 
fact that there has been a change of employers, even if the service of the 
workman is continued without interruption and the terms and conditions of 
his eervice remain unaltered. This has created difficulty in the transfer, 
reconstitution and amalgamation of companies and it is proposed to make 
the intention clear by amending sertion 25F of the Act. 


2. Questions have also heen raised whether a workman who is Inid-of 
for more.than forty-five days continuo‘isly is entitled to lay-off compensation 
for any period beyond the first forty-five days. Opportunity has been taken 
ty» remove the وھ‎ by specifying the circumstances under which such 
ঠা lear beyond the first forty-five days would be admissible to a 
workmun.

No. 6129P.—10th August 1956.—In exercise 
of the powers conferred by section 9 of the 
West Bengal Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1954 (West Bengal 
Act XXXIX of 1954), the (Géovernor is ‘pleased to make the 
following rules for the regulation of public exhibitions by 
meang of cinematograph, namely :— 


THE WEST BENGAL CINEMAS (RECULATION OF 
PUBLIC EXHIBITIONS) RULES, 1956. 


Preliminary, 


lL. (1) These rules may be called the West Bengal Short title and 
Cinemas (Regulation of Public Exhibitions) Rules, 1956, commencement. 


{2) They shall apply to public exhibitions by means of 
cinematograph. 


(3) They shall come into force at once. 
2, In these rules, unless the context otherwise Dofinttions. 
requires ,— 


(i) the ‘‘Act’’ means the West Bengal Cinemas 
(Regulation) Act, 1954; 


(ii) ‘‘licence’? means a licence granted under the 
provisions of the Act; 


(111) “licensing authority’? means the authority referred 
to in section 4 of the Act;

Kinds of licences. 3. There shall be three kinds of licences, namely :— 
(1) licences for permanent cinemas; 
(ii) licences for temporary indoor cinemas; and 
(111) licences for temporary open air cinemas. 


Part A.—-Permanent cinemas, 


Proud fer ie 4, (1) Any person desirous of building a permanent 

grant of حم"‎ cinema house shall, before commencing construction thereof, 

manent cinema make an application in writing giving all necessary parti- 

0809, culars to the District Magistrate for approval of the proposed 
site and plan of the building. 


(2) On receipt of the application, the licensing authority 
shall consider if the site is suitable for a permanent cinema 
house. If he is of the opinion that the site is suitable for 
a permanent cinema house, he shall publish in his office a 
notice calling for objections, if any, to the proposed 
permanent cinema house, from the local people within 
thirty days from the date of the notice and shall give due 

ublicity thereof by beat of drum or otherwise in the

District Boards or Municipal Commissioners’ concerned.

Conditions to be attached to a permanent licence issued under the provisions 
of the West Bengal Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1954. 


1. The lcensee shall not exhibit, or permit to be exhibited, in the 0۹ء‎ 

22 2 any film other than a 
sim which has been certified as suitable for public exhibition by an authority 
constituted under section 3 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (Act XXXVIL 
of 1952), and which, when exhibited, displays the prescribed mark of that 
authority, and has not been altered or tampered with in any way since such 
mark was affixed thereto. 


2 The licensee shall not exhibit or permit to be সদ in the said 
7557 any film which has 
been certified by the authority constituted under section 3 of the Cinemato- 
graph Act, 1952 (Act XXXVII of 1952), as suitable for public exhibition 
restricted to adults only, to any person who is not an adult, as defined in 
section 2(a) of the Cinematograph Act, 1952. 


_ Note.—This condition shall not be construed as prohibiting the exhibi- 
tion of such film to children below the age of three years. 


3. (1) There shall be prominently exhibited at each public entrance 
whenever the premises are open to the public a notice indicating in tabular 
form and in clear bold letters and figures— 

(a) the title of each film to be shown on that day, other than trailers 
and advertisement films; 


(b) the approximate times of commencement of each such film; 


(c) whether each such film has received an ‘‘A”’ or ‘'U” certificate from 
the Central Board of Film Censors; and 


(d) whether persons below the age of 18 years other than children 
below the age of 3 years will be admitted or not. 


(2) The ‘nature of any certificate received in respect of a film from the 
Central Board of Film Censors shall be clearly indicated by the letter 
“U" or “A” in any advertisement of the film displayed at the premises. 


4. The licensee shal] not display, or cause to be displayed any photo- 
graph, picture or poster which depicts or represents or purports to represent 
a scene or shot which has been excised from any film under the orders of the 
Central Board of Film Censors or the Central Government. 


5. Not more than three shows shall be held, at the place licensed, 
between 2 p.m. and midnight on any week day. 

Outside these hours, 7.e., before 2 p.m. or after midnight, no show shall 
be allowed at the licensed place on any week day except with the previous 
permission~of the licensing authority obtained in writing at least seven 
days in advance. 

Note.—There will be no restriction on the number of shows on Sundays 
and public holidays, provided that no show shall be allowed after midnight. 


G. Display of posters.—No obscene, immodest or objectionable poster, 
placard, hoarding or pictorial publicity. material shall be displayed at the 
show-windows or lobbies of cinema houses or at any other place within the 
licensed premises.

18. The relative positions of the picture sereen and seats shall be such

13. The relative positions of the picture sereen and seats shall be such 
as may be specified in each case by the licensing authority at the time of 
granting the licence so that undue eye-strain may not be caused to persons 
attending the cimematograph exhibition. 


In specifying the relative positions referred to in this condition the 
licensing authority shall see— 


(1) that the angle of elevation subtended at the eye of any person seated 
in the front row by the length of the vertical line dropped from 
the centre of the top edge of the picture to the horizontal plane 
passing through the observer’s eye shall not exceed 35 degrees, 
the height of the eye above the floor level being assumed to be 
3 feet 6 inches, and 


(2) that the angle between the vertical plane containing the upper 
edge of the picture and the vertical plane containing the 
observer’s eye and the remote end of the upper edge of the picture 
shall not be less than 25 degrees: 


Provided that, in the case of cinemascope, 3D, Vistavision, etc., the 
relative positions of the screen and the first row of seats shall be 
such as may be specified in each case by the licensing authority.

18. Hatt doors.—There shall be exit doors on the three sides of the

19. 17710195816 for apparatus.—The cinematograph machine shall he 
placed in a permanent enclosure. Such enclosure shall be at least 8 feet 
in height. If one machine is to be operated the floor space shall not be less 
than 48 square feet. If more than one machine is to be operated therein an 
additional 24 square feet shall be provided for each additional machine. 
The enclosure containing the cinematograph machine in these rules 
referred to as ‘‘the enclosure’? shall be substantially constructed of fire 
resisting materials. 


20. Entrance to the enclosure und means of rentilation.—The entrance 
to the enclosure shall be through a closely fitting self-closing door of fire- 
resisting material, suitably placed and opening outwards, and all openings, 
bushes and points shall be so constructed and maintained as to prevent, 
so fur as possible, the escape of any smoke into the auditorium. This door 
shall be kept closed at all times when not used for ingress or egress. 
Channels of ventilation shall not be allowed to communicate direct with 
the auditorium. The enclosure in which the machine is being operated 
shall be provided with a vent flue in its roof or upper part of its side wall 
leading tg the outdoor air, there being a separate vent flue for each cine- 
matograph machine. The vent flue shall have a minimum sectional area of 
50 square inches and shall be fire resisting. The vent flue shall fall below 
45° in each rise unless it has forced extraction. The vent flue shall be

Position of enclosure.—The enclosure shall, unless this requirement‏ .1ر 
is expresly waived in the licence, be so placed as to be outside the main‏ 
building forming the auditorium and where such auditorium consists of a‏ 
structure of a temporary or non-permanent character the enclosure shall be‏

less than 3 feet in width at the sides and in the front of the enclosure and‏ 
a space of 6 feet at the back in which the door is situated shall be kept clear‏ 
all round the enclosure.‏ 


22. Openings in enclosure.—In the front face of the enclosure there 
shall be an opening or porthole for each cinematograph machine in addition 
10 one opening or porthole for observation. The size of the opening or port- 
hole may vary with the type of cinematgryraph machine proposed to be used 
and shall in each case be such as may be determined by the Jicensing 
authority. Hach opening shall be fitted with a screen of fire-resisting 
material capable of being operated both from inside and outside the 
enclosure and such screens shall be sv suspended and arranged that they 
wil] automatically close the openings upon the operating of some suitable 
fusible or mechanical releasing device. 


23. The necessary pipes and cables shall enter through efficiently hushed 
openings. 


24. Temporary enclosure.—If{ a permanent enclosure is not provided, 
the cinematograph machine shall be contained in an enclosure formed of a 
smoke proof box constructed of sheet iron on substantial frame work and 
fustened together securely. The box shall be of sufficient dimensions 0. 
allow the operators to work freely and the floor shall, if boarded, be covered 
with asbestos or other fire-resisting material of sufficient thickness approved 
by the licensing authority. 


25. Combustible materials—No unnecessary combustible material shall 
be allowed within the enclosure and all necessary combustible material, filma, 
etc., except a film which is being passed through the lantern, shall be kept 
in metal boxes suitable for the purpose which shall be placed in an approved 
fireproof box. The latter shall be kept closed at all times except when it 
18 necessary to obtain or replace a film. Only those films which are being 
used at an exhibition shall be kept in the enclosure but in no case shall an 
amount in excess of 200 lbs. be kept at one time in such enclosure, any 
excess being stored, until required, in the place licensed under condition 44. 


20. There shall be no coils of slack electric cable within the enclosure. 
The ‘‘leads’’ to the cinematograph lamps shall, unless conveyed within a 
metal pipe or other suitable casing, be kept well apart both within and 
وہہ‎ the enclosure and so run that the course of each may be readily 
raced, 


27. No electric current at a higher pressure than 230 volts shall be 
used within the enclosure when a cinematograph apparatus is working. 


28. Electric light.—Within the encosure the insulating material of all 
electric cables, including ‘‘leada’’? to lamps in the enclosures, shall be 
covered with fire-resisting material. : 


29. Smoking, ete.—No smoking shall at any time be permitted within 
the enclosure, and no match or candle or other naked light shall be allowed 
in the enclosure.

30, Fire precaution tn enclosure.—Two liquid chemical extinguishers. 
two buckets of sund, two buckets of water and a blanket shall be kept inside 
the enclosure. <A large sponge shall be kept in one of the buckets of water. 
One liquid chemical extinguisher shall also be kept immediately outside the 
enclosure. 


31. General precautions in enclosure.—The management and the 
cinematograph operators shall take all due precautions for the preven- 
(101) of accidents und shall abstain from any act whatever which tends to 
cause fire and is not reasonably necessary for the purpose ot the exhibition; 
no unauthorized person ghall be allowed in the enclosure. 


32. Machine.—The cinematograpl machine shall be fixed to the floor 
and shall be preperly bonded and earthed. There shall be shock-proof 
rubber matting round the projector for the protection of the operators 
against electric shocks. 


33. The cinematograph machine shall be provided with a metal shutter 
which can be readily inserted between the source of light and the film gate. 


34. This shutter shall be immediately dropped in the event of any 
accident to the cinematograph machine or stoppage of the film and shall 
only be raised when the film is in motion for the purpose of projection. 


35. Film gate of the machine.—Except where the cinematograph 
machine is equipped with an automatic film gate, the film gate shall be of 
massive construction and provided with ample heat-radiating surface and 
the passage for the film shall be sufficiently narrow to prevent Hume travel- 
ling upwards or downwards from the light opening. 


36. Metal bores.—Except where the cinematograph machine is fitted 
with automatic spools for winding the films, each cinematograph machine 
shall be fitted with two film metal boxes which shall be of substantial 
construction and not more than 14 inches in diameter measured internally. 
The film shall-be made to travel from one box to the other. The boxes shall 
be so constructed as to close in a manner which will prevent the ingress of 


fire. 


37. The cable for the cinematograph machine shall be taken as a 
separate circuit from the source of supply and from the supply side of the 
main fuse to the general lighting circuit on such premises. Efficient 
switches and fuses shall be inserted at the point where the supply is taken, 
and, in addition, an efficient double pole shall be fitted in the cinematograph 
lamp circuit inside the enclosure. 


38. Spools.— Spools shall be chain or gear driven and films shall be so 
wound upon spools that wound film shall not at any time reach or project 
beyond the edges of the flanges of the spool. 


89. Use of acetylene gas prohibited.—Acetylene gas shall not be used in 
cinematograph machinces. 


40. Lighting.—No illuminant other than electric lights shall be used 
in a cinematograph lantern. The choking coils, switches and fuses shall 
be installed in accordance with the wiring rules for the time being issued 
by the Calcutta Fire Assurance Association for electric installations. 


41. Lighting of auditorium.—The general lighting of the auditorium 
anil exits shall not be controlled from within the enclosure.

operating room.

THE SCHEDULE 


Conditions to be attached to a temporary licence issued under the provisions 
of the West Bengal Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1954 


1. The licensee shall not exhibit, or permit to be exhibited any film 
other than a film which has been certified as suitable for public exhibition 
by an authority constituted under section 3 of the Cinematograph Act, 
1952 (Act XXXVII of 1952), and which, when exhibited, displays the 
prescribed mark of that authority, and has not been altered or tampered 
with in any way since such mark was affixed thereto. 


2. The licensee shall not exhibit or permit to be exhibited, any film 
which has been certified by the authority constituted under section 3 of the 
Cinematograph Act 1952 (Act XXXVII of 1952), as suitable for public 
exhibition restricted to adults only, to any person who is not an adult, as 
defined in section 2(a) of the Cinematograph Act, 1952. 


Note.—This condition shall not be construed as prohibiting the exhibi- 
tion of such film to children below the age of three years. 


3. (1) There shall be prominently exhibited at each public entrance 
whenever the premises are open to the public a notice indicating in tabular 
form and in clear bold letters and figures— 


(a) the title of each film to be shown on that day, other than trailers 
and advertisement films; 


(b) the approximate times of commencement of each such film; 


(c) whether each such film has received an ‘‘A’’ or ‘‘U” certificate from 
the Central Board of 1111) Censors; and 


whether persons below the age of 18 years other than childreu‏ رف 
below the age of 3 years will be admitted or not.‏ 


(2) The nature of any certificate received in respect of a film from the 
Central Board of Film Censors shall be clearly indicated by the letter 
“U” or “A” in any advertisement of the film displayed at the premises. 


4. -The licensee shall not display, or cause to be displayed any pholo- 
graph, picture or poster which depicts or represents or purports to re- 
present a scene or shot which has been excised from any film under the 
orders of the Central Board of Film Censors or the Central Government. 


5. Not more than three shows shall be held, at the place licensed, 
between 2 p.m. and midnight on any week day. 


Outside these hours, t.e., before 2 p.m. or after midnight, no show shall 
be allowed at the licensed place on any week day except with the previous 
permission of the licensing authority obtained in writing at least seven 
days in advance. 


Note.—There will be no restriction on the number of shows on Sundays 
লী سی‎ holidays, provided that no show shall be allowed after mid- 
night. 

6. Display of posters.—No obscene, immodest 01. objectionable 
poster, placard, hoarding or pictorial publicity material shall 
be displayed at the show-windows and lobbies of cinema houses or at any 
other place within the licensed premises. 


7. No loud-speaker or amplifier relaying music or commentary for the 
urpose of attracting customers shall be allowed to be fixed outside the 


icensed premises.

1954 (West Bengal Act XXXIX of 1954), the Governor, 
having considered it necessary so to do, is pleased to make 
this order for regulating exhibitions in West Bengal by 
means of cinematograph, other than public exhibitions, and 
to prescribe the following rules and conditions for the 
purpose, namely :— 


THE WEST BENCAL CINEMATOGRAPH 
(RECULATION OF রী EXHIBITIONS) ORDER, 
1956, 


' Rules and conditions 


1. In these rules and conditions, “private cinemato- 
graph exhibition’? meang indoor or open air cinematugraph 
exhibition for which no admission fee of any kind is 
charged and admission to which is restricted by issue of 
jnvitations, tokens or cards, or is restricted to members of a 
particular club, institution or organisation. 


2. Any person desirous of holding a private cinemato- 
graph exhibition expected to be attended by more than 
twenty-five persons at a time shall submit a written appli- 
cation to the Commissioner of Police in Calcutta or the 
District Magistrate elsewhere at least seven days in advance 
for the grant of a licence. The application shall contain the 
following particulars :— 


(a) Name and address of the applicant. 


(b) Name (if any) of the film or general description 
thereof. 


(c) The hour fixed for each show and its duration. 
(d) The venue of the exhibition. 


(9) Whether the venue provides for the safety 
precautions prescribed under condition 6 of the 
Schedule attached to the form of licence for 
private cinematograph exhibition. 


(f) The period for which the licence is required, 
(ج)‎ The purpose of the exhibition. 


(h) The maximum number of invitees proposed to be 
admitted to each show. 


(i) Declaration that the film is certified for unrestricted 
exhibition or for adults only or exempted from 
censorship by the Central Government. 


(j) The name of the producer of the film. 
(k) The country in which the film has been produced.

3. (1) On receipt of an application for a private 
cinematograph exhibition, the Commisioner of Police or the 
District Magistrate, as the case may be, may, at his 
discretion, grant to the applicant a licence for such private 
cinematograph exhibition as nearly as possible in the form 
appended to these rules and subject to the conditions set 
forth in the Schedule attached thereto for such period as may 
be considered by him to be necessary for holding the 
exhibition. 


(2) No fee shall be charged for granting such licence. 


4. No licence shall be required for holding any private 
cinematograph exhibition where the number of people 
attending the exhibition at any one time does not exceed 
twenty-five.

THE SCHEDULE 
Conditions to be attached to a licence for private exhibitions 


1. This licence shall remuin in force only 10],,১,০,১০০০১০০৪১০০০১০৪০৪০২৩৪০১০ ১০ 
2. No admission fee of any kind shall be charged. 


3. No film which has not been certified by the Central Board of Film 
Censors as suitable for public exhibition or has not been exempted from 
the provisions of section 9 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVII af 
1952), shall be exhibited or permitted to be exhibited. 


4. No film which has been certified by the Central Board of Film 
Censors as suitable for public exhibition restricted to adults only, shall be 
exhibited or permitted to be exhibited to a person who is not an adult as 
defined in clause (a) of section 2 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVII 


of 1952). 


5. The following safety precautions shall be observed in case of 35 m.m. 
cinematograph films سے‎ 


(a) Only non-inflammable films shall be exhibited or permitted to be 
exhibited. 


(b) No drapery and no combustible material, other than such material 
as may compose the floor, shall be within six feet of the 


cinematograph. 

(c) A bucket of sand and two buckets of water shall be placed close 
to the cinematograph and a large sponge shall be kept in one 
of the buckets of water. ا‎ 


(d) Not more than 200 Ibs. of film shall be kept in any place where 
such exhibition is being made, and all such films shall be kept 
in securely closed fire resisting receptacles. 


(e) No exhibition shall be held in a tent or any shelter or structure 
composed of, or covered with, combustible material or of a 
movable character, unless the cinematograph is operated from 
outside and at a distance of at least 6 feet from such structure. 


6. The licensee may shift the venue of the exhibition from place to 
place after giving due intimation of his programme and itinerary in advance 
to the licensing authority provided that all the rules and safety require- 
ments are duly observed. 


By order of the Governor,

Subscriptions for an issue of 4 per cent. West Bengal Loan, 1968 


1. Object.—The proceeds of the loan will be utilised towards 
meeting the capital expenditure on certain development schemes 
included in the Second Five-Year Plan of the State, viz., 
(i) Development of State Roads, (#2) Durgapur Coke-Oven, Gas- 
Grid and Power Plant Project, (871) Kangsabati Reservoir Project, 
i State Transport Service, (9 Electricity schemes, and 
vt) Slum Clearance, Housing and Industrial schemes. All the 
schemes except scheme No. (7) are fully productive. Against 
scheme No. (7), however, a considerable revenue is derived from 
Motor Vehicles Tax and Motor Spirits Sales Tax which provides a 
complete basis of repayment. 


2. Security for loan.—In accordance with Article 293(1) of 
the Constitution of India, the*loan will be secured on the whole of 
the Consolidated Fund of the Government of West Bengal. 


The consent of the Central Government has been obtained 66 
the floatation of this loan as required by Article 293(3) of the 
Constitution of India. 


8. Description.—The loan will be briefly described as the 4 per 
cent. West Bengal Loan, 1968. 


4, Amount of issue.—The amount of the loan will be Rs.700 
lalchs. 


5. Issue price.—The issue price will be Rs.100 for every 
Rs.100 of the loan applied for.

7., Partial allotment.—If the total subscriptions exceed the

made. 14 partial allotment is made, the balance of the sum paid 
at, the time of application will be refunded as soon as possible after

8. Date of repayment.—The loan will have a currency of 
twelve years trom 3rd September 1956 and will be repaid at par on 
3rd September 1968. 


9. Interest.—The loan will bear interest at the rate of 4 per 
cent. per annum from 38rd September 1956. Interest will be pay- 
able half-yearly on 3rd March and 3rd September and will be 
subject to 10600005-58۰ 

Refunds of income-tax will be obtainable by holders of the loan 
who are not liable to income-tax or who are liable to income-tax at 
a lower rate. An individual holder can also obtain on application 
a certificate from the Income-tax Officer of the district authorising 
deduction of income-tax at the rate applicable in his case when 
tax will be deducted at that rate instead of at the maximum rate. 


10. Place ot payment of interest.—Interest will be paid at 
any treasury or sub-treasury in the State of West Bengal and at the 
Public Debt Offices at Calcutta, Bombay, Delhi, Madras and 
Bangalore. 


11. Form of securities.—The loan will be issued in the form 
of— 
(1) Stock, the applicants for which will be given Stock 
Certificates, or 


" (2) Promissory Notes. 


If no preference is stated by the applicants, the securities will be 
issued in the form of Promissory Notes which are transferable by 
endorsement. 


The Promissory Notes will be in denominations of Rs.100, 
Rs.500, Rs.1,000, Rs.5,000, Rs.10,000, Rs.25,000, Rs.50,000 and 
Rs.1,00,000. 


12. Applications for loan.—(1) Applications for the loan must 
be for 116.100 or for a multiple of that sum. 


(2) Applications will be .received at— 


(2) the offices. of the Reserve Bank of India,-Calcutta, Bombay, 
۔‎ Delhi, Madras and Bangalore, 


(5) the brancheg and ser? pay offices of the State Bank of 
India located in the State of West Bengal. .—

the amount and description of thé+securities required, ‘the full 
name and address of the applicant and the Public Debt Office or

paid.

14. Brokerage.—Brokerage will be paid at the rate~of cne- 
eighth per cent. to recognised banks and brokers on allotments made 
in respect of applications for the loan hearing their stamp. 


15. Depreciation Fund.—The Government of West Bengal 
will provide in each financial year from 1957-58 to 1967-68 inclusive, 
a sum equal to 14 per cent. of the total nominal amount of the loan 
to be used for purchasing the securities of the Joan for carttellation. 


16. Sinking Fund.—The Government of West Bengal will also 
make such annual contributions to a Sinking Fund to he utilised 
for the repayment of this loan on 3rd September 1968 ag they may

located at the Public Debt Office, Calcutta.

An Act to amend the West Bengal Local Bodies (Electoral 
Offences and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1952. 


WHueEnEas it is expedient to amend the West Bengal Local 
Bodies (Electoral Offences and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 
1952, for the purposes and in the manner hereinafter 
appearing ; 

It is hereby enacted in the Seventh Year of the Republic 
of India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows:— 


1. This Act may be called the West Bengal Local 
Bodies (Electoral Offences and Miscellaneous Provisions) 
(Amendment) Act, 1956. 


2. In clause (a) of section 2 of the West Bengal Local 
Bodies (Electoral Offences and Miscellaneous Provisions) 
Act, 1952 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act), after the 
words ‘‘under the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951”’ the words 
‘for an election to fill a seat of a Councillor of the Municipal 
Corporation of Chandernagore under the Chandernagore 
Municipal Act, 1955 ’’ shall be inserted. 


3. In sub-section (J ) of section 6 of the said Act, after 
the words ‘‘poll is taken’’ the words ‘‘for an election’’ shall 
be inserted. 


4 In sub-section (4 ) of section 7 of the said Act, after 
the words ‘‘poll is taken’ the words ‘‘for an election’’ shall 


be inserted.

West Bengal Act XXV of 1956 


THE WEST BENCAL LAND (REQUISITION AND 
ACQUISITION) (AMENDMENT) ACT, 1956. 


[Passed by the West Bengal Legislature. ] 


[Aseent of the President was firat published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
Extraordinary, of the 13th August, 1966.] 


An Act to amend the West Bengal Land (Requisition and 
Acquisition) Act, 1948. 


WHEREAS it is expedient to amend the West Bengal Land west Ben. 
(Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, for the purpose and Act II of 
in the manner hereinafter appearing; 1948. 


It is hereby enacted in the Seventh Year of the Republic 
of India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows:— 


Short title. 1. This Act may be called the West Bengal Land 
(Requisition and Acquisition) (Amendment) Act, 1956. 


Insertion 2. After section 5 of the West Bengal Land (Requisi- 
rs mem ne tion and Acquisition) Act, 1948, the following section shall

No. P.H. | 2770/ W-68 /56.—28th July -1956.—In 
pursuance of rule (8) of the Rules for the Prepara- 
tion, Publication and Execution of Projects for 


Water Supply, Drainage or Sewerage 
by Municipal Authorities, it is hereby 


notified for general information that ۶6ط‎ 
scheme for augmentation — of _water-supply 
of the Budge Budge Municipality within the dis- 
trict of 24-Parganas has been approved by (tovern- 
ment and the particulars of the scheme are as 
follows :— 

1. (a) General description of the scheme.—The 
waterworks scheme of the Budge Budge Munici- 
pality has been prepared with a view to -aving a 
total population of 27,000 with 10 per cent. rise in 
population. The basis of per capita daily supply 
is about 124 gallons and the total daily supply of 
3,36,000 gallons has been provided. The supply 
mains hyve been proposed to be set up only where 
the demand is the greatest with provisions for 
adequate future extensions of the distribution 
system. 


Two supply zones have heen provided—one at the 
Municipal office compound and another’ on 
acquired land at R. N. Thakur Road. The 
following works are proposed in the scheme: سے‎ 


(i) Installation of two tube-wells having 
capacity of 14,000 gallons per hour to 
supply the respective zones. 

(77) Installation of two sets of bore-hole 
turbine pumping arrangements with 
pump houses. 

(711) Two Elevated Storage Reservoirs each with 
30,000 gallons capacity. 

(jr) Distribution system consisting of 8 inches 
diameter, 6 inches diameter, 5 inches 
diameter, 4 inches diameter, 3 inches 
diameter mains. 

(v) Installation of total sixty-eight street taps 
with platforms for distribution. 


The tube-wells will work 12 hours each day in two 
shifts. After extension of the distribution system, 
the working hours will be increased to 16 hours a 
day. Total supply of water will be available for 
consumption in ten hours. Provision of 150 house 
connections per zone has been contemplated. 


(b) An estimate of the cost of carrying it out.— 
Rs. 4,48, 000. 


(c) An estimate of the cost of maintaining it.— 


Rea. 18,214.

(28) Maintenance cost—By imposition uf water 
rates by the municipality.

by reason of the water-supply and to be met by a

(b) The percentage of such water-rate on the

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Coswami 
Flour Mills, 5/A Kalakar Street, Calcutta-7, and one ০0 their 
employees Shri Purosottam Prosad Misra, 2 Synagogue Street, 
Calcutta-1 (case No. VIII—310 of 1955), 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


রা PRESENT : 
burt SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sivth Industrial Tribunal. 


. Appearances : 
For the Company: Shri Gopal Chandra Das, Pleader. 
For the Employee: None. 


This reference made by the Government of West Bengal, by order 
No, 4769Dis./1)/111.-315/55, dated Caleutta, the 4th October 1955, is 
concerned with the discharge of Sri Purosottam Prosad Misra, by 
Messrs. Goswami Floor Mulls. 


The issues submitted for adjudicated are as follows :— 
(1) Is the discharge of Shri Purosottam Prosad Misra justified ? 
(2) What relief is he entitled to? 


The case set forth in the written statement presented by the employee 
is that he was in service under this Company since September 1954. On 
the 19th February 1965, the Company dispensed with the services on all 
of a sudden without assigning any reason. The salary due and compensa- 
tion for abrupt termination of services were promised to be paid but 
ultimately the Company tailed to redeem the promise. 


The Company in its reply submitted that this emplovee had left the 
service of his own accord on the Ist of February 1955, without rendering 
accounts. | 

The employee is fighting his own cause without receiving the support 
of any union or other employees of the Company. The question therefore 
anives whether this is an industrial dispute of which the Tribunal] can take 
cognizance. | 


And additional issue is accordingly framed. 


3138 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1960 [Parr] 
পাপ উস 
Issue No. 3 


Is this an industrial dispute which the Tribunal has jurisdiction to 
‘deal with? 


issue No. 3.—As pointed out above the cause of this employee has not 
been taken up by any union or other workers serving under this Company. 
This Tribunal had to deal with individual disputes of this type on a 
number of occasions and the view has been taken that such an individual 
dispute is not an industrial dispute as defined in the Industiral Disputes 
Acl. Reference may be made to two awards by this Tribunal which have 
been reported in 1956, ,ا‎ 114,105.) page 356, and 1966, 1, I..L.d., page 138. 
This view has been approved by a recent decision of the Hon’ble Calcutta 
High Court, reported in 66, C.W.N., page 856. The matter is therefore 
amply covered 2 authority binding upon this Tribunal. It must therefore 
be held that the dispute in question is not an industrial dispute and the 
Tribunal has no jurisdiction to deal with it. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


S. SENGUPTA, 
Judge. 
S. SENGUPTA, 
Judge, Sith Industrial Tribunal. 
The, 21st July, 1956. 


By order of the Governor, 
D.S. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy. 


ORDER 


No. 3304Dis./D/15L-5/56.—30th July 1956.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. (۱ 
15L-5/56, dated the 5th May 1956, the industrial dispute between Messrs. 
K. M. Sadhukhan and Sons, Rice and 011 Mills, Snanpiri Lane, Serampur, 
Hooghly, and their driver Shri Raghunath Shaw represented by the Motor 
Transport Workers’ Union, 249 Bow Bazar Street, ان‎ regarding the 
matters specified in the schedule thereto was referred for adjudication to 
the Second Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Second Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the 
State Government its award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased here- 
by to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. K, M. Sadhukhan 
and Sons, Rice and Oil Mills, Snanpiri Lane, Serampore, Hooghly, and 
their driver, Shri Raghunath Shaw, represented by the Motor 
Transport Workers’ Union, 249 Bowhbazar Street, Calcutta, 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT : 
Sari G. P. MUKHERJEE, Judge, Second Industrial 7 7৮৮2৫, 


Part 1[ THE CAIAUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 3139 


Appearances : 


For the Employee: Shri Sunil Roy, Member of the Executive Committee, 
Motor Transport Workers’ Union. 


Fur the Company: Shri Biswanath Ash, Advocate. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, by order 
No. 1886Dis./1)/157.-5/66, dated Sth May 1956, referred the above 
industrial dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication of the following issues 
as contained in the schedule to the order of reference :— 


Is the discharge of Shri Raghunath Shaw justified? To what relief 


is he entitled? 
AWARD 


Shri Raghunath Shaw was engaged as a driver by the firm on a monthly 
pay of Rs. 130. He worked there for more than one year with full satis- 
faction of the Company. On 25th October 1955 as usual, he came for duty, 
but he was not allowed to take up his work, and was told that his services 
were terminated with immediate effect. No reason was assigned, nor was 
any charge-sheet issued or enquiry held in the matter, This action of the 
Company has been stigmatised as illegal and unjust. The discharge, in the 
circumstances, 1s the basis of the grievance, which the Tribunal has to 
consider. Reinstatement with wages for the period of unemployment has 
accordingly been claimed. 


The Company’s version in short is that Shri Raghunath Shaw had 
voluntarily given up the job, and that his services were not terminated by 
the Company as alleged. It further stated that he, of his own accord, 
left the service of the Company on 24th October 1955, and did not report 
for duty on 25th October 1955 as stated. 


Shri Rabhunath Shaw has given his evidence, and on behalf of the 
Company, one of the partners, Shri Shyam Sundar Sadhukhan, and a 
darwan, Shri Krishna Bahadur by name, have been examined. Shri 
Raghunath Shaw has deposed that on 25th October 1955 when he came for 
duty as usual, he was all on a sudden discharged. He has denied of having 
relinquished his job of his own accord. But 0.P.W. 1 Shri Shyam Sundar 
Sadhukhan, one of the partners, bas stated that on 24th October 1955 Shri 
Raghunath Shaw has expressed his unwillingness to serve as their driver, 
and hence on that date he sent the key of the lorry, which he used to drive, 
through their durwan, Shri Krishna Bahadur, and that since then he did 
not turn up to work. He has emphatically denied that they dismissed or 
discharged him on 25th October 1955, at he turned up for duty. 
0.P.W. 2 Shri Krishna Bahadur is the darwan of the Company. His 
evidence 1s that on 24th October 1955 Shri Raghunath Shaw sent the key 
of the lorry, which he used to drive, through him stating that he would 
no longer serve under the Company. I have given my due consideration to 
the oral evidence as adduced on both sides. By view is that the version of 
the Company is acceptable. O.P.W. 1 Shri Shyam Sundar Sadhukhan, 
one of the partners, and O.P.W. 2 Shri Krishna Bahadur, darwan, deposed 
in a straightforward manner. It seems to me that they spoke the real 
truth, JI do not see any reason as to why they would depose falsely. 
0.۰۰ . 1 Shri Shyam Sundar Sadhukhan being.one of the partners of the 
firm appears to be a responsible person. It can hardly be believed that he 
would come to box to make a false statement. His evidence bears the stamp

to serve there. Of course, ‘Shri Raghunath Shaw has denied the 1081 that 
he voluntarily gave up the job under the Company. But his evidence did 
not impress me In the least. He suppressed the real truth, 8170 hig 
demeanour in the witness box was not also satisfactory. Hence, the

There is another fact, which points to the direction that Shri Raghunath

stating that Shri Raghunath Shaw was expert in driving and gave this

The points for ee 20 are as follows:— 


(1) Whether the retrenchment ‘of (1) Ramadhar Thakur, (11) Akkal 
Singh, (111) Ram Borai, (iv) Md. Yusuf, (v) Kalipada, (vi) 
Nayan and (vn) Tushar Kanti Ghosh, is justified? What 
relief are they entitled to? 


(2) Whether the dismissal of (1) Chand Gobin and (01) Subhanga, is 
justified? What relief are they entitled to? 


The Union’s written statement found fault with the Company for having 
retrench seven workmen by notice, dated 28th February 1955. According 
to the Union the retrenchment effected was unwarranted and was further 
vitiated by reason of non-compliance with the law which lays down that 
seniority rights must be safeguarded and juniormost employees have to 
make their exit first. Regarding the second issue the Union’s case is that 
there was no reasonable ground at all for refusal by the Company to allot 
duties to the two workmen from the 30th of March 1955. Those two 
employees are entitled to reinstatement with full compensation for the period 
of unemployment. 


The Company in its rejoinder expounded the case that it had lost the 
petronage of an important customer from whom the business was deriving 
handsome profits. The loss in business was such that the staff of the depart- 
ment concerned with the business had to be reduced. The management had 
its hand forced and had no other alternative but to eftect retrenchment. 
As the step was taken under stress of circumstances over which the manage- 
ment had no control it tried its level hest to provide the retrenched workmen 
with employment elsewhere. In fact one of the men retrenched has been 
given employment through the intervention of Mr. Hildreth, the Proprietor 
of the concern. Retrenchment was made on bona fide ground and not in 
pursuance of any ulterior object. 


Chand Gobin and Subhanga were guilty of misconduct in so far as they 
were involved in starting a lorry belonging to the Company and moving it 
out of its place in the absence of the licensed driver. They were warned 
but the employees did not take the warning in the right spirit. They 
became defiant and questioned the right of the Proprietor to give them 
any warning. They intentionally absented themselves and quitted the job. 
No order of dismissal was passed hy the Proprietor. 


issue No. 1.—The Glaxo Laboratories used to get their booking and 
despatching work done by this Company. In the month of January 1955, 
Glaxo Laboratories decided to withdraw the work hitherto performed by the 
Company. The letters Exts. A(1) and A(2), dated the 22nd January 1955, 
and 1188 February, respectively, bear upon this point. According to 
Mr. Hildreth the loss suffered by him on the termination of the contract 
by the Glaxo Laboratories amounted to approximately Rs. 3,000 per month. 
Tt is 1 the Union’s case that the business had suffered no loss. In para- 
graph 3 of the written statement of the Union the statement appears that 
services Of seven workmen were terminated on the ‘‘dubious পি 
that they had lost the patronage of a client. Properly construed this means 
that the Union was doubtful about the truth of the allegation that the Com- 
pany had lost custom. In paragraph 5 of the written statement there is no 
doubt that the termination of service waa not caused چنا‎ reason 
of trade necessity. But the fact remains that the services of this 
concern were no longer required by the Glaxo Laboratories. It goes without 
saying, that some loss was caused by the withdrawal of the commission. 
The statement Ext. C., prepared from the accounts produced before the 


Parc J] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 3145 


CR EN RENT EN ER NR جس وچیس موی جد ہی‎ 


TriMunal for verification, shows that the business wis on the down grade. 
Ram Adhar Thakur, P., W. 1, admitted that the Glaxo Laboratories had 
withdrawn their patronage and the Company was not given any work to he 
done by them. The witness further admitted that when Mr. Hildreth went 
home last in 1955, he called the workers and exhorted them to work to the 
peak of their capacity. On his return from home he told the workers again 
that unless they stretched themselves to the utmost and worked strenuously 
he would have no other alternative but to close the business. Unless the 
business had struck a bad patch, the Proprietor could have no occasion to 
go out of his way to address the workers in this strain. The testimony of 
thia witness therefore lends countenance to the case of the Company that 
the business had suffered to a large extent and the prospects were bleak. 
In the face of these facts the Tribunal must hold that the retrenchment 
was made for bona fide trade reasons. Ram Adhar admitted that he was 
on cordial terms with ‘the management. The Proprietor bore the workers 
no ill will. Since admittedly চা were friendly no suggestion can be 
made that retrenchment was decided upon as a measure of punishment or in 
pursuance of extraneous aims. The Company has proved that retrenchment 
was necessary because of loss of business and the Union witness had admitted 
that relations between the employer and the employed were peaceful and 
friendly. Against this backpround there 1s no scope for argument that 
retrenchment was mala fide. The Tnion’s contention that after the retrench- 
ment the Company engaged the services 01 fresh hands carries no weight 
in view of Mr. Hidreth’s evidence that according to exigencies of business 
only labourers (coolies) are engaged from time to time os before. There 
has been no addition to the staff. The Tribunal has supervisory jurisdiction 
and cannot arrogate to itself the right to sit as a court of appeal against the 
decision of the management. Its supervision is confined to find out whether 
the employer is acting bona fide and whether he has reasonable ground for 
wanting 10 pass the order or taking the action impugned. In this case the 
Tribunal is satisfied that the management acted bona fide and had reasonable 
ground for reducing its staff. The employer, it has been held, is prima facie 
the best judge to determine the strength of his labour force and when he 
acts bona fide and without any other ulterior motive, he has the right to 
retrench a number of workmen which he considers to be surplus. Applying 


this principle to the present case I hold that the retrenchment was fully 
justified. 


The Union raised a point that the principle of ‘‘last come, first (০১? was 
not observed. Ram Adhar Thakur stated generally that there are cooly 
sarders still in service junior to him. The Union did not however supply 
specific particulars and data. No suggestion was given in course of cross- 
examination of Mr. [11107611718 naming particular employees who were retain- 
ed in service though judged by the test of seniority they would have to 
leave. In the absence of positive evidenve the Tribunal is unable to hold 
that the principle aforesaid was actually violated. In the result it is held 
that the retrenched people are entitled to relief as provided in 25(f) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. There was a dispute as to the length of service. 
Ram Adhar Thakur is supposed to have been in scrvice since 1935. Mr. 
Hildreth deposed that records and registers are not preserved for more than 
3 years. He was uot therefore in u position to state that dates of appoint- 
ment of these employees. The length of service cannot hence be determined 
accurately, We have to follow a rough and ready method. According 
Ram Adhar Thakur, he joined in 19343 as a cooly in the soap godown of 
Lever Brothers. This Company had obtained a contract from Lever 
Brothers. In 1942 he was transferred to the lorry department of this 
Company, and in 1943 he was made a cooly sarder. Mr. Hildreth stated

that Ram Adhar Thakur entered service in this Company in 1942. From 
December 1940 or 1941 to April 1946, Mr. Iildreth was, on his own show- 
ing, not on the spot, being in military service during the period. It was 
urged on behalf of the union that his evidence regarding the commencement 
of Ram Adhar’s service is hence unworthy of credit. From the evidence of

in 1942 when according to his statement he was transferred to the lorry

be treated as in service from May 1952 as according to the Union hia service

issue No. 2.—The issue as framed assumes that Chand Gobin and 
Subhanga were dismissed. The Union’s case however in paragraph 10 of 
the written statement is that no notice was issued by the Company terminat- 
ing the services of these two employees. What the Company did was to

the Company which was standing at No. 2 Calcutta Jetty Subhanga had 
got into the driving seat, starting the engine he had backed the lorry at a 
high speed. He had no driving licence. Suinan and Chand Gobin, two 
coolies were in the same lorry. The driver of another lorry protested against 
these people moving the lorry in this way. Thereupon Subhanga and Chand 
Gobin had shouted to him that he had no authority to say anything, the 
lorry not having been entrusted to his care. Chand Gobin and رف‎ 
were warned that similar conduct in future would be visited with drastic

Suinan had thrown himself at the mercy of the Company and_ secured 
pardon. Chand Gobin and Subhanga took an intransigent attitude and 
approached the Union. According to Mr. Hildreth they stopped attending 
to their duties after the 30th of March. He had not seen their hide or 
hair after that day. The UWnion’s case on the other hand is that they were 
dismissed on 5th of April by the letter Ext. .(ج)(‎ Ext. |] ٢ is a letter of 
explanation addressed by Chand Gobin and Subhanga to Mr. Hildreth in 
which they stated that they had to move the lorry to make room for two 
carts to pass. In his evidence before the Tribunal Subhanga categorically 
denied the happening of any incident on the 12th of March. He was not 
prepared even to acknowledge the facts alleged in Ext. l(c). Be that as ۷ 
may, they indulged in some correspondences with the Proprietor regarding 
this matter. The Proprietor had warned them to be careful in future. No 
action was taken for the incident of the 12th. It is unfortunate that the 
workers did not accept the warning in a becoming spirit but sought the 
assistance of the Union to provoke a conflict creating bitterness. It seems 
these two workers having been taken under the wings of the Union felt that 
they were well protected and might tilt against the management. In the 
letter Ext. 162) Mr. Hildreth stated that he had not seen Chand Gobin 
at office or at the garage for about a week. Subhanga in his evidence stated 


Part [| THE 04140107014 GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 3147 


that he had been to his place of work throughout the whole month of March 
1965, but did not get any work. He did not say that he had attended in 
April. According to Mr. Hildreth these two employees had disappeared 
after 30th of March. The evidence given by Subhanga does not militate 
against Mr. Hildreth’s testimony. Balancing the evidence given by the Union 
and the Proprietor, I find that Mr. Hildreth’s evidence is entitled to greater 
weight. My conclusion therefore is that these two workers had of their 
own accord ceased to attend their duty and had by their own conduct thrown 
up their job. Their services were not terminated by the Proprietor. No 
question of relief can hence arise.

Issue No, 3.—WVerking hours.—Working hours in the workshop which

be off duty at 3 p.m. on Saturdays. 


Issue No. 4.—Leave and holtdays.—The shop employees will enjoy leave 
in accordance with section 12 of the Bengal Shops and Establishments Act, 
1940. 

The employees in the workshop will have annual leave, as prescribed under 
section 79 of the Factories Act. They will also get 7 days’ sick leave on 
full pay in a year on medical certificate granted by a registered doctor s0 
long as they are not entitled to sick leave in accordance with the Employees 
State Insurance Act. The workshop employees will also get 5 days’ casual 
leave in a year on full pay. 

The Company grants 5 days to all employees and 3 additional days to 
Muslim ازم‎ as holidays in a year. In my view no distinction should 
be made and all members of the staff should be allowed to enjoy holidays 
in the same way. I think the number of holidays is rather small. They 
should have 10 holidays as in the earlier award with full pay in connection 
with the festivals mentioned below :—

Issue No. 5.—Confirmation of service.—Confirmation would follow after 
a six months’ apprenticeship on service being approved. 


Issue No. 6.—Gratuity and Provident Fund.—Gratuity and Provident 
Fund are long-term reliefs: which appear inappropriate in a case of the 
present description. This is not a big scale business. Its future depends on 
uncertain factors. The reliefs already granted will put some strain upon 
the business. Any further strain will be too heavy to bear. I decline 
therefore to make any provision for gratuity or Provident Fund.

Issue No. 9.—Whether refusal of employment to Shn Chhediram was 
justified? To what relief is he entitled?—Chhediram had applied for leave 
which was refused. Not satisfied with the order rejecting his ۵٥۹ 
Chhediram moved the Assistant Labour Commissioner and Chief Inspector 
of Factories. The Company was ultimately compelled to grant leave for a 
month. After he had left it came to the notice of the Company that a shirt 
and a panjabi belonging to an outsider were washed and ironed by Chhediram 
on the tactory premises with factory materials. Chhediram had left instruc- 
tions with his cousin Ramlekha to hand over the shirt and panjabi to the 
owner. The washed articles could not however be taken out of the factory 
and were kept detained by the Manager. On his return from leave 
Chhediram was tendered a charge-sheet for misconduct on the ground that he 
had washed these articles with the Company’s materials. Chhediram’s case 
is that he wos not allowed to resume his duties and the Company’s case 18 
that being offered the charge-sheet Chhediram bridled up and left the tactory 
in a fit of temper. He did not return to report for duty. There was some 
controversy as to the ownership of the shirt and panjabi. Chhedi’s case 
18 that the shirt and panjabi belong to his brother-in-law Dewan Dhobi, 
an ex-emplovee of this Company. They were washed and ironed and kept in 
Chhedi’s box awaiting return. When he went home he instructed Ramlekha 
to make them over to Dewan Ram. The Company’s case 18 that these 
garments belong to one Mathuram of Bagmari Road. Chhediram _ had 
voluntarily offered to have them washed in the Company’s factory and had 
actually done so. Later Mathuraram claimed these articles as his own. It 
is immaterial to whom the shirt and panjabi belonged. The crucial point is 
whether the washing was an act of such misconduct as would justify refusal 
to give work to the employee. The issue as framed takes it for granted that 
Chhediram as refused employment. The Tribunal is to take the issue .s 
framed and give its decision whether the refusal was justified. The Company 
admits having placed Chhediram under suspension. Chhediram stated that 
during off hours the emplovees can wash thais clothes with their own 
materials and iron them. The Company could not produce any evidence 
that the Company’s materials were used hy Chhediram. As the employees 
were free to wash their clothes, no fault can be found for Chhediram under- 
taking the washing of the shirt and pan;aht so long it is not established that 
he had used উল materials helonging to the Company. As observed 
above evidence is lacking on this score. Chhediram had applied for leave 
but his prayer was refused by the Company in the first instance. He did 
not take the refusal lying down. Ultimately the Company was forred to 
concede his prayer. His attitude in thus challenging the authority of the 
management and succeeding in securing a victory over them maythave flicked 
the authorities in the raw. This probably accounts for the action against 
him. In the circumstances I must hold that the Company was not 
justified in refusing to give employment to Chhediram. Chhediram must 
be deemed to be in service all the time and will get his wages for the whole

The points for adjudication have been formulated in the order of refer- 
ence in the following terms :— 


(1) Pay and allowances.

Written statement was filed by the Union on behalf of the Union first 
on 25th January 1956. In this written statement the Union submitted that 
a charter of demands was presented to Proprietors on 6th September 1955, 
but the Proprietors treated the same with scant courtesy. Nothing was 
10716 to give relief as desired by the employees. Thereafter the employees 
banded themselves together and formed a Union. Charter of demands was 
again presented with no better results. The Labour Department was moved 
but efforts at conciliation having proved infructuous reference was made to 
this Tribunal. In the written statement filed subsequently on 20th June 
1956, the Union dealt with the issue subsequently added. According to the 
employees Md. Osman and his mate Yusuf were dismissed on 9th December 
1955 without any reason. All the remaining emplovees were dismissed on 
10th December 1955. The Proprietors resorted to these drastic measures 
simply because the employees had the temerity to form the Union. They 
claim reinstatement and compensation. 


The Proprietors in the original written statement submitted on 13th 
March 1956, alleged that the employees were being handsomely remunerated. 
Besides wages, they were provided with meals worth about Rs. 50 per 
month and each of them used to get anna I to annas 4 for pam and bir. 
Fixation of grade was objected to as the business was still in its infancy and 
had to pasa through hard times. 16 was also stated that out of 24 workers 
14 quitted service without any notice after receiving their wages on the 
4th of December 1955. In the additional written statement the Proprietors 
stated that on desertion by this group of workers a notice was put up on the 
Notice Board but none of them came back to resume their duties. This was 
not an incident of dismissal by the Maliks. 


Issue No. 1.—Annexure A to the Union’s written statement marked 
Ext. 3 is a statement of the designation of the workers, period of service, 
and monthly wages. ‘fhie was admitted to be correct more or less. The 
Proprietors’ case is that the restaurant was started five years back. It has 


3154 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 [Parr ] 


ee ee ee 
still to fight its way, to an nssured position, The period of service recorded 
in Ext. 3 lends support to the Proprietors’ version that the restauraut 18 in 
existence for a period of five years. The boy Nasir had put in 5 years’ 
service. All the rest served for 3 years or ھ7‎ None of the employeeg 
had to their credit service exceeding five years. I am therefore yersuaded 
that the restaurant is in being for o span of five years. The রা has 
claimed that pay and allowances should be fixed with a minimum of Rs, 40 
for certain categories, Rs. 50 for some other categories and Rs. 55 to Rs. 6 
for the remaining categories of workers. The maximum as claimed ranges 
from Rs. 110 to Rs. 150. This will appear in Annexure C to the written 
statement. In my view ao business of this type would be ruined if pay and 
allowances are settled as suggested by the Union. The prosperity and even 
continued existence of such a business is extremely uncertain. One cannot 
predict that it will have a successful career or grow from strength to strength 
as years roll by. The wages paid in cash and kind do not make a poor show, 
According to the evidence of O.P.W. 1 all the employees used to be pro. 
vided with morning tea with haluah and purt, and at 10 a.m. with two 
pieces of rott, one plate of dal and a cup of tea. The mid-day meal supplied 
to them consisted of rice or atta and dal cooked with meat. At night they 
were supplied with 792 and vegetables. As per evidence of O.P.W. 1], 
the foodstuff supplied to the employees were worth Rs. 2 to Rs. 2-8 per 
diem. Over and above this they used to get 1 anna to “4 annas for pan 
and birt. The Proprietors in the written statement assessed the value of 
the meals at Rs. 50 per month. The total emoluments in cash and kind 
taken together are nothing to sneeze at. No evidence was adduced that the 
wages paid in other establishments of like nature are more favourable. J] 
am noi therefore impressed that the Tribunal should interfere to disturb the 
existing pay and allowance. 


The learned gentleman appearing to press the case of the employees 
suggested that the tiffin and meals may be discontinued and cash payment 
of Rs. 50 might be made to supplement the cash wages. The suggestion is 
quite fair. It is hence directed that those employees who are so inclined 
may receive Rs. 50 in cash in lieu of tiffin and meals. Application must 
be made in writing to the Proprietors within 15 days’ from the date of 
publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette. 


Issue No. 2.—The hours of work as prescribed by section 10 of the Bengal 
Shops and Establishments Act, 1940, will be observed in this establishment. 


issue No. 3.—The holidays and leave will be enjoyed as provided in 
sections 9 und 12 of the Bengal Shops and Establishments Act. 


Issue No. 4.—The claim of the Union was that bonus should be made 
ayable at 12৫. and Pujah time. It is not the Union’s case that bonus 1s 
ed as a condition of service. As there is no contract for payment of bonus 
i the present claim is not for profit bonus, this claim must be turned 
own. 


issue No. 5.—For an establishment of this description no retiring benefits 
can be provided. 


Issue No, 6.—The Union’s case is that after the formation of the Union 
the Proprietors started a regime of persecution. Those employees who were 
the moving spirits were spotted and earmarked for victimisation. On the 
8th of December 1955, Usman and Yusuf were sudden} dismissed. 
According to paragraph 11 of the second written statement of 7 Dnion all 


Part 1] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 S155 


the femaining employees were dismissed on 10th December 1955. In course 
of hearing it appeared that a section of employees remained loyal and con- 
tinued working in the restaurant. It is not correct that all the employees 
were dismissed. It is quite clear that the Union indulged in exaggeration 
to some extent. As pointed out just now all the employees were not turned 
out. In his evidence before the Tribunal Md. Osman stated that he was 
threatened with assault by Lalaji. Nothing of the kind appears in the 
written statement. On the other hand, in paragraph 7, Mansoor is said 
to have been severely beaten by the cashier. Since the Union has departed 
in some measure from the truth, the case presented by 1t must be subjected 
to careful scrutiny. The case of the other party is that on the 4th of 
December, wages were paid and accepted by all the employees. From the 
next day 12 employees mentioned in the schedule to the order of reference, 
absented themselves from duty without notice. Srijut Kapoor put up a 
notice in the Notice Board re-calling them to join within three days but 
the deserters did not come back. One boy was appointed on the 7th of 
December and thereafter other appointments were made to fill up the 
vacancies caused by these people throwing up their job. On the other 
hand, the case of the employees is that they were dismissed on the 9th 
and 10th of December. The Proprietors’ case is that they had voluntarily 
relinquished their job. The suggestion made on behalf of the Union was 
that the Proprietors wanted to get rid of these members of the establishment 
who were engaged in carrying on agitation for better service conditions. 
Ii will appear that several of those employees who signed Ext. 1(b) are 
still in service. Among the persons alleged to have been dismissed are 
some who did not affix their signatures to the appeal forwarded to the 
Labour Commissioner. It is not hence correct that the wrath of the 
Proprietors had fallen upon the heads of the employees engaged in the 
agitation. The evidence 1s meagre but I am led to hold that the Proprie- 
tars’ case that the employees had suddenly quitted service reflects the 
correct picture. It was probably expected that by shock tactics the 
Proprietors could be brought down to their knees and the employees might 
get their demands granted. So many workers going out at a time, the 
management was likely to be seriously embarrassed. Probably the 
employees felt in that state of predicament the Proprietors would climb 
down and meet them at least half way but they had miscalculated. Consi- 
dering the circumstances and probabilities I have reached the conclusion 
that the employees mentioned in the schedule to the order of reference were 
not dismissd by the Proprietors but they had left of their own accord.

1955 for very slow production and bad workmanship. On 30th August 195 
this worker was found neglecting his work and was found raising subscrip- 
tion inside the Mills premises in course of which, he threatened some female 
workers and when questioned hy the overseer to stop raising subscription, 
he fared up and misbehaved with the supervisor and also threatened Janaki, 
another worker of the Mill. A charge-sheet wus framed against him and he 
offered his explanation denying the charge, whereupon the Management 
thought it necessary to hold an enquiry, for which two notices were issued 
ما‎ him by registered post with A/JI), but he refused to accept such notices. 
After due enquiry, the Management was convinced that this worker was in 
the habit of اس وی‎ other workers, negligent and insubordinate and the 
charges framed against him were proved. The Management decided that he 
should be dismissed from service, and as such an application was made 
before the Tribunal under section 33 of the কারন Disputes Act for 
permission to dismiss the man. The present petition made by the workman 
is clearly an after-thought and has been made as the Tribunal had become 
functus officio and was incompetent to decide any further issue and pass 
orderg under section 33 of the Act. The petition is not maintainable and 
the Tribunal would uphold the orders of suspension by the Management and 
reject this petition of the worker and pass an order of dismissal.
