ES‏ وب سد ححم سح تحت te‏ س تمس گقققییجبہ ید ھحہسی سیت سوب موس مرج یس تج چہوں یج سے یو جس وی جیدیجہ جو ججہ تہ ستحدجہ جج رسب جامس انی مر سی نمس دم رجات چمں جن ےچ موب زجوتیچ سالجا سے 66ا 


By Government order No. "1265 / Dis. /D/111-39/56, dated 23rd Makeh 
1956, the uforesaid dispute has been referred to this Tribunal for 


adjudication regarding the matters mentioned in the schedule to the order 
of reference, 


৩ issues contained in the schedule to the order of reference stand as 
follows :—— 


(1) Whether 75 retrenched employees as per attached list are entitled 
to gratuity in addition to retrenchment benefits? 


(2) Whether the said employees are entitled to wages for the period of 
leave not availed of by them? 


AWARD 


The employees in question were employed in the Brahmachari Research 
Institute, but they were retrenched from 17th October 1954. This 
retrenchment was effected with the permission of the Hon’ble Jabour 
Appellate Tribunal. The said Tribunal rassed order in this respect on 
13th October 1954, because an application under section 22 of the 
Industrial JTnisputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act was made on 30th August 
1954 by the Company ا‎ it for such retrenchment. ‘The employees so 
retrenched; were given the retrenchment relief as provided in section 26F 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is the contention of these retrenched 
employees that in addition to the retrenchment relief as paid 
by the Comrany, they were entitled to get gratuity as per award of Shri A. 
Das Gupta made on 18th August 1952, and also the wages for the period of 
leave not availed of by them. But the Company refused to pay them such 
gratuity and wages. Hence this reference. 


The Company in reply stated that the workers concerned were not 
entitled to get gratuity as provided under the award of Shri A. Das 
Gupte over and above the . retrenchment compensation payable under 
section 25F of the Act, which was paid to them at the time of retrenchment. 
Regarding the wages in lieu of the Jeave not availed of, the Company 
wanted to say that the workers were not also entitled to get the same, in 
view of the leave rules as made by this Company. There was and 18 no 
provision under the Company to pay wages in lieu of leave not availed of. 
But still the Company out of generosity paid the workers at the time of 
retrenchment wages for the leave found due to their credit according to the 
Company’s record. The Qompany finally contended that the claim of the 
workers as put forward by the Union was, in the circumstances, flimsy 
and speculative, and should be dismissed. 


Issue No, 1.—Whether 75 retrenched employees as per attached list are 
entitled to gratuity in addition to retrenchment Uenefits?—There is no 
dispute or controversy between the parties that the JTabour Appellate 
Tribunal gave permission to the Company to retrench these 74 workers. 
Admittedly, the employees who were so retrenched, got retrenchment relief 
as provided in section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act. It may be 
stated in this connection that out of these 75 workmen mentioned in the 
list attached to the order of reference, two workmen were not actually 
retrenched, and they are Shri Sudhansu Rov and Shri Puran Bahadur 
[Serial Nos. (34) and (88), respectively, of the said list]. These two 
emplovees are still in service of the Company. This fact was also admitted 
on behalf of the Union at the time of hearing. Therefore, no question 
about payment of gratuity or wages for the period of leave not availed of 


PartI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 3163 


আনতে নিত (regina تب سے‎ SS | لب‎ 


can “nrise, so far as those two workers are ' concerned. As regards the 
other workers, the Company paid them retrenchment relief under 
section 25F of the Act. The টি of the Union is that these workers in 
addition to the retrenchment relief payable under section 25F of the Act 
are also entitled to get gratuity as provided under the award of Shri A. Das 
Gupta. It is a fact no doubt that in the award passed by Shri Das Gupta 
on 18th August 1952, a scheme for gratuity was made for the workers in 
cases of retrenchment or termination of service by the Company. The 
relevant extract regarding the gratuity scheme of this award 1s 141. 2. 
The gratuity scheme as made in that award for cases of retrenchment or 
terminution of service by the Company for any reason other than 


misconduct, or for cases of resignation with the consent of the Management, 
was as follows :— 


(a) On completion of 15 years’ service or over 15 days’ basic pay for 
each completed year of service up to a maximum of 15 months’ 
basic pay, 

(b) On completion of 10 years’ service, but less than 15 years’ service— 
10 days’ basic pay for each completed year of service. 


(c) On completion of 5 years’ service, but less than 10 years’ service— 
7 days’ basic pay for each completed year of service. 


(0) Before the completion of year service, no gratuity will be paid. 


(e) Persons discharged at any period of service for misconduct, no 
gratuity will be paid. 


(1) In case of death of an employee, his widow or children or other 
dependents will be granted gratuity on the above basis. 


Now the question is, whether the remaining 73 workers of the list are‏ ۔ 
eglitled to get gratuity as provided under the award of Shri A. Das Gupta,‏ 
in addition to retrenchment compensation paid to them by the Company‏ 
under section 25F of the Act. Having heard the learned representatives‏ 
on both sides, and on a perusal of Chapter V(A) of the Industrial Disputes‏ 


Act, which was inserted in the Act 43 of 1953, I am of the view that these: 


workera are not entitled to get gratuity as was provided in the award of 
Shri A. Das Gupta. The gratuity scheme as provided in that award was 
by way of compensation only for the workers, who were retrenched or whose 
xervices were terminated for any reason other than misconduct. Since 
that award was made, Chapter V(A) of the 17110810101 Disputes Act was 
introduced, and it was introduced to standardise the liability of the 
employers and the rights of the employees in respect of payment of lay-off 
und retrenchment relief. The whole object of Chapter V(A) dealing with 
lay-off and retrenchment is to standardise compensation to be paid on the 
terraination of the services of an employee, and not to leave it to various 
Industrial Tribunals awarding different compensations 01] different basis 
| vide case reported in 1955)1( ٠۔1۰3.‎ 371 at page 874). In this connection, 
the provisions as made in section 25J of Charter V(A) of the Act are 
important and relevant. Section 257 is as follows :— 


(i) The provisions of this Chapter shall have effect notwith- 
standing anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law 
including standing ordera made under the Jndustrial Employment 


(Standing Orders) Act, 1946 (XX of 1946): 


Provided that nothing contained in this Act shall have effect to 
derogate from any right which a workman had under the Minimum 
Wages Act, 1948 (XT of 1948), or any notification or order issued 
thereunder or any award for the time being in. operation or’ any 
contract with the employer. 


3164 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 [Pant 1 


(11) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that 
nothing contained in this Chapter shall be deemed to affect the 
rovisions of any other law for the time being in force in any State, 
in so far as that law provides for the settlement of industria] disputes, 
but the rights and liabilities of employers and workmen, in so far as 
they relate to lay-off and retrenchment, shall be determined in 
accordance with the provisions of thts Chapter. 


I am mindful of the fact that the proviso of this section as quoted ahove 
protects the existing benefits, to which a workman 18 entitled to, on 
retrenchment, either under an award for the time being in operation, — or 
under any contract with the employer. But it must be remembered that 
the existing benefits must be higher than what is payable under section 
20F of the Act. This is clear from the words “Derogate from any right’’ 
as used in the proviso. The said words are significant, and manifestly 
mean some better rights already secured under an award or contract. The 
intention of the Legislature is not to pay both statutory compensation and 
gratuity otherwise payable according to the terms and conditions of service 
subsisting at the time of retrenchment. Furthermore, the gratuity scheme 
approved in the award of Shri Das Gupta provides for payment of an 
amount of 15 days’ basic pay for each completed year of service, and not 
15 days’ average pay as provided in section 25F of the Act. This is not 
all. That award provided 10 days’ basic pay for each completed year of 
service in case of workers who had completed Jess than 15 years’ service, 
and 7 days’ basic pay for each completed year of service for workers whose 
services were less than 10 years. This falls short of what is provided in 
section 251" of the Act. So, in any view, it cannot be said that the benefits 
as provided in the gratuity scheme of that award, were higher than what 
is payable under section 24F of the Act. My view is that the gratuity 
scheme as provided in the award of Shri A. Das Gupta stands superseded 
by the legislative enactment, in which provision for relief in cases of lay-off 
and retrenchment has been made. [n the face of this Statutory 111+ 
the workmen concerned in the present case, are not entitled to any 
gratuity under the previous award. They are entitled only to retrench- 
ment relief as provided in section 25F of the Industrial Disputes 401. 
The Company says that the payment of such retrenchment compensation, 
In accordance with section 25F of the Act, has already been made to these 
workers. This 1s not disputed in the present case. That being so, these 
retrenched employees, barring Shri Sudhansu Roy and Shri Puran Bahadur 
[serial Nos. (34) and (38) respectively, of the list attached to the order of 
reference] who are still in service of the Company, are not entitled to any 
gratuity under the award, over and above the compensation received by 
them under the provision of section 25F of the Act. This isaue is answered 
accordingly. 


Issue’ No. 2.—Whether the said employees are entitled to wages for the 
perind of leave not avatled of by them?—Regarding the workers Shri 
Sudhansu Roy and Shri Puran Bahadur [serial Nos. (94) and (98), 
respectively, of the list attached to the order of reference], the question of 
their getting wages for the period of leave not availed of, does not arise, as 
they are sti]] in service of the Company. Regarding the remaining 
73 employees of the list, the Tribunal is of the view that they are not 
entitled to get anv wages for the period of leave not availed of by them. 
From the materials placed before the Tribunal, it appears that the 
privilege leave allowed to the employees of this Company was more lavish 
and liberal than what was allowed under the Factories Act. The Company 
allowed such privilege leave all along to its workers. In the Standing 


Parr 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 3165 


نے 


Order which was certified on 4th January’1952, it has been provided 
inter alia that holidays with pay will be allowed as provided for in the 
current Factories Act, and other holidays in accordance with customary 
usage. In the said Standing Orders, nowhere it is to be found that any 
provision was made to pay wages to the employees, in lieu of leave not 
availed of. It could not be shown or proved on behalf of the Union that 
the employees of this concern got any wages for the leave not availed of. 
No mention is also made that the employees will get wages for the leave 
not availed of in the document—a _ letter, dated 13th December 1951, 
written by the Works Manager to the Secretary, Brahmachari Research 
Institute Karmachari Samity (Ext. 3), on which reliance was placed on 
behalf of the Union. All that is said in that document 1s that leave not 
availed of will be credited to the leave account of the employee concerned. 
Under the circumstances, the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that these 
19. 67719105968 are not entitled to wages for the period of leave not availed 
of by them. In this connection, it may be stated that another fact has 
come out from the evidence in the instant case, and in my opinion it 
completely demolishes the claim of the workers on this score. It is the 
Company’s contention that at the time of retrenchment, it paid the wages 
for leave found due to the credit of the workmen according to the 
Company's record, though strictly speaking they were 20% 
entitled to the same. Learned advocate for the Company has 
argued that the Company paid such wages, in lieu of leave 
to the workers out of generosity. The Company has produced a 70০0 
(Ext. I), from which it appears that almost all the workers retrenched, 
were given leave pay due, which means wages for the leave due to their 
credit, but not availed of. Only 7/8 such retrenched workers were not 
given leave pay due, and it is presumably because that they fully availed 
af the leave leaving nothing behind to their credit. No material was 
moduced before the Tribunal by the Union to show that these workers 
did not fully avail of their leave. In the result, the Tribunal holds that 
the claim of the workers for wages for the leave not availed of, is unten- 
able in any view of the matter. This issue is therefore answered in the 
negative, 


This is the award of the Tribunal.

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Mossrs. Metro

For Messrs. Metro Theatre Calcutta Ltd.: Shri ১, K Mullick (Jr.) of

Demand for bonus for the year 1953-54 submitted by the employees of 
the Metro Theatre Calcutta, Limited, gave rise to this reference made b 
the Government of West Bengal by order No. d63Dis. /D/11L-264/56, 
dated Calcutta, the 4th August 1955. 


The issue referred for adjudication is as follows :— 


Are the employees entitled to any bonus for the financial year 1963-54? 
If so, what amount? 


The case as made out by the Union in the written statement is that 
there is an established practice in the cinema trade of this State for payment. 
of bonus in every financial year. There is also a practice prevailing in 
this particular Company in conformity with which bonus had been paid 
regularly year after year up to 1952-53, though at different rates. In 
the year under reference the Company did not make any payment as the 
election of Professor Nirmal Bhattacherjee as President and that of Srijut 
Haripada Chatterjee as Secretary of the Union was not to their hking. The 
Union failed to bring the management round to a reasonable frame of mind 
and had therefore to move the authorities of the Labour Department for 
redress of the grievance. Claim has been laid for bonus at the rate of 8 
(eight) weeks’ total emoluments. 


The Company resisted the claim and alleged in the written statement 
that there was no established practice in the trade regarding payment of 
bonus nor was any such practice in existence, so far as the Company is 
concerned. JJuring years of prosperity the Company made payment of 
bonus. _In the years 1951, 1952 and 1953 the Company had trade reverses 
and did not make any payment of bonus. But on repeated representations 
made by the employees certain ez gratia payments at different rates had 
been made in those three years purely as a gesture of goodwill. In 1954, 
the losses rose to a dizzy height and hence the Company was unable to 
make even ex gratia payment as in the preceding three years. Regarding 
the allegation that the election of Professor Nirmal Bhattacherjee and 
Shrijut Haripada Chatterjee had caused annoyance or irritation to the 
management, the Company has given a categorical denial. 


The basis of the claim has been stated in paragraph 2 of the Union 
written statement. According to the Wnion there is an established prac- 
tice in the cinema trade for payment of bonus. Secondly, this particular

dealing with cases for aunual bonus on the footing that the right was

سا‎ my view those cases are inappropriate having regard to the case made 
out in paragraph 2 of the written statement. 


There is no evidence that a practice or convention hus grown up in the 
cinema trade which is binding on everybody engaged in this industry that 
bonus must be paid to the employees year by year. Leference was made io 
the practice followed by members of the Bengal Motion Pictures Associa- 
tion. ‘The witness appeariag tor the Metro Cinema deposed that all mem- 
bers of the Association did not pay bonus every year. The Elite Cinema, 
according to witness, never puid any bonus to its employees. The Union 
cannot in the circumstances rest its claim for bonus on practice prevailing in 
the industry. 


Admittedly the Company was floated in 1935. Bonus was being paid, 
wecording to P, W. 1, since 1948. Payment of bonus was made at varyiny 
rates up to 1958. The evidence of O.P.W. 1 is that bonus was paid up to 
1950. Thereafter the Company suffered losses. Ea gratia payments were 
made in the years 1951, 1952 and 19538, on representations made by the 
employees. These were ex gratia payments calculated to maintain cordial 
relations with the employees, To use the language of the witness, these 
were eagratia payments made os a gesture of goodwill. Ext. A is a docu- 
ment signed by the President, Secretary and members of the Union. The 
employees agreed to accept four weeks’ basic salary by way of ex gratia 
payment in full and final settlement of their claim for bonus in the year 
ending 3let August 1962. Ext. A(2) is the letter addressed by the 
Managing Director to the President of the Union intimating that the 
authorities at the Head Office in New York had accepted the recommenda- 
tion by the local office for er-gratia payment by way of gesture of poodwill. 
1556. 1 1) is a document by which the employees agreed to accept ez gratia 
payment for the year ending 915 August 1953. Ext. B series are the 
receipts granted by the employees in which this has been described as 
‘er gratia bonus.”’ These documents prove conclusively that the Company 
was not willing to concede the existence of any right in the employees to 
receive bonus in those years. They decided however to make some payment 
ما‎ keep them contented and the employees accepted the same without 
protest. (mn behalf of the Union learned Counsel cited a case reported 1p 
1954, 1..A.C., page 18. In that case claim was pressed on the footing that 
payment of annual bonus was a condition of service founded on 40 
agreement. I have already observed that in view of the pleadings this 
aspect of the case does not fall for consideration. Still the learned Counsel 
having relied on this case T may make my observation thereon. In the case 
cited, bonus had all along been paid since 1945 although the Company had 
incurred losses in all those vears excepting one year when the profits earned 
were negligible. According to their Lordships, the conduct of the Com- 
puny to a certain extent excluded the element of bounty. Although the 
evidence was not very strong an agreement to pay bonus irrespective of 
profits could. in their JT.ordships’ view. he implied. In the present case 
clement of bounty haa not been excluded, for, in express terms the Company 
yave the employees to understand that this was nothing better than er 
gratia payment. The employees accepted the payment with the string thus 
attached. They cannot therefore turn round and say that payment in years 
of loss excludes the element of bounty

treated as binding forever or of perpetual. effeet. Treated a ra More 
ftherally the case may be considvred to be one of a customary right. Tho 
low as adiministéred in courts of vivil Jurisdiction recognises customary 
rivits but in order to crystalise into a right u castom must be immemorial, 
reasonable, and certain and further the enjoyment must have been as of 
rivht and neither by violence nor by stealth nor by Jeave granted (86 )',1 
page 20). As in this case payment was made as a gesture of goodwill avd

employees had received bonus during these years as of right. Payments by 
agreement in the terms referred to is negation of the important element that 
ihe enjoyment must have been as of right. Secondly, a right to ripen into 
« customary right must be arment. That element is-also absent. In 
these circumstances the Tribunal cannot hold that the employees have 
xequired any right to receive bonus as claimed. The Company had the 
option to grant their prayer or to refuse it. It is hence awarded that the 
employees are not entitled to any bonus for 1953-54 as of right.

DECISION 


This appeal is preferred against the decision and award of the Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal. West Bengal, dated 4th February 1955, in a reference 
between Messrs. Martin Burn J.td., and all the associated companies of 
which Messrs. Martin Burn Ltd., are the Managing Agents, and their 
workmen represented by Martin Burn Indian Employees’ Unicon. 


2. The matters in dispute that were referred for adjudication ٠ہ‎ the 

Tribunal as contained in the schedule to the order of reference are as 
, follows ১ 

(1) Revisions of existing grades. 

(2) Tiffin. 

(3) Extent of medical aid. 

(4) Security of service. 

(5) Gratuity over and above Provident Fund. 


This appeal has been preferred by the Union against the award of the 
lower Tribunal. 


318 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956 [Parr IA 
তারা: a I I A پت ےت م0 کت سے‎ 


¢ 
3. In the course of arguments Shri Acharya stated before us, that he 
was not pressing the appeal so fay us the decision in respect of item No. (4) 
‘Security of service’? was concerned. The appeal has been argued in 
respect of the other matters in dispute. 


4. In the first place we shall take up the question of revision of exist- 
ing scales of pay for the clerical staff. The existing grades and rates of 
pay are set out in paragraph 4 of the award of the lower Tribunal. These 
grades are those laid down in the award of the Mercantile Tribunal, 
published in the Calcutta Gazette of 25th August 1949. The learned Judge 
of the lower Tribunal has held, that there is no case made out for revision 
of the existing scales in the manner contained in the Union’s statement, 
that the award of the Mercantile Tribunal is not liable to be disturbed in 
@ piecemeal manner, and that if there is any need for revision that should 
be done in a collective manner by another Major Tribunal. In the award 
of the Mercantile Tribunal, there are four grades, viz., A, B, C and D. 
Shri Acharya for the Union does not seek any revision so far as Grade A 
and Special Grade are concerned. He has confined his arguments 69 
Grades B, C and D. The learned Tribunal has awarded as below :— 


Grade D—Rs. 70—3—100—E.B.—4—140 (20 years.) 
Grades B and C—Ks. 70—4—110—E.B.—7—180. 


5. The first contention raised on behalf of the Union by Shri Acharya 
is, that the learned Tribunal is wrong in holding that the scales cannot be 
revised so far as this particular company is concerned, and that any revi- 
sions must be made in a collective manner by another Major Tribunal, 11 
is urged before us, that the scales as fixed by the Mercantile Tribunal have 
been revised in the case of other companies even without another Mercantile 
Tribunal being constituted to go into the question of grades of pay. Strong 
exception has been taken to the observation of the learned Tribunal which 
are as follows: ‘‘Even the wives of workmen do not sit idle. Besides, 
these workmen, working in-one province and having their native place in 
another, do generally hhave agricultural income. That implements the 
earnings obtained by serving in concerns here’’. Even granting that we 
ure not in agreement with these observations, still it can be, by no means 
be contended that the scales as fixed in the Mercantile award need revision 
in the present circumstances. That award was published in August 1949. 
In the Caltex case (1952 LAC, p. 402) the starting wage of a clerk was 
fixed at about Rs. 80. Shri Acharya has contended that in any case the 
starting salary must be raised from Rs. 70 to Rs. 80. 


6. It is well settled that fairness to workers requires that rewards for 
similar work be equal, and fairness to employers requires that cost of 
production be equal for similar kind of work. In other words, the wage 
should be such as amounts to average payment for tasks of equal difficulty 
and disagreeableness. ‘lhe argument on behalf of the workmen, that the 
capacity of Messrs. Martin Burn, Ltd., to pay wages demanded is not denied 
and therefore the scales of pay as মাহি by the Union should be adopted, 
does not commend itself to us. Messrs. Martin Burn, Ltd., are Managing 
Agents of a number of firms. It can by no means be said on the material 
on record that all the companies of which Martin Burn are Managing 
Agents have equal or identical paying capacity. It is argued on behalf 
of the Management that there are certain companies whose economic condi- 
tion is much inferior to that of other companies. There is no valid 
reasons to disturb the scales of pay as laid down in the award of the 
Mercantile Tribunal. We cannot also ignore the repercussions which may 
arise in respect of other companies governed by the Mercantile Tribunal 
award, if-the scales of pay laid down in the award of that Tribunal are 
revised in an upward direction in the manner claimed by the Union. 
Moreover as observed by the learned Tribunal, the Mercantile Tribunal 
and Bengal Chamber of Commerce have provided for trore handsome 
dearness allowance based on a sliding scale which neutralizes the deficit 
caused by the high cost of living to a great extent. Under the Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce scale 115 per cent. or thereabout is the dearness 
allowance given on the first Rs. 100 of the salary. The total wages and 
dearness allowance that are provided for as a result of the Mercantile 
Tribunal award, are fair and reasonable and no circumstances have been 
established on the facts of this case to have the scales of pay revised in an 
wpward direction. We must also not lose sight of the consumer, It is 
well recognised that a scheme of wages, is meant to subsist for some time, 
and such arrangements for scales and grades of pay are long-term affairs 
which cannot be interfered with except on proof of change of circumstances, 
vide Army and Navy Stores, 1851 I LJ, p. 51, and Union Drug Co., and 
their workmen 1954 I LLJ, p. 766. On the materials on record we are not 
satisfied that there is proof of such a change of conditious and circumstances 
as to compel revision of the scales of pay as demanded by the Union. 


7. Shri Acharya has argued that in any event the starting salary 
must be fixed at Rs. 80 as the lowest in the grade. Reliance is placed on 
the decision in Caltex case referred to above. We are not in agreement 
with this contention. The decision in Caltex case 1s distinguishable. That 
related to an oil company whose resources are vast and whose profits are 
generally undisclosed. That cannot serve as a model for raising the 
minimum to Rs. 80. Moreover we cannot lose sight of the argument ot

THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1956

Shri Bose, that 7خ‎ must make note of the New Companies Act which has 
1 


become law, that 
direction has been conwiderably restricted, that the expenses are multiply- 
ing, and that this is hardly a propitious time for increasing the scales or 
revising them jn the manner stated on behalf of the Union. It is also 
urged, that each of the associated companies of Martin Burn are not 01 
the same economic level, that for example the firm of Robert Hudson 18 
a small concern and cannot compare with Martin Burn Ltd., and that the 
wage structure that should be fixed must be consistent with the financial 
stability of the weaker units. It is further contended that: a downward 
tendency is noticeable in the matter of prices, and that it would be anomalous 
to raise the scales of pay at the present moment. On a consideration of 
all circumstances we are of opinion that no circumstances have been 
estnblished for acceding to the contention of the Union for a general 
revision of the scales of pay or for raising the starting salary to Rs. 80 in 
the vase of clerks. We may also notice the fact, that in Karam Chand 
Thapar's case 1953 LAC, p. 152, the starting salary was fixed at Res. 70 
only. We find no valid reason to raise the minimum to more than Rs. 70 
in the case of clerks. 


8. In the course of arguments Shri Acharya has contended that 
stenographers at least must start in any case at Rs. 110 and go up to Rs. 180 
the maximum of the grade. ‘lo this Shri Bose has no objection. 


9, Again Shri Acharya has drawn our attention to the case of 
Comptometer operators. It is argued that they should be given a starting 
salary of Rs. 78 and not at Ks. 70. Shri Bose has accepted this contention, 
and has agreed that the grades in their case may be from Rs. 78 to Rs. 140. 
But he urges that they cannot be placed on the same footing as steno- 
graphers. We agree with this view, but we fix the maximum of the grade 
at Rs. 142, annual increments being Rs. 4. 


10. However, objection is taken to the grades as fixed by the lower 
Tribunal. It 1s argued by Shri Acharya that there is no need for Grade 
D, that it may be abolished, and that grades B and C should be amaft- 
gomated. It is also urged that the learned Tribunal by introducing an 
efficiency bar, has interfered with the scales as laid down by the Mercantile 
Tribunal. It is pointed out before us that the scales as laid down by the 
lower Tribunal are even less advantageous than those fixed by the 
Mercantile Tribunal. We notice that there is no provision for efficiency 
bar in the scales of pay laid down by the Mercantile Tribunal. We do not 
consider that the grades and scales as laid down by the lower Tribunal 
with efficiency bar meet the needs of the case and in fact they operate to 
the prejudice of the workmen. We hold that there is no need for the 
existence of a separate Grade D. In the Mercantile Tribunal award the 
scale of pay for Grade D is Rs. 7O—3—130, and for Grade C it is 
Rs. 70-4184 In our opinion there is no need for the existence of two 
separate grades with the same starting salary and with a maximum of the 
grade with a difference of only Rs. 4. We are in agreement with Shri 
Acharya’s contention that Grade D should be abolished and ‘that B and ( 
should be amalgamated. We consider the following scales of pay will 
meet the ends of justice, viz., Rs. 70—4—138—7—180. We find on issue 
No. 1 that 03209 D should be abolished, Grades B and C should be amal- 
gamated, and that the scales and grades of pay should be as mentioned 
above. 


11. The next question is with reference to sub-staff. Even with 
reference to the question of wages and scales of pay of sub-staff, we are not 
prepared to hold that any revision is called for. The same considerations 
which apply in the case of the clerical staff alao apply here. We find that 
no change of circumstances has been established as to warrant interference 
with the scales of pay fixed for the sub-staff in the Mercantile ‘Tribunal 
award, 

12, Our finding on this question is that the grades and scales of pay for 
the clerical staff shall be as follows سے‎

Grade B—Rs. 70—4—138—7—~180. 
Stenographers—Rs, 110—4—180.

18. So far as sub-staff are concerned the same rates as fixed in the 
Mercantile Tribunal award shall prevail. 

14. The second question is with reference to ‘‘tiffin allowunce’’. The 
contention on behalf of the Union is that tiffin allowance of Re. 1 per day 
per head should he given. Reference has been made in this connection to 
the letter Ext. 1, dated 20th January 1948, There 1s a demand that the 
meagre allowance of Rs. 6 is inadequate and that the allowance should be 
raised to at least Rs. 15. Ext. 2 is the letter, dated 18th December 1947, 
by the management to the Secretary wherein it was said that the Company 
was prepared to grant cash payment of Rs, 6 per mensem to each clerk for 
the purpose as: from Ist Januury 1948 and that for non-attendance on any 
day as. 4 per day would be deducted.

15. The contention of Shri Acharya is, that a gens of companies 
have been granting 00100) allowance, and that therefere such’ allowance should 
be granted as demanded by the Urfion. We are not prepared to agree. 
In the first place the question of tiffin allowance is not one of the appealable 
items under section 7(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate 
Tribunal) Act. Secondly, the learned Judge has exercised his discretion 
in the matter and has found that there is no case made out for grant of 
tiffin allowance. We do not see any ground for differing from the said 
conclusion. The.learned Judge has observed that the Company has started 
a canteen also. We find that there is no case made out for the grant of 
tiffin allowance in the manner claimed on behalf of the Union; but the 
companies will continue to pay whatever tiffin allowance, if any, they have 
been paying till now, and our finding as above will not affect any existing 
arrangements about the tiffin. 


16. The next question is about medical assistance. The decision in 
Karam Chand Thapar case (1958 LAC, p. 162) lays down the manner in 
which provision should be made in the matter of medical assistance. ‘The 
arrangements are set out in pages 160 and 161 of the said decision. The 
directions given in the award of the lower Tribunal are substantially in 
accord with the said arrangements. We confirm the award of the learned 
Judge on this question. 


17. Issue No. (5):—The last question is with reference ہا‎ retiral 
benefit. The argument on behalf of the workmen is, that they should be 
given gratuity in the manner claimed in addition to Provident Fund. The 
learned Tribunal has rejected the claim for gratuity. We are in agreement 
with the said decision. It is in accordance with the decision of the 
Mercantile Tribunal and also another award referred to in the judgment of 
the lower Tribunal. It 1s well recognised, that the question of gratuity 
in addition to Provident Fund, depends upon the financial condition of the 
Company. We are not prepared to hold that such circumstances have been 
established in the facts of this case as to compel the conclusions that the 
workmen are entitled to gratuity in addition to Provident Fund, so far us 
Martin Burn and other associated companies of which they are Managing 
Agents are concerned. This finding however will not operate to the 
prejudice of any existing arrangements, if any, in any Company where 
boii gratuity and Provident Fund benefits are in existence. 


18. In the result the appeal is allowed in part and for the award of the 
lower Tribunal in the matter of grades and scales of pay we substitute the 
following grades and scales of pay so far as clerical staff is concerned,

of the lower Tribunal.

Ill. The following orders have been passed by the Vice- 
Chancellor and Syndicate of the University of Calcutta 
in respect of the cases of breach of ور‎ arising in 
connection with the B.Sc, Compartmental Examination, 
held in 1955:— 


_ (i) The Examination for 1955 of the following candidate

National Library. 


IN response to public opinion, the working hours of the 
Reading Rooms and the Lending Section at Belvedere have 
been extended with effect from the 16th August 1953. The 
revised working hours are specified below:—~ 


Reading Roome— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—9 a.m. to 8 p.m 
Sundays and holidays—10 a.m. to 6 p.m. 

Lending Section— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—1l0 a.m. to 5 p.m 
Sundays and holidays—1l0 a.m. to 1-80 p.m. 
The Reading Rooms and the Lending Section will, how- 


ever, remain entirely closed on the following days of the 
year سا‎ 


(1) 07 Day, (ii) Independence Day and (iii) 
ahatma Gandhi's Bi Day. 


Persons above 18 years of age are eligible to make use 
of the Library; which is a free lending Library open tw 
any one residing in any part of the Indian Union. There 
is no subscription to pay but security in cash is essential.

DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 6992/2A-23/50.—9th August 1956.—In exercise of the power con- 
ferred by section 35 of the West Bengal Development Corporation Act, 1954 
(West Bengal Act X1V of 1955), the Governor is pleased to make the follow- 
ing rules, namely :— 


Rules, 


1. These rules may be called the West Bengal Development Corporation 
Rules, 1956. 


2. In these rules unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 
context ,— ' 


(a) ‘‘the Act’? means the West Bengal Development Corporation Act, 
1954 (West Bengal Act XIV of 1955); 


(b) ‘‘section’’ means a section of the Act; 


(c) other expressions used in these rules but not specifically defined have 
the same meanings as in the Act. 


8. The Corporation shall include: 


(i) aah members representing the State Government to be nominated 
y ut; 


(11) one member being a shareholder, representing the shareholders, to 
be elected in the manner provided in rule 4 whenever the Cor- 
poration is constituted or reconstituted after the issue of shares. 


4. (1) The manner of election of a shareholder to represent the share- 
holders shall be by postal ballot. 


(2) The Chairman of the Corporation shall act as the Returning Officer. 
He shall invite, when so directed by the State Government, nominations, 
within such date as may be specified by him, of candidates from the share- 
holders in writing and each candidate must he proposed by a shareholder 
and seconded by another shareholder. He shall then make out a list of 
validly nominated candidates. 


(3) The Chairman shall thereafter send by registered post to each share- 
holder a list of validly nominated candidates and a postal ballot paper as 
nearly as possible in the form given in Schedule I to these rules and shall 
enter on the counterfoil of each such ballot paper the name of the share- 
holder and his serial number on the register of shareholders, 


(4) Each shareholder shall have as many votes as the number of shares 
owned by him. 


(5) A shareholder shall, on receiving his ballot paper, record his vote 
or votes thereon in favour of the candidate of his choice among those speci- 
fied in the list of nominated candidates and shall sign the declaration on the 
back of the ballot paper. The elector shall obtain the attestation of his 
signature but not of his vote on the postal ballot paper by a-Gazetted Officer 
of the State Government. He shall then send his ballot paper by registered 
post to the Chairman. 


8226 THE CAIXUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 28, 1956 [Panr I 


ere 1 Sra | 


(6) 11106 Chairman shall then count the votes and prepare a list showing 
the votes obtained by each of the candidates and declare the candidate who 
has obtained the largest number of votes to be elected and a shareholder so 
elected shall be a member of the Corporation on its constitution or reconstitu- 
tion after such election. 


®. The term of office of the members of the Corporation, including the 
Chairman, shal] be four years. 


6. (1) In the event of a casual vacancy among the members of the Cor- 
poration on account of resignation, removal or death, it shall be filled by 
nomination hy the State Government, provided that the person to be nomi- 
nated in place of the representative of the shareholders shall be the share- 
holder who may be available from amongst those who stood for election 
and who obtained the next largest number of votes. 


(2) A person nominated to fill a casual vacancy shall hold office for the 
unexpired portion of the term of the member in whose place he is 90 
nominated. 


7. (1) The members of the Corporation other than the Chairman shall 
be entitled to receive a fee of Rs. 100 each for attending every sitting of the 
Corporation : 


Provided that when a member of the Corporation is a salaried officer 
of Government he shall not be entitled to the said fee. 


(2) The members of the Corporation other than those who are salaried 
Government officers shall be entitled to travelling allowances for journeys 
made by them in the course of their duty as such members at the same 
rates as are admissible to Government officers of the First Class drawing a 
salary of over two thousand five hundred rupees per month. 


8. The Administrative Officer and the Chief Accounts Officer of the 
Morporation shall he Government officers whose services may be placed at 
the disposal of the Corporation by the State Government on such terms as 
to period of deputation, pay, allowances and leave and pension contributions 
as may be agreed upon between the State Government and the Corporation. 
These officers shall, in respect of disciplinary matters, continue to be under 
the control of the State Government. 


9: (1) The capital which the Corporation may be authorised to raise 
from time to time under sub-section (2) of section 19 or the additional 
capital which may be raised by the Corporation under section 20 shall he 
divided into shares of Rs. 100 each. 


(2) The Corporation shall not allot shares exceeding Rs. 50,000 in 
value to any one party other than the State Government, 


(3) Payment of the shares shall be made: 
(1) 1n cash or assets in the case of the State Government, and 
(৫1) in cash. or bonds issued by the State Government, in the case of 


any other party, such bonds being redeemable by the State 
Government. 


(4) The sharesof the Corporation shall not he transferred to any party 
other than the State Government or a party approved by the Government. 


part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 3227 


Pa 


(5) The Corporation shall maintain a register of shareholders and shall 
enter therein the following particulars separately in respect of each issu 
of shares: — | 


(a) the name of the shareholder and the number, value 00 serial 
numbers of the shares held by him, 


(b) the postal address of the shareholder and the address of his prin- 
cipal place of business, 


(c) the date on which and the manner in which he acquired his shares, 


(d) the date on which he ceases to be a shareholder and the reasons 
therefor. 


10. The net profits of the Corporation shall be utilised: 


(i) in paying the interest and repaying the principal of the money 
borrowed under section 22: 


(11) in building up a fund for the redemption of shares (to be called 
the Share Redemption Fund) where so directed by the State 
Government; 


(iii) in building up the reserve fund; and 


(iv) in carrying out any other purpose of the Act. 


11, (1) No redemption of share shall be resorted to if the amount to 
the credit of the share redemption fund referred to in clause (11) of rule 10 
ia less than five lakhs of rupees. 


(2) In redeeming the shares issued to parties other than the State 
(Jovernment ; 


(a) the shares issued earlier shall be preferred to those issued later, 


(b) ia 0 ۶ of the shares with guaranteed dividend stil] due shall 
e paid. 


12. (1) The financial year of the Corporation shall be from the Ist of 
April to the 8181۲ of March next following. ” 


(2) Annual Budget Statements shall be submitted by the Corporation to 
the State Government on or before the fifteenth day of November in each 
year as nearly as possible in the form given in Schedule II to these rules. 


(9) The Corporation may without the previous sanction of the State 
Government incur expenditure under any head or in connection with any 
particular scheme in excess of the budget allotments only up to a limit of 
twenty-five thousand rupees for recurring expenditure and one lakh of 
rupees for non-recurring expenditure in a financial year. The Corporation 
shall, however, report to the State Government the circumstances under 
which it has become necessary to incur such expenditure. 


۳ If in respect of any financial year, expenditure ovér and above the 
total amount provided for in the budget estimates becomes necessary or 18 
incurred in terms of sub-rule (3), a supplementary estimate shall be pre- 
pared by the Corporation and submitted to the State Government by the 
first day of January in the same manner as the annual budget, 


3228 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 238, 1956 [Part] 


13. The number of membexs necessary to constitute a quorum at a 
meeting of the Corporation shall be three, of whom at least one shall be a 
representative of the State Government, 


14. (1) The Corporation shall keep such books of account as the State 
Government may determine in consultation with the Corporation. 


2 All account books and registers shall be bound and all the pages there- 
of shall be numbered before being brought into use and all corrections and 
alterations in the accounts shall be made in ink and duly attested by a person 
authorised in this behalf by the Chief Accounts Officer. 


15. (1) The annual accounts of the Corporation shall be audited by an 
auditor appointed by the State Government as soon as may be after the close 
of each financial year. 


(2) The auditor shall see, while examining the accounts of the Corpora- 
tion ,— | 


(i) whether the books of account required to he kept under sub-rule (1) 
of rule 14 have been duly kept and whether the books of account 
and registers conform to the provisions of sub-rule (2) of rule 14; 


(21) 7 the items of receipt and expenditure are stated in sufficient 
6৮৪1] ; 


(iii) whether the payments were made under proper authority and are 
supported by vouchers; and 


(iv) whether all sums received have been brought into account. 


(3) The auditor may require the production of any document or the 
attendance before him of any person responsible for the preparation of the 
accounts of the Corporation, to enable him to obtain information for the 
proper conduct of audit. 


16. The Corporation shall furnish the State Government with— 


(a) an annual balance-sheet of the assets and liabilities of the Corpora- 
tion as on the 3lst March of every year; 


(b) statements of the grants made by the Corporation to the Boards from 
time to time for executing the schemes entrusted to the Boards 
under section 24; 


(c) such periodical reports as the State Government may direct showing 
the progress of development schemes, undertaken by the Corpora- 
tion; and 


(dy a report of the proceeding of each meeting of the Corporation as soon 
as possible after the meeting.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT. 


ORDER

Appearances: 


For Messrs. Metro Goldwyn Mayer Indta, Ltd: Shri ১. K. Mullick থে) of 


Messrs. Sandersons and Morgans, Solicitors. 


Kor Metro Goldwyn Mayer Employees’ Union: Shri 9. K. Acharyya, Bar.- 
at-luw, assisted by Shri Suprobhat Mukherjee. 


Demand for bonus for the year 1953-54 submitted by the employees of 
Messrs. Metro Goldwyn Mayer India, Ltd., gave rise to this reference made 
by the Government of West Bengal by order No. 20Dis. /D /111.-443/55, dated 
Calcutta, the 6th January 1956. 


The issue referred for adjudication is as follows:— 


Are the employees entitled to any bonus for the financial year 1953-54? 
if so, what? 


The case of the Union as set forth in the written statement is that the 
employees were receiving bonus every year and were thus entitled to have 
the same in customary right. In the year under reference the Company did 
not make any payment as the election of Professor Nirmal Bhattacherjee as 
President and that of Srijut Nartpada Chatterjee as Secretary of the Union 
was not to their liking. The Union failed to bring the management round 
to a reasonable frame of mind and had therefore to move the authorities of 
the Labour Department for redress of the grievance. Claim has been laid 
for bonue at the rate of eight weeks’ total emolumenty. 


3236 THE CATOUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 28, 1956 [Parr | 


The Company resisted the claim and denied that the employees had any 
customar right to receive bonus. It wag submitted that the Company had 
suffered Joss in the years 1951, 1952 and 1993-und hence no bonus was paid 
in those years. Asa result of representations-made by the employees during 
those years for some payment, the Company exercised its discretion in their 
favour and made ea gratia payment solely as a gesture and goodwill without 
creating any precedence for the future. In 1954, the losses were still heavier 
and hence no payment of any amount was possible. Regarding the allega- 
tion that the election of Professor Nirmal Bhattacherjee and Shrijut Haripada 
Chatterjee had caused annoyance or irritation to the management, the 
Company has given a categorical denial. 


The Union’s case appears in paragraph 3 to be one of customary right. 
Plainly this is not a case for bonus to be paid out of surplus profits, nor is 
this strictly speaking a case of a right to recover bonus, as a condition of 
service arising from implied agreement. Reported cases dealing with cases 
for annual bonus on the footing that the right was rooted in the conditions 
of service have been placed in course of argument. In my view those 
cases are inappropriate having regard to the case made out in paragraph 3 
of the written statement. P.W. 1 admitted in his evidence that he did not 
know if bonus used to be paid on profits or as a condition of service. 
According to P.W. 1 bonus is being paid since 1947. Ext. B(1) 1s a letter 
written by the Managing Director to the Secretary of the Union intimating 
that the authorities at the head office in New York had accepted the 
recommendation of the local office for ex 77050 payment to the employees 
for the year ending 3lst August 1953. Ext. B is the communication 
addressed to the Company by the Union and the members individually 
signifying their willingness to accept ex gratia payment of four weeks’ basic 
salary, in satisfaction of their claim for bonus. Ext. A is a receipt granted 
for the er gratia payment made in accordance with the letter aforesaid. 
These documents prove conclusively that the Company was not willing to 
concede the existence of any right in the employees to receive bonus in 
those years. They decided however to make some payment to keep them 
contented-and the employees accepted the same without protest. On behalf 
of the Union, the learned Counsel cited a case ا‎ in 1954, 1۰. 
page 18. In that case claim was pressed on the footing that payment of 
annual bonus was a condition of service founded on implied agreement. I 
have already observed that in view of the pleadings this aspect of the case 
does not fall for consideration. Still the learned Counsel having relied on 
this case I may make my observations thereon. In the case cited, bonus 
had all along been paid sinve 1945 although the Company had incurred 
losses in all those vears excepting one year when the profits earned were 
negligible. According to their Lordships, the conduct of the Company 
to a certain extent excluded the element of bounty. Although the evidence 
was not very strong an agreement to pay bonus irrespective of profits could, 
in their Lordships’ view, be implied. In the present case element of bounty 
has not been ات‎ for, In express terms the Company gave the employees 
to understand that this was nothing better than ez gratia payment. The 
employees accepted the payment with the string thus attached. They 
cannot therefore turn round and say that payment in years of 1088 excludes 
the element of bounty. 


The case set up by the Union is that a practice had grown up in terms of 
which bonus was being paid year after year. If it is treated simply as u 
practice there is nothing to prevent the Company from setting a period to 
it and withdrawing the concession. A practice of this nature cannot be 
treated as binding forever or of perpetual effect. Treated a little more 
liberally the case may be considered to be one of a customary right. The 


parr T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 3937 


law as administered in course of civil jurisdiction recognises customary 
rights but in order to crystallise into a right « custom must be immemorial, 
reasonable, and certain and further the enjoyment must have been as of 
right and neither by violenge nor hy stealth nor by leave granted (36, 
C.1..d., page 20). As in this case payment was made as a gesture of gond- 
will and was described as ex yratia payment, it is not possible to affirm that 
the employees had received bonus during these years as of right. VPayment 
by agreement in the terms referred to is negation of the important element 
that the enjoyment must have heen as of right. Secondly, a right to ripen 
into a customary right must be ancient. That element is also absent. In 
these’ circumstances the Tribunal cannot hold that the employees have 
acquired any right to receive bonus as claimed. The Company had the 
option to grant their prayer or to refuse it. It is hence awarded that the 
employees are entitled to any bonus for 1953-54 as of right. 


S. SENGUPTA, 
Judge, Siath Industrial Tribunal.

By Government order No, 12961)75.11)1101,-60150, dated 28rd March 1956, 


the aforesaid dispute was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The issues as contained in the schedule to the order of reference stand 
as follows:— 
(1) Should the Management subsidise the cunteen to enable the 
workmen to have mid-day meals at concessional rates? 


(2) Has there been any cut in piece-rates and if so, what should be 
the fair piece-rates? 

(3) Whether new recruits should be confirmed on completion of six 
months’ continuous service in compliance with the certified 
standing orders? | 

AWARD 


Notice of the aforesaid dispute having been served on the parties, the 
Union filed its written statement on dth May 1956 and the Company on 
23rd June 1956. The case of the Union is that the canteen maintained 
by the Company in the factory at present serves no good to the workmen. 
The workmen are not allowed to use the dining hall for recess, nor do they 
get cheap mid-day meals. The grievance of the Union on this score is that 
unless the Company meets the establishment charges and other necessary 
expenses for the maintenance of the canteen, the object of the canteen wil] 
remain unfulfilled. The Union has further stuted that there has boen cui 
in the rates of the piece-rated workers during the last two years, as a result 
of which their wages have gone down considerably in relation to their 
past wages. Accordingly, the Union claimed that fair wages should be 
given to the piece-rated workers with full compensation for loss of their 
wages during the period in question. The Union has further contended 
in its written statement that the Company dves not care to follow the 
provision of the certified standing orders in the matter of confirmation of 
new recruits on completion of six months’ continuous service. The Company 
discontinues the services of such workmen just before the expiry of the 
period of six months, thereby disentitling them to permanency of service, 
and again recruit new hands who also go out of employment in the same 
way, as a result of which the new recruits are never confirmed in their 
services. 


The Company, in reply, has stated in its written statement that it 
started a canteen according to the directions of the First Major Engineering 
Tribunal Award of 1948, and maintains the same in accordance with the 
provisions of the Factories Act and rules made thereunder. The Manuge- 
ment of the canteen is entrusted to a Managing Committee consisting of 
four~persons, two of whom are elected by the workmen and two are 
nominated by the Manager. Jt denied the statement of the Union that 
the workmen were not allowed to use the dining hall of the Canteen during 
recess hours. ٤٤٢ maintains that the dining hall is kept open during recess 
and lunch hours, and is utilised by the workmen everv day. Regarding the 
alleged cut in piece-rates, the Company denied the allegation of the Union 
that it indulged in wilful wage cutting of the piece-rated workmen. As 
regards confirmation of new recruits on completion of six month’ conti- 
nuous service, the Company wants to say that the question of such confir- 
mation arises only in cases of probationers recruited on permanent 
vacancies, and that the said provision of the standing orders does not extend 


part T] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 3239 


পা aa ea 
to tefh porary workmen, who are taken from time to time on account of 
temporary requirements, and whose period of service entirely depends on 
the duration of temporary work for whxh they are engaged. The 
Company has stated further that there is no such provision in the standing 
orders of the Company for confirmation of such temporary workmen. 


issue No. 1.—-Should the Management subsidise the canteen to enable 
the workmen to have mid-day meals at concesSonal rates ?—Admittedly, 
jhere is a canteen in the factory of the Company. It appears that the 
Company maintains the said canteen in accordance with the provisions of 
ihe Factories Act and rules made thereunder, O.P.W. 1 Shri V. S. 
Raghuvanshi, who is the Personnel Manager of the Company had deposed 
in this case. From his evidence, it appears that in the ganteen, which is 
maintained inside the factory, sweets, snacks, tea, etc., are catered, and 
ihat about 450 workers purchase the said materials from the canteen on an 
average per day. He has deposed that the dining hall in the canteen is 
also used by the workmen, who bring food from home, as they take the 
said food in the dining hall of the canteen during recess hours. In face 
of such positive testimony of the Personnel Manager, the version of the 
Union as made in the written statement that the workmen are not allowed 
to use the dining hall for recess, cannot be believed. It has further 
transpired from the evidence of the Personnel Manager that the Company 
provides crockery, cutlery, utensils, electricity, furniture, etc., for the 
canteen, and also pays Rs. 378 per month on an average for maintaining 
the staff of the canteen and for the cost of coal, fuel, etc. There is also a 
(‘anteen Committee, which consists of employers’s and employees’ repre- 
sentatives in equal number. In my view, the Company has done, what it is 
required to do in accordance with the provisions of the Factories Act and 
the rules made thereunder. The Management subsidises the canteen by 
paying a handsome amount per month. It is for the Canteen Committee 
to decide as to menu and price to be settled for mid-day meals. It is up to 
that Committee to take steps as to what would be the concessional rate for 
inid-day meals. Such a thing is a matter of detail, and it is for the 
(‘anteen Committee or for the Works Committee to settle it, and the 
Management cannot be directed to do anything further in this respect. 
This issue is decided accordingly. 


Issue NO. 2.—Has there been any cut in piece-rates and if so, what 
should be the fair piece-rates?——In fixing a piece-rate, one is to calculate 
everything to a nicety. This requires, among others, time and motion 
atudy and the degree of fatigue involved. There is no material before this 
Tribunal to enable it to consider whether the existing piece-rate is unfair, 
and should be revised. It must also be remembered that piece-rate once 
fixed in a scientific way, should not be easily disturbed. In the instant 
case, the grievance of the Union was that there has been cut in plece- 
rates, but the Union produced no material whatsoever before this Tribunal 
to support its contention. 0< the contrary, the Company has examined its 
Personnel Manager and has produced cost sheets (Ext. A-series). The oral 
and documentary evidence as adduced on the side of the Company, points 
to the clear direction that during the last few years, there has been no 
reduction or cut in piece-rates. So, on a consideration of the material 
placed before it, the Tribunal feels no hesitation in coming to the conclu- 
sion that there has been no cut or reduction in piece-rates. It being so, the 
question of fixing fair piece-rates does not at cannot arise at all in this 
cage, This issue is thus decided. ; 


Issue No. 3.—Whether new recruits should be confirmed on completion 
of sia months’ continuous service in compliance with the certtfied standing 
orders ?—The Company has produced certified standing orders, and it is 


3240 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 [14৮] 


ec NERO ara oh aoc ا‎ 


15৮ B. From the said standing orders, it is evident that the wobkmen 
in this concern are classified into four categories, (1) permanent or regulary 
workmen, (2) probationers,” (3) temporary workmen and (4). trade 
apprentices. It appears that only the probationers, who are provisionally 
employed to fill vacancies in regular posts, ure to be confirmed on comple. 
tion of six months’ continuous service in compliance with the certified 
standing orders. According to the Company, they have got some temporary 
hands in their factory. These temporary hands are recruited for some 
temporary work in anticipation of construction of some new factory. 
O.P.W. 1 the Personnel Manager has denied that these temporary hands 
were discharged and again reappointed. He, on the other hand, hag 
deposed on oath that the Company pays to these temporary hands the same 
wages as they do pay to other workmen, and they also enjoy other benefits 
and facilities, which the workers of the Company do enjoy. Whatever 
might be that, according to the provisions of the certified standing orders, 
such temporary workmen are not entitled to be confirmed on completion of 
six months’ service, as these temporary workmen are appointed for a 
limited period of work of an essentially temporary nature. Therefore, the 
new recruits who are taken as such temporary ‘workmen are not entitled 
to confirmation on completion of six months’ continuous service. The 
contention of the Union is, therefore, untenable and cannot be accepted 
regarding the new recruits, who are taken in as temporary workmen. This 
issue 19 answered accordingly. 


This is my award.

By Government order No. 16838Dis. /D/111.-12(A)Pt/56, dated 19th April 
1966, the above industrial dispute has been referred to this Tribunal for its 
ud judication. ٠ 


The issues as contuined in the schedule to the order of reference ure as 
follows :— 


(1) Is the discharge of Shri Prahlad Mistry justified? To what relief 
is he entitled? 


(2) Is any sum payable to the said workman on account of earned wages? 


AWARD 


The case of the employee, Shri Prahlad Mistry, in short is that he was 
continuously in the service of the Company since November 1952 on a salary 
of Rx 63 per month, but he was suddenly retrenched with effect from Ist 
Jvaistna of 1362 B.S. He was not given any retrenchment relief under 
the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is further alleged that at 
the time of his retrenchment, his salary for six months was due. Accord- 
ingly, retrenchment compensation for 14 months’ wages, one month’s wages 
in lieu of notice and also arrears of wages for ৪13 months have been claimed 
on behalf of the workman concerned. 


\ In reply, the Company stated that Shri Prahlad Mistry, who was a 
lumber, was not a regular workman of the Company, but he was something 
fa petty contractor engaged on a monthly basis. The Company has further 

contended that Shri Prahlad Mistry had not been in continuous service of 
the Company as alleged, and that he was, therefore, not entitled to any 
retrenchmont compensation as contemplated under the Act. The Company 
terminated the engagement of Shri Prahlad Mistry by way of retrenchment, 
in view of its financial difficulties. 


issue No, 1.—/s the discharge of Shri Prahlad Mistry justefied? To 
what relief is he entitled?—On a consideration of the matter, T am con- 
vinced that Shri Prahlad Mistry had to be discharged, in view of the bad 
financial position of the Company. This fact was not and could not be 
denied by Shri Prahlad Mistry himself, while giving evidence before the 
Tribunal. Accordingly, the Tribunal holds that the discharge of Shri 
Prahlad Mistry was justified. 


The workman concerned is entitled to get retrenchment relief as provided 
in section 26F of the Industrial Disputes Act. In my view, 11118 18 a case, 
which would attract the provisions of section 2917, and it makes no difference 
whether the discharge of the employee concerned hy wav of retrenchment 18 
justified or not. But the Company wanted to defeat this claim of the 
employee concerned by contending that Shri Prahlad Mistry was not a 
regular workman under the Company, but he was something of a petty con- 
tractor engaged on a monthly basis, and that the contract with him was con- 
tract, for service. and not contract of service. On a consideration of the 
evidence adduced by the parties, T feel no doubt or hesitation in saying that 
Shri Prahlad Mistry was a regular workman employed by the Company on 
a monthly pay. By no means, it can be held that he was a contractor, with 


3242 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 28, 1956 [Pant ] 


whom there was contract for service and not contract of service. The 
Company, in my view, has signally foiled 10 establish that Shri Prahlad 
Mistry was employed as thei contractor, On the contrary, the evidence of 
the witness examined on behalf of the Company points to the direction that 
Shri Prahlad Mistry came within the ambit of “‘workman”’ as defined in 
section 2(s) of the Act. So, there 1s no substance or merit in the contention 
of the Company that Shri Prahlad Mistry was not a workman, but was a 
contractor. The Tribunal is of the view that Shri Prahlad Mistry was 9 
workman within the meaning of the Act. That being so, Shrt ٥ز‎ 
Mistry is undoubtedly edited to get retrenchment compensation as provided 
im section 26F of the Act. 


Therefore, the point for decision in this respect 1s what would be the 
২1510181601 such compensation, It is laid down in clause (b) of section 257 
that the workman shal] at the time of retrenchment be entitled to get com- 
pensation, which shall be equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for every 
completed year of service or any purt thereof in excess of 6 months. Thig 
necessarily requires determination of the length of such service of the work. 
man concerned in the Company and also of his pay. Regarding pay, there 
is no dispute or controversy between the parties. The version of the (০1. 
pany is that Shri Prahlad Mistry used to get Rs. 63 as his pay per month, 
and that no dearness allowance was paid to him. Shri Prahlad Mistry has 
alsa admitted in his evidence that he used to get Rs. 63 only as his pay, and 
did not get any dearness allowance. But the dispute centres round the 
question of his period of service for the purpose of assessing the amount of 
retrenchment compensation payable under section 25F of the Act. As stated 
already, the workman concerned is entitled under the law to get compensa- 
tion equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for every completed year of service 
or any part thereof in excess of 6 months. Section 25B provides that for the 
purposes of sections 250 and 25F, a workman, who during a period of 12 
calendar months has actually worked in an industry for not less than two 
hundred and forty days, shall be deemed to have completed one year of con- 
tinuous service in the industry. In Explanation to that section, it has heen 
laid down that in computing the number of days, on which a workman has 
actually worked in an industry, the days on which he has been on leave with 
full wages, shall be included. In the instant case, 1t appears from the oral 
and documentary evidence furnished by the Company that this worker had 
gone on leave from 14th Ashar 1360 B.S. and joined on Ist Agrahayan of 
that vear, and that during this period he did not get any wages. The 
worker concerned has also admitted in his evidence that he had gone home 
for some months after taking leave in the year 1953, and that he got no pay 
while he was on leave. That he got no wages while on leave during the 
period from 14th Ashar 1360 B.S. to Ist Agrahayan of that year, is thus 
an admitted fact. It being so, the above period should be excluded while 
con puting the number of days, on which he actually worked in the Company 
for that year. Admittedly, this workman served the Company from 
November 1952 till 3rd May 1955, when he was retrenched. The period as 
noted above, that is the period while he was on leave without wages, cannot 
be taken into account in computing one year of continuous service within 
the meaning of section 257 for the purpose of section 25F of the Act. 
According to section 25B of the Act, in order to qualify for one year’s con- 
tinuous service, the actual work aggregating to at last 240 days should be 
done within a span of 12 calendar months. That section clearly lays down 
thot the actual work for not less than 240 days should be done during a 

eriod of 12 calendar inonths. The workman must satisfy two conditions 
efore he can claim the benefits offered by section 26F. The first condition 
is that he must have put in 12 eculendar wonths’ service with the employer. 
The second condition is that during this service of 12 calendar months, he 
must have actually worked for not less than 240 days. Judged by the above 


Pant T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 324! 
০০০০ ET PT RAAT YA ae TET i Sak Toe ee a 


tests, 11 appears that this workman in the year 1952 worked only for two 
months (that is for November and Decembey only), which waa far below 240 
days and less than 6 months during a penod of 12 calendar months, and 
that during the year 19538, he worked for 223 days only (that is from 
January 1903 to 27th June 1993=178 days and from 17th November 1958 
to dist December 1953=45 days). ہمت‎ for the years 1952 and 19438, this 
workman is not entitled to get any retrenchment compensation, For the 
year 1955 also, he is entitled to no com7ensation. He was retrenched on 3rd 
May 1955. This indicates that his service for this year fell short of six months. 
But it is abundantly clear that in the year 1944, he was in continuous service 
of the Company, and had actually worked for 318 days im course of 12 
ealendar months. 11ص٥١,‎ for the year 1954 only, Shri Prahlad Mistry 2৪ 
ertitled to get retrenchment compensation, which shall be equivalent to 15 
days’ average pay, that ia-Rs, 31-8. 


Next question for consideration is whether the workman concerned 19 
entitled to get one month’s wages in lieu of notice. In the present case, one 
month’s notice as required under section 25F was not admittedly given to 
the workman. But a letter was given to this workman by the দাদ পি 
Director of the Company on 7:10 May 1955 and it is Ext. 1. From this 
letter, 1t appears that the workman concerned was informed that his services 
woulda not be required with effect from Ist Jyaistha 1362 B.S. 38rd May 1955 
corresponded to 19th Baishakh 1362 B.§. From that letter (Ext. 1) 1t appears 
further that the Management agreed to pay wages to the workman till 
3lst Baishakh 1362 B.S. The workman concerned has also admitted in his 
evidence that he got his wages from the Company up to 9186 Baishakh 1362 
B.S., and that nothing was due to him for arrears of wages. So, on a consi- 
deration of the matter, I am of the view that this workman is entitled to 
get wages for 18 days more (that is for the remaining days 10 complete one 
month) in lieu of notice, and such wages shall be calculated at the rate of 
Rs. 63 per month, which was the basic salary of the workman concerned. It 
ia accordingly awarded that the above payments be made to Shri Prahlad 
'Mistry within 14 days from the date of publication of the award in_ the 
Caleutta Gazette. This issue is decided thus. 


issue NO, 2.—/s any sum payable to the satd workman om account of 
earned wages?—Jt was stated in the written statement filed on behalf of 
the workman that his earned wages for six months were also due from the 
Compuny, and accordingly a claim was laid for the same. But at the time 
of hearing, this part of the claim was abandoned by the workman con- 
cerned. fe has deposed that he got his arrears of wages for six months, 
which were due to him. He has also admitted that he got the same about 
§/6 months ago. Jn view of this clear and unequivocal statement of the 
worker, the Tribunal holds that nothing is payable to this workman on 
account of earned wages. This issue is accordingly answered 11) the 
negative.
