4. Before ا‎ discuss the issue specificalPy, I. would like to refer to the 
brief history of the dispute. According to the Union, the Tlowrah District 
Bus Workers’ Union was formed on 919 May 1954 in respect of workers 
punbering about 330 of buses plying in routes Nos. 51, 54, 56 and 60 in 
the district of Howrah. Thereafter the Union placed its charter of 
demands to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Howrah, and _ to the 
individual owners of buses on 245th August 1954. The present petitioner, 
Shri Mrinal Bose, who was a driver under the employer Shri D. N. Biswas, 
was the Organising Secretary of the aforesaid Union. Then, during the 
period between 9186 May 1954 and 6th September 1954 the owners of buses 
in the aforesaid routes discharged as many as 18 workmen serving under 
them without any reason being assigned and without any charge-sheet 
being given to them. Mrinal Babu along with one Sukharanjan Chakra- 
yorty and others championed the cause of the said victimised workers. 
They waited on a deputation before the District Magistrate, Howrah, and 
the Regional Transport Authority in September 1954. Eventually there 
had been a conciliation proceeding started by the Labour authorities, and 
those 18 workmen had their reinstatement in service in November 1954. 
But just before this Shri Mrinal Bose, the Organising Secretary of the 
Union, was discharged on Ist October 1954 without any charge-sheet and 
without any reason being shown. So Shri Mrinal Bose, the present peti- 
tioner, claims reinstatement, and also compensation for the period of forced 
unemployment. 


The employer contends that he is an East Bengal refugee, and owns a 
single bus. He purchased the bus at a heavy outlay, but his transport 
business proved to be a losing one. He accuses the driver Shri Bose with 
the charges of rash driving and causing damages to his bus in course of the 
driver’s 10 months and 15 days’ service. It is further said that Shri 
Mrinal Bose used to withhold a portion of the day’s collection without the 
employer’s permission. He was warned by the employer against commit- 
ting accidents by rash driving, and against allowing other drivers to ply 
the bus without the employer’s permission. Shri Mrinal Bose was a 
temporary workman employed in the leave vacancy of one Kartic Chandra 
Das. After his discharge Shri Bose was fully paid his dues. But 
Shri Bose, however, kicked up a ‘‘row’’ on 380th September 1954, and 
abused the employer in filthy ae This is the employer’s version of 
the story of the present case. The employer, later on, has taken legal 
objections that the present dispute being an ‘‘individual dispute’ as 
distinguished from an “industrial dispute’, the Tribunal has got no 
jurisdiction to adjudicate upon it, and also that Mrinal Bose is not compe- 
tent to raise a dispute after his discharge, as has been done in the present 
case, 


Now, I would like to deal with the legal objections first before I discuss 
the case on merits. 


Regarding the assertion that the present dispute is an individual dispute, 
it will have to be shown by evidence that the cause of the workman in 
question was not espoused either by any Union or by his fellow workers, 
priory to the date of reference. The evidence, of course, is rather meagre 
so far as the question that the fellow workers of this man*had made his 
grievances their own cause directly. But the evidence is abundantly clear 
that the inion had taken up his cause long before the date of reference. 
refer fo the Ext. 2, dated the 8th November 1954. This is a copy of the pro- 
ceedings of the joint discussions on the 8th November 1954, under the name 
of Shri B. .کا‎ Basu, Assistant Labour Commisssioner, Howrah, West 


3250) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 24, 1880 [Parr ] 
এ সা সনি তি 


Bengal. 1 quote from the paragraph بل‎ “As regards Subharanjan, 
Bharat and Mrinal, as emplovers concerned cannot ugree to reinstate 
them it is proposed that the dispute over their dismissal be 
referred to a Tribunal for adjudication, on the understanding that the 
Union will withdraw the contemplated strike’. Thus, it is clear that the 
Union had espoused the cause of Mrinal Babu as far back as the 8th 
November 1904, if not earlier, and that the Union was contemplating to 
resort to a strike over the dismissal of the above workmen. The Text. 2(a) 
gives the names of the other workers who were similarly discharged. The 
Ext. 2(b) also shows that the President of the Union wrote to the District 
Magistrate over the dismissal of Shri M. Bose on Ist October 1954. The 
date of the present reference is the 8th June 1955. So it is clear that 
Shri Mrinal Bose was discharged, and his discharge was taken up by his 
Union long before the date of reference. It 18 contended by the employer 
{hat there is no document to show that the Union was specifically authorised 
by Shri Mrinal Bose to represent his case. But that is neither here nor 
there. The question of ‘‘representation’’ by a Union is something different 
from the question of one’s cause being espoused by a Union. So far as 
the ‘‘representation’ is concerned the order of reference is explicit, and 
perhaps says the last word. So it is clear that the present so, 
though originally it had been between Shri Mrinal Bose and his employer 
was developed into a dispute between the employer and the Union of 
which the said Mrinal Bose was a member. So it developed into a 00]. 
lective dispute and, as such, there can be no question of the present dispute 
being an industrial dispute. 


The argument that Shri Mrinal Bose being an ex-employee cannot be a 
‘‘workman’’ is merely an attempt of a dying man to catch at a straw. A 
“dismissed workman’’ is a ‘‘workman’’ as defined in section 2(8) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as I shall show presently. A dispute raised 
in connection with his non-employment falls within the definition of 
industrial dispute in section 2(k). This was decided in the case of Ganesh 
Das Ramgopal versus the Government of U.P., reported at page 479 of the 
Indian. Faetories Journal of February 1953. Further reference may be 
made to the famous cases of Western India Automobile Association versus 
Industrial Tribunal (1949), reported in 1 F.J.R., page 97, and India 
Paper Pulp Co., Ltd., versus Workers’ Union, reported in 1 F.J.R., page 
119. Both are the decisions of the Hon’ble Federal Court. I may refer 
also to the decision of Mr. Justice Mack of the Madras High Court in the 
famous Kandan Textile Ltd. versus Industrial Tribunal case. I quote 
from His Lordship’s observations: ‘‘If such a dismissal, however, even 
of an individual workman is taken up by Workers’ Union or a substantial 
body of workmen who continue in employment and espouse his cause, 
then an industrial dispute may arise’’. 


His Lordship Bind Basni Prasad of the Allahabad High Court in the case 
of Ganesh Das Ramgopal observed: ‘‘It is admitted on behalf of the 
applieant that if any dispute is taken up by other workmen of the 
industrial establishment or by their Union, then it would become an 
industrial dispute’’. The most recent case of the Hon’ble Calcutta High 
Court can be found in the C.W.N., Vol. LX, dated the 16th July ۵۰ 
Mr. Justice Sinha found in the case of Bengal Club, Ltd. versus Sant: 
Ranjan as follows: ‘‘Where an individual workman is dismissed and his 
dismissal is not objected to by any Union of workmen or by a majority 
of his fellow workmen, that 19 an individual dispute between the employer 
and an individual workman, and is not an ‘industrial dispute’ and neve 
developed into one’. From this it 1s clear that if the majority of the 
fellow workmen or any Union of workmen espouse an individual dispute, 


“a 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 3251 


shen it turns into an industrial dispute even though it might not be 
originally so. So the position is perfectly clear. In the present case 
there is no question of the dispute being an industrial dispute, though it 
might look as an individual dispute in the context of circumstances. | 


Regarding the maintainability of the present dispute in law by an ex- 
workman, the position is not different. It can be maintained as such as 
ig clear from the aforesaid cases. Desides, the evidence makes it clear 
that there had been already o pre-existing dispute over the discharge of 
certain workmen, and Mrinal Babu was pushing their cause. Then 
followed his own dismissal. So he was discharged in course of a dispute 
and, a8 ৪001, comes within the definition of “‘workman’’. 


Next, I consider the question on merits. It is admitted that Shri Mrinal 
Bose was given no charge-sheet, and there was no enquiry held before his 
discharge, nor after that. The discharge certificate was given to him only 
when he refused to stop running the vehicle. That will appear from the 
Ext. 1, which is the discharge certificate. But it does not speak of any 
reason for his discharge. So it is clear that the employer had practically 
nothing before him to justify the discharge of Shri Mrinal Bose, It 18 
only in the written statement that the management comes forward with a 
statement that the facts pleaded in paragraphs 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the said 
written statement constitute the cause of his discharge. But in the 
evidence the employer could not substantiate any of them. By the Ext. C 
the employer wanted to show that Mrinal Babu was involved in an accident. 
But the Exhibit does not show that on its face. Besides, 16 might be that 
the accident was of such a nature over which the driver could not have 
any control. It does not appear that the driver was ever convicted and 
fined by any Court of Law for any accident. Then, regarding the charge 
of rash driving, there is no evidence at all. Then again, regarding the 
llezed unauthorised taking of a moiety of the day’s collection, some 
teceipts have been filed. But these may show that or practice was only 
usual. It is admitted that the driver defrayed the expenses of running 
repairs of the bus from the day’s collection and adjusted ‘the same later 
on. Had the employer really taken any exception to such conduct of the 
driver, he would certainly have demanded an explanation from the driver. 
But there is no evidence to that effect. So it appears that the employer 
is piling up these charges only to justify his action of discharge which could 
uot otherwise be accounted for. Besides, the employer practically keeps 
mum over the fact that Mrinal Babu had Union activities. There is ample 
evidence to this effect in writing. So 16 1s likely that Mrinal Babu had 
incurred the displeasure of his employer along with those of other employers 
of the aforesaid transport service who had an organisation of their own. 
That is why Mrinal Babu was served with the dismissal or discharge order 
without any charge-sheet, without any enquiry and without showing any 
reason. If such a conduct on the part of an employer is condoned, then 
that would put the cause of progress of the labour movement backward. 
In that case there would be hardly any employee who would be brave 
enough to have active part in Trade Union movement because that would 
entail loss of his service. Service now a days is hard to procure. Loss of 
service may mean starvation and ruin 10 a worker who generally lives from 
hand to mouth. So, in the circumstances, I set aside the order of dismissal 
or discharge of Shri Mrinal Bose, the present petitioner..I order his 
reinstatement within one month of the award coming into operation. 


_ Regarding compensation for the period of forced unemployment, I have 
in evidence that Mrinal Babu had casual services during this period 
altogether to two months or so. THe is also running a tailoring shop with 


3252 THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 [Parr J 
ee ee oe 


his brother. Of course, it 18 not to be expected that a man though unjustly 
thrown out of employment, would be sanguine enough of his reinstatemen} 
and .sit idle, therefore, in the hope of getting compensation for the period 
of unemployment. But at the same time we should remember that the 
employer also did not have the benefit of service of this man during that 
period, though for this he is to blame none but himself. So, in view of 
this, I Pec compensation at the tate of half his average monthly earnings 
during last two months just before his discharge, from Ist October 1954 
up to the date of his reinstatement in service. This should be paid in 
three equal monthly instalments after the award becomes operative.

(2) This application for interim relief is not a bona fide one, as on the

the case till the final ا‎ of the main case, in which all the employees

The two grounds which the petitioners advance are not sufficient to 
sustain a claim for interim relief as made. An interim relief can be asked 
for only in aid of the final relief that is likely to be given and in the case 
where money payments are prayed for as a measure of interim relief, the 
question of adjustment towards the final amount ا٦‎ be given must be kept 
in view (aide case of Messrs. Benett Colman & Co., 1944 T1.A.C. 24). The 
monty awarded in the interim relief should be capable of being merged und 
adjusted in the final relief, The question whether the petitioners are 
‘workmen’? and would be entitled to any relief by way of wages in the 
final adjudication of the case under section 38A of the Act, 19 of importance, 
in view of the claim for an interim relief of 50 per cent. of the wages for 
the period from the date of their discharge till] date. Although a decision 
of the question is necessary for the final determination of the case, a prime 
facie decision on the point would be sufficient for a consideration of the 
present petition (vide the case of National Tobacco Co. of India, 11. 1962 
L.A.C. 251). Again, even if this point were decided in favour of the peti- 
(101,618) inasmuch as the dispute relates to termination of service, an

In these circumstances, there is nothing to warrant advance payment of

By order No. 40241)78.11)1 14171117104) dated 30th August 1955, the Gov- 
ernment of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred an industrial 
dispute existing between Uttarpara Municipality and their workmen repre- 
sented by Uttarpara-Kotrung নিস শন Mazdoor Union to this Tribunal for 
adjudication regarding certain matters, as mentioned in the order of 
reference. One of the items in respect of that dispute was prohationary 
period of workmen, and it was issue No. (4) of the schedule to the said 
order of reference. This Tribunal duly gave its award on 25th January 
1956 regarding the dispute, and it was published in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazette’, 
dated 23rd February 1956. After its publication, the Municipal Authorities 
wanted certain clarification regarding the decision of the Tribunal on the 
above issue No. (4). So, the Government by its order No. 2785Dis./1)/ 
141,.-8/56, dated 25th June 1956, referred to this Tribunal for decision the 
following questions: 


(1) Whether under issue No. (4) of the said award the workmen are 
to be confirmed, after six months’ probationary period with 
benefits or without benefits. 


(2) Whether under the said issue, the conservancy menials, who work 
under ‘‘No work no pay’’ system, are also to be similarly con- 
firmed? If so, how? 


I am, therefore, required to give my decision on the questions. But 
1 doubt very much, if the Tribunal has got anything to do after the award 
is made and published in the Gazette. It seems that the Tribunal becomes 
functus officio after making a complete award, and has no power to clarify 
or interpret the award. This was the view taken in some cases, and the 
decisions in Pampa River Factory (1952 J..A.C., 591) and Kamdar, ۰ 
(1952. (ii) 11.7. 192] might be cited in this connection. Very recently, it 
has been held also in the case of Rajruani Transport, Ltd. versus Collector 
of Frichinapalli (1956 1 M.L.J., page 222), which has been printed also 
in notes portion (xci) of Calcutta Weekly Notes, volume LX, dated 7th May 
1956, that once an award has heen published in the Gazette, the Tribunal 
can do nothing further with the award—it has no power to alter, modify, 
clarify or even interpret the award. The State Government has made the 
present reference for interpretation of the award, presumably acting under 
rule 20A of the Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules) 1947. By notification 
No. 5268Dis./1)/1R-3(A)/54, dated 18th November 1954, the aforesaid 
rule 20A was inserted in the Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1947. The 


ےا 


part [I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 1956 3257 
i . 


Tribunal does uot hke to suy anything regarding the propriety or otherwise 
of the said rule, nor does it want to muke ‘any observation as to whether 
that rule 18 consistent with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


Though I am doubttul if the Tribunal can be required to offer inter- 
yretation of the award, 1 propose to consider the questions referred to the 
{ribunal, and give my decision on the same as desired by the Government. 
Notiee on both parties to appear before the Tribunal was duly given, and 
] had the advantage of hearing the arguments made by the learned 
representatives of both sides. 


Question No. 1.—While dealing with issue No. (4)—probationary 
period of workmen, this Tribunal observed as follows: 


“The demand of the Union is that on putting three months’ satis- 
factory services, every workman be made permanent with all the 
benefits, to which a permanent worker is entitled. The Municipality 
resists this demand by saying that no question of probationary period 
arises at all in case of methors or sweepers, as they are treated as con- 
servancy menials. I find no substance in this contention of the Muni- 
cipality. J direct that a worker should be confirmed, if found honest 
and satisfactory after a probationary period of six months.’’ 


It will be thus clear from the above observation that the Tribunal held 
that the workmen, who will be confirmed and made permanent after a proba- 
tionary period of six months, will get all the benefits, to which a permanent 
worker 18 entitled. This question is answered accordingly. 


Question No, 2.—In deciding the said issue No. (4) the Tribunal over- 
ruled the contention of the Municipality to the contrary, and was of the 
view that methors or sweepers, who were conservancy menials, fell also with- 
in the category of workmen concerned in the issue. So, according to the 
award, the conservancy menials would be entitled to be similarly confirmed. 
The first portion of this question Is answered thus. 


Regarding the last portion of question No. 2, I think that it does not 
call for any decision from this Tribunal. It is up to the Municipal 
authorities to decide whether they would confirm or discharge such con- 
servancy menials after a probationary period of six months. It will be 
quite open to the Municipality to discharge such of them, who are not 
found honest and satisfactory after this probationary period. Grant or 
refusal of leave to the conservancy menials during the probationary period 
will, however, be at the discretion of the Municipal authorities. It will be 
for the said authorities to decide also whether the period of leave taken by 
such conservancy menials beyond they were entitled to, should be treated 
continuity or break of service for calculating their probationary period as 
fixed under the award.

DECISION 


By Government of West Bengal, Lahour Department, order Na. 1989- 
Dis. /D/10L-10/54, dated 7th April 1954, five items of industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Bhartia Iron and Steel, Ltd., and their workmen, repre- 
sented by Bhartia Iron and Steel, Ltd. Workers’ UWnion, 249 Bowbazar 
Street, Calcuita, were referred for adjudication to the Second Industrial 
Tribunal, West Bengal. 


The Tribunal gave its award which was published m the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated 1761) March 1955. The items of industrial dispute for 
adjudication were— 

(1) Increment. 

(2) Bonus tor 1953. : 


(3) Whether Shri Ram and Shri Bishwanath are surplua ہا‎ the 
Jompany'’s tequirements for crane drivers. 


(4) Night shift allowance. 
(5) Duty hours of lorry drivers, 


92 


THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 23, 07 


০০৩ 


The Tribunal decided issues 1, 3 and 4 against the workmen and awarded 
1/8th of the total basic wages of the year 1953 as bonus and fixed the duty 
hours of the lorry drivers according to the provisions of the Motor Vehicles 
Act. The Company which appears to have denied its liability for bonus 
for 1953, has appealed against the decision on the issue of bonus. This is 
appeal No. Cal.-107 of 1955. The workmen’s appeal (appeal No. Cal.-111 
of 1955) is directed against the award on all the issues. These two appeals 
arising out of one and the same award have been heard together. We shall 
consider the appeals of both the parties on bonus last. 


The first point, we proposed to take up, relates to increment. The 
workmen demand ad hoc increment of Rs. 10 per month of the basic wages 
of all categories of workers and employees اٹ‎ effect from 2nd June 1953, 
i.e., the date of the submission of the charter of demand, 11) consideration 
of their low wages. The workmen also urge in support of their demand that 
no increment has been given for years together. The Company opposes the 
demand and pleads that the wages paid to the workmen of the concern are 
not low as compared to that paid in comparable industries in the region. 
The Company grants increments to deserving workers in recognition of 
their efficiency. Although this Tribunal has all along appreciated the 
importance of periodical increments as an incentive for better and efficient 
work, it has consistently discouraged ad hoc increments where there are no 
fixed grades and scales of pay for the workmen. The Union complains that 
iucrements at the discretion of the employers for efficiency encourages 
discrimination. In the absence of specific cases of discrimination, we 
shall not be justified to speculate and in the case of Messrs. Simbhauli 
Industries, Ltd., where some workers were rewarded by increments, this 
Tribunal held that there was no justification to increase the wages of all 
workmen. Management’s right to reward increments of efficiency cannot be 
interfered with. The remedy against such apprehended discrimination 
does not lie in ad hoc increments to all workmen. The lower Tribunal 
was perfectly justified in rejecting the demand of the workmen on this 
point. 


The third issue 18, whether Shri Ram and Shri Bishwanath are surplus 
to the Company’s requirements as crane drivers. For a correct apprecia- 
tion of the issue and the findings thereon with a view to ascertain whether 
the decision admits of any appeal, a short résumé of the facts which relate 
10 the dispute may be relevant. Tho undisputed facts are that these two 
grane drivers were found surplus to requirements and were served with a 
notice terminating their services on the 10th August 1953, but immediately 
after the service of the notice and before the actual termination of their 
services, when it was realised that conciliation proceedings were pending 
and the necessary permission had not been obtained from the Conciliation 
Officer, the notice was not enforced, and two workers were allowed to 
continue in their work as spare crane drivers till December 1958, when they 
were transferred to the electric furnace department. They refused to work 
in the electric furnace department and were charge-sheeted and suspended 
for four days, for wilful and persistently refusing the work. Qn expiry 
of the period of suspension they were permitted to resume their duties in 
the electric furnace department. The Company thereupon applied to the 
Conciliation Officer for permission to retrench these two workmen, but this 
application has not been disposed of. Shri Ram applied for sick leave on 
the 17th December 19538, but the Company doubting the bona fides of this 
application, asked him to appear before the Works Medical Officer for 
examination, by a letter, dated 18th December 1953. He did not respond 
to the said letter. Both these two workmen continued absenting ene 
selves, and the Company’s case is that by absenting themselves without 
notice, they must be presumed to have abandoned the services of the 
Company. The workmen on the other hand plead that the transfer to 
impossible duties was intended to force them to go out of work and was 
an act of unfair labour practice. Be whatever that might have been, the 
fact remains that the order of the reference called upon the Adjudicator 
to decide whether these two workmen were surplus to requirements as crane 
drivers. They were not discharged as surplus to requirements. They were 
transferred. This does not amougt to retrenchment. Without termination 
of the services of the employee by the employer there cannot be retrench- 
ment. Retrenchment is one of the specific appealable items listed under 
section 7(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. 
The order of reference calls upon the adjudicator to decide whether these 
two workmen were surplus to requirements as crane drivers. Although 
surplusage is one of the direct causes of retrenchment, the question about 
surplusage of workers in the abstract is not appealable, unless there is 
either actual retrenchment. In the instant case, the notice of retrenchment 
was not acted upon. The decision of the management that these two 
workers were surplus to requirements as crane drivers, was followed by a 
transfer of these workers to other departments. The events which followed 
the transfer of these workers from the department of crane drivers 
to the electric furnace department raise the question whether they were 
dismissed by the management, rightly or wrongly, or they themselves 
abandoned their services with the Company. These questions are not 
covered by the order of reference, and the learned Tribunal did not consider 
this point. In the circumstances of the present case, the findings of the 


[Pang 1A 


Party | 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 28, 1956 


learned Adjudicator that these two workers were surplus to requirements as 
crane drivers, does not admit of any appeal. The workmen's appeal on 
this point is accordingly rejected as incompetent. 


Next we come to the question of night shift allowance. The Union’s 
case is that extra night shift allowance was in existence before 1948, and 
that this allowance was withdrawn and discontinued, although the Major 
Mngineering Tribunal did not purport by its award to curtail the existing 
benefits. This is denied by the Company. The claim for night shiit 
allowance came before the First Major Engineering Tribunal. The learned 
Tribunal while rejecting the workmen’s claim for night shift allowance, 
appears to have considered the facts that some firms were payimg a small 
allowance for night shift works. The Tribunal’s finding was that such 
payments were only war-time measures. The present firm and _ these 
workmen were parties to the Adjudication proceedings, but there is nothing 
in the award that they claimed the benefits otherwise than as a war-time 
measure. The direction of the Engineering Tribunal under issue No. 12, 
clearly shows that payment of night shift allowance as a war-time measure 
was ignored and the claim of the workers was rejected without reservation. 
The observation of the Engineering Tribunal under the head that the 
‘application of the award’’, did not safeguard the night shift allowance 
as a war-time measure. The relevant observation of the Engineering 
Tribunal on which Shri Rain Sen, relies, reads as follows :— 


“This award will not affect adversely any other kind of existing 
advantage which the employees of a firm may be enjoying in excess of 
the benefits given by this award, unless an express provision has been 
made in this award concerning such advantage.’’ 


The Engineering Tribunal gave a definite direction on the demand about 
night shift allowance. This Tribunal has consistently discouraged special 
allowance for night shift work, where workers are employed, as in the 
present concern, in day and night by rotation. The workmen’s appeal on 
this point is also rejected. 


Now we come to the issue of the duty hours of the lorry drivers. It is 
not a specific appealable item under section 7(1)(b) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. o appeal is competent on this point unless it is shown 
that a substantial question of law is involved, but Shri Ram Sen could 
not make out any such substantial question law. The appeal is on this 
point accordingly rejected as incompetent. 


Lastly we come to the question of bonus. This is a public limited 
Company. The workmen claimed bonus both as a condition of service and 
a legitimate share in the profits. The claim has been laid at 24 months’ 
wages for monthly paid workers, 65 days’ wages for daily-rated workers 
less what has been received by the workers as advance during Pujas. 


The Company denies that bonus had ever been a condition of service 
and trading result does not warrant any bonus. The Company, however, 
pleads that the workers had been offered bonus during conciliation proceed- 
ings, in spite of unsatisfactory trading results, 35‘days’ basic wages as bonus 
have been paid to.the workers, as a gesture of goodwill. The Company 
now withdraws this offer on the ground that it was not accepted by the 
workmen and the industrial dispute between the parties was not settled 
during conciliation proceedings. 


The learned Adjudicator has awarded bonus to the workmen equivalent 
to one-eighth of their respective total wage of the year. Both the work- 
men and the Company have appealed against the award of the Adjudicator. 
The workmen fall back upon their original demand, while the Company 
pleads financial inability to pay bonus. We do not propose to enter into 
the question whether bonus can be claimed as a condition of service, for 
even assuming that it can be so claimed, there is not material on the record 
to warrant a decision either way. Although the ex gratia theory of bonus 
has long been exploded, it has been established that on principles of social 
justice the claim of the workmen would arise only if there is a surplus, 
after making “provision for prior charges, for distribution among the 
workmen as bonus. The Hon'ble Supreme Court observed in the case of the 
Muir Mill, Ltd., 1955, 1. LIT. page 1, that ‘it is, therefore, clear that the 
claim for bonus can be made by the employees only if as a result of the 
joint contribution of capital and labour the industrial concern has earned 
profits’, 


The learned Adjudicator has relied on the published balance sheet of 
the Company, and we have no reason to differ from him on this point, 
The surplus profits available for distribution for bonus to the workmen have 
got to be determined with reference to this balance sheet. Both parties 
appeared to have submitted before the Tribunal their estimatés of the 
available surplus and we need hardly say that these estimates differ widely. 
I’xhibits 1 to 1(b) are the estimates of the workmen about capital invested 
in the business, income-tax payable for the year and depreciation permia- 
sible under the Income-tax Act. Exhibit 4 ia the estimate about the 
surplus of profits available for distribution to the workmen as bonus. 
লিন A(6) to A(7) are the estimates of the Company. According to

804

Shri Khaitan who: represents the Company, after providing of all the prior 
charges uccording to the accepted Full Bench Formula, there would be a 
deficit of about Rs. 3,60,000 in the year 1953, while the workmen contend

In 1952, the Company voluntarily paid bonus to the workmen equi-

bonus. In 1953, the yvross profit after appropriation of Rs. 6,00,000 as

The learned Adjudicator has allowed the workmen bonus equivalent 
to one-eighth of the anuual basic wage less what had been voluntarily paid. 
We are called upon to decide if the trading result of the Company for 
1953 can bear the additional burden and also if further increase is 
warranted. 


We have already pointed out that both the Company and the workmen 
appear to have submitted before the Adjudicator statements indicating, 
in their own way, the permissible deductions from the gross profits for the 
purposes of ascertaining the surplus available for distribution of bonus. 
The Company has claimed as a prior charge arrear depreciation of the 
previous years, the statutory depreciation permissible under the Income-tax 
Act, income-tax payable on the balance of the gross profit after deducting 
the depreciation, return on the share capital at 6 per cent. and return at 
4 per cent, on the reserve which is said to have been utilised as working 
capital during the accounting year. 


The Union’s contention is that for the purpose of the Full Bench 
Formula, initial and additional depreciations, although a permissible 
deduction under the Income-tax Act, cannot rank as a prior charge. The 
Union also disputes the Company’s claim for arrear depreciation and for 
return of the hae capital and the working capital at the rates claimed. 


The Company with a view to modernise the rolling mill department has 
spent Rs. 23,29,977 in block and Rs. 1,16,082 in stores at Khardah and 
the evidence shows that the Khardah block did not operate in 1953. The 
I)irectors’ report, dated 2ud July 1954, shows that the Khardah block was 
expected to start after three or four months. 


The Company did not provide for any depreciation of the Khardah 
block up to 1952, nor did it provide full depreciation from 1948 to 1962 
even on the blockthat was in operation during the period. The Company 
has claimed the arrear depreciation for the years 1948 to 1952 amounting 
to Rs. 12,85,743 and Rs. 2,43,291 for 1953 in four equal instalments. 
Deduction of arrear depreciation from the account of a subsequent year is 
allowed by the Income-tax Act and the rules framed thereunder only 
under circumstances indicated in proviso (b) under section 2(b)(vi) of the 
Act. In the years 1948 to 1952 the Company earned considerable profits 
and large reserves were accumulated and these accumulations were utilised 
in bonus shares. If the arrears of depreciation in such circumstances 
are allowed as a prior charge out of the profits for the subsequent years 
the workers will be deprived of their due shares in the prosperity of 
concern which they have earned. We reject the Company’s claim for arrear 
depreciation as a prior charge on the trading profits of 1953. A similar 
view was taken in Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills, Ltd., reported in 1954, 
LAC, p. 716. Shri Khaitan referred to the decision in the Hastern 
Chemicals Co., Ltd. (1954, I. LLJ, p. 818). In this case the Company 
could not on account of unsatisfactory trading result, provide for depre- 
ciation in past years and sought to recoup the arrear depreciation from 
the trading profits of 1950, 1951. It was decided that provision for arrear 
depreciation should be gradually made. The facts of the case are different 


- from the facts of the case under consideration. The Income-tax Act 


prescribes depreciation under three heads: 


(1) Normal depreciation. 
(11) Initial depreciation. 
(111) Additional depreciation. 


Rule 8 of the rules framed under the Income-tax Act as amended by 
notification No. 31-[.T. of 15th May 1948 limits the annual depreciation 
for buildings, plants and machineries, ete., only to the period of their 
user. As the Khardah block did not operate in 1952 and 1953 the 
Company is not entitled to any annual depreciation for this block for 1953. 
But 36110016918 from the departmental notes incorporated in the Income- 
tax Manual (10th edition, p. 450), that the change in the rule which was 
necessitated by some decisions of the High Courts allowing full depreciation 
for buildings, plants and machineries without any regard whether they 
had been used in the previous year or not, does not affect the initial 
depreciation which should be allowed in full for the whole year in all cases. 
Thus under the Income-tax Act, the Company is not entitled, ag an item of 


{Pawr TA 


سمسو وی _. ক্র * ক‏ اسلمنہ

THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 28, 1956

permissible deduction, to normal depreciation for the Khardah block, but 
the Company may fairly claim for the purpose of income-tax initial depre- 
ciation for the new construction of buildings and new installation of plants 
aud machineries for the Khardah block in 1953 under section 10(2)(v1) 
clauses (a) to (০), The question is whether this initial depreciation is a 
০ deduction as a prior charge under the Full Bench Bonus 
formula. 


The Union relying on the Full Bench decision in the Electricity Supply 
Industry, reported in 1955, LAC, p. 665, urges that the Company is not 
entitled to initial an additional depreciation under the Full Bench Bonus 
Formula. This contention of the Union deserves careful consideration. 
In the Full Bench case of the Millowners’ Association, Bombay, this 
Tribunal was not called upon to decide whether for the purpose of bonus 
formula, depreciation is permissible under all the three heads, initial, 
normal and additional, as indicated under the Income-tax Act. What was 
required for the bonus formula was the annual requirement for rehabilita- 
tion, replacements and modernisation of buildings and machineries. In 
fact the quantum of bonus appropriated in the past and accumulated has 
no direct bearing on the bonus formula, except for the purpose of ascer- 
taining what sum of money was available for rehabilitation and moderni- 
sation. The quantum of permissible depreciation for the accounting year 
is relevant nate for the purpose of income-tax to be provided out of the 
trading profits of the year, and for ascertaining what additional sum of 
money is to be provided for rehabilitation, etc. It may be noted that 
where the trading profit of a year does not permit any additional provision 
beyond the permissible depreciation for the year, the depreciation has got 
to be ascertained and allowed as a prior charge. Absence of any specific 
indication in this direction in the Full Bench decision in the Bombay 
Millowners’ case created some confusion and different benches held different 
views, The second Full Bench was constituted to decide the issue of bonus 
in some units of the Electricity Supply Industry and this point was 
clarified in 1955, LAC, p. 659, at pp. 678-79, as indicated below: 


“Under the Income-tax Act, the initial depreciation and addi- 
tional depreciation in the early years raise the quantum of deprecia- 
tion very considerably, to the detriment of the available surplus. 
Considering that the initial depreciation and additional depreciation 
are allowed in the main so that on monies utilised for purchases in 
augmentation of the block a relief in income-tax results, it is evident 
that considerations which apply to the grant of initial and additional 
depreciation are different to the considerations of social justice and fair 
appointment which formed the basis of the Full Bench Formula. 
Benches of this Tribunal held different views on the subject of initial 
and additional depreciation. But considering that the initial and 
additional depreciation are an abnormal addition to the income-tax 
depreciation designed to meet particular contingencies and for a 
limited period, it would not be fair to the workmen that these two 
depreciations should be rated as prior charges before the available 
surplus is ascertained, for in many cases, if allowed, there would be 
no available surplus left, even though the workmen may have laboured 
during the year to the best of their ability and the concern was for all 
purposes prosperous. Upon a careful consideration of the matter we 
are of the view that only normal depreciation, including multiple shift 
depreciation, but not initial or additional depreciation, should rank as 
৪ prior charge in applying our Full Bench Formula.”’ 


We accordingly hold that the initial and additional depreciation cannot 
rank as a prior charge for the purpose of ascertaining the surplus available 
out of the trading profit of a year for distribution as bonus to the workmen.

Shri Khaitan prayed that the rehabilitation charges might be cal- 
culated on the principle adopted in the case of Messrs. Saxby & Farmer 
(India), Ltd., reported in 1955, LAC, p. 707, and filed before us a chart 
indicating the particulars required for the scheme. We are not inclined to 
accept the chart at this stage. In the case of Messrs. Saxby & Farmer 
(India), Ltd., there was specific evidence when different plants and 
machineries actually came into existence and also about their initial cost, 
their age and the fluctuation in the price since they were installed. There 
is no such evidence on any of the points in the present case. Shri Khaitan 
prayed that an opportunity might be given to him to place positive evidence 
on the relevant points and that the case might be remanded to the Primary 
Tribunal, if that was deemed necessary for the purpose, We do not accede 
to the prayer. The claim is for bonus for 1953, and now we are in 1956. 
No new principle was Jaid down in the case of Saxby & Farmer (India), 
Ltd. The Full Bench Formula laid down in the case of Millowners’ 
Association, Bombay, was followed. In all, bonus cases the cost of rehahi- 
litation of buildings, plants and machineries which ranks first as a prior 
charge on the gross profit of the industry should be ascertained and it is 
the duty of the parties concerned to place before a Tribunal all the relevant 
রি for calculation of the rehabilitation cost as accurately as possible. 
This was possible jn the case of Messrs. Saxby & Farmer (India), Ltd., 
because all the relevant materials were placed on the record and there was 
sufficient evidence for definite findings on all the relevant points that were 
necessary to calculate the annual requirements which were to be deducted 
from the trading profit of the Company per year for the purpose of rehabi- 
litation. The Company could not make out before us a sufficient case for 
a remand. The Company could place necessary evidence before the 
Adjudicator, but this was not dene. We are not inclined either to call 
for further evidence before us or to remand the case to the Primary 
Tribunal for further evidence. Although we feel the importance of 
rehabilitation allowance as a prior charge on the gross profit of a year for 
the purpose of the bonus formula, we are afraid that we are not in a 
position to work out correctly the exact requirements. The importance 
of setting apart some portion of the profit out of the revenue of the business 
of every year for Rael acinar and rehabilitation of plants, machinery and 
buildings cannot be exaggerated. It has been rightly observed in the Full 
Bench case (1952, LAC, p. 433). ‘‘It is essential that the plant and 
machinery should be kept continuously in good working order for the 
purpose of خر شا‎ that return, and such maintenance of plant and 
machinery would also be to the advantage of labour, for the better the 
machinery, the larger the earnings, and the better the chance of securing 
a good bonus. The first charge on the gross profits should, therefore, be 
the amount of money that would be necessary for rehabilitation, replace- 
ment and modernisation of machinery. As depreciation allowed by the 
Income-tax authorities is only a percentage of the written down value, the 
fund set apart yearly for depreciation and designated under that head 
would not fe sufficient for these purposes. An extra amount would have to 
be annually set apart to make up that deficit.’”’ The primary duty of the 
Industrial Tribunal is to establish peace in the industry between the 
employers and the workmen, but for settlement of an industrial dispute 
with a view to establish industrial peace, it should not lose sight of the 
interest of the industry. Any settlement of dispute ignoring the interest 
of the industry is likely to have a far reaching detrimental reaction on the 
workmen themselves. To deny rehabilitation and replacement cost would 
be to cut short the life of an industry with the result that the workmen 
employed in the industry would be thrown out of employment and add 
complications to the question of unemployment which is gradually increas- 
ing in volume.

We may in this connectiop quote the observation of the Full Bench of 
this Tribunal in the case of 7 Millowners’ Association, Bombay, “having 
regard to the uncertain tendency of the price level of. machinery, we 
think that a liberal estimate should be adopted.’’ In the absence of any 
positive evidence about the relation between the present value and the 
initial cost in different years prior of 1948 of buildings, plants and machi- 
neries, we cannot but act upon what has hitherto been generally followed 
for calculating rehabilitation charges. 16 cannot be denied that the present 
value of the buildings, plants and machineries has considerably increased 
since the pre-war period and the period immediately following the cessation 
of the second war. The requirement for rehabilitation is calculated on 
the present day price level te is obtained by multiplying the cost price 
by a co-efficient which indicates the ratio of the rise. It has become a 
convention with this Tribunal to multiply the cost of buildings constructed 
prior to 1948 by 2.25 and the cost of کے‎ and machineries installed prior 
to 1948 by 2.7 for the purpose of equating the requirement to the present 
market value. It has also been a convention with the Industrial Tribunals 
to assess the total life at 27 to 30 years in case of buildings and 15 years 
in the case of plants and machineries. We do feel that these conventions 
are not always favourable to the industries. But there is no help. 


We may safely infer from the Directors’ report on the trading result 
9 1948 that this indusiry has completed 20 years of its age at the end of 
1948. We may accordingly presume, in the absence of any evidence, that 
the construction of buildings and installation of plants and machineries in 
use on Ist January 1948 leaving out what have since been 9010 away and 
replaced since then were spread over during these 20 years and we may 
safely say that these buildings, plants and machineries had spent on 8184 
December 1953, at least 10 years of their life on an average. Thus for the 
buildings and plants and machineries that were in existence and were in 
use on Ist January 1948, we may fix the residuary life at 20 years and 5 
years, respectively. In calculating the total rehabilitation requirements, 
5 per cent. of the cost price as breakdown value must be deducted. The

The annual depreciation including the multiple shift depreciation on 
the written down value of the blocks (buildings, plants and machineries) 
in operation in*1952 leaving out the Khardah block which was not in use 
works out to Rs. 40,950 for buildings and Rs. 2,90,892 for plants and 
machineries. There were some additions in 1989, but that is no evidence 
when these additions came into existence and for what period they were 
used. We have not accordingly allowed any depreciation for these 
additions. We need hardly repeat that depreciation for the accounting 
year has no material bearing except for the purpose of working out the 
income-tax. The tota] depreciation for the year 1953 permissible under the 
Full Bench Formula for buildings, plants and machineries works out to 
Rs. 3.381 lakhs. It appears that the Tariff Board requires the concern to 
set apart every year an additional sum of Rs. 30,000 on account of partial 
rehabilitation of the electric furnaces. The total depreciation works to 
Rs. 3.61 lakhs. 


Gross profit as per balance sheet in 1953 is Rs. 9.33 lakhs. This was 
arrived at after deducting Rs. 6.30 lakhs as depreciation. If we add back 
this amount, the gross profit would be 18. 15.63 lakhs. Deducting 
Ra. 3.31 lakhs as depreciation permissible under the Full Bench Formula, 
the taxable amount is Rs. 12.31 lakhs. An additional sum of Rs. .380 lakh 
has to be provided per annum under the directions of the Tariff Board on 
account of partial rehabilitation of the electric furnaces. This will leave 
Rs, 12.01 lakhs. Income-tax on this amount at 6.95 as in the rupee works 
out to Re. 5.25 lakhs approximately. After making provision for income- 
tax, there will be left Rs. 6.77 lakhs. Out of this amount, the annual 
charge of rehabilitation should be টো The annual rehabilitation 
requirement, after deducting the total depreciation provided for the year is 
Rs. 3.05 lakhs (Rs. 6.66 lakhs minus Rs. 3.61 lakhs). The depreciation 
provided for the year represents partial rehabilitation requirement for the 


year. 


The share capital is Rs. 50,00,000 and a major portion of this is made 
up of bonus share. The recent trend is to treat bonus and cash shares at 
par and to allow return on both cash shares and bonus shares at 6 per cent. 
per annum except where such shares came into existence in the accounting 
year in which case a lower rate of dividend is allowed without any dis- 
tinction between bonus and cash shares. In the present case, the bonus 
shares came into existence prior to 1953, but out of the bonus shares 
Rs. 24.46 lakhs appears to have been employed for the Khardah block 
which was unproductive at least till the end of 1953. We are definitely of 
the opinion that dividend should be allowed at 6 per cent. on the balance 
of Rs. 25.54 lakhs (Rs. 50 lakhs minus Rs. 24.46 lakhs). This works out 
to Rs. 1.53 lakhs. Rupees 10 lakhs in the general reserve and Rs. 6.88 lakhs 
being the balance of the Taxation reserve (after deducting advance pay- 
ments of Rs. 14.67 lakhs) came up to a total of Rs. 16.88 lakhs. This 
amount appears to have been employed during the accounting year as 
working capital. The Company is entitled to return on this amount at 
4 per cent. This works out to Rs. 76 lakhs. After providing these amounts 
out of the gross profit of the year 1953 there will be left only Rs. 1.45 lakhs.

We shall not be justified to increase the bonus as demanded by the 
Union. We may in this connection repeat the observations in the Full 
Bench case, ‘‘After the aforesaid deductions there remains a surplus and 
the issue is whether the employees are entitled to any, and if so, te what 
bonus. The answer to this issue is not easy, for we have to consider in 
this context, the needs of the employees, the claims of the share-holders 
and the requirements of the industry’’. 


The Adjudicator’s decision on the issue of bonus is affirmed.

PART Ii—Advertisements, Notices 


Procedure regarding sending Manuscripts for publication of Advertisements, Notices, etc., in the 
‘‘Calcutta Gazette’? (Part 11), 


1, Manuscripts should be properly edited and complete in Itself. 
2. Manuscripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. The name of the signatory should be type- 
written below the signature. 


3. Manuscripts intended for advertisement In the next issue of ‘Calcutta Gazette” shall be received by ۸۲3 
Sales Office at New Secretariat Bulldings, 1 Hastings Street, Caloutta, up te 11 a.m. on Saturday and at 81850 Office 


at Alipore up to 12 noon on Monday. 
4. All costs shall be paid in advance and deposited along with the Manuscripts. 


6. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressed to SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING 
(PUBLICATION BRANCH), WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE. 


The Press shall not be held responsible for delay in publication of any advertisement due to the non-observance of the 


instruations detalfed_above.

PART V—Acts of the Parliament of India assented to by the President 
and Ordinances promulgated by the President 


COVERNMENT OF INDIA. 
Ministry of Law 


The Following Act of Parliament received the assent of 
the President on the 13th June, 1956 and is hereby published 
for general information :— 


ACT NO. XXIX OF 1956 


THE TRAVANCORE-COCHIN STATE LEGISLATURE 
(DELEGATION OF POWERS) ACT, 1956 


[18th June, 1966.] 


An Act to confer on the President the power of the Legis- 
lature of the State of Travancore-Cochin to make laws. 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Seventh Year of the 
Republic of India as follows: — 


1. This Act may be called the Travancore-Cochin Short title. 
State Legislature (Delegation of Powers) Act, 1956. 


2. In this Act, ‘‘Proclamation’’ means the Proclamation Definition. 
issued on the 23rd day of March, 1956, by the President 
under clause (4) of Article 356 of the Constitution. 


3. (1) The power of the Legislature of the State of conferment 
Travancore-Cochin to make laws, which has been declared on the 
by the Proclamation to be exercisable by or under the autho- President 
rity of Parliament, is hereby conferred on the President. ۰ ۵ 


(2) In the exercise of the said power, the President may, 
from time to time, whether Parliament is or is not in.session, ature. 
enact as a President’s Act a Bill containing such provisions 
as he considers necessary : 


Provided that before enacting any such Act, the President 
shall, whenever he considers it practicable to do so, consult 


THE CALOUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 86 


[5487 


smilie ia a ৯টি নন রন সিসির সি নি 


a committee constituted for the purpose consisting of four- 
teen members of the Kouse of the People nominated by the 
Speaker and seven members of the Council of States nomi- 
nated by the Chairman. 


(3) Every Act enacted by the President under sub-section 
(2) shall, as soon as may be after enactment, be laid before 
each House of Parliament. 


(4) Hither House of Parliament may, by resolution passed 
within seven days from the date on which the Act hag been 
laid before it under sub-section (3), direct any modifications 
to be made in the Act and if the modifications 
are agreed to by the other House of Parliament during the 
session in which the Act has been so liad before it or the 
session succeeding, such modifications shall be given effect 
to by the President by enacting an amending Act under 
sub-section (2): ۱ 


Provided that paige in this sub-section shall affect the 
validity of the Act or of any action taken thereunder before 
it is so amended.

SUPPLEMENT—Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 9th August 1956. 


Summary.——During the wock under report there was rainfall in thirty-six subdivisions. Tho weather conditions were unfavourable 
in seven subdivisions. Transplantation of Aman continued in some subdivisions. 


The condition of the standing crop was on the whole fair. The fodder was reported to be insufficient in eighteon subdivisions and 
cattle-disease was reported from two subdivisions. 


The wages of the labourer varied from rupee one to rupees two and annas eight during the week under report.

{Note.—The figures of average yield rates of the 
composite crops, ۶٥٠ر‎ bhadoi fruits, bhadoi 
vegetables, other bhadoi food crops, bhadoi 
fodder crops (other than jowar, bajra, marua 
and maize), lbhadoi non-food crops (other 
than fodder and fibres) and bhadoi fibres 
(other than jute and sunnhemp) as shown in 
the forecast have been shown as percentages 
of their normal yields sper acre. | 


Season.—The weather conditions have generally 
been favourable in all the districts of West Bengal 
except Jalpaiguri. 


Area and yield.-—-The total area sown with 
\lifferent bhadoi crops included in the forecast is 
estimated at 336,000 acres this year compared to 
405,200 acres of last year. 


Juwar.—4,]00 acres are estimated to be under 
jowar crop this year compared to 3,900 acres 
last year. The total outturn of the crop for the 
State as a whole ia estimated at 1,100 tons this 
year compared to 1,100 tons last year. The 
average yield rate per acre of the crop for the 
State as a whole 19 estimated at 7.05 maunds this 
year compared to 7.62 maunds last year. 


Bajra.—300 acres are estimated to be under 
bajra crop this year compared to 400 acres last 
year. The total outturn of the crop for the State 
as a whole is estimated at 100 tons this year com- 
pared to 100 tons last year. The average yield 


rate per acre of the crop for the State as a whole 
is estimated at 6.50 maunds this year comparad 
to 6.60 maunds last year. 


Maize.—125,600 acres are estimated to be 
under maize crop this year compared to 117,200 
acres last year. The total outturn of the crop 
for the State as a whole is estimated at 37,000 
tons this year compared to 33,300 tons lust year. 
The average yield rate per acre of the crop for the 
State as » whole is estimated at 8.03 maunds this 
year compared to 7.74 maunds last year. 


Ragt.—23,800 acres ure estimated to be under 
ragi croup this year compared to 23,900 acres last 
year. The total outturn of the crop for the State 
as a whole is estimated at 5,500 tons this year 
compared to 5,200 tons last year. The average 
yield rate per acre of the crop for the State as a 
whole is estimated ut 6-30 maunds this year com- 
pared to 5.97 maunds last year. 


Other cereals.—9,500 acres are estimated to he 
under other cereals this year compared to 6,300 
acres last year. The total outturn of other cereals 
for the State as a whole is estimated at 2,100 tons 
this vear compared to 1,400 tons last year. The 
average yield rate per acre of other cereals for the 
State as a whole is estimated at 6.12 maunds this 
year compared to 6.11 maunds last year. 


Sunnhemp.—13,200 acres are estimated to be 
under sunnhemp crop this year compared _ to 
14,100 acres last year. The total outturn of the 
crop for the State as a whole is estimated at 
23,500 bales this year compared to 20,070 bales 
last year. The average yield rate per acre of the 
crop for the State aaa whole is estimated at 
1.78 bales this year compared to 1.42 bales last 
year.

AWARD 


DECISIONS 


Issue No. 1.—The rates of wages on Broad Looms of 210” R.S. and 168’ 
5.5. for the weavors. 


The ordinary hessian weaving loom in a jute mill has a reed space 
ranging from 40 inches to 90 inches. There are a very few looms in one or 
two mills with reed space of 94 inches and 102 inches. In the North Brook 
Jute Mills, which will be mentioned hereafter as the Company, the hessian 


Patt 1] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUG. 25, 1956 2033 
| | ০১০১১০০০০০০ See ree ne ee 70 


looms have reed space from 46 inches to 90 inches. The Company installed 
some additional looms of broader reed space. They are ot two classes, 
having reed space of 210 inches and 168 inches respectively. Fifteen looms 
of 210 inches reed space were installed between the dates of 18th March 
1955 and 2nd November 1955 and 15 looms of 168 inches reed space were 
installed between the dates of 165th July 1955 and 13th October 1909. 
These dates are detailed in Annexure A to the Company’s written statement. 
The Union states that the task of operating these broad looms entails great 
strain and hardship on the weaver concerned, and that the work 1s also 
attended with great personal hazard and risk. The Company, however, 
states that due to automatic devices fitted for the operation of these looms, 
the work involved there is even less strenuous than the ordinary lino looms. 
It is also recounted that during the two months of treble shift working 
of the broud looms prior to the filing of the Company’s written statement, 
which is virtually equal to six months of single shift working there was 
only one minor accident in the broad loom shed, due to a worker stepping 
on a nail on the floor, which was unconnected with the operation in the 
loom and that this fact would show that the Union’s plea of special 
hazards attended with a broad loom was unworthy of support. I may 
mention here that I inspected the new broad looms and watched while 
they were being worked. The automatic device was a great help to the 
operator. The loom automatically stopped when a piece of yarn snapped. 
It does not appear to me that the work in these broad looms was speciall 

strenuous to a worker, or that there was any special hazard attended wit 

the operation in these looms. Owing to the very nature of the work the 
production was bound to be slower than that in a narrower loom. The 
weavers were initially put on time-rates, being at Rs. 20-4 per week over 
and above the fixed dearness allowance of Rs. 8-10 per week. On 27th 
June 1955 these weavers were put on piece-rates, It may be mentioned 
that all other weavers in the Jute Textile Industry are on piece-rates. 
The wages of the workmen in the Jute Textile Industry were revised by 
the award of the Third Major Jute Textile Tribunal and the revised piece- 
rates of the weavers appear in Appendix IX of the award. These piece- 
rates were upheld by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of India. 
While the basic wages in time-rates and piece-rates of the workers 
including the weavers in the Jute Textile Industry in West Bengal were 
revised to their advantage, their dearness allowance was reduced from 
Rs, 37-6 in the month or Rs. 8-10 in the week to Rs. 32-8 in the month 
or Rs. 7-8 in the week. This award was in operation from 6th November 


1956. 


The weavers of the broad looms of the North Brook Jute Mills resented 
the change-over from time to piece-rates on 27th June 1955. After this 
date, the wages earned by the weavers fell. The Union accounts for this 
fall in wages to the introduction of the piece-rates in place of time-rates 
and the Company complains that this fall in earnings of the weavers was 
caused by the fall in production consequent on deliberate ‘‘go-slow tactics’’ 
employed by these weavers. A conciliation proceeding followed and there 
was a settlement on 27th June 1955, which appears in Annexure A to the 
Union’s written statement and Annexure D to the Company’s written 
statement. The rates fixed by this settlement are of a composite character, 
being in a time-rate of Rs. 16-6 per week of 48 hours, supplemented by 
additional earnings in the form of an incentive bonus’ contingent on 
reaching certain targets of production rates. The agreement was to remain 
in force for a period of three months. This would indicate that these rates 
were fixed for a period of transition till the weavers could finally be put 
on piece-rates. Corresponding wage rate scales were also adopted for the 
168-inch looms, which appear in Appendix D(1) to the Company’s written 


2034 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUG. 25, 1956 [Para] 


statement. Till 15th August 1955 the broad looms were being operated 
in double shifts, named A and B shifts. A third shift, the C shift, was 
started from 16th August 1955. The Union made some demands for the 
broad looms weavers including those to be employed in the C shift, which 
was to be all-might shift, and an agreement was arrived at on 12th August 
1955 between the parties. This agreement appears as Annexure B to the 
Union’s written statement and Annexure EK to the Company’s written 
statement. There were special concessions agreed to be given to the C 
shift men and also other broad loom weavers. Some of the terms will 
appear below: | 


(a) The C shift will work from 10 p.m. ito 2 a.m. and 2-30 a.m. to 
6 a.m. 


(b) Housing accommodation for workers engaged on broad looms shall 
be provided by the Company as soon as possible. 


(c) The workmen on C shift broad looms will be paid 48 hours’ wages 
for 45 hours’ work per week. 


(d) Weavers transferred from narrow to broad looms will be given 
three weeks’ time in which to learn, and if they are found 
incapable of working on broad looms, they will be sent back to 
their original narrow looms, 


(9) Workers of the C shift will be given two cups of tea and one piece 
of snack per head for each half of the night shift. ٰ 


Now comes the stage in the dispute that culminated in the present 
reference. The Union complains that it appeared on 27th August 1955 
that in paying wages to the weavers of the C shift, the Company did not 
implement the terms-of the aforesaid agreements and in paying wages to 
three of the weavers each of A and B shifts, the terms of settlement on 
26th July 1955 were violated. The weavers of the broad looms thereupon 
went on strike on 27th August 1955. There was a conciliation proceeding 
and o settlement was. arrived at between the parties on 2nd September 
1955. This settlement appears in Annexure C to the Union’s written 
statement and Annexure F to the Company’s written statement. In 
‘accordance with the terms of this settlement, dated 2nd September 1958, 
work was to be resumed on 3rd September 1955, and the three issues of 
the present proceeding were to be referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. 
The reference was, therefore, made by the Government in view of the 
terms of the settlement. 


We are concerned in this issue with the rates of wages to be paid to 
the weavers for working on the broad looms of 210 inches and 168 inches 
reed space. P.W. 1 Juman Miah, a broad loom weaver, deposed for the 
Union, and document, Ext. 1, was marked for the Union. The Company 
did not examine any witness. Documents, Exts. A to D, were marked 
forthe Company. P.W.1 Juman Miah states that he works in a 210 inches 
loom. There was again a dispute between the Company and the broad loom 
weavers regarding the wages to be paid to them in December 1955, The 
witness states that there was an agreement between the Union and the 
Company as to the rates to be payable for work on these broad looms and 
they are as shown in Ext. 1. Document, Ext. 1, shows that it was agreed 
that the settlement arrived at in the conciliation meeting, dated 26th July 
1955, for a period of three months, shall be extended up to the week ending 
8rd December 1955, and that thereafter from week ending 10th December 
1955, without prejudice to the case regarding the wage rates for the weavers 
on broad looms which is under adjudication, weavers would be put on 
plece rates as per the schedule attached to the terms of the settlement.

This shows that the broad loom weavers were paid up to 38rd December 
1955 basic time-rate at Rs, 16-6 per week স)1 48 hours plus the dearness 
allowance of Rs. 8-10 per week of 48 hours, plus the incentive bonus 
contingent on reaching certain production targets as mentioned in the 
Union’s written statement. Thereafter from week ending 10th December 
1955, the weavers of the broad looms were paid the basic rates as 
mentioned in Ext. 1, without prejudice to their claim in the present pro- 
ceedings. In cross-examination, P.W. 1 Juman Miah states that the 
broad টি weavers were now getting the proper wage and they pray for 
a continuation of the present wage rate. The witness, therefore, states 
that the piece-rates of wages, as mentioned in Ext. 1, are satisfactory to 
them and may be continued. 


Exhibit D filed by the Company shows the weaving rates for the hessian 
fabric woven on 210 inches reed space and 168 inches reed space looms. 
Exhibit D shows the same rates as appearing in Ext. 1. Exhibit D, 
however, shows rates for a greater number of variety of fabrics than 
appearing in Ext. 1. These hessian fabrics are called carpet backing 
fabrics, because these hessian clothes are used ag a background of carpets. 
Exhibit D shows the various kinds of hessian fabrics that are made on these 
broad looms and the rates of wages that follow from the weaving piece- 
rates formulated in the First Award and the Third Award of the Major 
Jute Textile Industry Tribunal. This wage chart also shows that the 
weaving rates as given by the North Brook Jute Mills in Ext. 1 are much 
higher than the weaving rates formulated by the First and the Third Awards. 
The North Brook rates are with dearness allowance of Rs. 8-10 per week, 
The Kinnison Jute Mills, under the same Managing Agents as the present 
Company is, also works the same broad looms. ‘They also pay similar wage 
rates and their wage rates have been calculated with the weekly dearness 
allowance of Rs. 7-8, the balance of Re. 1-2 per week having been included 
in the weaving rate. For that reason, corresponding to the present North 
Brook rate of 170 annas per 100 yards of 196 inches hessian plain of 16 
porter 15 shots with a weight per yard of 68.60 ozs. woven on a loom of 
210 reed space, the Kinnison weaving rate is 189 annas per 100 yarda. 


It is clear that the weaving rates as given by the Mill accounts for 
higher emoluments to the broad loom weavers than what is justified by 
the wage rates formulated in the Major Tribunal Awards principally for 
narrower looms. There can be no doubt that this advance in wage rate 
fully compensates for any additional strain that may be involved in 
working on the broad looms. Exhibit 1 also shows that in calculating the 
weekly wages, due allowance will be made for time lost through changing 
beams. They are as follows: 


On 210° R.S. Looms: Five hours’ allowance on all fabrics except 
12x12 plain where four hours will be allowed. 


On 168° K.S. Looms: Four hours’ allowance on all fabrics except 
12x12 plain where three hours will be allowed. 


Weavers will also receive wages in proportion when loom is standing for 
major repairs. Exhibits A and 401) are the actual production and the 
wages of the carpet backing weavers in ten weeks ending 2nd June 1955 
for all weavers working in the three shifts. They show quite satisfactory 
wages. Exhibit B(1) is a statement filed by the Company showing the 
average earnings excluding dearness allowance for 48 “hours from week 
ending 3rd March 1956 to week ending 5th May 1956 on all the broad 
looms as well as earnings of weavers in 48 narrow lino looms during the 
same period, The average per worker in the 30 broad looms during this 
period is Rs. 20.98, whereas the average per worker in the 48 lino looms 
during the period is Rs. 16.74. Exhibit B is a statement showing these

earnings in the broad loom and the lino loom during the period mentioned 
ahove. This statement shows the average total earnings of the broad loom 
weaver per week to be Rs. 29.605 and the average total earnings for the 
lino loom weaver to be only Rs. 24.24 per week. This statement clearly

the lino loom weavers on the rates as shown in Ext. D or Ext. 1. In these 
circumstances, it is clear that the weavers of the broad looms are getting 
more than Rs, 20-4 per week was fixed for them by way of basic wages 
when these looms were first installed, and which the Union wanted to be 
assured to the weavers even when piece-rates were introduced. P.W. 1 
Juman Miah states that the weavers wanted a basic wage of Rs. 20-4 per 
week exclusive of the dearness allowance of Rs. 37-6 per month. In the 
result, 1 1s awarded that the weavers on the broad looms of 210 inches reed 
space and 168 inches reed space shall get the same wages as were given to 
them under Ext. 1, or in other words, the same wage as is mentioned as 
the North Brook wage in Ext. D with a dearness allowance of Rs. 8-10 per 
week. These rates are the same as the Kinnison rates, mentioned in 
Ext. D, with dearness allowance of Rs. 7-8 per week. In view of the 
fact that the whole industry is now earning Rs. 7-8 per week as the 
dearness allowance, the broad loom weavers alsu shall get the same amount 
of dearness allowance, that is, at Rs. 7-8 per week, and they shall get 
their wage rates revised to include the balance of the dearness allowance 
and therefore shall get the same rates as mentioned for the Kinnison Mills 
in Ext. D. These wage rates are mentioned in Appendix A to this award. 
The concessions for time lost, as mentioned in Ext. 1, shall also continue 
and are mentioned in Appendix A. This issue is accordingly answered. 


19586 No. 2.—Are the weavers concerned entitled to wages for the period 
from 27th August 1955 till 2nd September 1955, both days inclusive, 
on account of stoppage of work? 


The broad loom weavers were on strike for the period from 27th August 
1955 till 2nd September 1955. The proceedings of the Third Major Jute 
Textile Industry Tribunal were pending from 7th April 1954 to 5th 
November 1955. The North Brook Jute Mills and their workers were 
parties to that proceeding. The strike resorted to by the broad loom 
weavers during the period from 27th August 1955 to 2nd September 1955 
was, therefore, illegal, in view of section 28, clause (b), of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. It is an established principle that an illegal strike absolves 
the liability of the employer to pay wages during the period of absence of 
the striking workmen [vide Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills case, 1952 L.A.C. 
310, Punjab National Bank’s case, 19538 L.A.C. (1)]. It is, therefore, 
awarded that the broad loom weavers who were on strike during the period 
from 27th August 1955 to 2nd September 1955 shall not get any wages 
for this period from the employer. This issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue NO. 3.—Are the weavers concerned entitled to wages for the paid 
holiday on 29th August 1955 on account of Muharram ? 


During the period of strike from 27th August 1955 to 2nd September 
1955 there was a paid holiday on 29th August 1955 on account of Muharram. 
The Union prayed for payment of wage to the broad loom weavers for this 
date only on the ground that it was a paid holiday. P.W. 1 Juman Miah 
states in his evidence that the holiday for Muharrum on 29th August 1954 
was notified in the beginning of the year. The broad loom weavers should 
get the pay for the holiday (Muharrum) on 29th August 1955. This issue 


is accordingly answered. | 
M. C. BANERJT, 


Judge, First Industrial_Tribunal.

Jails 


NOTIFICATION 
No. 2398H.J.—<8th August 1956.—The following draft of rules 


which in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 of the 
West Bengal Offenders (Release on Admonition and Probation) Act, 
1954 (West Bengal Act XXXVIII of 1954), read with section 23 of the 
Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899 (Bengal Act I of 1899), the Governor 
proposes to make 18 hereby published as required by sub-section (3) of that 
section for the information of persons affected thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 7th 
September 1956 and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto 


which may he received by the undersigned before that date will be

i!.—Inspector-Ceneral—Powers and Duties 


৫. The Inspector-General shall exercise throughout the State general 
supervision over the administration of probation. The Chief Probation 
کا‎ and other Probation Officers shall be under his administrative 
control, 


3. The Inspector-General shall prepare and submit an annual report 
to the State Government on the working of the system of probation. 


4. The report referred to in rule 3 shall be incorporated in the 
Inspector-General’s annual administration report for the year ending on 
the 3lst December immediately preceding the date of the report and shall 
contain, tnter-alia, the following particulars, namely; 


(a) Number of Probation Officers employed in each district. 


(b) Salary and other expenses paid to Probation Officers and subsidy 
to the societies or organisations providing Probation Officers 
recognised by the State Government.
