111.—Chief Probation Officer—Duties and Functions 


5. An officer shall be appointed for the State of West Bengal by the 
State Government designated as the Chief Probation Officer. Subject to 
the control and supervision of the Inspector-General, the Chief Probation 
(06061. stall administer the work of probation throughout the State, and 
shall direct, supervise and be responsible for the proper performance of 
the work of Probation Officers. 


6. The Chief Probation Officer shall submit to the Inspector-General 

half-yearly, in July and January, reports on the work and conduct of 
‘Probation Officers during the half-year immediately preceding the date of 
the report and such other reports and particulars as may be called for by 
the Inspector-General from time to time. 
7 The Chief Probation Officer shall meet every Probation Officer 
periodically and shall examine the case records of all important cases. In 
particular, he shall pay attention to the manner in which the probationer 
in such cases has been looked after generally, the number of times he has 
been met and visited at home, in office or 10 his place of employment, the 
nature of the vocation selected for the probationer, the job fixed for him, 
the manner in which his family ond other difficulties have been handled, 
how he spends his leisure, who his associates and what his earnings and 
savings are. 


\ 


8. In carrying out his duties, the Chief Probation Officer shall have 
regard to the following matters, namely :— 


He shall see that the Probation Officers work properly and exercise 
their influence for the rehabilitation of probationers. He shall 
also issue necessary orders to this end and ensure that his orders 
are carried out. He shall endeavour to make his inspection help- 
ful and shall not merely look for faults and defects but shall try 
to help the Probation Officers by giving them the benefit of his 
greater experience and wider view of life. 


1V.—Probation Officers 


9. The headquarters of a Probation Officer shall ordinarily be the 
headquarters of the district but the Inspector-General may, in consulta- 
tion with the District Magistrate, fix a sub-divisional headquarters as the 


2050 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUG. 28, 1956 [Parr آ‎ 


Someone 


headquarters of a Probation Officer. The jurisdiction of a Probation Officer 
shall cover the whole of the এ in which he is posted, or any other area, 
specified for the purpose by the State Government. The headquarters of 
a female Probation Officer shall be fixed by the Inspector-General and her 
jurisdiction shall cover such area as the Inspector-General may determine 
with the approval of the State Government. The posting and transfer of 
Probation Officers shall be made by the Inspector-General. 


10. Every Probation Officer shall, on appointment or recognition by 
the State Government, be furnished with an Identity Card os nearly as 
possible in Form I, which shall be returned to the Inspector-General when 
the Probation Officer is placed under suspension or ceases to hold office. 


11. The Inspector-General shall, as soon as possible, give notice to all 
Courts, concerned if any person ceases or is about to cease to be a 
Probation Officer. 


V.—Absence of Probation Officers on leave 


12. The Inspector-General may grant casual leave to the Chief Proba- 
tion Officer and the Chief Probation Officer may grant casual leave to other 
Probation Officers. The granting of all other kinds of leave to the Chief 
Probation Officer or any other Probation Officer shall be subject to the orders 
of the Inspector-General on application made to him in this behalf by or 
through the Chief Probation Officer, as the case may be. 


Vi.—Duties of Probation Officers 


13. When directed by a Court, a Probation Officer shall make prelimi- 
nary enquiries into the circumstances and home surroundings of an offender 
in respect of whom the question of making an order under the Act may 
arise. . _ 


14. The report on enquiries made under rule 13, shall be made as 
nearly as possible in Form II, and shall contain, inter-alia, the information 
indicated in rule 15 and such other information as may from time to time 
be laid "2 by the Inspector-General or as may be required by the Court 
concerned. 


15. In making enquiries under rule 18, the Probation Officer shal] have 
regard to the following :— 


(1) Circumstances connected with the offence. 
(2) Antecedents. 
(3) Personal factors— 

(৫) Age, place of residence, ete. 

(৮) Physical characteristics, if any. 


(6) Psychological traits—personality, character, and emotional 
stability. 


(d) Education. 
(e) Work and record of work, income. 


(f{) Leisure time activities.

pe a a 
(4) Family history, relations with members of family, economic condi- 
tion of the family. 


(6) Associations. 


16. All information collected on enquiry referred to in rule 18 shall be 
concisely stated, evaluated and presented in the report submitted to the 
(Court under rule 14 not later than the day on which it is due. 


17. Probation Officers shall not divulge any information concerning 
their enquiries or work of probation to any person other than the authorities 
to whom they are required to report, except in so far as 1٦١ 18 necessary to 
do so in the interest of the probationer. ۱ 


18. Female probationers shall be placed under the supervision of female 
Probation Officers where the services of such officers are available. 


All cases where a female probationer is placed under the supervision of 
a male Probation Officer, shall be reported immediately to the District 
Magistrate and the Chief Probation Officer. 


19. A Probation Officer shall explain to the probationer the conditions 
of the supervision order, and shall by warning and persuasion and by the 
exercise of personal influence, endeavour to ensure the observance thereof 
by the probationer. If the probationer disregards any of the conditions, 
the Probation Officer shall make a report as 5 provided. 


20. The Probation Officer shall maintain a case record in respect of 
every probationer in which shall be recorded every important event and 
significant change in the behaviour, activities, attitude and associations 
01 the probationer during the period of probation. 


21. In recording cases the Probation Officer shall be objective and 
factual, The records kept by him shall, as far as practicable, indicate all 
rituation and developments affecting the probationer. The sources of 
information shall be clearly stated. 


22. All Probation Officers shall, subject to any directions given by the 
Court (whether in the probation order or otherwise) or by the Chief 
Probation Officer, visit the houses of the probationers. The Probation 
کت‎ shall supplement such visits by making enquiries in the neighbour- 
001. 


23. The Probation Officer shall keep in close touch with the probationer 
and shall during the first month of probation meet him as frequently as is 
necessary. Jater the number of visits or meetings shall depend on the 
conduct and mode of life of the probationer, but shall not normally be less 
than once a month. A Probation Officer shall advise and befriend a proba- 
tioner and, where necessary, endeavour to secure suitable employment for 
him. He shall also assist him in averting evil influence and victimisa- 
tion, and to this end secure the assistance of public authorities, if 
necessary. 


<4. In planning out the course of reformation the Probation Officer 
shall have regard to the matters mentioned in rule 15. In the case of 
young probationers particular attention shall be paid to the family 
conditions and associations of the probationers. 


_ #0. The probationer shall be required by the Probation Officer occa- 
sionally to report himeelf at the Probation Officer's office. The Probation 
Officer shall also decasionally visit the probationer at his residence. The 
time and place of reporting shall be so arranged as not to cause unnecessary

hardship to the probationer afd to secure proper privacy and to avoid 
probationers associating with each other.

26. In the case of school-going boys or girls, the Probation Officer shall 
make enquiries regarding the boy or girl from his or her teacher 88 to 
his or her attendance and progress, but the boy or girl shall not be visited 
in the school premises. 


27. In the case of young probationers under 16 years of age, the Proba- 
tion Officer shall endeavour to secure the probationer’s membership of some 
recognised organisation for the care and protection of the young such ag 
the Sunday School, club, the Association of the Boy Scouts and Girl 
Giuides of other similar associations. 


8. A Probation Officer shall not unnecessarily disclose his identity or 
functions to those with whom he may come in contact in the course of his 
duties. 


29. A Probation Officer shall not wear any badge distinctive of his 
office. 


Vil.—Report By Probation Officers 


30. When an offender is released on probation and placed under the super- 
vision of a Probation Officer by a Court, the Probation Officer shall, without 
delay, send to the Chief Probation Officer a statement as nearly as 
possible in Form III containing the particulars of the offender entrusted 
to him. 


31. A Probation Officer shall report on the conduct and mode of life 
of a probationer and generally on his progress to the Court before which the 
probationer is bound by his bond, in accordance with any direction 
riven by the Court. Copies of the report shall also be sept at the same 
time to the Chief Probation Officer by the Probation Officer. Reports 
shall be made, unless otherwise directed by the Court, once every month; 
they تا الله‎ marked secret and addressed to the Presiding Officer of the 
Court by name. They shall not be published. 


de. Ifa probationer fails to observe any of the conditions of the bond 
and supervision order, and if the failure is not such as ¢an be 1۳50076 or 
if the matter cannot be set right by the personal influence of the Probation 
Officer without the intervention of the Court, the Probation Officer shall 
report the matter to the Court before which the probationer is hound by 
his bond and pray for the Court’s order. A copy of the report shall also 
he sent at the same time to the Chief Probation Officer by the Probation 
Officer. A copy of the Court’s order when passed shall also be sent by the 
Probation Officer to the Chief Probation Officer. 


33. A Probation Officer shall send to the Court and the Chief Proba- 
tion Qfficer a final report on the conduct and progress of each probationer 
on the termination of the period for which he is placed under supervision. 


Ps Every Probation Officer shall submit to the Chief Probation 
Officer, — 


(1) a half-yearly report in January and July on the conduct and 
progress of all probationers in his district during the half-year 
immediately preceding the date of the report containing, 
inter alia, the following particulars, namely :— 

(a) number of probationers at the beginning of the half-year; 


(6) number of offenders placed on probation during the half-year;

(2) such other reports as may be required hy the Inspector-General or

86. Every Probation Officer shall maintain the following records: — 


(1) A diary showing his day-to-day work including preliminary 
enquiries, attendance at Courts, visits to probationers, contact 
made in the advancement of probation work and other duties. 
A copy of the diary shall be submitted to the Chief Probation 
Officer every week. The diary shall be closed on the 84 
December each year and deposited as a confidential record in the 
Office of the Chief Probation Officer. 


(2) Separate files in respect of each probationer containing a history- 
sheet for each recording all important events during the period 
of his probation and reports including copies of preliminary 
reports submitted by him and orders passed by the Court 
during the preiod of probation. In case ৪ probationer 
is permitted by the Court to live in another district, the

Probation Officer. 


(3) An index card and chronological record as nearly as possible in

(4) Such other records as may be directed by the Inspector-General 
from time to time. 


37. The District Magistrate or any other officer, not below the rank of 
a Deputy Magistrate, duly authorised by him, may inspect the work of any 
Probation Officer and any record in the Office of the Probation Officer 
working within his jurisdiction. 


48. After the expiry of the period of probation, the history-sheets shal] 
he maintained in the (ffice of the District Magistrate in the district and 
in the Office of the Inspector-General in Calcutta. The history-sheets, 
index cards and chronological record shall be maintained as 17 Class 
records and preserved for 12 years. Other papers mentioned in rule 36 
shall be preserved for 3 years.

NOTIFICATION 


No. 14780L..Ref.—27th August 1956.——-The following draft of amend- 
ments which, in exercise of the power conferred by section 59 of the West 
- Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 (West Bengal Act I of 1954), the 
(toverner proposes to make in the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Rules, 
1954, as subsequently amended (hereinafter referred to as the said rules), is 
hereby published, as required: by sub-section (1) of the said section, for the 
information of persons likely to be affected thereby. 

2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 10th 
September 1956, and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto, which 
may be received by the undersigned before that date, wel be considered : 


Draft Amendments 


1. For sub-rule (8) of rule 10 of the said rules, substitute the following 
sub-rule, namely— 
“(3) Applications for ad-interim payment under section 12 shall be 
pe eee to the Collector or any other officer authorised by the 
‘ollector in this behalf. The application shall contain all parti- 
culars of the estates and interests of the intermediary situated 
in the district. Where the applicant held estates situate in more 
than one district, such application may be filed before the 
Collector of the district on the Tauzt Roll of which such estates 
are borne. Every such application shall be in Form 3A appended 
to these rules or in a form substantially similar thereto. Where 
the application is for ad-interom payment under sub-section (2) 
of section 12, true copies of the Deed of Trust or Dedication or 
Arpannama or any other document in support of such claim shall 
also be furnished along, with the application.” 
2. For sub-rule (2) of rule 11 of the said rules, substitute the following 
sub-rule, namely— 

‘“(2) For the purpose of sub-rule (1), the Collector may take into con- 
- gideration any return furnished by an intermediary in pursuance 
of the proclamation issued under rule 6, or the attested record 
of the revisional settlement operation, where available, or the 
record-of-rights prepared according to the provisions of the 
Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 and kept in the District Record Room. 
He may, if necessary, reguive an intermediary to produce

No. 3648Dis./D/100-1138/55.—18th August 1956.—Whereas under ‘the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No; 4697Dis./D/ 
10L-113/55, dated the 27th Septefiber F955, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Victery Iron Works, Behares Road, Salkia, Howrah and their 
workmen reptesented by Iron & Steel Workmen's Union, 172 Benares Road, 
Salkia, Howrah, regarding the matters specified in the schedule thereto was 
referred for adjudication to the Third Industrial Tribunal; 

And whereas the said Third Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the 
State Government its award on the said industrial dispute; . 

Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the. 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the (Governor is pleased 
hereby to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between Victory Iron Works, Benayes 
Road, Salkia, Howrah and their workmen represented by Iron & Steel 
Workmen's Union, 172 Benares Road, Salkia, Howrah. 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 
PRESENT ; 
Suri J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Third Industral Tribunal. 


For the Umon: Surat KALI CHAKRAVARTI, Vice-President. 
For the Company: Strr1 P. R. MUKHERJI, Pleader. 


AWARD 


1. By order No. 4697Dis./1D/10L-113/55, dated the 27th Septentber 
1955, the Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Victory Tron Works, Benares Road, Salkia, Howrah and their 
workmen represented by Iron & Steel Workmen’s Union, 172 Benares 
Road, Salkia, Howrah, regarding the matters specified in the schedule, to 
the Third Industrial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of the Industrial 
J)isputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 592Dis.//12L-5/52, dated the 281 _ 
February 1953, for adjudication. 


2. After usual summons the parties entered appearance and filed their 
written atatements, The pleadings were completed on 19th December 1955. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file their lists of documents. Then 
after adjournments the case was taken up for hearing., 


3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the Order of 
Reference are as follows: — 


(1) Pay and Dearness Allowance. 
(2) Leave. 7 
(3) If Joykissen, Bhaglu and Chhotolal should be made permanent? 


DECISION 


Lssues Nos, 1 to 3.—The parties filed a joint petition of compromise 
relating to the issues and prayed for an award in terms thereof. Heard 
the representatives of both sides. The terms are fair. I, therefore, give 


3300 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 = [Parr I 


ee

The issue that falls for decision is as mentioned in the order of refer- 


ence and is as follows: 
issue 


(1) Production bonus. 


AWARD 
DECISIONS 


The Company is the manufacturer of hydrogenated vegetable product, 
commonly known as ‘‘Vanaspati’’. ا1‎ started production in 1940. The 
processes in the manufacture are as follows: (1) Vegetable oil is refined; 
(2) thereupon it is hydrogenated; (3) then it is again refined; (4) then 
deodorised; and (5) thereafter the same is filled in tins. In 19438, the 
Company introduced a production bonus for payment exclusively to some 
of the mistries, who took part in the actual manufacture of the product. It 
will appear from Ext. D, being a list of the categories of workmen employed 
in the industry, that there are in all 130 workmen inasmany as 19 categories. 
In all these, the men in categories 1 to 12 numbering 26 are skilled workers 
and mistries, those in categories 13 to 16 numbering 30 are semi-skilled 
workers and those in categories 17 to 19 numbering 74 are unskilled workers. 
It is the admitted case of both parties that production bonus when introduc- 
ed was paid to only 14 men covered by the categories 1 to 6 in Ext. D. The 
hydrogenation of the oil is done in the machine at the rate of 5 tons of the 
product per charge. The production departments work for full 24 hours in 


Part (( THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 6 3303 
three “shifts. The normal output in 24 hours has been fixed at 5 charges 
giving out 25 tons and for each extra charge of 5 tons in the course of the 
sume 24 hours a bonus of Rs. 10 was agreed tp be paid to the 14 men in the 
category Nos. | to 5 in 1786, D. The production bonus of Rs. 10 per day 
for an extra charge of 5 tons was earned since 1943. This rate was 
increased to Rs. 15 in September 1948, and was further increased to Rs. 17 
in April 1950. Tn June 1958, the production bonus was increased {from 
Rs. 17 to Rs. 20 per batch of 5 tons after the production of 25 tons per day. 
Ii was further agreed that Rs. 10 out of the sum was to be distributed to 
those workers who were getting the production bonus so far, or in other 
words, the 14 men comprising the category 5 in Ext. D and the balance of 
Rs. 10 was to be distributed to the other permanent workers who were not: 
getting any bonus so far. This arrangement of the production bonus is 
continuing till today, 


The Union, in its written statement, complains that the present system 
for the payment of production bonus in which the total production is divided 
into two equal halves, then one half is paid to 10 per cent. of the favoured 
workers and the other half to 90 per cent. of the workers 18 unjust and un- 
equitable and is followed with the ulterior purpose of wrecking the unity of 
the workers. The Union has been repeatedly requesting the Company to 
change the present system of production bonus for a just and equitable 
system but without any result. After an unsuccessful conciliation proceed- 
ing over this matter, the dispute has been referred to the Tribunal. The 
Union claims that the production bonus should be raised to Rs. 40 per 
hatch instead of Rs. 20 and that the production bonus should be paid to 
each worker in proportion to his wage. 


The Company opposed this claim on the ground that on the present cost 
of production and selling price of the product, the target which has been 
fixed as normal production over and above which production bonus is to be 
gaven is very low and the workmen can easily produce and they actually 
stoduce 30 tonsa per day. It is, therefore, stated that it 1s not only 
impossible to lower down the target for the purpose of payment of production 
honus, but it is necessary to raise it to a higher level. The present ratio of 
distribution of Rs. 10 to the Refinery Hardening Mistries, and Rs. 10 to the 
other workers was fixed by a settlement by the workers themselves, and any 
alteration of the same will create difficulties and unrest amongst the workers 
eoncerned. The demand for the revision of the production bonus scheme 
now tn existence should be rejected. 


P. W. 1 Shri Bimal Chandra Basu, a semi-skilled workman working in 
the Pump House, was examined for the Wnion and 0.P.W. 1 Shri P. N. 
Mathur, the Manager of the Factory, was examined for the Company. 
Documents, Kxt. A to Ext. F(8), were marked for the Company. Exhibit 
A is a proceedings of the Works Committee held at the Mill premises on 
26th June 1953, in which the production honus of Rs. 17 was increased 
to Ra. 20 per batch of 5 tons after the production of 25 tons per day and 
the scheme of distribution of production bonus waa changed. Exhibit B is 
a letter, dated 4th March 1954, by which the President of the Union, Shri 
Shib Nath Banerji, called upon the Company to alter the scheme of distri4 
bution of production bonus on the ground that the existing scheme was 
unjust and inequitable. Exhibit C is a statement of working analysis show- 
ing the expenses of the ‘“‘Vanaspati” product per maund and the sale 
realisation per maund, showing the profit or loas per maund’in the years 
1961-52, 1942-58, 1953-54 and 1954-55. This document shows that there 
was a loss per maund of the manufactured product in 1951-42 and in 1954- 
65, and there was profit per maund of the manufactured product in 1952-53 
and 1953-54. Exhibit D is a list of the categories of workmen with their 


3304 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Pant I 
সিপিএ 
rates of wages per day and the number of workmen working in the different 
categories. Exhibit K is a statement showing the details of wages given to 
unskilled workmen in the Company, as well as in three local ‘‘Vanaspati’’ 
factories, indicating that the Company was paying the highest wages to the 
unskilled workers. Exhibits F to 1°(3) sre the Report and Statement of 
Accounts of the Company for the years ending 30th April 1952, 30th April 
1953, 30th April 1954, and 30th April 1955. 


The evidence of P. W. 1 Shri Bimal Chandra Basu shows that the 
present system of payment of production bonus is that half of the amount 
is paid to only 14 men and the other half is paid to the other workers, that 
there are 130 permanent workers besides 40 temporary workers in the 
Company, and that the temporary workers do not,get any production bonus. 
P.W. ۱ states that the grievance of the workers is that the production bonus 
should be distributed equitably amongst the workers and that an equitable 
distribution may be attained by distributing the bonus proportionately to 
the pay received by the employees. O.P.W. 1 Shri P.N. Mathur states that 
it is not possible for the Company to increase the bonus to more than 
Rs. 20, as it will be uneconomical. He states that it is not possible to 
distribute the bonus equally to all workmen, because there will be discontent 
umongst the mistries who are the real producers. He states that these 14 
mistries who received the production bonus are the persons who can increase 
the production and therefore they are given this incentive bonus. He fur- 
ther states that on an enquiry ۳ found that the skilled workers in the 
categories of 1 to 5 in Exhibit D were getting less pay than similar workers 
in other factories in Calcutta, and that the unskilled workers in other 
factories were getting more wages than similar workers in this factory. 
He, therefore, justified the present scheme of paying half of the production 
bonus, being Rs. 10 per day to 14 mistries and the other half of Rs. 10 to 
the rest of 116 workers. It appears that in June 1953, when the production 
bonus payable to the 14 mistries was reduced from Rs. 17 to Rs. 10, their © 
daily. wage was increased from annas four to annas seven. ‘he other 
mistries also got increase in their daily wage from annas four to annas seven 
per day and the other workers were given an increase of 6 pies per day. It 
appears in the evidence of O.P.W. 1.that the Foreman No. 1 in Exhibit D 
got more than annas seven increase in the daily wage, No. 2 got slightly 
less than annas seven, and the mistries in item Nos. 3, 4 and 5 got a little 
less than annas six increase per day. It is stated that the 14 mistries are 
the key-men for increasing production, although they cannot do so without 
the others. The balance-sheets, Exhibit I’ series show loss in the year 
1951-52, profit in the years 1952-53 and 1953-54. There was also a working 
loss in the year 1954-55. It appears that no provision for depreciation was 
made in any of these years, and no dividend was paid to the share-holders 
and no Managing Agents commission was paid. It is, therefore, argued by 
the learned advocate for the Company that the production bonus should not 
be increased in any way. It also appears from the document, Exhibit 8, 
which is the first letter of the President of the Union formulating the 
demdhd of the production bonus, that no increase of the production bonus 
was demanded at that date. The learned President for the Union, who 
addressed the court at the hearing of the case, admitted that no claim for 
increase of the quantum of the production bonus was made prior to the 
reference of the dispute to the Tribunal, although the Union has ۵۸8 
demanding for better and more equitable distribution of the production 
bonus since 1954. Considering all these circumstances and the fact that 
the financial condition of the Company is not strong, it is decided that 
there should be no increase of the quantum of the production bonus, and that 
the production bonus shall continue to be Rs. 20 per extra charge of 5 tons . 
after the production of 25 tons per day, as it is in existence at the present 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3305 


time. There can be no doubt that the scheme of distribution of the bonus 
is inequitable inusmuch as half the amount goes to only 14 men and the 
other half goes to the rest 01 116 permanent workers. This scheme of dis- 
tribution cannot be defended by the statement of the Manager, O.P.W. را‎ 
that the mistry Nos. 1 to 14 were getting less basic wage than the 
mistries in other ‘‘Vanaspati’’ factories in Calcutta. On this point, the 
only evidence was the statement of the Manager, O.P.W. 1. In any case, 
the scheme of distribution of the production bonus as it is availing at the 
present time is inequitable and is a potent cause of industrial dispute. It 
is awarded that the production bonus shall be distributed to the permonvent 
workmen in proportion to the basic wage earned by the individual ۰ 
nent workmen. The mistry Nos. 1 to 14 have already got an increase 8 
the daily basic wage in*1953. Should the Company find it necessary, a 
further increase in the basic wage may be given to them, but the deficiency 
in their basic wage should not be sought to be made up by an unjustly large 
share in the production bonus, as was being done so long. This issue is 


accordingly answered. 
M. C. BANERJT, 


Judge, First Industrial Tribunal.

The aforesaid dispute has been referred to this Tribunal for adjudication 
under Government order No. e 66Dis./D/11L-416/55, dated 24th April 
1956. 


The issues as per schedule to the order of reference stand as follows: 


(1) Whether the action of the Management in reducing the supply of 
raw materials and curtailing the work ef the workers was 
justified ? 


(2) To what relief are the workers entitled? 


AWARD 


The Union in its written statement has stated that the Company 1s an 
old one, and is a prosperous concern with about 600 workmen in its employ. 
There was no rule of service, no rule of leave and holidays, and no 
provision for Provident Fund and ratuity, and the minimum basic wages 
were also less in many cases. So, the workmen in order to better their lot 
and remove legitimate grievances formed a Union in 1950, which, however, 
was not accepted in good grace by | the Company. Two disputes between 
the parties were referred to two. Tribunals. The Tribunal presided over by 
Shri G, Palit passed an award on 14th June 1952 (which was published on 
26th June 1952 in the Calcutta Gazette) on several issues including 
minimum basic wages, bonus and involuntary unemployment for some time 
in a year. The Tribunal presided over by Shri M. N. Gan fixed dearness 
allowance for the workers. This award was made on 29th December 1953 
and was published in the Calcutta Gazette on 28th January 1954. But 
these awards have not been implemented by the Company. On the 
contrary, the Company in order to victimise the workers, who were 
members of the Union, pursued a policy of discrimination, and made two 
groups—one with the Union workers known as Russian Fauz, and the other 
with the workers who were loyal to the Company known as American Fauz. 
The Russian Fauz were given very meagre supply of materials, while the 
American Fauz as much materials aa they hiked and were capable of 
working with. In consequence of this reduction of the supply of raw 
materials there was curtailment of wages of workers during the period from 
6th June 1954 to 6th November 1954 and again from 4th Tale 108955 to 
10th October 1955 in this Company to the great sufferings of the workers 
and consequent loss of their income. The Union wanted to say that the 
action of the Management was unjustified, and accordingly it claimed that 
the workers should be paid normal wages, which they were entitled to get 
during the period when there was curtailment of work. 


The Company contested the claim on merits, and in its written statement 
has stated, among others, that it manufactures rubber shoes, and that these 
articles are sold mostly during the winter and rainy seasons, as in other 
seasons there is practically no market for the same. Its products are 
restricted between June and November. The Company has denied the 
allegation of the Union that it made discrimination in the matter 01 
distribertion of raw materials and curtailment of work among the workers. 
It has also denied the allegation of the Tnion that it termed one group of 
the workers as American Fauz and the other group as Russian Fauz. It 
further denied having recruited new hands during the dull season. 


issue No. 1—Whether the action of the Management in reducing the supply 
of raw materials and curtailing the work of the workers was 
justified? 


At the very outset, T may say that the scope of adjudication is limited 
by the issue No. 1, which is hased on the assumption that there was 
reduction in the supply of raw materials and curtailment of work of the 


issue 05 framed by the Govertiment in the schedule to the order of reference 
it ig admitted on behalf of the Company in its written statement that the 
rubber shoes and canvas shoes, which this Company manufactures, are sold 
mostly during the winter and rainy seasons, and its productions are being 
restricted between June and November every year, when there is practically 
no market for such articles. 0. P. W. 1 Shri M. S. Saigan, who is the 
General Manager and Director of the Company, has also deposed 17) ۵ 
case that the rubber and canvas shoes, which the Company manufactures, 
are sold mostly during the months of November, December, January, 
February, March and April, and also in May and June, but in the months 
of July, August and September and also in the first part of October there 1s 
practically no sale of such shoes in the market. The Union has specifically 
mentioned two periods in its written statement, when there was reduction 
in the supply of raw materials and curtailing wages of workers in this 
Company. One period is from 6th June 1954 to 6th November 1954 and 
the other period is from 4th July 1955 to 10th October 1955, In the issue 
appearing in the schedule to the order of reference no mention is made of 
the period. In view of what has been stated in the written statement of 
the Union, there is no difficulty in accepting the said period as the period 
when there was curtailment of wages of workers in this Company. The 
moot question for consideration in this dispute is whether there was 
justification for such curtailment of wages of the workers in consequence of 
reduction in the supply of raw materials. Both parties have adduced 
evidence, and I have carefully considered the same. On a consideration of 
the matter it is extremely difficult to say that the Management pursued a 
policy of discrimination amongst the workers employed in the factory in the 
mutter of distribution of work or supply of raw materials. The evidence of 
P, W. 1 Shri Ram Babu Saha, who is the General Secretary of the Union, 
is not at all helpful in this respect. He has frankly stated that he has no 
‘personal knowledge regarding the facts deposed to by him, but he heard 
the same from the workers who came and reported so to him. He _ has 
no doubt stated in his evidence that the Comrany adopted the policy of 
discrimination in order to victimise the workers, who were associated or 
connected with the Union. His version is that those who were loyal to the 
Management were called American Fauz and those who were connected 
with the Union were known as Russian Fauz, and that the Russian Fauz 
were given less work, while the American Fauz were given more work. 
But as his knowledge in this respect is based on hearsay, no importance or 
weight can be put to his version. P. ভা. 2 Shri Subai, who is a piece-rated 
worker of this Company, does not fullv support the version of P. W. 1, the 
General Secretary of the Union. He has stated clearly that the workers of 
both the groups—American Fauz and Russian Fauz—used to get work from 
the Company, and so also the new recruits. All that he wanted to say 38 
that those workers who were connected with the Union were given (۵ 
work. As againat this, there is the positive testimony of 0. P. W. 1 Shri 
M.S. Saigan, General Manager and Director of the Comrany, to the 
effect that in this Company there is no group of workers known as American 
Fauz and Russian Fauz, and that the Management does not make any 
discrimination in the matter of distribution of work or supply of raw 
materials to the workers. He has also denied the fact that the Company 
recruited new hands during the dull season. That there waa no recruitment 
of new hands during the last few years is also evident from the materials 
placed before the Tribunal. The Union in its written statement has 
stated that this Company emplovs about 500 workmen. In the written 


statement filed in connection with an industrial dispute before Shri 


3308 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Part T 


ےس یی سے 


dg 
G. Palit, it appears that the Union claimed then also that the Company 
employed 500 workman or more. P. W. 1 General Secretary of the Union 
was constrained to admit this fact in his cross-examination. An industrial 
dispute between the parties was referred to Shri G. Palit in the year 1951, 
and it appears that the Union filed written statement in connection with 
that dispute on 5th November 1951. There is also the statement of the 
General Manager and Director of the Company that the strength of their 
workmen will be about 400, and such number fluctuates from time to time, 
and that they have been maintaining that strength since the inception of 
the Company. In view of what has been stated ا‎ there cannot possibly 
remain any scope for argument that the Company recruited new hands in 
order to victimise the workers who were connected with the Union by 
curtailing their wages. After giving my careful and anxious consideration 
to the materials on record. J hold that the Union has not succeeded in 
establishing that the Company pursued a policy of discrimination amongst 
the workers in the matter of distribution of work or supply of raw ee ph 


That there was some curtailment in the wages of the workers during the 
periods as specifically mentioned in the written statement of the Union is 
an udmitted fact. Presumably, this was due to the fact that there was 
rractically no market for canvas and rubber shoes, which this Company 
manufactures. From the evidence 1t appears that such shoes are sold 
mostly during the months of November, December, January, February, 
March and April and also in May and June, but in the months of* July, 
August and September and also in the first part of October -there is 
practically no sale of such shoes in the market. The General Manager and 
Director of the Company has deposed that during the period when there is 
no sale of such shoes in the market, the Company closes its factory at 
12 o’clock instead of 5 p.m. P. W. 1 Shri Ram Babu Saha, General 
Secretary of the Union, has also admitted in his cross-examination that 
during: the periods as mentioned in the written statement of the Union the 
fectory, which opened as usual at 8 a.m., used to be closed sometime at 
12 o’clack, fihd in no Case after 12 o’clock the work continued 11) the 
factory. P. W. 2 Shri Subai, who is one of the workers, has also deposed 
in the same line. Their evidence does not indicate or suggest for a moment 
that some workers were allowed to work in the factory even after 12 o’clock. 
This also negatives the contention of the Union that the Company pursued 
a policy of discrimination in the matter of distribution of work amongst the 
workers. It appears from the award given by Shri G. Palit that the 
question of such closure of the factory also cropped up before him. Shri 
Palit while dealing with the issue No. ‘—1involuntary unemployment 
observed that such involuntary unemployment of the workers was unavoid- 
able, because there were seasons in which the rubber work was brisk and 
when it was dull and it all depended on the market. He further observed 
that in the winter and the rainy seasons the demand for rubber goods was 
more than the other times of the year. Thus, it is apparent that the 
question of curtailment of work of the workers and of their wages during 
the dull season did not arise for the first time during the periods as 
specifically mentioned in the written statement of the Union, but as a 
matter of fact, this practice has been going on in this factory all along 
since its very inception. Regard being had to the nature of the Company’s 
business, and on a consideration of the fact that it manufactures canvas and 
rubber shoes only, which are sold mostly during the winter and the rainy 
seasons for which there is no market at other times of the year, it cannot 
be said that the action of the Management in Closing the factory at 
12 o’clock during the periods specifically mentioned in the written 
statement of the Union, which were admittedly dull season of the years in 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3300 


yfestion, was mala fide and illegal. The Management best knows how to 
regulate its busimess. Tt could not be proved that the Management closed 
its factory at 12 o’clock during the saig periods to put the workers ۵٥ 
sufferings. It cannot be believed for a moment that ۶9 Management will 
arbitrarily and capriciously close its factory after 4 hours’ work instead of 
8 hours’, and stop production when it fetches profits. Such closure of the 
factory at 12 0’clock during the dull season was inevitable and unavoidable. 
If by such closure of the factory there was any curtailment of work and 
wages of the workers, there was no helr for it, and the Management cannot 
be blamed for that. So, the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the 
action of the Management in reducing the supply of raw materials and 
curtailing the work of the workers during the periods in question was 
justified. The Tribunal is unahle to hold that the Management سا‎ this 
respect acted with any mala fide motive, This issue is answered in the 
affirmative. 


issue No. 2—To what relief are the workers entitled? 


Tn view of what has been stated above, the question of giving any 
relief to the workers does not and Cannot arise. Hence, the workers are not 
entitled to any relief. This issue is answered accordingly.

AWARD 


Babcock & Wilcox of India, Ltd. (hereinafter called the Company), 18 
a private limited Company, which was registered in India on July 1, 1947 
Prior to that, the business was carried on in India by a Branch office of 
Babcock & Wilcox, London, from 1906. It does no manufacturing. It 
imports water tubes, boilers, guper-heaters, stokers, coal conveyors, steel 
chimieies, cranes, etc. and also spare parts of those articles. It also 
erects new boilers. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3311 


শপ রর ক রা 


Babcock & Wilcox Workers’ Union (hereinafter called the Union) 
wants to say that the dismissal of seven workmen as per attached List A 
regarding issue No. 1 was illegal and unfair, and against all principles of 
natural justice. So, their reinstatement with full compensation for the 
period of forced unemployment was claimed by the Union. The Union 
further submitted that the suspension of eight workmen as per attached 
List B regarding issue No. 2 was illegal and mala fide, and as such the 
Company might be directed to allow them to resume their work. The 
Union further demanded payment of bonus to each worker for the years 
1953 and 1954 equivalent to three months’ total wages in addition to one 
month’a bonus that has been granted by the Company. It was also 
submitied by the Union that the workmen concerned have been deprived 
of increments since 1953, and as such an annual increment of Its. 5 was 
claimed on their behalf. 


The Company says that the dismissal of these seven workers as per 
attached List A was justified, as they were found guilty of gross mis- 
conduct. The Company stated that in dismissing those workmen, it 
followed scrupulously all principles of natural justice. Regarding the 
Union’s claim for bonus, the Company wanted to say that such claim is 
not at all tenable, inasmuch as the trading results as disclosed 1 the 
balance sheets for the years 1953 and 1954 were not satisfactory, and there 
was no available surplus to be distributed amongst the workmen as bonus, 
after meeting all the prior charges. The Company paid one month’s basic 
wage as bonus for some years to the workmen, because the trading results 
of the Company were favourable, and there were some profits to justify 
payment of annual bonus, but the Company had at no time made any pay- 
ment in a year, in which the Company suffered trading losses. The 
Company had made ea gratia payments in 1958 and 1954, because it had 
some small profits for which such payment could be made, but this pay- 
ment was not a condition of service of the workmen. Regarding annua 
increment for the Hide Road godown staff, the Company has contended 
that it engages about 45 workmen in the said establishment, most of whom 
are unskilled workers. The Company grants increment only in deserving 
cases, and there is no grade system with time-scale of increment. The 
total remunerations paid by the Company to its workmen employed in the 
aforesaid godown are fair, reasonable and adequate, and ৪০ there is no 
justification of any increase in their existing wages. 


Issue No. 2—Whether the suspension of the eight workers as per attached 
List B was justified. What reliefs are they entitled to? 


This isaue is taken up first. It needs no more any adjudication by the 
Tribunal, inasmuch as both the parties have amicably settled this dispute, 
and filed a joint petition of compromise on 2]s{. June 1996 hefore the 
Tribunal. The said joint petition of compromise is on the record, and I 
have persued the same. The terms appear to he fair and reasonable, and 
as such they are accepted. It is, therefore, ordered that an award in terms 
of the settlement arrived at between the parties with reference ٥ this 
issue be made. The joint petition of compromise together with Annexure A 
do form part of the award as Appendices. This issue No. 2 is thus 
disposed of, 


Issue No. ---Annual increments for the Hide Road godown workmen. 


It appears from the evidence that about 48 workmen work in the Hide 
Road godown, and the majority of them are coolies. They come under the 
category of unskilled workers. 4 1s admitted that there are no fixed 
[70195 or scales of pay for these workers 1n this Company. The Union has 


3312 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Parr 1 


urged that annual increment should be awarded to all the workmen. as 
the Company grants increment to some of them. It is true no doubt that 
the Company granted increment to'some of the workers, but such increment 
was granted to them in consideration of their merit and efficiency. 4 
seems that granting of such increment lies absolutely at the discretion of 
the Management, but this fact by itself does not justify that annual 
increment should be awarded to all the workmen as a matter of right. In 
the absence of any fixed scales of pay or grades it is not possible to give any 
effective order calling upon the Company to give increments. The minimum 
basic ss of a worker in this godown, if taken alone, appears to he some- 
what inadequate. But the fact remains that the workers in this godown are 
getting dearness allowance according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scale, which is a generous and lavish one. So, the total emoluments paid 
to the workers of the godown are indeed decent and handsome, and 
compare favourably with similar concerns in the locality. In my view, 
the minimum total emoluments of a worker in this godown cannot, by any 
means, be said to be inadequate or low, so as to justify any increase regard 
being had to the length of service. Another thing is to be considered in 
this connection. Before incremental scales can be imposed hy an adjudica- 
tion, it is essential to see whether the employer would be able to bear its 
burden. The financial condition of the Company must be such as to lead 
to the condition that it would be able to pay increments year by year for 
an appreciably number of years, for wage scales when settled are intended 
to be long-term schemes. Thus, not only financial ability, but financial 
stability are also essential. In my view, as the evidence indicates, both 
the elements are wanting in the instant case. It has transpired from the 
evidence of 0.۲.۱۲۷۰ 3 Mr. K. J. Holt, who is Assistant Secretary of the 
Company, that the profits of this Company from the year 1950 to 1995 are 
gradually declining. He has deposed no doubt that during the next few 
dori it is hoped that the financial position of the Company might improve, 
mut simply on the basis of such mere expectation incremental scales for 
the workers cannot be thrust upon the Company. There is nothing to 
indicate that such hope as expressed by Mr. Holt would spurt into sudden 
prosperity. of the Company of a lasting nature. In my view, no ad hoc 
increments should be given, when there are no fixed grades and incremental 
scales already in existence. Incremental scales can be settled no doubt 
by the Tribunal, but the materials on the record are not adequate enough 
for laying down such incremental scales. In fact, materials are not of 
such a nature which would make it advisable to settle incremental scales 
in this case. There can be no doubt that ordinarily speaking there should 
be fixed annual increment, which would offer encouragement to the workers 
for better work and would provide for their proper maintenance, as they 
advance in age, but as the matters stand, there is no help. The workmen 
concerned would do well to co-operate with the Company for some time 
more with a view to improve its condition and to renew their claims there- 
after. So, considering the matter in all its bearings, I do not find my way 
to introduce any annual increment for the Hide Road godown workmen at 
present. ~This issue is decided accordingly. 


Issue No, : ‘Bonus for the years 1953 and 1954 


Regarding bonus, the Union’s claim is that the Company should pay 
the workmen concerned bonus equivalent to three months’ total wages for 
the years 1958 and 1954, in addition to one month’s bonus, which the 
Company has paid to such workers at Puja time. The Union’s claim, as 
I understood from its written statement, is that the Company has been pay- 
ing one month’s bonus to the workmen at Puja time for a long time past, 
without any reference to profit and loss, and that over and above that 


15711) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3313 


লিপ রা সা‏ 9ة ت0 
ar a‏ 1 :44 0 وو وو رو و CT‏ 1 


bonus. which the workers get as customary bonus, they are entitled to get 
profit bonus. I do not like to enter into the merits of the claim for such 
Puja bonus, because this is not an issuesin the present reference. The 
leading case in this respect is the Mahalakshmi Cotton Mills reported in 
no '× [ : 

1952 L.A.C. 370. A claim for such Puja bonus must depend on as to 
whether there was an agreement to pay it irrespective of profit as a condi- 
tion of service. That agreement might be either express or implied, and 
where not express, past practice may lead to an inference of an implied 
agreement. But the practice must be unbroken, and should have continued 
for an appreciably long period to exclude the hypothesis of these payments 
being ex gratia ones or out of bounty. In the present case, the claim for 
bonus has been based on the general principle that labour and capital 
should share the surplus left after meeting the necessary and prior charges. 
All the Tribunals now follow in this respect the well-established principles 
laid down by the Labour Appellate Tribunal in its Full Bench decision in 
the case of Mill Owners’ Association, Bombay v. Rastriya Mill Mazdoor 
Sangha, Bombay (1952 L.A.C. 433). It has been clearly laid down in the 
above case that the claim for bonus is to arise, if there is any surplus 
profit left after making provision for prior charges and fair return on 
pail up capital and on reserve employed as working capital. Thus, all 
previous theories regarding bonus have been exploded and replaced by one 
single theory of bonus, which is payable only out of profits of an industry. 
Hence, the question of bonus does not arise, until and unless there has 
been substantial profits leaving sufficient margin after meeting the prior 
charges, depreciation, reserve for rehabilitation of machinaries, a fair return 
for the yoney invested and some return on the working capital to meet the 
demands of bonus of the workmen. Income-tax is a legitimate deduction 
according to the Full Bench formula. The financial year of this Company 
is from October to September. In the present case, the claim for bonus 
fis for the years 1959 and 1954. That being so, we are to consider the 
financial position of this Company for the years ending 30th September 
1953 and 1954. The Company has accordingly produced the balance sheets 
for those two years, and they are Exts. A and B. These balance sheets 
have been audited by Messrs. Lovelock & Lewes, Chartered Accountants. 
The balance sheets produced by the Company must be presumed to be 
correct, unless the contrary is shown by definite evidence. In the present 
case, the Union could not show anything that the balance sheets were not 
correct. It appears from the balance sheets that in the year 1953 the net 
profit of this Company was Rs. 1,64,489-0-9 pies, and in the year 1954 1t 
was Rs. 1,59,867-5-f1 pies. It further appears from the balance sheets 
that subscribed, issued and paid-up capital was Rs. 34,00,000. If 6 per 
cent. return on the above paid-up capital is allowed, the figure comes to 
2,04,000. Over and above this, there is also the payment of income-tax 
for these years. It appears from Ext. J(1) series, which are the copies 
of the income-tax assessment issued by the Income-tax Authorities, that 
in the year 1953-54 Rs. 69,542-15 was payable as income-tax by _ the 
Company, and Rs, 68,186-14 in the year 1954-95. O.P.W. 3 Mr. K. J. 
Holt, who is the Assistant Secretary of the Company, has deposed that the 
said amounts of income-tax have been actually paid to the Income-tax 
Authorities. If 6 per cent. return on the paid-up capital and income-tases 
paid be deducted from net profits for the years in question, it is crystal clear 
that there remains no available surplus, but on the contrary there remains 
a deficit to the tune of more than one lakh in each year. Other items, such 
as depreciation, reserve for rehabilitation of machineries, etc., are not 
taken into account, although the Company is entitled to get deduction of 
the amounts required to meet those charges. Hence, the claim of the 
Union for profit bonus for the years 1903 and 1954 cannot be sustained, 
and is accordingly rejected. This issue is decided thus.

issue No. 1—Whether the dismissal of the seven workers as per attached 
List A was Justified. What relief are they entitled to? 


Now I would like to take up issue No. 1. Regarding the dismissal of 
the seven workers as per stacked List A of the order of reference, it is 
the contention of the Company that they were dismissed from service, as 
they participated in the stay-in-strike on 22nd April 1955, and also refused 
to do overtime work on 16th April 1955 and 23rd April 1955 according to 
the instructions of their superior officer Shri A. Mukherjee, Supervisor of 
the Hide Road godown. The said charges have been denied on behalf of 
the workmen concerned. The Union wanted to say that the workmen 
concerned were not guilty of the charges levelled against them, and that 
they had done nothing which might warrant dismissal, The Whion’s 
contention 1s that the Company in sacking them was actuated by ulterior 
motive, the motive being to crush the Union, because these workmen were 
more or less active organisers of the Union. It is necessary, therefore, to 
decide which version is correct. Ceratin facts require to be stated for 
appreciating the true position, and the matter should be judged 
dispassionately behind the background of those facts. The workmen of 
the Hide Road godown have all along been doing overtime work beyond 
normal scheduled working hours. It appears from the standing orders, 
which have been exhibited in this case, that such overtime work is their 
condition of service. The normal working hours for a workman in this 
godown is 36 hours in a week. This is also admitted by the Secretary of 
the Union, P.W. 1 Shr Gour Mohan Das. We further get from ithe 
evidence of the said Secretary and two other workmen who have deposed 
on behalf of the workers concerned, that overtime work is done in this 
godown. So, it is established beyond doubt that overtune work in the 
godown is the condition of service of the workers. For such overtime 
work the workers get extra remuneration. The majority of the workors 
in the godown being coolies are employed in loading and unloadiny of goods 
in railway wagons. That being so, the provisions of sections 51, 52, 64) 
55, 56 and 61 of the Factories Act do not apply to such workers, and this 
has been made clear by rule 10 of the West Bengal Factories (15610006107) 
Rules, 1954. But the Union that was formed in February 1953 demanded 
double wages for such overtime work from the Management. Its demand 
was that a worker working one hour overtime would get wages with dear- 
ness allowance for two hours. A letter was also আর to that effect 
to the Company on 4th April 1955 (vide Ext. 0). ie that letter 1 was 
perfectly made clear that unless such double wages fof overtime work were 
paid, the workers would not do any overtime work in future. P.W. 1 
Shri Gour Mohan Das, who is the Secretary of the Union, has admitted to 
have addressed such a letter to the Company. Thus, it is evident that 
the workers were willing to do overtime work, which they were doing all 
along and which they knew also to be a condition of service, but they 
were unwilling to do the same, unless double wages were paid to them for 
such overtime. The Company was not, however, willing to pay such 
double wages to them for overtime regard being had to their nomal work- 
ing hours and the conditions of service. In this state of things, a clash 
was inevitable between the Company and the workers. This is what exactly 
happened in the godown within a few days from the date of the letter 
addressed by the Secretary of the Union to the Company as mentioned 
above. According to the written statement of the Company, on Saturday, 
the 16th April 1955, at about 12 noon, a wagon came at the godown siding 
containing some boiler tubes. The Godown Supervisor in order to save 
demurrage charge asked eight workmen to unload the wagon, but those 
workmen refused to carry out the instructions of the Supervisor, unless 
they were paid double wages, and stopped work at 12-30 p.m. as usual.

The Supervisor reported the matter to the Head Office, and these eight 
workmen were charge-sheeted for this. The Company seut charge-sheets

While the Supervisor was explaining the charge-sheets to the workmen 
concerned on 22nd April 1955, all workmen of the godown in general left

withdrawal of the charge-sheets. The Supervisor informed the Manage-

work on both occasions, that is on 16th Apri] 1955 and 28rd April 1950

him, because on 17th July 1954 he left the Howrah Station without book- 
ing the Company’s goods for which purpose he was deputed there, end ٥0

overtime work on 28rd April 1955. Now it is for the Tribunal tu consider 
whether the dismissal of these seven workers. as mentioned in the attached

Tribunal is unable to hold that the Management in dismissin these 7

activities. Nor can it say that there was want of bona fides or there was 
victimisation or unfair labour practice, or anything of the kind on the part 
of the Management in the instant case. On a careful scrutiny of ae 
materials placed before the Tribunal, I am definitely of the view that these 
seven workers were guilty of wilful insubordination and disobedience of a 
lawful and reasonable order pf a superior officer. That they detiberatel 
refused to carry out the order of the Supervisor Shri A. Mukherjee ا‎ 
the latter asked them to do overtime work, has been amply proved by the 
evidence furnished on behalf of the Company. According to the Standin 
Orders of the Company [vide Appendix 1002) (1), Ext. C(1)] such wilful 
insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a 
superior officer constitutes a major misdemeanour for which a workman 18 


liable to dismissal. No company can afford to tolerate such repeatod 
Snsubordination and insolence on the part of its workers. This sort of 


Part ]] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3317 
insubordination and grave misconduct undermines discipline, and the 
gravity of such action and conduct cannot be under-rated. The workers 
concerned behaved rather in a disorderly thanner, and their conduct was 
highly subversive of discipline. So, the Tribunal, on a careful considera- 
tion of the merits of the case and after examining critically the propriety 
of the Management’s order, js satisfied that the decision of the Manage- 
ment in dismissing the said workers was a possible view on the evidence 
before it. That being so, the Tribunal should refrain from substituting its 
own judgment for the judgment of the Management, as in such matters the 
Tribunal does not act lke a Court of Appeal, but rather as a supervisory 
body. So, the Tribunal holds that the action of the Company in dismissing 
the said workers was quite justified. It is not open to the Tribunal to 
reduce the punishment or to substitute any other punishment for the one 
imposed by the Management, 


The Tribunal, therefore, comes to the conclusion that the dismissal 
of the seven workers as per attached List A was justified. In this view 
of the matter, the question of their getting any relief does not arise, 
This issue is decided accordingly.

BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL

Appearances: . 


For the employees: Shri Rajani Mukherjee, Vice-President, V. A. S. T.
