For the Company: Shri K. B. Basu, Bar.-at-Law, and Shri R. L. Maitra, 
| Acting Labour Adviser of I.J.M.A. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, by order 
No. 1589Dis./D/4L-6/56, duted 19th April 1956, referred under section 10 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, f947, the industrial dispute existing between 
Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Ltd., 3 Clive Row, Calcutta, and their 
workmen represented by V. A. 8. I. Launches Workmen’s Union, 51 Chitta- 
ranjan Avenue, Calcutta-12, to this Tribunal for adjudication regarding the 
matters specified in the following schedule: 


৫ Schedule 
(1) Duty hours, 

(2) Grades and scales, 

(3) Annual inerement. 


The issues framed for adjudication were the same as (1996 mentioned 
above in the schedule. 


Notices were issued to the parties. The Union filed 163 written statement 
on 28th May 1956, -and the Company on 12th June 1956. The case was 
taken up for hearing on 28th July 1956, | 


The case of the launch crews in question as presented in the written 
statement filed on their behalf by the Union in short is that they have to 
work for 24 hours without any holiday or weekly rest, and that the existing 

rades and scales of their pay are low and not sufficient enough for their 

ecent living. Hence, the Union has demanded that their duty hours should 
be fixed at 8 hours daily and 48 hours weekly, and that the grades and scales 
of pay with provision for annual increment as stated in the written statement 
should be introduced with retrospective effect from J anuary 1954. 


The Company, in reply, resists the demands put forward on behalf of 
the launch crews. Regarding duty hours, the Company wants to say that 
nowhere among such crews or River Transport staff are working hours fixed, 
and that duty hours cannot be fixed, because such workers being tidal 
workers are expected to be available for duty according to navigational 
considerations of the river and during periods when they are expected to 


3324 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 380, 1956 [Parr I 


make trips to and from. the Calcutta Port area. Regarding wages, 0 
Company’s contention is that these launch crews, who have all along been 
considered by the Omnibus Jute Tribunal] awards as Jute Mall employees, 
have alrendy received substantial Increases in their pay, and as such are not 
entitled to any further increases in pay as claimed or to incremental scales 


ef ۰ 


The Company has further raised Jegal objections as to the maintainabilit 
of the present reference. In this respect its contention is two-fold. 
Firstly, it is contended that Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co, peso Ltd., who 
have been made a party to the present dispute, are not the employers of the 
concerned workmen, who are really the workmen of the Samnuggur Jute 
Factory Co., Lid., Titaghur Jute Factory Co., Ltd., Victoria Jute Factory 
Co., Ltd., and Angus Company, Ltd., and that in the circumstances the 
present reference is bad in Jaw and not maintainable. The second objection 
as raised on behalf of the Company is that the Jaunch crews in question have 
all along been considered by the Omnibus Jute Tribunal awards as Jute 
Mill employees for the purposes of the Tribunal, and have thus been given 
all wages, service condition, etc., applicable to Jute Mill employees, and 
have been specifically included in the occupational nomenclature of the 
First Omnibus Jute Tribunal Award (Appendix IV). The issues 2 and 3 
in the present reference regarding grades and scales of pay, and annual 
increment, are fundamentally questions of wages payable to these workmen, 
and as such were the subject-matter of reference to the Third Omnibus Jute 
Tribunal constituted by the Government in 1954, and in that reference the 
aforesaid Jute Mills, whose workmen these launch crews are, were parties. 
This Union under their leader, late Shafatullah Khan, put forward the 
question of grades and scales of pay and annual increment on behalf of these 
workmen, which was duly considered by the Tribunal. The Third Omnibus 
Jute Tribunal gave its award, which came into force on 6th November 1955. 
In that award, directions were given regarding wages of the cargo boat 
crews and their working hours, but the said Tribunal did not think it 
necessary to interfere with the existing wages of launch crews, for whom it 
awarded along with other workmen not specifically mentioned a general 
increase of Rs. 8 per month, All the Jute Mill companies have fully 
implemented that award, and all the launch crews have received an increase 
on the lines specified in the award with effect from 6th November 1955. The 
said award was the subject-matter of an appeal before the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal, which delivered its judgment on 3lst May 1956. The Appellate 
Tribunal confirmed the award, so far as the present workmen are concerned. 
Accordingly, it is contended by the Company that the aforesaid award of the 
Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal bars a fresh reference and a fresh adjudica- 
tion regarding issues 2 and 3, at least during the statutory period of its 
operation. 


As the validity and the propriety of the present reference were challenged 
by the legal objections raised on behalf of the Company, the Tribunal, at 
the desire of both parties, heard the said objection first.. Learned represen- 
tativeS of both sides addressed at length the Tribunal regarding maintain- 
ability of the reference in question. Both parties placed before the Tribunal 
some documents, which have been marked exhibits. The Company further 
gave the Tribunal the copies of awards of the Jute Textile Tribunals as well 
as the copy of the judgment of the Labour Appellate Tribunal on appeal from 
the award of the Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal. 


On a perusal of the relevant documents and after hearing the elaborate 
arguments of learned representatives of both sides, I am of the view that 
there is considerable force in the legal objections raised on behalf of the 


Parr 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 19568] 3325 


জে 


ae a) এপস 


Company as to the maintainability of the present reference, and that the 
said objections must prevail. On a consideration of the matter, the Tribunal 
18 convinced that the workmen in the instant case are not workmen of 
Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. ا‎ *Ltd., but they are workmen of 
Samnuggur Jute Factory Co., Lid., Titaghur Jute Factory Co., Ltd., 
Victoria Jute Factory Co., Lid., and Angus Company, Ltd., and that Messrs. 
Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Ltd., are the only beter et Agent of those 
Jute Mill companies. This is established from Exts. A and B. Exihibit A 
is a copy of the rules and regulations affecting the terms and conditions of 
service of the River Transport staff in the Thomas Duff group. It appears 
therefrom that this River Transport staff includes all crews of steam launches 
and cargo boats belonging to the companies, and that the general direction 
and control of such staff shall be exercised through authorised representatives 
of the companies concerned at the Head Office. It further appears there- 
from that at the Head Office of each company, a permanent register of all 
launch and cargo boat crews shall be maintained. Exhibit B is a sample 
service record card of a launch crew, in which it is clearly stated that he is 
in the service of a particular company—Angus Jute Works or the Angus 
Company, Ttd. Fhe Wage and Attendance Registers of these companies 
were also brought before the Tribunal at the time of hearing. Learned 
counsel appearing on behalf of Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Ltd., 
placed before me some of these bound registers. ‘They showed that these 
workmen used to get their wages from the concerned Jute Mill companies. 
Thus it 1s abundantly clear that Samnuggur Jute Factory Co., Lid., 
Titaghur Jute Factory Co., Ltd., Victoria Jute Factory .Co., Ltd., and 
Angus Company, Ltd., were really the employers of these workmen, and 
that Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Ltd.—their Managing Agent— 
used only to look after the day-to-day management of those Mill companies, 
and whatever they did they did it in the name of those companies. 
Learned spokesman of the Union produced a document, Ext, 1, for showing 
that what was being contended by the Company now was not correct. 1 
have perused the said document which is a written statement filed by 
Samnuggur Jute Factory Co., Ltd., in connection with an application 
under section 338A. But ] may say that nowhere in this written statement 
it is stated that the workmen concerned were employed under Messra. 
Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Litd., the Managing Agents. On the contrary, 
it is asserted there that the applicants are all the employees of Samnuggur 
Jute Factory Co., Ltd., and are under the direct control and discipline of 
the Head Office, and that Samnuggur Jute Factory Co., Ltd., through its 
Managing Agents, are the proper employers of the above workmen. So, 
this document does not help the workmen concerned. It, on the other hand, 
lends support to the contention of the Company. I, therefore, hold that 
Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. (India), Ltd., are not the employers of the 
concerned workmen. 


But the fact remains that the real employers of the concerned workmen 
are not parties to the present dispute. Messrs. Thomas Duff & Co. (India), 
Ltd., who have been mentioned as a party to the dispute, are not the 
employers of these workmen. It is very unfortunate that in spite of specific 
objection taken by the Company in their written statement filed on 12th 
June 1956, the Union took no steps whatsoever for making the Jute Mill 
companies mentioned above, under which the workmen concerned work, 
parties to the present dispute. It could have moved either the Government 
or the Tribunal in this respect, but nothing was done by it. Now what 
would be the legal position of the present reference? The Tribunal, in the 
absence of proper and. necessary parties to the dispute, cannot obviousl: 
make any award. Certainly it would not be just and proper for the Tribunal 


3326 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Parr I 


to do so. If any award is passed in the circumstances, such award canftot 
possibly be implemented, nor can any relief be secured from the appropriate 
parties, because such award canngt be binding on the concerned Jute Mull 
companies. Strictly speaking, an award, if made, will involve the 
liabilities of the said companies, but they being no parties to the present 
dispute can easily avoid such liabilities. There might be many complica- 
tions in future if an award is passed in absence of the proper and necessar 

parties. It is not, therefore, desirable that the Tribunal shal] = suc 

an award, which can neither be implemented nor can have any binding force 
and effect. In this view of the matter, I hold that the reference as made, 
and as it stood at the time of hearing, was bad in law and not maintainable. 
Learned spokesman of the Union has argued that section 10(1) of the Act 
gives the Government absolute power to make a reference, and that when 
the Government has made the reference, the Tribunal must give an award, 
and the validity of the reference cannot be questioned or canvassed. In 
reply to this argument, I would say that Government is only concerned with 
deciding whether an industrial dispute exists, and whether in_ the 
circumstances of the particular case it should be referred to a Tribunal. 
But once the reference is made, it is for the Tribunal te consider whether 
it should pass an award after considering the matter ow merits. Even in 
spite of the reference by the Government, the Tribunal could enquire and 
decide for itself whether it should assume jurisdiction over the subject- 
matter of the reference, and simply the fact that a reference has been made 
by the appropriate Government will not stand in the way of any enquiry 
by the Tribunal. <A duty is cast upon both the Government and the Tribunal 
to work gut the scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act. It might have 
escaped the notice of the Government while making the reference that the 
real employers of the concerned workmen were no parties to the present 
dispute, but that does not necessarily mean that the Tribunal shall also kee 

its eves shut regarding this broad and important fact, and pass an shorn 
knowing fully well that such an award cannot be enforced against the 
appropriate party in securing relief for the workmen concerned. Jf it be 
done, it will lead not only to chaos and absurdities, but it will also frustrate 
the scheme_.of the Act and defeat the purpose for which the Industrial 
Disputes Act has been enacted, namely, settlement of industrial disputes. 


Now, I will deal with other legal objection raised by the Company. It 
appears from the awards of the Omnibus Jute Tribunal that launch crewg in 
question have been considered all along as Jute Mill employees. These 
launch crews have been specifically included in the occupational nomenclature 
of the First Omnibus Jute Tribunal Award, vide Appendix 1V, page 138 of 
the said award. The Jute Mill companies, where these workmen are 
employed, were parties to all references made to the Omnibus Jute 
Tribunal. The last reference was made to the Tribunal constituted under 
the chairmanship of Shri M. C. Banerjee, and it is called as the Third 
Omnibus Jute Tribunal. Very recently, that Tribunal gave its award which 
came 1010 force with effect from 6th November 1955. The question of wages 
payable to these workmen was also the subject of reference to the Third 
Omnibus Jute Tribunal. It appears that the present Union under their 
leader late Janab Shafatullah Khan of the Howrah Zilla Chatkal Mazdoor 
Union submitted to that Tribunal what should be the grades and scales of 
pay and annual increments of these workmen, The Tribunal considered the 
same, and in its award gave directions regarding wages of the cargo hoat 
crews and their working hours, This would appear from page 61 of the 
said award. But the Tribunal did not think it necessary to disturb the 
existing wages of launch crews. Jt, however, awarded to them along with 
other workmen not specifically mentioned a general increment of Rs. 8 per 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 3397 


কত‏ حسم জজ‏ جو اہ সিট শত hp‏ ہے 


month in basic wage. ٤ quote below what was said by the Tribunal in this 
respect [vide 9(7), page 74 of the said award]: 

“Any monthly paid workman, ‘who has not been covered by our 
observations in the preceding paragraphs, should be given an increment 
of Rs, 8 per month in his basic wage, and shall be paid a dearness 
allowance of Rs. 32-8 per month in place of Rs. 37-6.” 


The issues 2 and 3 of the present reference, which are regarding grades 
and scales of pay and নিপা increment, are fundamentally questions of 
wages puyable to these workmen. But it is abundantly clear from the award 
of the Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal that such questions were the subject of 
references to that Tribunal, which considered the same and gave its award, 
That award, as stated above, became operative with effect from 6th November 
1955. Although an appeal was preferred to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, 
the said Tribunal did not modify in any way the award, so far as the present 
workmen are concerned. Furthermore, the Labour Appellate Tribunal has 
clearly stated in paragraph 34 of its judgment that the appeal against the 
award related to the revision of basic wages and dearpess allowance of the 
workmen of all catekories in the Jute Textile Industry of West Bengal. The 
award of the said Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal is still in force and opera- 
tion. So, in view of what has been stated above, it must be held that the 
present reference relating to items of dispute as mentioned in issues 2 and 
8, 18 without jurisdiction, inasmuch as the said items of dispute are covered 
by the award of the Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal. In my view, this 
award of the Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal bars a fresh reference and a 
fresh adjudication in respect of issues 2 and 3, at least during the statutory 
period of its operation. Section 19(6) of the Act stands in the way. It 
might be that even after adjudication of an industrial dispute the parties 
may remain dissatisfied, and the industrial dispute may still continue in 
spite of the adjudication, but in the eye of law the industrial dispute must 
be deemed to have merged in the award and to have lost 118 existence. So 
long as the prior award is operative and. binding, neither the Government 
tan re-open the award just by a reference of the same matter to another 
Tribunal, nor can the parties avoid the consequence except strictly in the 
manner provided for under the law. During the operation of that award 
the Tribunal, in spite of the Government reference, wil] not be able to deal 
with the matter. It may amount not only to incompetence of the Tribunal 
for want of authority, but it may also amount to want of jurisdiction. So, 
this Tribunal cannot superimpose any award regarding issues 2 and 3 over 
another binding and operative award. The Tribunal, therefore. holds that 
it is not competent to adjudicate on the matter regarding grades and scales 
of pay and annual increment of these workmen as stated in issues 2 and 3, 
because such questions were the subject of the award of the Third Omnibus 
Jute Tribunal. It is true no doubt that the question of duty hours of these 
launch crews (which is issue No. ] in the present reference) was not the 
subject of reference to the aforesaid Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal, but this 
matter cannot be gone into and decided in this reference, because the real 
employers of the concerned workmen are not parties to the dispute. I have 
already recorded my reasons in this respect, and I do not like to repeat the 
same here. 


1 would, however, like to say a few words in this connection. Regard 
being had to the nature and condition of work of the launch crews, it is 
extremely difficult to fix duty hours for their work. Their work depends on 
the tides, and the launches and boats are their home for the period of their 
work. They are expected to be available for duty according to navigational 


considerations of the river. Their main work and duties consist in the 


3398 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Parr I 


| SS 
transhipment of goods to and from the respective mills, to and from other 
mills and the Caleutta Port area. It so happens that they are to remain 
idle for over a week at a time‘and also for months together, when their 
launches are laid up for repairs, etc., but without any loss in wages. 


The present reference is thus disposed of, 
Dictated and corrected by me. 


G. P, MUKHERJEE, 


Judge.

DECISIONS 


Point Nos, 1 and 2.—Exhibit B shows that the Company filed an appli- 
cation under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for permission to 
terminate the services of the petitioner, Shri Gujor Singh, on the ground 
of misconduct. The application states that at 10.5 p.m. on edrd September 
1955 the petitioner was found sleeping while on duty and that the said 
act of the petitioner is a misconduct under rule 14(C)(IX) of the Standing 
Orders. The charge-sheet was served on the petitioner on 24th September 
1955. The petitioner submitted his explanation and the Manager after 
holding an enquiry ordered that the petitioner should be dismissed but until 
the permission of the Tribunal was obtained he should continue to be 
suspended. Qn these facts the Company prayed for permission to dismiss 
the petitioner. The application, Exhibit B, also shows a copy of the charge- 
sheet on the petitioner and his explanation. A copy of the said charge- 
sheet also shows the Manager’s decision made on 28th September 1955. 
Exhibit A is an order of the Tribunal, dated 7th November 1955, showing 
that as the Award in the proceedings arising out af the Order of Reference 
in the main case was published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 6th October 
1955, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to deal with the application under 
section 33 of the Act. The application was, therefore, struck off. It has 
been decided by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Products of India, Limited, reported in 1955 1.۵۸.08. page 221, that it is the 
contravention by the employer of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, that gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the workman to 
approach and move the Tribunal and this contravention is the condition 
precedent to the exercise by the Tribunal of the additional jurisdiction 
under section 335A of the Act. It is, therefore, clear that aos the opposite 
party Company applied under section 33 of the Act for permission to ter- 
minate the services of the petitioner, no contravention of section 33 of the 
Act was committed by the opposite party. The present complaint under 
3A of the Act was, therefore, not competent, and should be rejected. 


section 3: ۱ 
The sk ogre is, therefore, not entitled to any relief. These points are 


accordingly answered.

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, be rejected.

Lhe Company in its written statement stated as follows: 


The petition under section 338A of the Industria] Disputes Act, 1947, 
ig misconceived, and 18 not maintainable in law as the Company has not, 
In any way, violated section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The peti- 
tion filed by Shri Nagendra Nath Surai contains various vague, misleading 
and incorrect allegations, and the Company denies the same. The facts of 
the case are as follows: On 12th November 1954 Shri Nagendra Nath Surai 
was examined by the Mill Medical Officer and was found medically unfit to 
continue his work asa mistry. Shri Nagendra Nath Surai was 65 years old 
when he was medically examined. As the workman was found medically 
unfit for further service, he was laid-off pending the permission of the Tri-

in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes (Amendment)

as claimed by him. The Company, therefore, prays that the application 
should be rejected. 


The points that arise for decision are— 


(1) Is the petition under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
maintainable? 


(11) Is the petitioner entitled to any relief in this ۶ءء‎

DECISION 


Point No. 1.—Exhibit 18108 that the Company filed an application 
under section 33 of the Act for permission *to terminate the services of the 
petitioner Shri Nagendra Nath Surai on medical ground on account of 
continued ill health. Annexure ‘'A”’ of Exhibit 1 1s the report of the 
Medical Officer. This report states that Shri Nagendra Mistry was aged 
65 years by his own statement, and also in the opinion of doctor, that he 
was suffering from breathlessness and senile debility, and was, therefore, 
unfit to carry on the work of a mistry. Annexure “B’ to Exhibit 1 is the 
notice, dated 17th November 1954, for laying off the petitioner till per- 
mission 18 obtained from the ‘Tribunal for termination of his’ services. 
Exhibit 2 18 an order of the Tribunal, dated 7th November 1955, showing 
that as the Award im the proceedings arising out of the Order of Reference 
in the main case wag ahead in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 6th October 
1955, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to déal with the application under 
section 83 of the Act. The application was, therefore, struck off. It has 
been decided by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Automobile 
Products of India, Limited, in 1955 L. A. C. page 221, that it is the 
contravention by the employer of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, that gives rise to a cause of action in favour of the workman to 
approach and move the Tribunal and this contravention is the condition 
precedent to the exercise by the Tribunal of the additional jurisdiction 
under section 38۸ of the Act. It is, therefore, clear that as the opposite 
party Company applied under section 33 of the Act for permission to termi- 
nate the services of the petitioner, no contravention of section 93 of the Act 
was committed by opposite party. The present complaint under section 934. 
of the Act was, therefore, not competent, and should be rejected. This 
point is accordingly answered, 


(৯: Point No, 2.—From what has been decided in the foregoing point, it is 
‘clear that the petitioner is not entitled to any relief in the proceeding. It 
may also be added that his prayer for lay-off compensation for the entire 
period of lay-off or, in other words, beyond the first 45 days, is not worth 
of support. The petitioner cited the decision of the Hon’ble Labour Appel- 
late Tribunal in the case reported in 1954 L. A. ©., page 871, in his 
petition. This decision supports the claims of the petitioner, but the decision 
of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, reported in 1956(1) L. L. J., page 749, in 
the case of Modi Food Products, Ltd., negatives the claim of the petitioner 
In view of the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the matter, the 
petitioner is not entitled to get any relief, even on merits. 


In the result, the application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, 18 rejected.

hereby to publish the said award as shown in the Annexure hereto.

2. The reference was received here on 15th June 1955. After usual 
notices the Union filed written statement on 25th July 1955. The employer 
filed written objection on 15th September 1955. Then after several 
adjournments the case was taken up for hearing on 7th June 1956. The 
evidence was concluded on that day. The argument was heard partly, on 
18th June 1956 and finally on 24th July 1956. The award was reserved. 


3. The only issue contained in the schedule to the Order of Reference 
stands as follows :— 


(1) If the discharge of (1) Shri Sukha Ranjan Chakraborty and (2) 
Shri Bharat Tala was justified, to what relief includin 
reinstatement and/or any other compensation are they entitled f 


AWARD 


4. Before ] discuss the issue in question, J would like to preface it by 
a brief history of the dispute, as I find from the written statement of the 
parties before the Tribunal. 


According to the Union, this Howrah District Bus Workers’ Union was 
formed on 9181 May 1954. The Union comprised among its members the 
conductors, drivers and cleaners numbering about 330 of the 84 buses 
plying in the routes Nos. 51, 54, 56 and 60. Thereafter when the Union 
found that the employers were in no mood to redress the grievances of the 
workers who were being exploited by them, it submitted a charter of 
demands both to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Howrah, and to the 
individual owners of buses including Shri P. K. Chatterji of the bus 
No. WBU 825 of the present case on 25th August 1954. Shri Sukharanjan 
Chakravorty, the driver of the bus owned by Shri P. K. Chatterji above, 
happened to be the Vice-President of the Union. Bharat Lala was another 
driver of this employer. He was also an active organiser of the Union. 
It so happened that during the period between 9181 May 1954 and 6th 
September 1954 as many as 18 workmen of the buses in the aforsaid routes 
were discharged by their employers without any notice and without any 
charge-sheet. No reason was assigned for their discharge. Then their 
cause was espoused by Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty and one Shri Mrinal 
Bose, and they moved the District Magistrate and the R.T.A. in the matter 
in September 1954. Eventually in course of conciliation proceedings, 
those 18 workmen were reinstated in their service in November 1954. But 
when the above conciliation proceedings were in progress, Shri Sukha- 
ranjan Chakravortv himself and Bharat Lala aforesaid were dismissed from 
their service on 14th September 1954 and 26th September 1954 respectively 
by their emplover Shri P. K. Chatterj). Bharat Lala was thereafter 
re-employed in service, but he was deprived of any compensation for the 
unemployment period. Thus has arisen the present dispute. Bharat Lala 
has since died after his re-employment. ; 


The employer contends that he is a political sufferer, and a refugee from 
Kast Bengal. He purchased the aforesaid bus at a cost of Rs. 32,000 
payable in instalments. But his transport business proved to be a losing 


3338 THE CATILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 [Parr I 


ہیی جج 


রব রর 1‏ ہے 
পপ স্পা এপস পারা ০০০‏ رد دوہ جد ور ہن رانا 9ناج باہش یو تح ۱ا9 نے ےس سے ے سے سر 


Bharat Lala was also dismissed for misconduct, but he was re-employed 
on his জগ regret and apology. He has since died. The claim for 
compensation and reinstatement is resisted by the employer. 


Later on, the employer has taken certain legal objections, viz., 


(1) that the present dispute is an “individual dispute’, and not an 
‘industrial dispute’. So the Tribunal is not competent to 
adjudicate upon it; and 


(2) that Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty after his dismissal has become 
an ex-workman and, as such, he is not a ‘‘workman’’ as defined 
in the Act. So he is not competent to raise a dispute against 
the employer after his dismissal. 


Now, let. me dispose of the legal objections first. The position in law is 
now pretty well established. If a dispute is originally an ‘‘individual 
dispute’’, and af it continues as such up to the date of reference, then it 
will not be an industrial dispute. The Tribunal] will not be competent to 
adjudicate upon it in spite of the same heing described as an ‘‘industrial 
dispute’? in the Order of Reference. The latest decision on this point by 
the Hon’ble Calcutta High Court is reported at page 865 of the Calcutta 
Weekly Notes of July 1956, Volume LX in the case of Bengal Club, Ltd. 
and Santi Ranjan. If the workmen or other fellow workmen espouse the 
cause of the workman concerned, then the individual dispute develops into 
a collective dispute where the Tribunal has jurisdiction to adjudicate upon 
the same. If any authority is needed, I can refer to the famous observa- 
tion of Mr. Justice Mack of the Madras High Court in the case of Kandan 
Textile, Ltd. versus Industrial Tribunal. I quote from his observation as 


below: 


“Tf euch a dismissal, however, even of an individual workman is taken 
up by Workers’ Union or a substantial body of workmen who 
continue in employment and espouse his cause, then an industrial 
dispute may arise.” 


To the same effect is the observation of Their Lordships of the Allahabad 
High Court in an application for writ in the form of mandamus under 
Article 226 of the Constitution of India No. 851 of 195) in the case of 
Ganesh Das Ramgopal] versus the Government of the State of Uttar Pradesh. 
Now, if I turn to the evidence, I find that the case of Shri Sukharanjan 
Chakravorty was taken up by the Union long before the date of reference, 


Pary 1۱| THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 380, 1956 3339 
Kven a strike was contemplated by the Union on this issue (vide para- 
graph 4 of the proceedings of the tripartite conference held by the A.L.C., 


Howrah, on 8th November 1954 (Ext. 2Y. The said paragraph runs as 
follows :-— 


“‘As regards Sukharanjan, Bharat and Mrinal, as employers cannot 
agree to reinstate them it is proposed that the dispute over their 
dismissal be referred to a Tribunal for adjudication, on the 
ee that the Union will withdraw the contemplated 
strike.’ | 


Sukharanjan’s name also finds mention in the letter of the President of the 
Union addressed to the A.L.C., dated 21st September 1954 [Ext. 2(a)]. 
So it is clear that the dispute centring round the dismissal of Shri Sukha- 
ranjan Chakravorty and Bharat Lala was espoused by the Union long before 
the date of reference. The date of the present reference is the 8th June 
1955. So it is clear that the present dispute, though originally it was an 
individual dispute, ultimately developed into a collective dispute. As such, 
it is an industrial dispute, and the Tribunal has jursdicton to adjudicate 
upon it. The employer contends that there is no evidence that the employees 
in question gave any written authority to the Union to take up their case. 
That is not necessary. A Union is constituted to redress the grievances 
of the workmen. So where it tukes up the cause of any workman against 
the employer, such authorisation must be presumed in every case. So this 
contention is disposed of. 


The second legal objection is that Shri Sukharanjan and Bharat Lala 
ere ex-employees on the date of reference. So they were not ‘‘workmen’’ 
dates the Act. But if we refer to the definition of “workmen’’ in section 
2৪) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, we find that a workman discharged 
during the dispute also comes within the defimtion of ‘‘workman’’. In 
this extended sense the present workmen are attracted by the said definition. 
The evidence is clear that they were dismissed when there was a_pre- 
existing dispute pending before the Conciliation Officer. I may also refer 
to the case of India Paper Pulp Co., Ltd. versus Workers’ Union reported 
in L. I. J. 1955, paze 541. So this contention cannot hold water. 


Next I turn to the evidence to consider the merits of the case. It 1s 
admitted that none of these two workmen was given any charge-sheet. No 
reason was assigned for their discharge. Sukbaranjan in his evidence says 
that when he went to join bis work on 14th September 1954 after his hath, 
he was suddendly told by Shri P. K. Chatterji, the employer, that his 
services would no longer be required. He demanded 4 charge-sheet which 
was sternly refused. The employer, P.W. 1, says that he dismissed 
Sukharanjan for his bad driving and for putting him into troubles on three 
occasions when he did not pay the prices of petrol, and also for causing loss 
to him in the matter of tyre vulcanizing, and also for misappropriation of 
money by the conductor in collusion with Sukharanjan. But I find from 
the evidence that none of these charges has been substantiated. In the 
watter of misappropriation of money, the employer admits that the conduc- 
tor returned the entire money. So the money alleged to have been 
misappropriated did not come from Sukharanjan. It is also stated that 
Sukharanjan was also pardoned on that occasion, The employer Shri P. K. 
Chatterji admits also that in the matter of discharge of Sukharanjan, he 
took into consideration all his past offences which he had _ previously 
pardoned. So it appears that he auddenly raked all the past sins of Sukha- 
ranjan, if there were any, and dismissed him. The employer does not say 
what was the present provocation that led him to take such an action. | 


40 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 = [Parr I 


ately ES ےی سم‎ 


en] +,‏ جیےے

مسسمیٔمٔصحسىسمسحح دسج 


think that the present provocation lay in the fact that Shri Sukharanjan 
Chakravorty was the Vice-President of the Union. The employers were 
not slow to realise that if the'Union became strong, they would become 
week. They had an organisation of their own, but still they did not feel 
secure. So Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty was victimised by dismissal. 
When no present fault whet be picked up on the part of Shri Sukharanjau 
such as to justify the employer’s action, the employer fell back on his past 
acts of omission and commission. Strangely enough, though Shri Sukha- 
ranjan appeared to be so very delinquent, yet no warning was given to him 
at any time in writing. So I have no means to find whether these alleged 
charges for offences have been set up only when the employer found him- 
self in a tight corner. The employer says that Shri Sukharanjan was a 
temporary hand working for 11 years, and so he could be dismissed at the 
employer's pleasure. I have got in evidence that in this bus service no man 
is made permanent. So I have to suppose that the destiny of the employees 
here, no matter for how long they serve, lies on the sweet will and whim 
of employers. This is certainly not a situation which can be viewed with 
any equanimity by an Industrial Tribunal. So 1 am not prepared to accept 
this plea of the employer as a justification for causing Sukharanjan’a 
discharge. Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty is said to be a rash driver, but 
there is no record of any police case against him, That he misappropriated 
the money of petrol remains to be proved. ‘he employer admits that there 
is nothing in writing regarding the tyre vulcanizing atory. So in the 
circumstances, I set aside the order of discharge or dismissal on Shri Sukha- 
ranjan Chakravorty in the present case. 


Regarding Bharat Lala, I get in evidence that he was re-employed and 
that later on he went home and died there. So it 1s clear that he nequiesced 
in the circumstances and did not claim any compensation. I cannot allow 
this matter to be revived after this length of time. So I can grant no relief 
‘to Bharat Lala either by way of reinstatement or by way of compensation. 


Regarding Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty,, I award that he must be 
reinstated within one month of the award coming into operation. He is 
ranted compensation at the rate of half his average monthly earnings 
uring last two months just before this discharge or dismissal, from 
l4th sel 1954 up to the date of his reinstatement in service. This 
amount should be paid in three equal monthly instalments. Regarding 
inability to pay compensation, I do not find that the employer has made 
out any case. Besides, the employer has got to blame himself for this 
penalty. As Shri Sukharanjan Chakravorty did not render any service to 
the employer during this period, and also because he earned something by 
casual work during this time, I do not grant him more than half average 
wages as above.

IN THE HONOURABLE LABOUR APPELLATE TRIBUNAL OF 
INDIA, CALCUTTA 


Bhartia Electric Steel Co., Ltd., Calcutta ... Appellants, 
versus 
Bhartia Iron and Steel Workers’ Union, Caleutta ... Hespondents. 


In the matter of appeals against the award of Shri M. N. Can, Judge, 
Second Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, which was published in the 
‘Calcutta Cazette’’, dated 17th March 1955, in respect of an industrial 
dispute between the above parties 


Dated, the 5th April 1956. 
PRESENT : 
Sarr A. DAS GUPTA, President. 
ওরা 8. B. SINGH, Member. 
Appearances : 


For the مس ن‎ : Shri B. P. Khaitan, S. K. Bose, Bar.-at-law, Shri 
P. R. Bagri, Director, Shri N. K. Saraf and Shr K. P. Mukherjee. 


For the Respondent: Shri Ram Sen. 


State: West Bengal. 
Industry: Tron and Steel. 


DECISION 


Two issues were referred to the Second Industrial Tribunal, West 
‘Bengal, for adjudication. 


7 a 
۲٤ 


(1) Establishment costs of the works canteen. 


(2) Weekly off and overtime pay and the provision of uniforms to the 
durwans, 


The Learned Adjudicator. decided the first issue against the Company 
and the second issue againat the workmen. The award was published in 
thy Calcutta Gazette on 17th March 1955. The Compuny has appealed 
epainst the decision of the Tribunal on issue No. 1. This is Appeal Cal.- 
108 of 1965. Appeal Cal.-110 of 1955 has been filed by the workmen 
against the decision on issue No, 2. 


We take up first the Company’s appeal which relates to establishment 
cost of the works canteen. It is not covered by the list of appealable items 


392 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1966 


[Panr TA 


শিব Eater 


under section 7(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribu- 
nal) Act, 1950. ence the appeal is incompetert unless it is shown’ that 
it involves a substantial question of law. Shri B. P. Khaitan, who 


represents the Company before us urges that the decision involves an 
interpretation of the award of the Major Engineering Tribunal, the reie- 
vant section of the Indian Factories Act and the rules framed thereunder. 
For a correct application of the contention of Shri Khaitan, a short résumé 
of the facts of the case may be relevant. In 1947, the Government of 
West Bengal constituted a Tribunal to adjudicate upon the industrial dis- 
putes in 119 Engineering Firms of which the present appellant was one 
This Tribunal was commonly known as the Major Engmeering Tribunal. 
This Tribunal gave its award which was published in the Calcutta Gazette 
under Government of West Bengal, Labour Department,’ order No. 2161 /- 
Lah., dated the 80th June 1948. ‘‘Canteen’’ was one of the subject matters 
of the adjudication. The Indian Factories Act of 1948 came into force on 
18: April 1949. Its predecessor, namely, the Indian Factories Act of 1934 
which was in force during the adjudication proceedings did not provide for 
any canteen. But the Major Engineering Tribunal টড the rele- 
vant provision of the Act of 1948 which was then pending before the 
Central Legislature and recommended that food may be supplied at a price 
just sufficient to meet the cost of the canteen. 


The Company admittedly maintains o canteen and bears a substantial 
portion of its costs, although there is slight difference between the parties 
as to the exact amount paid by the Company and the number of servants 
enployed. According to the Company 16 servants are employed for the 
canteen, while the Union contends that only 14 servants are employed. 
Out of these servants four are directly paid by the canteen committee out 
of the sale proceeds of foodstuff and the rest are paid by the committee. 
The Union demands that the Company should bear the entire establishment 
costs of the canteen including the salary of the servants employed for the 
canteen and the Lower Tribunal relying on a.decision reported io 
1954 I LLJ., page 774 (Burn & Co., Ltd.) has allowed the demand of the 
Union. The Company denies its liability to bear any portion of the 
establishment costs of the canteen. The decision in the present case 
hinges on the correct interpretation on the relevant section of the Indian 
Factories Act, the rules framed under the Act and the relevant portion in 
the award of the Major Engineering Tribunal. We accordingly agree with 
Shri Khaitan that the appeal involves a substantial question of law and is 
maintainable. 


As we have already pointed out that the Major Engineering Tribunal 
recommends that food may be supplied at a price just sufficient to meet 
the cost of the canteen. In the absence of any direction to the contrary, 
we may presume that the establishment cost would count in fixing the sale 
price of the foodstuff in the canteen. Section 46 of the Indian Factories 
Act, 1948, providés for canteen. It directs that in a factory where there 
are more than 250 workers, a canteen should he provided and maintained 
by the occupier for the use of the workers. It also authorises the State 
(Jovernment to frame rules in respect of such canteens under five specified 
heads. Rules 66 to 71 of the rules framed by the West Bengal Govern- 
ment, deals with the maintenance of canteen, equipment, price to be 
charged for foodstuff. Rules 66 and 67 deal with the site, ventilation, 
lighting and accommodation of the canteen including kitchen, pantry, 
store room and the dining hall. These two rules also provide for the 
hygienic measures in respect of the building including the kitchen, pantry 
and store room and the dining hall. Rule 68 deals with equipment and rule 
69 with the prices of food. Rule 68 runs as follows :— 


68. Equipment.—(1) There shall be provided and maintained 
sufficient utensils, crockery, cutlery, furniture and any other equip- 
ment necessary for the efficient running of the canteen. Suitable 
clean clothes for the employees serving in the canteen shall also be 
provided and maintained. 

(2) The furniture, utensils and other equipment shall be main- 
tained in a clean and hygienic condition. A service counter, if pro- 
vided, sha]l have a top of smooth and impervious material. Suitable 
facilities including an adequate supply of hot water shall be provided 
for the cleaning of utensils and equipment. 


Rule 69 directs that food and drink 210 other items served in the 
canteen will be sold and the prices charged shal] be sulsject to the approval 
of the managing committee. For our purpose rule 68 is relevant, and the 
piece decision on the issue before us involves an interpretation of this 
rule. 


It has been urged on behalf of the workmen that the employer has a 
statutory obligation to maintain a canteen and that to discharge this 
statutory obligation he must bear the entire establishment cost including 
the salary of servants employed in the canteen. This contention raises 
the question whether the employer has any statutory obligation to subsi- 
dise the canteen and if so to what extent. This is a much larger issue 
than what is involved in the present appeal. The question before us is 


۴ 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 


whether the peo a has any statutory obligation to pay for the four 
servants employed by thp canteen. Rule 68 does not specifically meun 
‘servants’ us one of the equipments. In interpreting this rule we must 
apply the principle of ejusdem gencris. By no stretch of imagination, 
the words ‘‘any other equipments necessary for the efficient running of 
the canteen” include servants, Servants have not been enumeraicd in 
rule 68 as one of the equipments, although the tule provides for suitable 
clean clothings for the servants serving in the canteen. 


Furniture, utensils and other equipment necessary for the canteen are to 
be maintained in a clean and hygienic condition and hot water is 60 be 
rovided for the cleaning of the utensils und other «equipments. Rule 
$(2) clearly indicates that the words ‘“‘any other equipment’ are not 
intended by the’ Government to include servants. We are accordingly of 
the opinion that the Company is under no obligation to pay the salary of 
the four servants employed by the canteen committee. The salary of these 
four servants should be taken into account in fixing the price of foodstuff. 
This will not offend the statutory provision for canteen under the Indian 
Fectories Act of 1949 and the a framed thereunder. The direction of 
the Adjudicator on this point is vacated. It is, however, hoped that the 
Company will not mata the existing subsidy. 


The facts of the case reported in 1954 I LLJ., page 774 (Burn & Co., 
lid.) is different from the facts of the present case. In the said case the 
Company was under an obligation under the award to maintain a cheap 
canteen and a Bench of this Tribunal held that a cheap canteen could not 
mean supply of food on the basis of ‘‘no profit and no loss’’. This decision 
does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


Now coming to the appeal of the workmen’s appeal No. Cal.-110 of 
1955 on issue No. 2 we may at once reject as incompetent the appeal so far 
as it relates to weekly off and the provision of uniforms to the durwans. 
Shri Ram Sen who has appeared before us for the workmen has not been 
able to establish any substantial question of law involved in the appeal. 
The appeal is competent only in respect of overtime pay of the durwans. 


The durwans working in the watch and ward department are not work- 
men under the Indian Factories Act and are not hence entitled to the bene- 
fit provided in the Act for factory workers. They do not also come under 
the Shops and Establishments Act. The Union claims overtime pay for 
the durwans for work on weekly day off. The Company states in its written 
statement that all the durwans excepting the durwans posted at the gates 
and in the stores get weekly holidays and that all durwans are alluwed one 
month’s leave with pay and 15 days’ leave on half pay in a year and are 
provided with free quarters. The durwans are the gurdians of the pro- 
perty and materials of the factory, and their services are required through- 
out the day and the week. It is not the Union’s case that they are 
eniployed for intension duty for 24 hours in a day without any recess. The 
durwans are provided with free quarters and free fuel and they even enjoy 
holidays. This is the condition of service of the durwans. The Learned 
Adjudicator turned down the Union’s demsaud for overtime pay as compen- 
sation for loss of weekly rest day. We are not inclined to interfere. 


In the result, appeal No. Cal.-108 of 1955 is allowed on contest and the 
direction of the Adjudicator to the appellant Company to bear the salaries 
of the four servants of the works canteen which are now paid by the canteen 
committee is vacated. Appeal No. Cal.-110 of 1955 is dismissed on contest. 
The award on issue No. 2 shall stand. Parties shall bear their own costs. 


A. DAS GUPTA, 
President. 


S. B. SINGH, 
Meinber.

ORDER 
The following facts have given rise to this application. 


2. During the pendency of appeal No. Cal.-207 of 1955 the opposite 
party, the National Carbon Company (India), Ltd., introduced piece-rate 
system in their packing department and thought that as a result of it six 
of the permanent 7 would become surplus in the line. On the 
218 of December 1955, this introduction of piece-rate system was taken up 
in hand when the six workmen who were to be retained in the line were 
called and explained the implications of the new system. On the following 
day these six workmen who were considered surplus were required to leave 
the packing line and take up some other work in that very department. 
The workmen did not agree to do so and they resisted it. For continuous 
10 days they refused to obey the orders of the management requiring them 
to take up work in some other line in the department. They were, there- 
fore, charge-sheeted and suspended pending enquiry. The domestic enquiry 
was held on the 12th of January 1956. The officer making the enquiry 
came to the conclusion that the workmen complainants were guilty of mis» 
conduct by violating factory’s standing orders and that they deserved to be 
dismissed and made a report to that effect on the 13018 January 1956. On 
the 19th of January 1956, they were informed that the Company was mak- 
ing an application under section 22 for permission for their dismissal and 
that they were to continue on suspension pending grant of permission. 
Within a weak of receipt of the letter communicating this order, the present 
application under section 23 was made on the 25th of January 1956. It 
took some time for the Company to make an application under section 22 
which was made on the 7th of February 1956. In the meantime, the appeal 
which had already been heard was decided on the 27th of January 1956. 
On the 19th of March 1956, the Company’s application under section 22 
being application (Misc.) case No. C-612 of 1956 was dismissed as infruc- 
tuous. Four days thereafter, i.e., when the pendency of the appeal had 
ceased the Company dismissed the complainants, 


3. The first question that presents itself for decision in this case is 
whether on the date the present application was made the Company had 
committed any act which could be called contravention of section 22. 
Pointed attention of the learned representative of the workmen was drawn 
to show that any action which could be called violation of the provisions of 
section 22 of our Act bad been committed by the Company, but he has 
failed to do so. Repeatedly he harped on the fact that the Company had 
not paid these workmen wages for the speriod from 21st of December 1955 
to the 818۲ of December 1955 and the Company had, with ulterior motives, 
suspended these workmen. Thus, he maintained that these, acts constituted 
contravention of section 22. , 


4. & very careful consideration has been bestowed upon the contention 
of the learned representative. Suspension pending enquiry—including 
enquiry by this Tribunal in application under section 22—has been held by 
this Tribunal times out of number to be no contravention of section 22 of 
our Act and, besides suspension pending enquiry no action express or 
implied of the Company giving rise to a cause of action for the present 
application could be cited. As regards nun-payment of wages tor the 
period from the 21st December 1955 to the 8150 December 1965, suffice 1t 
to say that in the particular circumstances of this case it would not 
constitute contravention of section 22 though it may be possible to raise a 
dispute over the matter. I do not want to go into the merits of this aspect 
and would leave the workmen to raise a dispute in the matter if they are ao 
advised, as any ০3010188101) of opinion on my part at this stage may prejudice 
the case if and when raised. 


5. A point was raised on behalf of the complainants that the enquiry 
made into their alleged misgonduct was devoid of all principles of natural 
justice. T have gone through the proceedings of enquiry and find nothing 
to uphold the contention. The enquiry was conducted in the presence of the 
complainants and two representatives of the Union. The workmen were 
asked to crosa-examine the witnesses Nagin on behalf of the Company 
but they refused to do so and though at the end of examination of the 
complainants it is not so stated that they were required to produce their 
witnesses, it 14 sufficiently clear from the report made on the day following 
the enquiry, i.e., on the 1900 of January 1956, that the complainants did 
not produce any evidence. 


Part IA] 


(০০০০০ এরাও ক মিটি সা স্পা পা পপ ے‎ পপর مو‎ 


0. It is then argued that the enquiry was devoid of all principles of 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 30, 1956 


شش 
Se‏ ——

natural justice inasmuch عو‎ Shri Panchanan Bhattacharyh, President of the 
_ Umon to which the complainants belonged, was not allowed ما‎ be present 
durjug the enquiry and to cross-examine the witnesses produced on behalf 


ef the Company. 


Shri Bhattacharya may be President of the Union but 


certainly was not an employee of the Company and the Company could not 
be compelled to allow an outsider to conduct the enquiry which is a domestic 


enquiry, 


7. Tam satisfied that the enquiry cannot be called against the principles 


of natural justice. 


8. The result is that this application under section 23 is not maintain- 


uble and is hereby dismissed.

GOVERNMENT OF HYDERABAD 
Home Department 
NOTIFICATION 
No. SPL/R/139/PS/56-—8rd August 1956.— 


Whereas the Rajpramukh of Hyderabad 18 satished 


that the publication of the photo depicting the 
Prophet of Islam along with Hazrat Ali, address- 
ing a gathering of Muslims and bearing the name 
of printers as ‘‘Nadeeb Photo Publishers Co., 
lTyderabad, Deccan’”’ is deliberately and maliciously 
intended to outrage the religious feelings of a class 
of Muslims and the publication of which is 
punishable under section 153A of the Indian 
Penal Code, 1860 (Act XLV of 1860); 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers ¢on- 
ferred by 28801) 99۸ of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), the Rajpramukh 
herehy declares every copy of reprint of the-~sajd 
photo to be forfeited to Government. 


B. A. KULKARNI, Dy. Secy.

OFFICE OF THE ACCOUNTANT-GENERAL, WEST 


BENGAL 


A COMPETITIVE examination will be held early in 
October 1956, to recruit about 60 Senior Accounts Clerks 
for employment in the various offices of the Executive 
Engineers under the Government of West Bengal. The 
subjects in which the candidates will be examined are (1) 
Essay or Precis and Draft, (ii) Elementary Book-Keeping, 
and (iii) Arithmetic and Mensuration. The precise dates 
of the examination will be intimated individually only to 
those whose candidatures are accepted. 


The scale of pay is Rs, 80—4—160—5—180 (Efficiency 
Bar after the 12th stage) plus the usual dearness and other 
allowances as admissible from time to time under the rules 
of the Government of West Bengal. Appointments will bo 
temporary for the present but may become permanent in 
due course. Successful candidates have also the prospect 
of becoming Divisional Accountants on passing the 
prescribed departmental examination. All appointments 
carry liability to serve anywhere under the Government of 
West Bengal. 


Candidates should be Qraduates of a _ recognised 


‘University. They should either be domiciled in West 


Bengal or have domiciliary qualifications for service under 
the Government of West Bengal. Age should not exceed 
24 years on the Ist October 1956. Relaxation may be 
permitted up to 30 years ordinarily and up to 33 years in 
very special cases in favour of clerks with experience of 
two years in the Accounts Branch of a P.W. Division or 
in the Works Audit Department of the Accountant- 
General’s Office. The age-limit in rospect of bone fide 
displaced persons may be relaxed by three years, if approved 
by the State Government. Any candidate, who is سیف‎ 
in service, should apply through the Head of hia office. 


Application forms and further particulars may be obtain- 
ed from the Superintendent, W.M. Section of this office, 
between 2 p.m. and 3 p.m. on any working day except 
Saturdays, or by sending him a self-addressed large-sized 
stamped envelope. 


Application forms, duly filled in, should be either handed 
in personally in return for an acknowledgement or sont by 
3 post. In either case, they should be accompanied

¢ TENDER NOTICE 


SEALED TENDERS are invited for printing of Electoral 
Rolls (Addenda and Corrigenda) of Cooch Behar district. 
Rates for prmting of full page of foolscap (folio) 0 
names, half-page and one-third page may be quoted. 


The rates will be inclusive of heading lines (i.e., top 
headings, two sets of column headings, ete.). Printing 
papers will be supphed by the undersigned. 


Tenders will be received by the undersigned up to 
5 p.m, of 10th September 1966 and will be opened on the 
llth September 1956, at 11 a.m. 


The tendorors will have to submit along with the tender 
a Clearance Certificate of income-tax and that of sales tax 
without which the tenders will not be recognised. 


Selected tenderers will have to deposit a security money 
the amount of which will be settled after selection of the 
Press, and to execute a security bond for due execution 
of work hefore printing order can be issued. 


The undersigned does not bind himself to accept the 
lowest tender and to reject any tender without assigning 
any reason, whatsoever. 


Accepted tenderer will be required to give delivory of 
the printed Rolls within 10 (ten) days from the date of 
delivery of papers. 


Other necessary particulars may be obtained from the 
District Election Office, Cooch Behar. 


A. K. BANERJEE, 
for Deputy Commissioner, Cooch Behar. 


Deputy Commissioner's Office, Cooch Behar (Election 


Branch), 14th August 1956.

forporation to be capable of being conveniently

culated directly or indirectly to render profitable

THE FIRST SCHEDULE 
(See section 16) 
PRINCIPLES FOR DETERMINING COMPENSATION 
۲۸2" A 


The compensation to be given by the Corporation to an 
insurer having a share capital on which dividend or bonus 
is payable, who has allocated as bonus to policy-holders the 
whole or any part of the surplus as disclosed in the abstracts 
oy a in accordance with Part II of the Fourth Schedule 


‘to the Insurance Act in respect of the last actuarial investiga- 


tion yelating to his controlled business as at a date earlier 
than the Ist day of January, 1955, shall be computed in 
accordance with the provisions contained in paragraph 1 or 
paragraph 2, whichever is more advantageous to the insurer. 


Paragraph 1.—Twenty times the annual average of the 
share of the surplus allocated to share-holders as disclosed in 
the abstracts aforesaid in respect of the relevant actuarial 
investigations multiplied by a figure which represents the 
proportion that the average business in force during the calen- 
dar years 1950 to 1955 bears to the average business in force 
during the calendar years comprised in the period between 
the date as at which the actuarial investigation immediately

Dated Calcutta, the 24th August 1956 


Notice is hereby given under Section 4(2) of the Calcutta Improvement

(90.১ 8 Roval Exchange Place, Caleutta, to be a Member of the Board of 
Trustees for the Improvement of Calcutta with effect from 23rd August, 1956. 


S. K GUPTA, Chairman.
